It continues through much of the documentary evidence with a 1334 Lay Subsidy but in most it is included with other settlements. In essence this is a shrunken settlement as it was probably not much bigger than currently survives. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Cainhoe
e179_last: 1624 three fifteenths and tenths

description_full: The settlement of Cainhoe is thought to be located somewhere between the remains of the motte and bailey castle at Cainhoe to the north and Cainhoe Manor to the south. The grid reference has been altered from the original (TL 100 367) to reflect this location more closely. Earthworks close to the castle that were originally thought to have been part of the settlement are now thought to be a continuation of the castle features. [1] A hollow way has been spotted on the earlier aerial photographs but this area has been heavily quarried. [1] Cainhoe was recorded in Domesday with a minimum population of 15 and later in the 1334 Lay Subsidy the village was taxed alongside the village of Clophill. There is also an E179 date of 1624 for the settlement. The site was held by the d'Albini family following the conquest, and it is suggested that the village was deserted soon after 1349 as a consequence of the Black Death. [1] An inquisition post mortem of 1375 found ten cottages that were empty ‘since the pestilence’. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_snippet: Traces of the village earthworks are visible to the north and the west of St Nicholas’s Church. description_full: Traces of the village earthworks are visible to the north and the west of St Nicholas’s Church. [1] The principal remains are a hollow way which bisects the site running east to west, bounded by a moat to the east and two building platforms to the west. Other surrounding features include further building platforms to the south of the hollow way and a possible moat or fish pond. [1, 2] A large moated site is present to the northeast of the church and to the north of the present hall which was built in 1847. [3] Landwade is first mentioned in 1060 however there is no mention of the settlement in the Domesday Book. [4] In 1279, it is recorded with 12 households not including the Manor House. [1] By 1327, this number had increased to 15 households. In 1334, the tax quota was well below the national average at 40s. [5] There was a boom during the later fourteenth century when the village went through a revival and the 1377 records showed 44 tax payers. [4] However by 1664 only 8 households remained in the village and by 1674, there were only 4 [1]. It would appear that the village had begun its decline around 1563. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Chalgrave

description_full: The village of Chalgrave was once situated immediately south and east of All Saints’ Church. The earthworks were characterised by a series of enclosures and a possible track way. [1] Today the physical remains are no longer visible and have been destroyed by a golf course. Before it was destroyed a small motte and bailey castle to the south of the church was excavated. [2] The Domesday record suggests a sizable population in the area. The 1291 Taxatio shows the church in place by this time. The 1334 Lay Subsidy is above average for the area. By the 1525 Lay Subsidy Chalgrave is recorded with its neighbouring hamlet of Wingfield. The Medieval Village Research Group suggested that it may never have been more than a handful of cottages, a church and manorial complex. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Chellington
e179_last: 1678 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: Extensive physical remains of the deserted village of Chellington are located close to the Church of St Nicholas spreading to the south-east. These have been identified as a tri-focal settlement.  The main focus of activity was close to the church, with two other smaller areas close to the farms.  The earthworks are characterized by a series of rectilinear enclosures and a hollow way running north to south.
description_full: Extensive physical remains of the deserted village of Chellington are located close to the Church of St Nicholas spreading to the south-east. These have been identified as a tri-focal settlement. [1] The main focus of activity was close to the church, with two other smaller areas close to the farms. [1] The earthworks are characterized by a series of rectilinear enclosures and a hollow way running north to south. There is also evidence of ridge and furrow extending over a considerable area. Chellington has been identified as the location of an un-named manor in Domesday with a minimum population of 23. [2] The earliest mention of the Chellington place-name is in 1242. [3] In the lay taxations Chellington was recorded with the neighboring village, Carlton, and in 1359 the manors of Chellington and Carlton were amalgamated into the same family, the Traillys. [4] At this time it is suggested that the settlement shifted to a new location, where the modern settlement of Chellington is located. [5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The site can be seen on the ground as faint crop marks in an area of ploughing. An east-west hollow way is visible with possible field boundaries. The manor of Etonbury seems to be combined with Arlesey which has extensive Domesday and later evidence. Etonbury itself does not appear in any taxation records and it may be the case that there was no extensive settlement at Etonbury, instead a manorial complex is present with the population located at Arlesey. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The remains of a medieval settlement can be seen, characterized by several rectilinear enclosures, hollow ways and bounded to the east, west and south by large areas of extensive ridge and furrow, still well preserved although some of the surrounding area has been ploughed. The place-name evidence appears in c. 1125 and runs through to the fourteenth century. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: There are no clear visible remains for the village of Lower Gravenhurst. St Mary’s Church is located surrounded by ploughed fields, although the area of the present houses to the south does have some pasture and may contain some field boundaries. Medieval pottery and brick have been recovered from the area immediately east of the church which would suggest the original location of the village. [1] Recent analysis of the aerial photographs for the area surrounding the current houses has revealed a number of features suggestive of medieval settlement. [2] Gravenhurst was recorded in the Domesday Book and a church and rectory existed by the reign of Henry II. [3] It paid a high 1334 Lay Subsidy along with Ion. The poor survival of fourteenth-century tax records makes it difficult to plot the fortunes of Lower Gravenhurst. The present church is built in the fourteenth century suggesting a sufficiently large population still existed. [3] By the sixteenth century 12 people pay the 1525 Lay Subsidy and five households are recorded in 1563. In 1637-8 there is a record of two people refusing to pay a ship tax, suggesting a population still existed. [3] By the time of Jeffrey’s map in 1765 there are buildings in some places, but the concentration of settlement has disappeared. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: Higham Gobion should be classed as a shrunken settlement. There are a number of houses still present at the site. Surrounding this cluster of houses and the church are a number of earthworks. To the north there is an east-west boundary that may be a hollow way, with evidence of ridge and furrow to the north. To the east of the houses, an area is scheduled due to the presence of medieval settlement remains although this area is now under plough. [1] Excavation in this area in 1954 revealed a wall and sherds of twelfth-century pottery. [2] To the north of the settlement is a monument known as The Camp, which is now interpreted as medieval fishponds. [3] A sizable manor is recorded at Domesday. Place-name evidence records the settlement as Higham in the eleventh-thirteenth centuries with the first record of Higham Gobion from the 1290s. [4] In the 1334 Lay Subsidy Highham is recorded with Faldo, but jointly they pay an above average amount. Unfortunately there are no other fourteenth-century tax records available. By the sixteenth century, only two people pay the 1525 Lay Subsidy and two households are recorded in 1563. This would suggest the settlement shrank to its present size sometime in the fifteenth/sixteenth century. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

An estate map of 1596 does show buildings in the area of the settlement. [2] This suggests that the settlement saw a slow gradual decline probably in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries with a change to isolated farmsteads. description_full: Few visible earthworks can be seen at the site. A church and a number of house sites still exist and this is more a shrunken settlement. There is evidence from early aerial photographs of ridge and furrow and field boundaries, all of which has since been ploughed. [1] Stondon is recorded at Domesday, but not as Lower and Upper. The current church at Upper Stondon is dated to the nineteenth century replacing its predecessor that had burnt down. [1, 2] There is clear evidence of the church from the thirteenth century with a rector recorded in 1289, and taxation in 1291. [1] There are few surviving documentary references in the fourteenth century. By the sixteenth century two households are recorded in 1563. On the 1851 enclosure map seven buildings are shown to the east of the church. [2] There is really no clear evidence of a large settlement at this location. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The main area of settlement has been engulfed in the development of Biggleswade. A large part of this has been excavated during this development throughout the 1990s and 2000s. The evidence of the village from excavations demonstrates extensive occupation. There is Saxon evidence with sunken featured buildings, before the settlement shifts and is focused along a north-south hollow way. The occupation is dated to the tenth to the fourteenth century with post-built long houses in enclosures. Some evidence of activity continues into the sixteenth century. [1] A chapel is recorded at Stratton in the fifteenth century and the excavation uncovered a number of burials which may relate to this chapel. [2] Stratton is recorded at Domesday and in the Lay Subsidy of 1334 when an average payment was made. It was a substantial settlement but by the fourteenth century it was eclipsed by Biggleswade, and thereafter recorded as a hamlet. [3] The 1670 Hearth Tax records eight houses and Jeffrey’s map of 1765 shows eight buildings. [3] By the time of the 1838 Tithe Map only the former manorial centre of the Stratton Park moated site and another moat to the north, are shown. [3] The Stratton Park moated site would seem to signify the manorial centre up until the late sixteenth century when it is abandoned for the new Stratton Park. [3] The excavation and documentary evidence show a complex history at Stratton. It would appear to be a long-lived settlement with origins back in the seventh century. The settlement gradually shifts focus eastwards until the seventeenth century. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Arborfield
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Arborfield has been suggested as a shifted medieval village on the basis that its ruined medieval church (perhaps originally itself a thirteenth-century rebuild of the completely ruined ‘old wooden chapel’ of 1220 ) and the former site of Arborfield Hall stand in relative isolation near the River Loddon, separated from the main focus of local settlement further east.
description_full: Arborfield has been suggested as a shifted medieval village on the basis that its ruined medieval church (perhaps originally itself a thirteenth-century rebuild of the completely ruined ‘old wooden chapel’ of 1220 [1]) and the former site of Arborfield Hall stand in relative isolation near the River Loddon, separated from the main focus of local settlement further east. [2, 3, 4] The current church dates only from 1863, [5] whilst most of the houses along Church Lane are also recent, so a significant shift in focus as far as Arborfield Cross might be envisaged. It has been suggested that 'low earthworks' in grassland adjacent to the ruined church could represent the earlier area of settlement, [6] but beyond this there is currently little evidence to demonstrate this shift, as opposed to the long-term existence of a dispersed settlement pattern. A recent archaeological watching brief of a gas pipeline close to the ruined church found only undated or ninteenth-century features. [6] Future research on the date of the various settlement foci in Arborfield, including the impact of the grounds around Arborfield Hall would be useful. Site identified by the HER.

name: Ardington Wick
e179_last: 1563 subsidy
description_snippet: The evidence for depopulation at Ardington Wick comes from three sets of former rectilinear boundaries to the north-east, north, and north-west of the settlement, identified by Brendan Grimly from aerial photographs. [1, 2, 3, 4] Two sets of photographs are thought to show the remains as earthworks in 1946 and as cropmarks in 1969, apparently after being ploughed level.
description_full: The evidence for depopulation at Ardington Wick comes from three sets of former rectilinear boundaries to the north-east, north, and north-west of the settlement, identified by Brendan Grimly from aerial photographs. [1, 2, 3, 4] Two sets of photographs are thought to show the remains as earthworks in 1946 and as cropmarks in 1969, apparently after being ploughed level. [1] Whilst each set of cropmarks is thought to include possible tofts and crofts, and the north-western group may have sections of a hollow way, it is also possible some of the features represent field boundaries or even drains. [1] The documentary evidence consulted provides little evidence for a settlement of substantial size. Although Gelling notes that the ‘Wick’ was mentioned in an Inquisitions Post Mortem in 1326, [5] there are only two references to this place in the E179 database, both linked with the main settlement at Ardington, in the Lay Subsides of 1559 and 1563. The map evidence indicates that by the time of Rocque’s 1761 map and the 1808 enclosure map [6] the settlement consisted of only three or four farmsteads (the western group apparently being omitted from the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing). All but two of the seven houses now present at Ardington Wick were apparently first built after the 6 inch first edition Ordnance Survey map was surveyed in 1875-7. Although classified as a DMV by the Oxfordshire HER, [2] the ambiguity of the archaeological evidence and the apparent paucity of documentary information both suggest a classification of this site as a deserted hamlet may be more appropriate, pending any further research. Site identified from aerial photographs.

name: Avington
depop_text: Medieval (14th century) and Post-Medieval decline (final stage post-1761)
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The present day settlement at Avington essentially consists of the church, Manor Farm (the Manor House burnt down in 1769)  and a row of modern houses on plots first developed in the late Victorian period. Although physical evidence is not reported by the NMR or HER, there is however a limited case for classing Avington as a shrunken village.
description_full: The present day settlement at Avington essentially consists of the church, Manor Farm (the Manor House burnt down in 1769) [1] and a row of modern houses on plots first developed in the late Victorian period. Although physical evidence is not reported by the NMR or HER, there is however a limited case for classing Avington as a shrunken village. The vill paid an above average amount of tax in 1334, placing it in the upper 30% within Berkshire, although the 10 taxpayers in the 1327 Lay Subsidy and 12 in 1332 suggest a more modestly populated vill. [2, 3] The returns of the 1381 Poll Tax and the 1524 Lay Subsidy suggest the vill’s population was relatively small (with percentile rankings within Berkshire of 0.16 and 0.09 respectively), perhaps indicating a degree of fourteenth-century decline. Further post-medieval shrinkage is attested by the cartographic evidence. Rocque’s map of 1761 shows what appear to be two rows of buildings to the west of Manor Farm. The northern one of these seems to have disappeared by the 1808 Ordnance Survey drawing, with the southern row gone by the time of the 1878 Ordnance Survey mapping for the 25 and 6 inch maps. More recently (possibly in the 1960s) the rectory buildings to the south of the church have also been lost. Identified during Beresford's Lost Villages Project.

name: Barcote
e179_last: 1563 subsidy

Beresford and Hurst classed the documentary evidence as ‘excellent’, but this perhaps overstates our knowledge.  Barcote is recorded in Domesday Book as a modestly populated vill (with a percentile ranking of 0.28 within Berkshire), and was also recorded separately in the 1327 Lay Subsidy with 10 taxpayers (a ranking of 0.24).
description_full: The evidence for a deserted settlement at Barcote is, to date, purely documentary. [1] Beresford and Hurst classed the documentary evidence as ‘excellent’, but this perhaps overstates our knowledge. [2] Barcote is recorded in Domesday Book as a modestly populated vill (with a percentile ranking of 0.28 within Berkshire), and was also recorded separately in the 1327 Lay Subsidy with 10 taxpayers (a ranking of 0.24). Beyond this there are very few references to the settlement in the medieval taxation records, with just four records in the fourteenth century and another four in the sixteenth century. Barcote was usually grouped with other vills, in particular Buckland, including in the 1381 Poll Tax. Perhaps this suggests that decline came early to this settlement, although Beresford and Hurst suggest a retreat between 1450 and 1700, [2] and Buckland parish did see some enclosure activity in the early sixteenth century. [3] There is little to indicate the former size of Barcote, although it had its own chapel in 1371. By 1761 Rocque’s map shows the settlement reduced to a farm or hamlet. Barcote Farm is thought to be early seventeenth century, [4] whilst Barcote House is a later nineteenth-century addition. [5, 6] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Basildon
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Basildon is listed as a migrated settlement by the West Berkshire HER,  giving the grid reference of Lower Basildon, with migration to this area presumably thought likely from the site of the church and Church Farm, set 0.5km away in low-lying fields near the River Thames.
description_full: Basildon is listed as a migrated settlement by the West Berkshire HER, [1] giving the grid reference of Lower Basildon, with migration to this area presumably thought likely from the site of the church and Church Farm, set 0.5km away in low-lying fields near the River Thames. John Brooks has suggested that settlement movement here may have occurred after the Black Death and was also influenced by attraction to a line of communication, in this case towards the A329 Streatley-Reading road, along which Lower Basildon is now mainly situated. [2] There is no obvious evidence as yet for abandoned areas of settlement near the church site, although little archaeological work has yet been carried out there. A watching brief during the lowering of floor levels at Church Farm House did find layers pre-dating the sixteenth-century house, some of which might have been associated with outbuildings, perhaps belonging to an undiscovered medieval farmstead nearby. [3] Most archaeological attention in recent years has been focussed to the south-west of the church site and north-west of Lower Basildon, where a Roman villa is thought to have been destroyed by the building of the railway line in the nineteenth century. [4] The current church building of St. Bartholomew’s, dating from the thirteenth century is presumably also the site of one of two churches mentioned in the Domesday Book for Basildon – the other is usually assumed to have been at Ashampstead, which may have been included with the manor of Basildon in Domesday. [5, 6] As with many possible migrated or shifted settlement sites, the relative lack of archaeological evidence leaves open a further possible scenario, that the modern dispersed settlement within Basildon parish may have early origins. Certainly settlement is already shown in a dispersed pattern by the time of Rocque’s 1761 map, including the more distant area of Upper Basildon, then known as Basildon Green. Identified by the HER and John Brooks.

name: Baulking
e179_last: 1679/80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Baulking’s status as a shrunken settlement is suggested by both the gaps in its plan, scattered along the western side of a large village green,  and earthworks on the green itself. A sketch plan of the earthworks has been produced,  and it has been suggested the settlement formerly had a ‘planned’ layout,  perhaps even intended as a 'medieval new town'.
description_full: Baulking’s status as a shrunken settlement is suggested by both the gaps in its plan, scattered along the western side of a large village green, [1] and earthworks on the green itself. A sketch plan of the earthworks has been produced, [2] and it has been suggested the settlement formerly had a ‘planned’ layout, [1] perhaps even intended as a 'medieval new town'. [3] During the fourteenth century it appears that Baulking was a reasonably populous settlement – the 16 taxpayers in the 1327 Lay Subsidy give the vill a percentile ranking of 0.49 within Berkshire, [4] whilst the vill’s tax assessment for the 1334 subsidy has a percentile ranking of 0.73. The percentile ranking by inhabitants by the time of the 1801 census was only 0.25. Within this timeframe the date of the settlement retraction at Baulking is not clear, but some loss clearly occurred as late as the nineteenth century. The tithe map is said to include a dozen buildings now no longer present, and the Ordnance Survey drawing of 1811 and Rocque’s 1761 map also show areas of housing subsequently lost in various places along the green frontage. Rocque’s map in particular shows house plots along the southern end of the green’s eastern side, which seem to have largely disappeared by the early nineteenth century, with only one house currently existing in this area today. Identified by the MVRG.

name: Beckett
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Beckett seems to have been obscured by later emparking and the creation of the military college. No physical trace has been found of the medieval village, save some thirteenth-century pottery sherds said to have been found in the ‘seed beds’.  Beckett House or Hall was built in the early 1830s, [2, 3] but an earlier Beckett House and a driveway (and a probable parkland area) is shown on Rocque’s 1761 map.
description_full: Beckett seems to have been obscured by later emparking and the creation of the military college. No physical trace has been found of the medieval village, save some thirteenth-century pottery sherds said to have been found in the ‘seed beds’. [1] Beckett House or Hall was built in the early 1830s, [2, 3] but an earlier Beckett House and a driveway (and a probable parkland area) is shown on Rocque’s 1761 map. Part of a manor house on this site is said to have burnt down during the Civil War. [3] An archaeological watching brief in the area just north of the house found only post-medieval features. [4] The vill had an above average tax assessment in 1334, but seems to have suffered considerably in the Black Death with tax reliefs of 24% and 72% granted in 1352 and 1353. [5]. Although no returns survive for the 1524/5 subsidies, Beresford and Hurst suggest that there is early sixteenth-century taxation evidence that the village had 'fallen victim to some depopulating force by that date'. [6] Presumably any remaining settlement was removed at the time of emparkment. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Benham Burslot
description_snippet: A small collection of five buildings are shown on the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1878-82. Buildings are also visible in this vicinity on the 1812 Ordnance Survey drawing and Rocque's 1761 map. This appears to be a common edge settlement on the boundary of Wickham Heath. It is not known if the settlement had medieval origins, but seems unlikely in any event to have been a 'village'.

Buildings are also visible in this vicinity on the 1812 Ordnance Survey drawing and Rocque's 1761 map. This appears to be a common edge settlement on the boundary of Wickham Heath. It is not known if the settlement had medieval origins, but seems unlikely in any event to have been a 'village'. Last buildings demolished some time after 1960. [1] Not recorded in the Domesday Book or the Taxatio 1291, although there are entries for Benham. Identified by the HER.

name: Bessels Leigh
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The twelfth-century church at Bessels Leigh now stands in isolation within parkland,  but Rocque’s map of 1761 shows a collection of buildings surrounding it. These seem to have been removed by the early nineteenth century, perhaps as part of an emparkment. The original manor house which lay near the church was demolished in 1784.
description_full: The twelfth-century church at Bessels Leigh now stands in isolation within parkland, [1] but Rocque’s map of 1761 shows a collection of buildings surrounding it. These seem to have been removed by the early nineteenth century, perhaps as part of an emparkment. The original manor house which lay near the church was demolished in 1784. [2] The settlement pattern in the parish may have been polyfocal, since a further area of settlement around Bessels Leigh Farm (about 800m north-east of the church) was also present in 1761. The medieval taxation records suggest that the population of this vill was always relatively small. Identified by the HER.

name: East Betterton
e179_last: 1671 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions (Betterton)
description_snippet: Betterton may represent two DMVs – East and West, but in the absence of any physical remains (save some earthworks more likely to be associated with East Lockinge) we are forced to rely on the documentary record, which usually grouped both places together simply as ‘Betterton’. Whether there was originally a single settlement is not clear. Domesday Book has two holdings, both simply named ‘Betterton’.
description_full: Betterton may represent two DMVs – East and West, but in the absence of any physical remains (save some earthworks more likely to be associated with East Lockinge) we are forced to rely on the documentary record, which usually grouped both places together simply as ‘Betterton’. Whether there was originally a single settlement is not clear. Domesday Book has two holdings, both simply named ‘Betterton’. A document thought to date from c. 1300 may list both East and West Betterton, and references to both places can be found in other fourteenth-century documents, including an inspeximus suggesting that West Betterton may have been differentiated as early as 1244. [1, 2] The 1334 Lay Subsidy mentions only ‘Betterton’ and gives the lowest assessment of any vill in Wantage hundred, suggesting that both places covered by this description are likely to have been small, perhaps never more than hamlets. The 1381 Poll Tax assessment confirms this impression, with ‘Betterton’ again easily the least populous vill in the hundred. Beresford and Hurst classified the most likely period of depopulation at Betterton to be between c. 1450 and 1700, [3] although the nature of the documentary evidence and the small medieval assessments means the scale and timing of any reduction is unclear. By the time of Rocque’s 1761 map the place was represented by Betterton House to the west (constructed mid-eighteenth century [4]) and Betterton Farm to the east. Whilst these have been used as the National Grid References for West and East Betterton respectively it cannot be assumed that these represent the sites of medieval settlements. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968 as Betterton.

name: Binfield
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Binfield has been suggested as a shifted village, based on the isolation of its church and rectory from the main focus of the village about 0.5 to 1km further south along Terrace Road. Fieldwalking as part of the East Berkshire Archaeological Survey (EBAS) has provided some supporting evidence, with medieval pottery scatters (presumably EBAS nos 22 and perhaps 28)  indicating a possible 'intermediate stage in the...
description_full: Binfield has been suggested as a shifted village, based on the isolation of its church and rectory from the main focus of the village about 0.5 to 1km further south along Terrace Road. Fieldwalking as part of the East Berkshire Archaeological Survey (EBAS) has provided some supporting evidence, with medieval pottery scatters (presumably EBAS nos 22 and perhaps 28) [1] indicating a possible 'intermediate stage in the shift of settlement from a presumed focus close to the church to the present day focus 600m to the south'. [2] However, even if it is correct that the area around the church is the earliest settlement [3], it seems as if the shift in focus may have taken place relatively late. Rocque’s map of 1761 (and to a lesser extent, the 1809 Ordnance Survey drawing) shows a dispersed settlement pattern extending across the parish, north and south of the church, which might reflect an older, scattered pattern being reflected in fieldwalking finds. The creation of post-medieval parkland around both Allanbay Park and Binfield Park also appears to have had some influence in isolating the church from other settlement elements and producing the modern pattern. This was exacerbated by an intensification of settlement in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries south and south-west of Binfield Park. Identified through fieldwork.

name: Bockhampton
depop_text: 15th-16th cenury, final stage between 1761 and early 19th century
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Earthworks including 'building platforms, [a] hollow way track, field banks and lynchets' were recorded at Bockhampton in 1975 by Julian Richards, with the site subsequently being scheduled.  To the north and north-west modern housing now covers parts of the probable medieval village footprint.
description_full: Earthworks including 'building platforms, [a] hollow way track, field banks and lynchets' were recorded at Bockhampton in 1975 by Julian Richards, with the site subsequently being scheduled. [1] To the north and north-west modern housing now covers parts of the probable medieval village footprint. The village possessed a chapel in the late twelfth century, [2] and the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map marks the site of a chapel south of the River Lambourn. The medieval documentary evidence shows that Bockhampton was once a reasonably sized village, and it appears to have supported two separate manors, named East and West Bockhampton. In 1334 it may have been recorded with a lost settlement named 'Blagrave' but this settlement has not been identified. The relatively low 1525 Lay Subsidy assessment perhaps hints that the village may have started to contract, but the settlement was still large enough in 1761 (as shown on Rocque’s map) to occupy areas north and south of the River Lambourn and north of the main road. Parliamentary enclosure took place in 1778, [3] and by the early nineteenth century the settlement was seemingly reduced to just three farms, also shown on the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map surveyed in 1878. The site is sometimes classified as a shrunken settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Borough Farm, Sonning
description_snippet: Borough Farm is situated nearly 2 miles north-east of the village of Sonning, occupying the south-western part of an island formed by the Thames, the Loddon and Borough Lake. The earliest reference to the place-name is found in the surnames of Roger and William de Burgeia in a list of Sonning tenants made during the visit of the Dean of Salisbury in 1220,  and the surname persisted in the 1327 Lay Subsidy for...
description_full: Borough Farm is situated nearly 2 miles north-east of the village of Sonning, occupying the south-western part of an island formed by the Thames, the Loddon and Borough Lake. The earliest reference to the place-name is found in the surnames of Roger and William de Burgeia in a list of Sonning tenants made during the visit of the Dean of Salisbury in 1220, [1] and the surname persisted in the 1327 Lay Subsidy for Sonning (as Borgheye). [2] Gelling has suggested that a meaning of “island meadow belonging to the borough” should be preferred, [3] i.e. It need not refer to an ancient earthwork or settlement at this site. Nevertheless it would seem the site was occupied from the medieval period, and finds of this era, including a brooch, buckle, pottery and a coin of Henry IV, are thought to have come from this area. [4, 5] There is also a tradition of a former chapel here, with 'the site of Burrough Chapel' appearing on the 1840 tithe map. However contemporary documentary references to a chapel appear to be lacking, and foundations said to have been visible in 1912 were not located during field investigation in 1963. [6] Moreover it has been suggested that carved stonework found near the site (as marked on the first edition Ordnance Survey map) could have derived ultimately from Reading Abbey. [7] Taken together, there is little as yet to suggest that Borough Farm was once more than a hamlet or farm, and it is possible it has retained this status since medieval times. Identified by the NMR.

name: Buscot
e179_last: 1678 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The main focus of modern settlement at Buscot, arranged along a north-south lane off the A417, is situated over 500m from its church. The fields in between contain earthworks and cropmarks indicating an area of lost settlement, with a hollow way and the rectilinear units of former house plots or small fields.
description_full: The main focus of modern settlement at Buscot, arranged along a north-south lane off the A417, is situated over 500m from its church. The fields in between contain earthworks and cropmarks indicating an area of lost settlement, with a hollow way and the rectilinear units of former house plots or small fields. [1, 2] Partial ploughing of the site was reported in 1978, [3] and aerial photographs indicate that the southern half of the deserted area has been under the plough since at least 2001. Finds of pottery from fields at the site date from the twelfth to fifteenth century. [1, 2, 4] Although the usual later medieval taxation records used in this database are lacking for Buscot, it is clear that the vill was once very populous, with the minimum number of 64 Domesday individuals placing it in the upper 10% of vills for Berkshire. Thirty-six individual taxpayers were listed in the 1327 Lay Subsidy [5] and the vill’s communal assessment for 1334 still placed it in the top 20% for the county. Whilst the latest pottery reported from the site is apparently fifteenth century, the map evidence indicates that depopulation continued into the post-medieval period. A number of buildings are shown immediately south and east of the church on Rocque’s map of 1761, which had largely disappeared by the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing. Whether this site is best classified as shrunken, shifted, or (as Brooks suggested) migrated, [6] would require further research into both the abandoned and surviving settlement areas. Identified from earthworks.

name: Calcot
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Calcot is truly a ‘lost’ place – it is plotted at an approximate grid reference of SU 340 698 suggested by Beresford and Hurst,  although the basis for this suggestion is not clear, other than that the settlement lay near Leverton.  The NMR lists a number of cropmarks of possible field boundaries and tracks in the general vicinity although there is no evidence currently to link them to a deserted settlement.
description_full: Calcot is truly a ‘lost’ place – it is plotted at an approximate grid reference of SU 340 698 suggested by Beresford and Hurst, [1] although the basis for this suggestion is not clear, other than that the settlement lay near Leverton. [2] The NMR lists a number of cropmarks of possible field boundaries and tracks in the general vicinity although there is no evidence currently to link them to a deserted settlement. Calcote appears in Domesday Book, and - surprisingly given the complete disappearance from memory of its location - it appears in some taxation records throughout the period of the E179 database, into the late seventeenth century. The settlement must always have been small. It had a relatively low Lay Subsidy assessment in 1334. By 1381 there were just four poll tax payers – the lowest of any assessed vill in Berkshire and suggesting the settlement can have been no more than a farm or tiny hamlet by this stage. Beresford and Hurst suggest a general period of desertion of c. 1450-1700. Rocque’s map of 1761 shows a single unnamed building slightly to the east of the estimated grid reference for Calcot. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Carswell
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Carswell was represented by just a main house and a couple of other buildings on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1876-7, and Rocque’s map of 1761 appears to show a similar situation. No physical evidence for a former village in this vicinity has been identified.
description_full: Carswell was represented by just a main house and a couple of other buildings on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1876-7, and Rocque’s map of 1761 appears to show a similar situation. No physical evidence for a former village in this vicinity has been identified. The 1334 Lay Subsidy and 1381 Poll Tax indicate a modestly populated vill at Carswell in the fourteenth century, but by the Lay Subsidy of c. 1525 it was grouped with surrounding vills. In any event the presence of Carswell Marsh, about 1km to the north complicates matters. This name is recorded as early as 1467, [1] and population here may have contributed to tax assessments of the medieval vill. A fuller understanding of the history of this northern settlement may be necessary before it can be established if Carswell should be classed as a DMV. There may even be a case for depopulation at Carswell Marsh. Beresford and Hurst assumed a depopulation in the seventeenth or eighteenth century. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Catmore
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Catmore today consists of a church, farm and a couple of cottages. The late nineteenth-century 6 inch Ordnance Survey maps show a few additional cottages, barns or outbuildings, whilst Rocque’s schematic representation of 1761 also indicates a church alongside a farm or small hamlet. Nevertheless there are indications that medieval Catmore was once a more substantial place.
description_full: Catmore today consists of a church, farm and a couple of cottages. The late nineteenth-century 6 inch Ordnance Survey maps show a few additional cottages, barns or outbuildings, whilst Rocque’s schematic representation of 1761 also indicates a church alongside a farm or small hamlet. Nevertheless there are indications that medieval Catmore was once a more substantial place. Julian Richards has noted a possible house platform close to the church, [1] and within the churchyard itself 19 sherds of mostly twelfth and thirteenth-century pottery were recovered from a disturbed area of ground. [2] On the northern side of the road the surrounding fields are now cultivated. Catmore’s entry in Domesday Book suggests the vill was modestly populated (with a percentile ranking in Berkshire of 0.31), perhaps enough to form a village within its small parish at some stage. However the 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment for the vill had a slightly lower percentile ranking within Berkshire (0.19) and the four taxpayers there in 1327 indicated an even lower county ranking (0.05). [3] Moreover, it is also possible that Lilley, at the south-east corner of the parish, may have contributed to the medieval population. Catmore was a substantial enough place to be granted a market in 1306, although nothing further is known about it. [4] In 1517 the Enclosure Commission heard that 400 acres had been enclosed at Catmore, displacing 14 people from work. [5] In a relatively small community this may have instigated a significant episode of depopulation. The 1841 Census records 22 inhabitants at Catmore itself but noted that in the entire parish including Lilley there were 96 inhabitants. Identified through fieldwork.

name: West Challow
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The village of West Challow is surrounded in a number of directions by a series of parallel earthworks, which may variously be evidence of ridge and furrow or drainage systems, the latter perhaps associated with the management of water meadows.
description_full: The village of West Challow is surrounded in a number of directions by a series of parallel earthworks, which may variously be evidence of ridge and furrow or drainage systems, the latter perhaps associated with the management of water meadows. One set of earthworks north of the village, near a large fish pond formed in the Childrey Brook, has been suggested as possibly indicating a former settlement area, with one possible house platform. The aerial photographic evidence for earthworks has been plotted by the Lambourn Downs National Mapping Project. [1, 2, 3, 4] The road layout of the village itself consists of two ‘loops’, forming a figure of eight. In maps from the mid eighteenth to late nineteenth centuries, only the northern part of the northern loop, and the two ‘sides’ of the southern loop were occupied, raising the question of whether the unoccupied areas within the village are evidence of former shrinkage, or the persistence of a polyfocal settlement layout. The documentary evidence for West Challow is complicated by its relationship to East Challow. The Domesday Book entry for ‘Challow’ was assumed by Morris to refer only to West Challow, [5] and the minimum number of inhabitants there (20) made it a manor of middling population size. The 1327 Lay Subsidy records only West Challow, as a moderately populous vill with 16 taxpayers, [6] whilst the 1334 Lay Subsidy records ‘Challow’ as a single entry, with a large assessment in the upper quartile for Berkshire. The Lay Subsidy returns of 1524/5 did give separate entries for the two Challows, and in both cases West Challow was the less populous, with 12 taxpayers in 1524 and 13 in 1525, giving the vill percentile rankings within Berkshire of just 0.13 and 0.19 respectively. This might hint at a degree of late medieval settlement retraction. West Challow was still the less populous of the two Challows in 1801, although its Berkshire percentile ranking by then was 0.27. Identified from earthworks.

name: Chapelwick
e179_last: 1371 lay subsidy on parishes
description_snippet: First identified as a possible shrunken settlement by Beresford,  Chapelwick is today represented by a single farm in the north-west of Ashbury parish. The settlement previously had a chapel, situated about 250m south of the farm and sitting within a sub-rectangular moat, which is still visible as a cropmark on aerial photographs although the entire chapel site is now under the plough.
description_full: First identified as a possible shrunken settlement by Beresford, [1] Chapelwick is today represented by a single farm in the north-west of Ashbury parish. The settlement previously had a chapel, situated about 250m south of the farm and sitting within a sub-rectangular moat, which is still visible as a cropmark on aerial photographs although the entire chapel site is now under the plough. [2, 3, 4, 5] The chapel was built in c. 1230 and is said to have become disused after the reformation, [4, 6] although the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing still shows a building in the vicinity. South of the farm there is an area of small paddocks, which might represent candidates for former amalgamated house plots, but site visits to the farm and chapel site in 1964, 1977 and 1996 failed to notice any evidence for surviving earthworks. [2, 3, 4] Aerial photographs suggest that the settlement site was once surrounded by ridge and furrow, [3] although a charter of 1536 also records pasture land and woodland named after Chapelwick in the vicinity. [7] Although this place warranted the building of a chapel, the documentary records for Chapelwick offers little evidence for a significant former settlement. The name occurs only once in the E179 database, in a subsidy from parishes for 1371, where it is listed as a chapel with Shrivenham parish rather than Ashbury. Gelling has noted that Chapelwick, along with the nearby farms of Stainswick and Ruffinswick may all derive their place-names from the thirteenth-century manor of Wick, which also bore several alternative names (e.g. East Wick, Notteswick). [6, 8] Possibly the medieval chapel served a number of outlying farmsteads rather than a single nucleated settlement. This site is therefore currently best classified as doubtful. Identified by Maurice Beresford.

name: Charlton
e179_last: 1678 Act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: An aerial photograph from 1946 shows evidence for earthworks of tofts and crofts in the centre of Charlton, indicating settlement retreat, although these have subsequently been built over. [1, 2] Whilst it is unclear if these earthworks were medieval or post-medieval in date, map evidence suggests that some of the settlement shrinkage at Charlton occurred relatively late.
description_full: An aerial photograph from 1946 shows evidence for earthworks of tofts and crofts in the centre of Charlton, indicating settlement retreat, although these have subsequently been built over. [1, 2] Whilst it is unclear if these earthworks were medieval or post-medieval in date, map evidence suggests that some of the settlement shrinkage at Charlton occurred relatively late. The loss of buildings along the main east-west street and elsewhere in the village can be charted between Rocque’s map of 1761 and the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing, and again by the time of the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map (surveyed 1875-7). The enclosure map of Charlton for 1868 also indicates a greater sub-division of the rear plots on the north side of the main street compared to a decade later, in the same general area as the aerial photographic evidence. [3] Although sixteenth-century subsidy sources are lacking, the documentary record confirms that Charlton maintained its status as a substantial vill at the time of the 1381 Poll Tax (with 81 taxpayers) but was in the bottom 40% of Berkshire vills measured by population for the 1801 Census. Identifed from the NMR and HER.

name: Charlton (Charnham Street)
description_snippet: The vill of Charlton is recorded in the Wiltshire sections of Domesday Book, the 1334 Lay Subsidy and the Poll Taxes of 1377 and 1379. The entry in 1334 is disputed - and Glasscock thinks the identification is unlikely. The entry for 1379 may include the settlement of North Standen. It was situated in the vicinity of Hungerford, albeit that the precise location of the settlement was thought to have been lost.
description_full: The vill of Charlton is recorded in the Wiltshire sections of Domesday Book, the 1334 Lay Subsidy and the Poll Taxes of 1377 and 1379. The entry in 1334 is disputed - and Glasscock thinks the identification is unlikely. The entry for 1379 may include the settlement of North Standen. It was situated in the vicinity of Hungerford, albeit that the precise location of the settlement was thought to have been lost. Margaret Gelling has shown that the name ‘Charnham Street’ (which seems to appear from the fourteenth century onwards) has the etymological meaning 'street of the people of Charlton’, linking it with the ‘lost’ vill. [1] Charnham Street is now the main east-west street in Hungerford, joined to the main High Street by Bridge Street, but seems to have emerged as a separate settlement. The idea has therefore been mooted that Charnham Street is a ‘re-settlement’ of the lost place of Charlton, [2] which could have been nearby, although Hopgrass Farm has also been suggested as a possibility. [3] The former suggestion seems more likely in the light of excavations carried out by Thames Valley Archaeological Services in advance of a new development at Charnham Lane, situated to the rear of Charnham Street. Here a medieval ‘bi-focal’ settlement, probably consisting of two neighbouring farms started in the eleventh or twelfth century, but seems to have been abandoned around the fourteenth century. [4] Identified from documentary and place-name evidence.

name: Chieveley
description_snippet: An aerial photograph of 1955 is believed to show evidence for earthworks of medieval or post-medieval boundaries running parallel to Chieveley’s main north-south street on its west side,  perhaps relating to an area of lost settlement or enclosures at the rear of the existing settlement. It would appear that these earthworks have now been either built over or subsumed into gardens.
description_full: An aerial photograph of 1955 is believed to show evidence for earthworks of medieval or post-medieval boundaries running parallel to Chieveley’s main north-south street on its west side, [1] perhaps relating to an area of lost settlement or enclosures at the rear of the existing settlement. It would appear that these earthworks have now been either built over or subsumed into gardens. In the near vicinity, the grounds of Chieveley Manor are also thought to have produced medieval pottery and a series of (undated) features including ditches and pits. [2] Rocque’s map of 1761 does show some buildings (perhaps outbuildings) to the rear of the high street near the church, which were lost by the time of the 1812 Ordnance Survey drawing, as well as several houses further north fronting the west side of the High Street which had also disappeared, suggesting a degree of post-medieval settlement retreat. Whether Chieveley also suffered settlement shrinkage in the medieval period itself is less clear. For the sources consulted in this project the vill was amongst the larger in Berkshire (ranked in the top quartile) at the time of Domesday and in the sixteenth-century lay subsidies, although it was ranked slightly lower in the fourteenth-century subsidies. The taxation records from this period contain evidence of an apparently difficult time for the settlement. Between the 1327 and 1332 Lay Subsidy returns Chieveley saw a drastic decline in its taxable wealth of 54%, although the number of taxpayers (19) remained the same. [3, 4] Possibly the fact that Chieveley had a set of tax assessors to itself in 1332 ensured this more lenient assessment, however. Nevertheless in 1341 the Nonarum Inquisitiones also recorded that seven carucates (perhaps c. 840 acres) of arable land lay uncultivated on account of the poverty of the parishioners. [5] Identified from the NMR and HER.

name: Cholsey
e179_last: 1679/80 - grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Cholsey has been classed by John Brooks as a migrated village, with its focus of settlement shifting from the area around the parish church south-eastwards towards the core of the modern village, a process Brooks suggests may have occurred shortly after the Black Death.
description_full: Cholsey has been classed by John Brooks as a migrated village, with its focus of settlement shifting from the area around the parish church south-eastwards towards the core of the modern village, a process Brooks suggests may have occurred shortly after the Black Death. [1, 2] The parish church is probably late Anglo-Saxon in date – it has been suggested that the central tower preserves part of Aethelred II’s monastic foundation of the early 990s, with the church returning to secular status before the Norman Conquest. [3] The area opposite the church, east of Church Road has produced pottery from as early as the eleventh century and contains areas of probable medieval ridge and furrow. [4, 5] The full story of Cholsey’s later medieval history is not yet clear however, and pre-development archaeology at a number of sites in the main village area (i.e. several hundred metres south east of the church) has produced pottery perhaps dating from as early as the thirteenth century, and possibly even early medieval features [6, 7], indicating some occupation here before the suggested fourteenth-century shift of focus. The documentary evidence for Cholsey suggests it was always one of the largest vills within Berkshire, although a substantial tax relief of almost 80% was received in 1352. [8] A survey of the manor made in 1551 also suggests a degree of later decline with a number of tenants holding multiple messuages, some of which were noted as ‘decayed’. [9] Whilst the NMR simply classes Cholsey as ‘shrunken’, [10] in light of the emerging archaeological picture for both parts of the medieval settlement it seems that the village could yet be best characterised as a ‘shifted settlement’. Identified by John Brooks.

name: Clapcot
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The location of the medieval settlement of Clapcot is uncertain. Beresford and Hurst suggest Rush Court (SU 605 916) as the location,  and the VCH notes that a Clapcot House was demolished half a mile south of this location in the late eighteenth century,  to be replaced by cottages, although the house does not seem to appear on Rocque’s map of 1761.
description_full: The location of the medieval settlement of Clapcot is uncertain. Beresford and Hurst suggest Rush Court (SU 605 916) as the location, [1] and the VCH notes that a Clapcot House was demolished half a mile south of this location in the late eighteenth century, [2] to be replaced by cottages, although the house does not seem to appear on Rocque’s map of 1761. Perhaps a more likely location for the medieval village (if indeed Clapcot was such) is close to Wallingford Castle, an idea suggested by Gelling on etymological grounds. [3] It has been suggested that the nearby Park Farm was formerly known as Clapcot Farm c. 1550, [2] and the site is plotted at this location. The name Clapcot seems once to have referred to an area extending from the Castle over a mile northwards to the bank of the Thames, [2] and medieval taxation documents perhaps therefore included population from other farms and the manor at Rush Court in their assessments. Nevertheless, Beresford and Hurst note that 'the agglomeration of lands in the hands of two owners at Clapcot suggests that it...was dead by the end of the middle ages.' [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Coleridge
description_snippet: Coleridge survives today only in the name of a copse, but appears in a number of documentary sources from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.  References to a series of grants in the Close Roll for 1340 describe four arable crofts lying together at Coleridge, and a reference to a ‘Coleridge Green’ lying outside the park pale of Beche Park.
description_full: Coleridge survives today only in the name of a copse, but appears in a number of documentary sources from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. [1] References to a series of grants in the Close Roll for 1340 describe four arable crofts lying together at Coleridge, and a reference to a ‘Coleridge Green’ lying outside the park pale of Beche Park. [2] Given this limited documentary evidence and in the absence of archaeological finds to date it seems unlikely Coleridge was ever more than a hamlet. Certainly no trace of a settlement remained by the time of Rocque’s 1761 map. Identified from documentary sources.

name: Combe
e179_last: 1678 Act for rasing money by a poll
description_snippet: The National Monuments Record lists Combe as a shrunken medieval village, based on evidence in the MVRG archive,  although an initial search of the Berkshire files of this archive failed to find details of this place, which was in Hampshire until 1895. Nevertheless the modern settlement layout of Combe does hint at past shrinkage and/or relocation.
description_full: The National Monuments Record lists Combe as a shrunken medieval village, based on evidence in the MVRG archive, [1] although an initial search of the Berkshire files of this archive failed to find details of this place, which was in Hampshire until 1895. Nevertheless the modern settlement layout of Combe does hint at past shrinkage and/or relocation. The church and Manor Farm are isolated from the main village focus to the east, and some post-medieval settlement retreat can be attested in the latter area by nineteenth-century map evidence. The 1808 Ordnance Survey drawing shows several buildings both in the main village focus and in outlying farms that no longer exist, with some disappearing by the time of the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map (surveyed in 1873). More information on the medieval settlement history of the parish would require archaeological fieldwork. Identified by the NMR.

name: Compton
e179_last: 1679-8 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: This site is sometimes referred to as East Compton, and was initially classed as a DMV by Beresford and Hurst.  John Brooks and the West Berkshire HER have preferred to categorise the site as ‘migrated’, [2, 3] with the settlement shift envisaged being from the area around the church formerly known as East Compton, to the larger area of settlement formerly known as West Compton.
description_full: This site is sometimes referred to as East Compton, and was initially classed as a DMV by Beresford and Hurst. [1] John Brooks and the West Berkshire HER have preferred to categorise the site as ‘migrated’, [2, 3] with the settlement shift envisaged being from the area around the church formerly known as East Compton, to the larger area of settlement formerly known as West Compton. An area of scheduled earthworks immediately west of the church has been assumed to represent at least part of the abandoned settlement area at East Compton, with possible tofts and crofts suspected. However, a recent English Heritage field visit in November 2013 has noted that the earthworks are not typical of medieval deserted settlement remains, and may instead be post-medieval in character, perhaps even remains of garden features. [4] The documentary record makes it difficult to discern the relative sizes of the eastern and western components of Compton through time, as they were usually grouped together for taxation purposes, with the vill or manor of ‘Ashden’ usually assumed to indicate the area of West Compton. Documentary references to ‘East’ and ‘West’ Compton are found at least as early as the thirteenth century. [5, 6] There is some evidence that East Compton survived as a substantial area of settlement into the post-medieval period, with a Hearth Tax return of the 1660s separately listing 20 householders for that vill. [3, 4] The map evidence also suggests that some of the depopulation at East Compton occurred in the post-medieval period, since housing plots shown there on eighteenth-century maps and the 1808 Ordnance Survey drawing, especially to the south of the church, were absent by the late nineteenth century. Beresford and Hurst’s initial DMV list for Berkshire classified East Compton as being deserted in the seventeenth or eighteenth century, [1] although the general link between desertions of that period and the emparking process noted in that list does not seem to apply to Compton. John Brooks has suggested that settlement shift towards West Compton could have been an example of attraction towards a line of communication, [2] although the locational advantage of this area over East Compton is not immediately obvious. The eighteenth and nineteenth-century map evidence also does not appear to indicate a notable increase in the size of West Compton to match the contemporary retraction around the church. Given the ambiguous evidence and the close proximity of East and West Compton, it is difficult to classify the site satisfactorily. Archaeological work to establish the chronology of settlement growth and change at both locations is needed to better understand the village’s history, particularly whether the depopulation around the church started in the medieval period. The only attestable period of decline so far is eighteenth/nineteenth century in date, but the lack of growth in West Compton at this time would appear to rule out a ‘migrated’ classification, whilst a ‘shifted’ settlement, which would envisage movement in several stages, cannot yet be supported. Given that East Compton is not entirely deserted, a ‘shrunken’ designation seems most appropriate for the time being. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Compton Beauchamp
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed force
description_snippet: A field west of Compton House is thought to contain earthworks related to the deserted settlement of Compton Beauchamp, and ploughing in its eastern part is said to have uncovered the foundations of two buildings.  The medieval tax assessments for the vill of Compton Beauchamp probably contained other settlements (e.g. Hardwell Farm) and continued right through the period of the E179 database.
description_full: A field west of Compton House is thought to contain earthworks related to the deserted settlement of Compton Beauchamp, and ploughing in its eastern part is said to have uncovered the foundations of two buildings. [1] The medieval tax assessments for the vill of Compton Beauchamp probably contained other settlements (e.g. Hardwell Farm) and continued right through the period of the E179 database. However a study of other medieval documentation has suggested that the village had ceased to exist by 1522, perhaps as part of general move towards depopulation in a number of local manors under the ownership of Sir Thomas Fettiplace. [2] Compton House is generally thought to have sixteenth-century origins, [3] although its formal parkland was probably laid out in the early eighteenth century. [4] Only the country house and church survived by the time of Rocque’s 1761 map. Identified by John Brooks and the MVRG.

name: Cox's Farm, Cholsey
description_snippet: The possible earthwork remains of hollow ways, house platforms and ridge and furrow have been detected in the vicinity of Cox’s Farm by an Environment Agency LIDAR survey in 1996.  The Oxfordshire HER has classed these features as possible evidence of former medieval settlement. The map evidence confirms the likelihood that the settlement previously extended beyond the single farmstead present today.
description_full: The possible earthwork remains of hollow ways, house platforms and ridge and furrow have been detected in the vicinity of Cox’s Farm by an Environment Agency LIDAR survey in 1996. [1] The Oxfordshire HER has classed these features as possible evidence of former medieval settlement. The map evidence confirms the likelihood that the settlement previously extended beyond the single farmstead present today. Rocque’s map of 1761 shows nine buildings, although presumably some are intended to represent outbuildings, perhaps of two or three farmsteads. A similar group of buildings seems to be shown on the 1809 Ordnance Survey drawing, but these had been reduced to the courtyard of the current farm by the time of the 1851 Enclosure map. [2] The surviving farmhouse itself is said by Historic England to be seventeenth century based on external inspection. [3] The group of small fields adjacent to the modern farmhouse is perhaps an indication of the house plots of a former hamlet here, and the earliest maps make clear these would have been strung along the north-eastern edge of Cholsey Common, in a similar fashion to nearby Hillgreen (see separate entry). It is unclear as yet whether the settlement had medieval origins, but it does not seem to have featured in the medieval documentary record and is unlikely to have been more than a hamlet. Identified by the HER.

name: Cruchfield
e179_last: 1624-5 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: Although no physical evidence is known for the medieval village of Cruchfield,  it appears to have been a modestly populated vill in the 1334 Lay Subsidy and had 10 tax payers in 1327 and 11 in 1332 [2, 3]. Beresford and Hurst suggested that the period of depopulation should be attributed to between c. 1450 and c. 1700.
description_full: Although no physical evidence is known for the medieval village of Cruchfield, [1] it appears to have been a modestly populated vill in the 1334 Lay Subsidy and had 10 tax payers in 1327 and 11 in 1332 [2, 3]. Beresford and Hurst suggested that the period of depopulation should be attributed to between c. 1450 and c. 1700. [4] However, Rocque’s schematic representation of 1761 still shows eight buildings on the south side of the main east-west road, which had largely disappeared by the late nineteent century. Modern housing has now been built west of Cruchfield House at ‘Hawthorn Hill’. The house itself is eighteenth century and is perhaps represented on Rocque’s map. By the late nineteenth century an area surrounding the house (except to the south) is mapped as parkland, and could perhaps have obscured further parts of a medieval settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: North Denchworth
e179_last: 1671 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: A small estate at North Denchworth is seemingly delineated in a late Anglo-Saxon charter,  and a five hide estate, one of the three Domesday Book vills named as Denchworth, has been identified as probably being North Denchworth.  Rocque’s 1761 map shows three sets of buildings here in an area it names as ‘Little Denchworth’.
description_full: A small estate at North Denchworth is seemingly delineated in a late Anglo-Saxon charter, [1] and a five hide estate, one of the three Domesday Book vills named as Denchworth, has been identified as probably being North Denchworth. [2] Rocque’s 1761 map shows three sets of buildings here in an area it names as ‘Little Denchworth’. These seem to be present on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1875-7, and are named as Hyde Farm, North Denchworth Farm and Flapp’s Barn. North Denchworth Farm is named as Grange Farm on modern Ordnance Survey maps. In a field west of Grange Farm modern vertical photographs show a limited area of possible earthworks, although much of the general area surrounding the farm seems to be occupied by ridge and furrow. About 350m to the south-east of Grange Farm the modern Ordnance Survey map also maps a moat, marked as Hyde Copse on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map. North Denchworth appears in only two documents in the E179 database – a Lay Subsidy of 1322 and (as Little Denchworth) in 1671. The name is also found in thirteenth-century documents, with the main settlement sometimes distinguished as South Denchworth. There are entries in 1334 Lay Subsidy and 1381 Poll Tax for South Denchworth, and for Denchworth in the census. Possibly North Denchworth was normally assessed for taxation with the southern settlement or elsewhere. The VCH article for Denchworth suggests that Hyde Farm was perhaps the site of a fourteenth-century manor of the Hyde family, and may have had other manor houses nearby in 1383 called 'Loveday's Place and Cleet's Place'. [3] Although the documentary evidence for the site being a medieval village appears to be somewhat limited, it is listed as a DMV by the Brooks. [4] The site certainly appears to have been a long-lived settlement of some form, although it is unclear yet whether it would be better to classify it as a hamlet or a village. Identified by John Brooks.

name: Draycott
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: No physical evidence is known for a DMV at Draycott,  and most of the surrounding fields are under cultivation. The vill appears in Domesday Book as ‘Draycott’, but often occurs as Draycott Moor in later documents.
description_full: No physical evidence is known for a DMV at Draycott, [1] and most of the surrounding fields are under cultivation. The vill appears in Domesday Book as ‘Draycott’, but often occurs as Draycott Moor in later documents. The tax assessments and population counts for the place in later medieval documents seem to have included settlement further south at Southmoor, making it difficult to discern the fortunes of the settlement from this source. Southmoor seems to have existed by at least the thirteenth century. [2] Rocque’s map of 1761 shows that Draycott itself was by then a single farm, as today. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Drayton
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Evidence for possible shrinkage of a medieval settlement at Drayton has been noted in a set of paddocks situated to the north-west of Manor Farm and south of Henleys Lane. The Oxfordshire HER notes a bank and a possible separate enclosure, and has a plan of the earthworks.
description_full: Evidence for possible shrinkage of a medieval settlement at Drayton has been noted in a set of paddocks situated to the north-west of Manor Farm and south of Henleys Lane. The Oxfordshire HER notes a bank and a possible separate enclosure, and has a plan of the earthworks. [1] The NMR mentions that parallel ditches forming property boundaries are visible in this area from 'poor quality' aerial photographs, as well as the presence of a further set of earthworks to the south of the village at SU 4791 9394. [2] Two archaeological interventions have taken place in the area north-west of the Manor. A test pit dug by the Abingdon Area Archaeological and Historical Society at SU 47718 94379 found 'cut features of prehistoric, Roman and medieval date'. [3] Slightly further south, in an area around the northern fringe of Manor Farm a series of ten evaluation trenches were excavated by TVAS. These discovered ditches and gullies from the Saxon and medieval periods, as well as postholes of modern or uncertain date, and a small assemblage of pottery including late Roman, mid Saxon and twelfth to fourteenth-century wares. [3] The documentary evidence consulted provides little clue to Drayton’s decline – the Domesday vill seems to have been quite small, but from the fourteenth century onwards and up to the first census records the vill was one of the more populous in Berkshire. The suggestion that the remains in the paddocks north-west of the manor are medieval in date is supported by the fact that these fields appear to be shown as uninhabited on both Rocque’s 1761 map and the 1811 Enclosure map. [4] More modern development at Drayton has affected the settlement pattern and effectively joined the village with Sutton Wick, with the exception of the paddocks where this entry has been plotted. Identified by the HER and NMR.

name: Eaton Hastings
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The earthworks of the Thames-side DMV of Eaton Hastings appear to be situated in two fields between the church and Lower House Farm, named as ‘Old Town’ and 'Little Old Town’ on the 1842 Tithe map.  Although past ploughing may have removed some of the details, a sketch of the earthworks and maps from aerial photographs have been produced, with a hollow way, ditches and two possible tofts still discernable.
description_full: The earthworks of the Thames-side DMV of Eaton Hastings appear to be situated in two fields between the church and Lower House Farm, named as ‘Old Town’ and 'Little Old Town’ on the 1842 Tithe map. [1] Although past ploughing may have removed some of the details, a sketch of the earthworks and maps from aerial photographs have been produced, with a hollow way, ditches and two possible tofts still discernable. [2] The documentary evidence has been surveyed in detail by John Brooks. [1] Eaton Hastings was once an average-sized village, shown by its 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment and an extent of 1333 which recorded 39 households. The tax reliefs of 1351 (24.7%) and 1352 (28.4%) suggest that the village was not disproportionately affected by the Black Death. However depopulation as a result of enclosure for pasture probably started in the late fourteenth century and perhaps continued into the poorly documented fifteenth century. If the allegations of a court case are to be believed the most substantial blow for the village came between 1509 and 1523 when Thomas Fettiplace was alleged to have enclosed 200 acres, threatening the ‘destruction’ of the village. Certainly by the 1540s only four taxpayers remained and desertion was already 'an accomplished fact'. [1] Eaton Hastings appears to be unusual in Berkshire as an example of a parish where wholesale enclosure had been achieved before 1600. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Egrove
description_snippet: The first mention of Egrove recorded by Margaret Gelling is in the late twelfth century, and the place-name is also mentioned in the 1316 Feudal Aids,  but the name is absent from the E179 database. There is no obvious indication therefore that this farm was once a village. It is listed as doubtfully deserted by John Brooks.  Identified by the HER.
description_full: The first mention of Egrove recorded by Margaret Gelling is in the late twelfth century, and the place-name is also mentioned in the 1316 Feudal Aids, [1] but the name is absent from the E179 database. There is no obvious indication therefore that this farm was once a village. It is listed as doubtfully deserted by John Brooks. [2] Identified by the HER.

name: Farnborough
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The scattered nature of Farnborough’s settlement pattern, with buildings interspersed with substantial gaps on the road frontage, is indicative of a probable shrunken village. This pattern has changed relatively little since the 1812 Ordnance Survey drawing, albeit with some losses and new building since.
description_full: The scattered nature of Farnborough’s settlement pattern, with buildings interspersed with substantial gaps on the road frontage, is indicative of a probable shrunken village. This pattern has changed relatively little since the 1812 Ordnance Survey drawing, albeit with some losses and new building since. The main areas of obvious earthworks indicating settlement withdrawal are thought to be between the church and Manor (Lower) Farm, including the area further back from the road frontage, and to the south of the church, where a building platform, pond and hollow way have been noted [1]. The hollow way may represent a south-western continuation of Copperage Road, perhaps a former pack horse route [2]. Other areas of possible former enclosures or earthworks have been noted to the north-west of the Old Rectory, and between Keeper’s Cottage and the Old Smith in the north-west of the village, [3] whilst other parts of the road frontage (e.g. east of the church) are also notably unoccupied. It has been suggested that Rocque’s 1761 map may indicate some buildings between the church and Manor Farm, [2] suggesting a late removal in this area, but Rocque’s map is perhaps too schematic to be of use for this area. Although some of the depopulation was certainly post-medieval it is difficult to date any earlier retraction, although the fact that some of the supposed tofts and crofts to the north-west of the village apparently differ from the modern settlement layout, [3] perhaps hints at medieval retraction. Farnborough’s surviving taxation returns suggest that the vill was a little below the median size for Berkshire in the early fourteenth century and the sixteenth century, although it is recorded as receiving relatively high tax reliefs (of 57% and 68%) shortly after the Black Death in 1352 and 1353. [4, 5] Identified by the HER.

name: Frenches, nr Sulham
description_snippet: There is a ninteenth-century workhouse which may have its origins in a medieval tenement.  A schematic building is shown in the location by Rocque's 1761 map. However it is unlikely to have have been a village or hamlet. Identified by the HER.
description_full: There is a ninteenth-century workhouse which may have its origins in a medieval tenement. [1] A schematic building is shown in the location by Rocque's 1761 map. However it is unlikely to have have been a village or hamlet. Identified by the HER.

name: Fulscot
e179_last: 1624-5 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: No evidence for a deserted site has yet been found on the ground or on aerial photographs for this site, although it is possible earthworks survive of a moat (of uncertain date). [1, 2, 3 4] A buried stone near the ‘moat’ has been postulated as the remnant of a lost chapel.
description_full: No evidence for a deserted site has yet been found on the ground or on aerial photographs for this site, although it is possible earthworks survive of a moat (of uncertain date). [1, 2, 3 4] A buried stone near the ‘moat’ has been postulated as the remnant of a lost chapel. The main support for a DMV at Fulscot is the size of its 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment, which was below average for all vills, but above average for DMV sites. The 1327 and 1332 Lay Subsidies recorded eight and 10 tax payers at the vill respectively.
