[5, 6] By 1525 only five tax payers were recorded for the vill and Rocque’s map shows a small site, presumably including the current house, part of which is said to be 'no...earlier than the 16th century'. [7] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Gainfield in Buckland
description_snippet: Earthworks in an area of pasture east of Gainfield Farm, observed on aerial photographs of 1969, have been suggested as a possible deserted settlement site. The layout is said to be 'an interrupted, ordered, rectilinear, ditch-defined linear system with `units' of on average 55m by 35m'.  Another description refers to the earthworks as 'house plots'.
description_full: Earthworks in an area of pasture east of Gainfield Farm, observed on aerial photographs of 1969, have been suggested as a possible deserted settlement site. The layout is said to be 'an interrupted, ordered, rectilinear, ditch-defined linear system with `units' of on average 55m by 35m'. [1] Another description refers to the earthworks as 'house plots'. [2] More recent analysis concluded that further research would be necessary to resolve the site [1]. There appears to be no documentary support for a DMV at this site. This part of Buckland parish area is thought to have served as a large open area hundred meeting place in the Anglo-Saxon period. [3, 4] Rocque’s 1761 map shows a single farm at the site. Identified by the NMR and HER.

name: East Ginge
description_snippet: East Ginge has been listed by Brooks as a potential shrunken village,  although to date no evidence of settlement earthworks has been identified.  Some support for the idea might come from the medieval taxation returns, where although amongst the smaller or less wealthy vills in 1086 and 1334, East Ginge did have a middling number of tax payers (34) in the 1381 Poll Tax.
description_full: East Ginge has been listed by Brooks as a potential shrunken village, [1] although to date no evidence of settlement earthworks has been identified. [2] Some support for the idea might come from the medieval taxation returns, where although amongst the smaller or less wealthy vills in 1086 and 1334, East Ginge did have a middling number of tax payers (34) in the 1381 Poll Tax. Whether this population was concentrated at the current settlement site or more widely scattered is not certain, but by the time of Rocque’s 1761 map East Ginge was already a small hamlet. Identified by John Brooks.

name: West Ginge
description_snippet: West Ginge was listed by the MVRG as a potential shrunken village in 1981, with a sketch survey of earthworks being carried out by John Brooks.  Further evidence for shrinkage may come from an aerial photograph of 1946 showing a possible 'scarp...in an area of disturbed ground' which may be a medieval or post-medieval boundary.
description_full: West Ginge was listed by the MVRG as a potential shrunken village in 1981, with a sketch survey of earthworks being carried out by John Brooks. [1] Further evidence for shrinkage may come from an aerial photograph of 1946 showing a possible 'scarp...in an area of disturbed ground' which may be a medieval or post-medieval boundary. [2] The documentary record certainly suggests that West Ginge may once have been a more substantial place. The Domesday vill had a greater than mean number of individuals listed for Berkshire, and the number of Poll Tax payers in 1381 (33) placed the vill as just below the mean size for the county. It seems some of the settlement retreat at West Ginge may have come about quite late, with Rocque’s map of 1761 appearing to show some areas with buildings that had disappeared by the time of the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing. Identified by the MVRG.

name: Goosey
e179_last: 1678-9  Act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The modern settlement pattern of Goosey, set around an extensive green with numerous gaps in the ‘frontage’, is immediately suggestive of a shrunken settlement, [1, 2, 3] but the history of the village’s morphology may be more complicated than at first sight. The green itself contains well preserved earthworks, perhaps of tofts and crofts and including possible building platforms.
description_full: The modern settlement pattern of Goosey, set around an extensive green with numerous gaps in the ‘frontage’, is immediately suggestive of a shrunken settlement, [1, 2, 3] but the history of the village’s morphology may be more complicated than at first sight. The green itself contains well preserved earthworks, perhaps of tofts and crofts and including possible building platforms. [2] It may be significant that a former ‘corpse path’ across the Green leading to Stanford-in-the-Vale (of which Goosey was a chapelry) is said to have consisted of ‘ancient stones’ which were reported to have been pulled up in the early twentieth century. [4] The medieval taxation evidence for Goosey suggests that it may once have been a moderately sized place. Although the vill had a low communal assessment in 1334 (a percentile ranking of 0.13 within Berkshire), there were 19 taxpayers present in the 1327 Lay Subsidy (a ranking of 0.57) and 16 in 1332. [5, 6] The vill received reliefs of 78% and 20% on its small communal assessment in 1352 and 1353 respectively, [7, 8] but was still moderately populous by the 1381 Poll Tax (28 tax payers and a percentile ranking within Berkshire of 0.34). The 1524 Lay Subsidy recorded just five tax payers, but 14 were recorded the following year. Even so, the latter still placed Goosey in the bottom fifth percentile of Berkshire vills and it seems likely that some depopulation may have occurred by this stage. Cartographic evidence also shows however that the pattern of houses around the green continued to change in maps of 1761 (Rocque), 1811 (Ordnance Survey drawing) and 1880 (Ordnance Survey), with both removals and new buildings. Some of the large gaps on the north-western frontage of the green also post-date the 1880 Ordnance Survey map, whilst new housing has been built along Goosey Lane to the south-west of the green. The medieval economic history and topography of Goosey was also influenced by its ownership by Abingdon Abbey, with a fish-pond surviving to the rear of a farm thought to have belonged to the Abbey. [1] Identified by the MVRG.

name: Hamstead Marshall
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: A series of earthworks near the church at Hamstead Marshall have been suggested as a small deserted settlement site.  Although Hamstead Marshall Park was created in the thirteenth century the most likely context for the desertion is thought to be the seventeenth-century park landscaping to accompany the now destroyed mansion (built 1633) to the south-west of the church.
description_full: A series of earthworks near the church at Hamstead Marshall have been suggested as a small deserted settlement site. [1] Although Hamstead Marshall Park was created in the thirteenth century the most likely context for the desertion is thought to be the seventeenth-century park landscaping to accompany the now destroyed mansion (built 1633) to the south-west of the church. [1, 2] The documentary evidence for Hamstead Marshall may be relatively uninformative about the size of any settlement, if the dispersed settlement pattern within the wider parish has medieval origins. However the 21 tax payers in the entire vill in 1381 would seem to confirm that any village near the church must then have been small. Identified by the HER and NMR.

name: East Hanney
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Physical evidence for settlement retraction in East Hanney has been identified at two places on the western edges of the village. To the west of Snuggs Lane (where this entry has been plotted) the lane can be seen continuing across a field as a hollow way as far as Letcombe Brook, with earthworks of two house platforms and crofts alongside and ridge and furrow on the far side of the brook.
description_full: Physical evidence for settlement retraction in East Hanney has been identified at two places on the western edges of the village. To the west of Snuggs Lane (where this entry has been plotted) the lane can be seen continuing across a field as a hollow way as far as Letcombe Brook, with earthworks of two house platforms and crofts alongside and ridge and furrow on the far side of the brook. [1] About 300m further north a set of earthworks is said to surround Poughley Farm. [2] The Oxfordshire HER suggests that Poughley Farm might represent a former hamlet of its own, based on the reference in the 1803 Enclosure Award to a division of East Hanney as the ‘hamlet or tithing of Paufrey’, [3] but given its proximity to the main village it has been classed as part of the potential shrinkage of this settlement. Although the modern farm is absent from Rocque’s 1761 map and the earthworks have apparently not been investigated, the site of the farm perhaps has medieval origins. Poughley is presumably named after the priory in Chaddleworth parish, and appears as a surname in the 1327 Lay Subsidy and 1381 Poll Tax returns for East Hanney. [4, 5] However the Poughley place-name at East Hanney might have earlier origins, deriving from the ownership of a half virgate of land there by the priory, mentioned in a confirmation charter of 1248, preserved in a later inspeximus. [6] Domesday Book and the fourteenth-century taxation returns suggest that East Hanney was one of the more populous Berkshire vills. The Lay Subsidy returns for 1524 and 1525, with just eight and nine taxpayers respectively are misleading, since they include only the part of the vill that fell within Ock Hundred. Another part of the medieval vill fell within Wantage Hundred, and the fourteenth-century returns make clear this was the more populous portion. Identified by the HER.

name: Hardwell Farm in Compton Beauchamp
e179_last: 1662-6 Hardwell
description_snippet: An area of uneven ground seen on aerial photographs, surrounded by ridge and furrow, has been suggested as a deserted settlement at Hardwell Farm. However the remains have not been positively identified on the ground.  A programme of fieldwalking in the general vicinity of the site did recover medieval pottery, mainly of twelfth and thirteenth century date.
description_full: An area of uneven ground seen on aerial photographs, surrounded by ridge and furrow, has been suggested as a deserted settlement at Hardwell Farm. However the remains have not been positively identified on the ground. [1] A programme of fieldwalking in the general vicinity of the site did recover medieval pottery, mainly of twelfth and thirteenth century date. [2] Unusually Hardwell appears more commonly in the E179 database in taxation documents of the sixteenth and seventeenth century, with just a handful of medieval references. Fourteenth-century extents indicate the size of the demesne holdings on the manor, but apparently give no clue to whether a village existed. The settlement is thought by Brooks to have shrunk to a single farm by the time of the dissolution of Abingdon Abbey. [3] The former house dates perhaps from the sixteenth century (although a fourteenth-century date has been postulated) and is accompanied by the remains of a moat. [1, 4] Whether this site was ever more than a medieval manor or hamlet is a possibility. Identified by the NMR and HER.

name: Hartridge
e179_last: 1624 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The West Berkshire HER makes no reference to earthworks or cropmarks at this site.  The medieval taxation records are ambiguous – the Domesday Book entry and early fourteenth-century lay subsidies suggest a small vill, with just three tax payers recorded in 1327 and 1332.
description_full: The West Berkshire HER makes no reference to earthworks or cropmarks at this site. [1] The medieval taxation records are ambiguous – the Domesday Book entry and early fourteenth-century lay subsidies suggest a small vill, with just three tax payers recorded in 1327 and 1332. [2, 3] However the incomplete 1381 Poll Tax record for Hartridge lists at least 46 people, suggesting it was reasonably populated, assuming it covered a similar area to the previous assessments. A courtyard of perhaps as many as eight buildings is shown on Rocque’s 1761 map at this site, but it is unclear if this represents a hamlet, or the courtyard of a single farm, as indicated on later maps. The HER is doubtful that this site was ever a nucleated village [1] and further research on the local medieval settlement pattern would be worthwhile, to investigate its possible dispersal. Identified by the HER.

name: Hatford
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Hatford has been suggested as a shrunken village by John Brooks,  who identified a significant area of desertion to the west of the modern village.  The documentary record suggests that Hatford was a modestly sized place both at the time of Domesday Book and in the fourteenth-century taxation returns.
description_full: Hatford has been suggested as a shrunken village by John Brooks, [1] who identified a significant area of desertion to the west of the modern village. [2] The documentary record suggests that Hatford was a modestly sized place both at the time of Domesday Book and in the fourteenth-century taxation returns. The Lay Subsidy for 1525 may indicate that some depopulation had occurred by this time, as it recorded only five taxpayers for the vill, placing it in the bottom 5% for Berkshire. A decline in population by the sixteenth century may have facilitated the enclosure of the small parish of Hatford, a process that may have largely taken place in a single episode in 1588. [2] Rocque’s map of 1761 essentially depicts Hatford in its shrunken state, although it is possible that some buildings shown on this map along the west side of Sandy Lane were subsequently lost by the time of the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing. Identified by John Brooks.

name: Old Hayward Bottom
description_snippet: Although Old Hayward does not appear in the medieval taxation records in the E179 database, a series of earthworks recognised by Julian Richards, extending over 3 hectares, may mark the site of a DMV.  The earthworks are said to be in 'pasture either side of the farm buildings'  by the NMR and more specifically 'in [a] field surrounding existing farm buildings to s[outh] of the road'  by the local HER.
description_full: Although Old Hayward does not appear in the medieval taxation records in the E179 database, a series of earthworks recognised by Julian Richards, extending over 3 hectares, may mark the site of a DMV. [1] The earthworks are said to be in 'pasture either side of the farm buildings' [1] by the NMR and more specifically 'in [a] field surrounding existing farm buildings to s[outh] of the road' [2] by the local HER. These descriptions refer, it seems, not to Old Hayward Farm, but to buildings (now ‘Globe Cottage’) further north in Old Hayward Bottom. These fields have more recently been under cultivation. A single building is marked at this location on Rocque’s 1761 map. Identified by the MVRG.

name: Henley
description_snippet: Henley is listed by the West Berkshire HER and John Brooks as a DMV, although it is not clear whether any archaeological evidence for the designation exists. [1, 2] The documentary evidence is also unpromising: the place-name appears in the 1316 Nomina Villarum (alongside West Shefford and Fawley),  but is entirely absent from the E179 database.
description_full: Henley is listed by the West Berkshire HER and John Brooks as a DMV, although it is not clear whether any archaeological evidence for the designation exists. [1, 2] The documentary evidence is also unpromising: the place-name appears in the 1316 Nomina Villarum (alongside West Shefford and Fawley), [3] but is entirely absent from the E179 database. The place-name is found as a local surname from 1241, [4] and again in the 1327 Lay Subsidy, where two taxpayers for the vill of Great Shefford, Edmund and Richard de Henle (or their ancestors), may have lived at the settlement. [5] Clearly any depopulation at Henley had occurred before Rocque’s 1761 map which shows only a single farm there, as today. As such it seems possible Henley was always a small place and it is provisionally classed as a doubtful DMV site. Identified by the HER and John Brooks.

name: Henwick
e179_last: 1662 Hearth Tax
description_snippet: Although analysis of aerial photographs from 1947 and field investigation c. 1963 produced no evidence of physical remains of Henwick DMW, later work for the NMP identified (from vertical aerial photographs) earthworks and soilmarks of 'field banks and ditches, ridge and furrow fields and a possible hollow way' near Henwick Manor.
description_full: Although analysis of aerial photographs from 1947 and field investigation c. 1963 produced no evidence of physical remains of Henwick DMW, later work for the NMP identified (from vertical aerial photographs) earthworks and soilmarks of 'field banks and ditches, ridge and furrow fields and a possible hollow way' near Henwick Manor. [1] The area between the Manor and Henwick Cottages is also said to contain 'several small enclosures... which may be garden enclosures or crofts'. [1] It is not clear if this refers to earthworks or field boundaries which are extant or shown on maps. The documentary evidence for Henwick seems encouraging. The 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment was above average for a Berkshire vill and the 79 poll tax payers recorded in 1379 shows a substantial population remained. Beresford and Hurst suggested that Henwick was depopulated between c. 1350 and c.1450. [2] Although the vill does not feature in the 1524/5 Lay Subsidies it can be found in other sixteenth-century documents in the E179 database. However its incidence is curtailed after 1624, being recorded in just two hearth tax returns of 1662 beyond that date. The surprising figure of 99 houses recorded in 1662 perhaps reflects the inclusion of houses at Ashmore Green. [3] Study of the later documents might provide more information at what stage the vill began to suffer depopulation. However, as noted, the size of the vill in medieval and later documentation may not automatically be an accurate guide to the fate of any village. The first 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1877-8 shows that in addition to Manor Farm and Little Henwick Farm (now Manor Cottages) three other farms existed nearby – Lower Henwick Farm, Henwick Farm and Old Henwick Farm. All of these seem to be depicted on Rocque’s 1761 map, raising the question of the degree of dispersal in the medieval settlement pattern. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hillend
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: To the north of Hill End Farm the earthworks of possible deserted settlement platforms are cut into the slope of the hillside. One assessment concluded that these platforms were perhaps too large for buildings and in any case 'are too vague to be surveyed'.  Alternatively the features have been described as 'likely to be house sites' and 'three or four well formed house platforms' [2, 3].
description_full: To the north of Hill End Farm the earthworks of possible deserted settlement platforms are cut into the slope of the hillside. One assessment concluded that these platforms were perhaps too large for buildings and in any case 'are too vague to be surveyed'. [1] Alternatively the features have been described as 'likely to be house sites' and 'three or four well formed house platforms' [2, 3]. Hillend has been identified with the tithing of “Hill” in the medieval taxation records, which had a relatively small communal assessment in 1334 (a percentile ranking of 0.15 within Berkshire), but by contrast 14 tax payers for the 1327 Lay Subsidy (a ranking of 0.42). [4] Few taxpayers were present by 1524 and 1525 (seven and six respectively, percentile rankings of 0.06 and 0.05). It is not clear whether these assessments included possible population centres further afield (e.g. Woodend), but if so it is possible that Hillend itself was never much more than a hamlet. Only two farms or clusters of buildings are shown in the area by Rocque’s map of 1761 and the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map. It is not immediately clear on what basis Beresford and Hurst suggested a seventeenth or eigtheenth-century date for depopulation. [5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hillgreen, Cholsey
description_snippet: The settlement of Hill Green is shown on Rocque’s 1761 map as a linear sequence of buildings along the north-west edge of Cholsey Common, stretching from the site of Old Hithercroft (formerly Heathercroft) Farm in the north to Hillgreen Farm in the south, a distance of about 750m.
description_full: The settlement of Hill Green is shown on Rocque’s 1761 map as a linear sequence of buildings along the north-west edge of Cholsey Common, stretching from the site of Old Hithercroft (formerly Heathercroft) Farm in the north to Hillgreen Farm in the south, a distance of about 750m. The post-medieval decline of the settlement is charted by the map evidence with buildings in the northern area apparently disappearing by the time of the 1809 Ordnance Survey drawing. Those in the southern half were still present on the 1851 Enclosure map, [1] but had largely disappeared by the 1876-7 survey for the first edition 6 and 25 inch Ordnance Survey maps, leaving much the same pattern as the modern settlement with the two farms at the northern and southern extremities and a single farm or house in the centre of the settlement, succeeded or replaced by the house today named as ‘The Haven’, near where the NGR for this site has been plotted. In the absence of any archaeological evidence or intervention it is not clear whether the settlement had medieval origins. Hillgreen does not seem to feature in the medieval taxation documentation, but it is likely the settlement was simply grouped with the nearby main village. The site has been classified as a deserted hamlet rather than a village, although neither category reflects its status as an extensive scatter of green-edge settlement. Identified during the Beresford's Lost Villages Project.

name: Hodcott
e179_last: 1624 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The only evidence of physical remains at Hodcott known to date are some limited banks marked on the 1913 edition of the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map.  Otherwise, apart from the casual find of three medieval potsherds,  this site is only known from documentary records. Beresford and Hurst suggested a period of desertion between c. 1350 and 1450.
description_full: The only evidence of physical remains at Hodcott known to date are some limited banks marked on the 1913 edition of the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map. [1] Otherwise, apart from the casual find of three medieval potsherds, [2] this site is only known from documentary records. Beresford and Hurst suggested a period of desertion between c. 1350 and 1450. [3] The vill contained two Domesday Manors, and a chapel is recorded in the late thirteenth century, [4] but Hodcott’s few lay subsidy taxpayers (five in 1327 and 1332) and low 1334 assessment suggests it was a small settlement that may have been vulnerable to post-Black Death desertion. [5, 6] Although absent from the 1524/5 Lay Subsidies, the vill did continue to appear in the documents of the E179 database until 1624. The seventeenth-century Manor House at the site (apparently attributed to Inigo Jones) was demolished and rebuilt c. 1826 revealing a human skull in the foundations. [4] Rocque’s map of 1761 shows the courtyard of a probable farm, as well as two other buildings, perhaps part of the farm or house, or possibly the last remnants of a hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Holt
e179_last: 1624 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: Holt was listed as a DMV by Beresford and Hurst,  and is plotted at the grid reference of Holt Manor Farm. However no evidence from aerial photographs or earthworks of former settlement has yet been identified at this site. The documentary evidence shows that the vill of Holt had a moderately sized assessment in 1334, although the 23 poll tax payers in 1381 suggests a fairly thinly populated place.
description_full: Holt was listed as a DMV by Beresford and Hurst, [1] and is plotted at the grid reference of Holt Manor Farm. However no evidence from aerial photographs or earthworks of former settlement has yet been identified at this site. The documentary evidence shows that the vill of Holt had a moderately sized assessment in 1334, although the 23 poll tax payers in 1381 suggests a fairly thinly populated place. The key to interpreting the history of medieval settlement in this vicinity may be an understanding of the degree of settlement nucleation or dispersal. It may be of note that Rocque’s map of 1761 shows a number of farms or hamlets to the west and north of ‘Holt Farm’, some of which no longer survive. Perhaps the medieval settlement pattern was similarly dispersed. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hurst
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Hurst has been suggested as possible shrunken village site by Paul Chadwick,  and it is certainly the case that the church, alongside an inn, former vicarage, school and almshouses, forms a small and isolated area of settlement.
description_full: Hurst has been suggested as possible shrunken village site by Paul Chadwick, [1] and it is certainly the case that the church, alongside an inn, former vicarage, school and almshouses, forms a small and isolated area of settlement. Archaeological evidence for settlement contraction in this area seems to be limited to an earthwork said to be near the church [2], whilst medieval features (ditches, pits, ridge and furrow) and pottery were found during evaluation works to the west in Whistley Park. [3] The influence of the grounds of Hurst House (originally a sixteenth-century building) [4] on the local settlement pattern would be worth further investigation, since the church sits at their southern edge. As an alternative to the idea of village shrinkage, it is also worth considering that the local medieval and post-medieval settlement pattern (as shown by Rocque’s 1761 map) could always have been dispersed. Identified by Paul Chadwick.

name: Inglewood
e179_last: 1624 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: As with many DMVs in Western Berkshire, there are no physical remains at Inglewood.  The site has been plotted at the former Inglewood House, rather than Inglewood Farm. The medieval documentary evidence suggests a relatively thinly populated vill.
description_full: As with many DMVs in Western Berkshire, there are no physical remains at Inglewood. [1] The site has been plotted at the former Inglewood House, rather than Inglewood Farm. The medieval documentary evidence suggests a relatively thinly populated vill. Some of the surrounding farms (e.g Anvilles, Templeton) which originally took their name from the Inglewood [2] are separately recorded in the fourteenth-century taxation documents. Nevertheless it is still possible that the medieval vill of Inglewood included other outlying farms as part of a dispersed settlement pattern, rather than a nucleated village. [3] If a village did exist at Inglewood, Beresford and Hurst suggested that it was depopulated in the period c. 1450-1700. [4] The first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map shows parkland between Inglewood House and Farm. The HER notes that 'from 1592 much of the land around Inglewood was owned by the Blandy family, probably involved in the wool trade', which might provide a context for any depopulation. [5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Langley
e179_last: 1624 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: To date the only evidence on the ground for the DMV of Langley seems to be 'a few fragmented sections of ditch and bank' seen on an aerial photograph by the Lambourn Downs National Mapping Programme.  The general area was given over to parkland at some point presumably in the post-medieval period, which may have further masked any remains.
description_full: To date the only evidence on the ground for the DMV of Langley seems to be 'a few fragmented sections of ditch and bank' seen on an aerial photograph by the Lambourn Downs National Mapping Programme. [1] The general area was given over to parkland at some point presumably in the post-medieval period, which may have further masked any remains. It has been suggested that Langley formed part of the unnamed Domesday Book vill in Rowbury Hundred held by Gilbert of Ghent. [2] Together with its sub-manor this holding included at least 17 individuals (four villeins, 10 borders, three slaves). [3] Langley’s 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment was of an above average size for a Berkshire vill, offering perhaps the strongest evidence for a former village here, although only 11 tax payers were present in 1327. [4] The vill received large tax reliefs of 71% and 50% in 1352/3, [5, 6] although this may have partly reflected the disproportionate size of its tax quota rather than any recent episode of post-Black Death decline. Unfortunately no records survive from the Poll Tax for the area, and the vill is not recorded in the 1524/5 Lay Subsidy records. Beresford and Hurst suggested that Langley may have succumbed in this late medieval period (c. 1350-1450). [7] In the mid sixteenth-century manor court rolls survive covering the combined manor of West Bradley and Langley. They do not give the impression that the manor included a substantial settlement, transacting little business. In March 1539 the only item of business was to report that the granary or barn (“orreum”) of John Hobbs was in dire disrepair, although we cannot be sure if this relates to a building at West Bradley or Langley. [8] By the time of Rocque’s 1761 map the settlement consisted mainly of the house and farm, with a few additional buildings. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Leckhampstead
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Listed by the West Berkshire HER as a possible 'shifted' village, since the original church is situated east of the main area(s) of settlement at SU 449 759.  This chapel was demolished in 1859. It is sometimes claimed to have been Anglo-Saxon (based on a probable misreading of an Abingdon Chronicle reference) but was probably at least thirteenth century in origin,  and mentioned in the Patent Rolls in 1308.
description_full: Listed by the West Berkshire HER as a possible 'shifted' village, since the original church is situated east of the main area(s) of settlement at SU 449 759. [1] This chapel was demolished in 1859.[2] It is sometimes claimed to have been Anglo-Saxon (based on a probable misreading of an Abingdon Chronicle reference) but was probably at least thirteenth century in origin, [2] and mentioned in the Patent Rolls in 1308. [3] Although a sixteenth-century farmhouse lies north of the chapel site there is no further evidence to date for a village in the immediate vicinity. Hill Green, further north, has also been claimed as the 'original Leckhampstead', but there appears to be no evidence to confirm this suggestion. The grid reference given by the West Berkshire HER (SU 439 760) is to the main settlement rather than the chapel site. Identified by the HER.

name: Little Town
description_snippet: The main evidence for a former settlement at Little Town – situated about 1km north-west of Little Wittenham, near the parish boundary with Long Wittenham – comes from eighteenth and nineteenth-century maps.
description_full: The main evidence for a former settlement at Little Town – situated about 1km north-west of Little Wittenham, near the parish boundary with Long Wittenham – comes from eighteenth and nineteenth-century maps. Although not named, two buildings are depicted at this site by Rocque’s 1761 map, whilst the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing shows what appears to be a small row of cottages on a north-south alignment, named as Little Town. These cottages were demolished in the early nineteenth century, [1] a specific date being suggested by the 25 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1912, which contains a note that the settlement was destroyed in 1838. This map shows the site in the far north-west corner of Little Wittenham parish, but the true location was seemingly about 120m further east, as confirmed by both the Ordnance Survey drawing and the 1812 Enclosure map of neighbouring Long Wittenham (which labels the site as “Little Houses”). [2] References to this site in medieval documents were not found amongst the E179 database nor in the material consulted for Gelling’s survey of Berkshire place-names, [3] and its medieval pedigree seems doubtful. No earthwork remains were noted at the site by a field investigator in 1964, [4] and suggestions that the site was once more sizeable than the few cottages shown on eigthteenth/nineteenth-century maps seem to have derived from cropmarks seen to the north of the site showing a north-south trackway and rectangular enclosures to the east. However the Oxfordshire HER suggests these are more likely to represent an area of Iron Age or Romano-British settlement, [5] and a number of cropmark sites of similar assumed date are known from the vicinity. Identified by the HER and NMR.

name: East Lockinge
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: East Lockinge has been identified by John Brooks as a rare example of a migrated village in Berkshire where emparking (of Lockinge Park) explains the demolition of buildings and their reconstruction elsewhere.  The reconstruction is thought to have taken place in 1860 as an attempt to create a ‘model village’,  but as Brooks acknowledges, there may also have been earlier changes to the settlement pattern.
description_full: East Lockinge has been identified by John Brooks as a rare example of a migrated village in Berkshire where emparking (of Lockinge Park) explains the demolition of buildings and their reconstruction elsewhere. [1] The reconstruction is thought to have taken place in 1860 as an attempt to create a ‘model village’, [2] but as Brooks acknowledges, there may also have been earlier changes to the settlement pattern. The archaeological evidence for settlement retreat or migration comes in the form of two sets of earthworks, apparently representing tofts and crofts as well as ridge and furrow, visible on aerial photographs of 1946 and 1964. [3] The first is thought to be located within the centre of the village (at approx SU 4254 8744), east and north-east of the modern main north-south road. These may represent a relatively late period of settlement retreat, perhaps from earlier post-medieval emparking, since it appears that some buildings are shown near this area on Rocque’s map of 1761 and perhaps the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing, but had been lost by the time of the 1853 Enclosure map. [4]. The second set of earthworks has been suggested to the south of the village at approx. SU 4271 8706. [3] Rocque’s map shows no buildings in this area, and the settlement here may have retreated long before the creation of Helena’s Park. The cartographic evidence may also help us further chart some of the post-medieval settlement shrinkage at East Lockinge and its relationship to emparking. Rocque’s map shows a series of houses along the north side of the east-west street which was later incorporated into Lockinge Park, but these houses seem to have disappeared by 1811. Although not named, a smaller Lockinge Park is clearly shown on the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing, and might have been responsible for the loss of these dwellings. The former mansion house itself was rebuilt sometime between c. 1730-50 [2, 5, 6] and perhaps this was accompanied or followed by a degree of landscaping work. Houses along the south side of the east-west road taken into Lockinge Park are shown by the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing (but not Rocque) and the 1853 enclosure map, and are surely those chiefly removed by the mid nineteenth-century expansion of the park, being absent from the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map, surveyed in 1875-7. These are perhaps the buildings referred to by a parish history, published in 1900, which noted how the expansion of the park had overtaken 'spots still remembered by the older inhabitants as their early dwellings'. [7] The replacement (and therefore ‘migration’) for these lost dwellings was presumably those built (c. 1860) along the west side of the main north-south village street. The wider picture therefore is that the migration of settlement at East Lockinge perhaps did not occur solely in a single episode, and further research on the dates and geography of the post-medieval emparking would be useful. Information on the medieval fortunes of East Lockinge relies for the moment on documentary evidence, but this is complicated by its relationship to West Lockinge (which formerly fell into Wantage parish). Morris identifies the two references to ‘Lockinge’ in Domesday Book with the east and west parts, both being moderately populous vills. [8] Although place-name references to the east and west elements date from the thirteenth century onwards, [9] Lockinge was taxed as a single unit in the fourteenth-century lay subsides and poll tax, making it impossible to unpick the potential fortunes of the two elements. By the 1801 Census West Lockinge, perhaps always the smaller of the two settlements, was a small hamlet whilst East Lockinge was larger, albeit that it had probably experienced some post-medieval settlement retraction by that stage. Identified by John Brooks.

name: West Lockinge
e179_last: 1671 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: Although no earthworks or cropmarks have been noted for West Lockinge, it appears to be a shrunken settlement based on documentary and cartographic evidence. The documentary evidence for the East and West components of Lockinge is discussed in the database entry for East Lockinge.
description_full: Although no earthworks or cropmarks have been noted for West Lockinge, it appears to be a shrunken settlement based on documentary and cartographic evidence. The documentary evidence for the East and West components of Lockinge is discussed in the database entry for East Lockinge. The Domesday entry identified by Morris as West Lockinge [1] was slightly less populous than East Lockinge (18 minimum individuals compared to 23) although the former still had a percentile ranking of 0.37 within Berkshire. West and East Lockinge were originally situated in different parishes and had a separate manorial history throughout the medieval and most of the post-medieval period. [2] However they were assessed together in some of the medieval taxation returns such as the 1327 and 1334 Lay Subsidies and 1381 Poll Tax and were absent from the sixteenth-century lay subsidies, so it is difficult to assess whether West Lockinge experienced a medieval episode of depopulation without further research. Certainly by the time of the 1801 Census West Lockinge township had only 14 inhabited buildings and 60 inhabitants including outlying farms (compared to 57 and 245 respectively for East Lockinge). The percentile ranking by population for West Lockinge in 1801 was only 0.06 within Berkshire. The map sequence provides evidence for a post-medieval episode of depopulation, with several houses along both sides of the road heading north from West Lockinge Farm being shown on Rocque’s 1761 map but not the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing. The village’s layout then seems to have remained largely unchanged for about 150 years, with several remaining houses near the farm demolished shortly after 1960 according to the modern Ordnance Survey map sequence, although two rows of new houses were also built further north at about the same time. Identified by John Brooks.

name: Lollingdon
description_snippet: Lollingdon has been listed as a DMV by John Brooks,  although the NMR and HER record no archaeological evidence for medieval settlement here beyond the manor house. This house sits within a moat, which is said by the HER to be post-medieval,  but the house itself does appear to contain medieval features, in the form of re-used timbers from a fourteenth-century hall and evidence for a medieval service block.
description_full: Lollingdon has been listed as a DMV by John Brooks, [1] although the NMR and HER record no archaeological evidence for medieval settlement here beyond the manor house. This house sits within a moat, which is said by the HER to be post-medieval, [2] but the house itself does appear to contain medieval features, in the form of re-used timbers from a fourteenth-century hall and evidence for a medieval service block. [3] The documentary evidence for Lollingdon does not seem to point towards a substantial former settlement. It is not recorded in the documents used for the E179 database, and whilst it did appear in Domesday Book, the three villeins and three cottars then present at the manor meant Lollingdon had a percentile rank of just 0.08 within Berkshire for its Domesday population. The manorial descent for Lollingdon has been charted in detail, and from 1392 onwards the manor was attached to Brightwell, as a possession of the Bishopric of Winchester. [3, 4] The cartographic evidence suggests that Lollingdon was little more than a farmstead at the time of Rocque’s map of 1761, which shows four or five buildings in the vicinity, although perhaps all intended to depict a single farm. A close-knit collection of buildings at the farm was shown on the 1851 Enclosure map for Cholsey parish. [5] Possibly it would be worth investigating the archaeological potential of some of the small paddocks in the immediate vicinity of the farm, in case they reflect the amalgamation of former house plots, but a doubtful classification currently seems most appropriate for this site. Identified by John Brooks.

name: Longcot
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The modern village of Longcot is mainly focussed along the Shrivenham Road and King’s Lane, but a significant element of the settlement to the west has been lost since the late eighteenth century. Rocque’s map of 1761 shows a series of houses along a lane (apparently known as ‘the Dash’ ) which headed westwards from King’s Lane before curving south-westwards in a loop to rejoin the Shrivenham Road.
description_full: The modern village of Longcot is mainly focussed along the Shrivenham Road and King’s Lane, but a significant element of the settlement to the west has been lost since the late eighteenth century. Rocque’s map of 1761 shows a series of houses along a lane (apparently known as ‘the Dash’ [1]) which headed westwards from King’s Lane before curving south-westwards in a loop to rejoin the Shrivenham Road. Most of the houses along the Dash appear still to have been present on the 1796 Longcot Enclosure map, [2] whilst the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing fails to depict any of these houses or the lane itself. It seems possible there may also have been some loss of houses along the north side of the Shrivenham Road part of this ‘loop’ at a similar period. A series of earthworks within the area of the ‘loop’ formed by the Dash were assessed in 1977 and said to consist of 'low banks and very shallow ditches but no building platforms...[they] may indicate former shrinkage of the village, but they appear to be of very minor importance'. [3] Analysis of aerial photographs of the area by Brendan Grimley also identified the cropmarks of two possible medieval tofts. [4, 5] It is notable that the depiction of settlement around the Dash on Rocque’s map still indicated some gaps in the lane frontage, so it is possible a degree of settlement shrinkage occurred in this area earlier than the late eighteenth/early nineteenth-century episode indicated by the map evidence. The documentary evidence sampled for Longcot is too fragmentary to give an indication of the settlement’s fortunes over time, but it is worth noting that the relatively low lay subsidy assessment of taxable goods in 1334 probably did not reflect the population size of the vill, which had 24 tax payers present in 1327 (a percentile ranking of 0.695 within Berkshire). [6] Identified by the HE and NMR.

name: Longmoor
description_snippet: Said to have been first recorded in the late seventeenth century, mainly built between 1810-40 and demolished by the early twentieth century.  A settlement on the waste, marked on Rocque's map of 1761, but no evidence it should be regarded as a nucleated 'village' or that it was medieval. Identified by the HER.
description_full: Said to have been first recorded in the late seventeenth century, mainly built between 1810-40 and demolished by the early twentieth century. [1] A settlement on the waste, marked on Rocque's map of 1761, but no evidence it should be regarded as a nucleated 'village' or that it was medieval. Identified by the HER.

name: Maidencourt
e179_last: 1624 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: No physical remains of a DMV are known from the site of Maidencourt Farm. A curious note is recorded from a field investigator in 1963, relating the comment of the local farmer that much of the land near the farm had been ‘bulldozed’. [1, 2] The documentary evidence however does point towards the likelihood of a more substantial settlement once existing.
description_full: No physical remains of a DMV are known from the site of Maidencourt Farm. A curious note is recorded from a field investigator in 1963, relating the comment of the local farmer that much of the land near the farm had been ‘bulldozed’. [1, 2] The documentary evidence however does point towards the likelihood of a more substantial settlement once existing. A list of 1220 notes 22 individuals owing arrears on the carrucage tax for land within the vill. [3] The 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment is about average for accepted DMV sites in the county, whilst the 23 poll tax payers recorded in 1381 suggest a viable population may still have existed, assuming that these tax payers mainly lived in a nucleated settlement. By the Lay Subsidy of 1525, however, Maidencourt was grouped with nearby East Garston. Beresford and Hurst suggest that depopulation took place in the period c. 1450-c. 1700. [4] By 1761 only a single farm is marked on Rocque’s map. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Marlston
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: In common with so many potential DMVs in West Berkshire, there is no known evidence on the ground for a medieval village at Marlston. [1, 2] However, the documentary evidence suggests that the place was once more substantial. Although not specifically mentioned in Domesday Book it has been suggested that one of the smaller Bucklebury entries (for 4 hides) refers to Marlston.
description_full: In common with so many potential DMVs in West Berkshire, there is no known evidence on the ground for a medieval village at Marlston. [1, 2] However, the documentary evidence suggests that the place was once more substantial. Although not specifically mentioned in Domesday Book it has been suggested that one of the smaller Bucklebury entries (for 4 hides) refers to Marlston. [3] The church at Marlston was first built, as a chapel, in the twelfth century. [3] The vill’s 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment is about average for accepted DMVs, although the 14 poll tax payers in 1381 probably indicates a relative decline. Beresford and Hurst suggest a period of depopulation between c. 1450 and 1700 for the village. [4] Rocque’s map of 1761 has some extra information of value in this case. In addition to three buildings shown around the church in the area now occupied by Marlston House (itself apparently rebuilt in the late nineteenth century and now a school) there were two buildings north of the road, lost by the time of the 1808 Ordnance Survey drawing. The possibility also needs to be considered that the medieval settlement pattern could have been partly dispersed (several other farms or buildings near Marlston House have buildings depicted on Rocque’s map). The first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map shows a small area of parkland surrounding Marlston House. The site has been plotted at a grid reference near the House and church. Marlston Farm, further to the east, appears to have been built initially as a barn between 1761 and 1808. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Newton
e179_last: 1563 subsidy
description_snippet: Newton was listed as a DMV in the 1968 gazetteer, located at the grid reference of Upper Newton Farm (SU 360 980),  although this seems to have been built between 1761 and 1811. A more likely location for a medieval settlement is Lower Newton Farm. The farm house there was demolished in the 1920s, apparently producing sixteenth and seventeenth-material for re-use at Newton House.
description_full: Newton was listed as a DMV in the 1968 gazetteer, located at the grid reference of Upper Newton Farm (SU 360 980), [1] although this seems to have been built between 1761 and 1811. A more likely location for a medieval settlement is Lower Newton Farm. The farm house there was demolished in the 1920s, apparently producing sixteenth and seventeenth-material for re-use at Newton House. [2, 3] The site is said to have the remains of a manor house, dovecote, fishponds and 'earthworks' [4]. Finds from fieldwalking and metal detecting in the vicinity include late Anglo-Saxon/early Norman mounts and coins from the twelfth to fourteenth century. [5] The documentary evidence for Newton seems to be rather sparse. It is recorded as a small Domesday vill, with four bordars and two slaves. A description of a landholding which seems to have included an area of both Newton and Hatford in 1348 referred to 10 messuages, [6] but it is not clear how many of these were at Newton. The vill only appears on the E179 database of medieval and post-medieval taxation records in three documents – the Lay Subsidies of 1523-5, 1559-60 and 1563. In each of these cases Newton was grouped with Buckland and several other places. Perhaps Newton was normally assessed with Buckland in medieval taxation assessments. The paucity of the documentary evidence does however prompt some doubts about whether Newton was once a village rather than a manorial site or hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: nr Lamb's Farm, Swallowfield
description_snippet: A DMV was suggested south of Lamb’s Farm, Swallowfield on the basis of cropmarks on an aerial photograph of 1970, showing ditches that may have formed enclosures typical of a medieval settlement.  However, further significant archaeological evidence for this site has not yet been found.
description_full: A DMV was suggested south of Lamb’s Farm, Swallowfield on the basis of cropmarks on an aerial photograph of 1970, showing ditches that may have formed enclosures typical of a medieval settlement. [1] However, further significant archaeological evidence for this site has not yet been found. A scatter of 12 undated (but most likely medieval) pottery sherds was discovered north of the site by the Loddon Valley Fieldwalking Survey, [2] but two watching briefs in advance of building works in and around the farm itself failed to produce any archaeological finds or features, albeit that in one case any deposits had likely already been truncated. [3, 4] Lamb’s Farm itself is not show on Rocque’s 1761 map, although it is found on the 1806 Ordnance Survey drawing for the area. There is no obvious documentary evidence for a substantial lost settlement in the immediate vicinity, and it seems unlikely that the site represents a deserted village. The generally dispersed local settlement pattern suggests that a hamlet is more likely in any event, and for the time being the site has been classed as doubtful. Identified by the HER.

name: nr Thrupp in Littleworth
description_snippet: Listed by the NMR as an early medieval or later deserted settlement and referred to in its description as a possible deserted village, but the description also suggests this site is the cropmark of a single enclosure.  There are Domesday and taxation records for Littleworth but not for a settlement at Thrupp. There are census records for Littleworth and Thrupp. Identified by the NMR.
description_full: Listed by the NMR as an early medieval or later deserted settlement and referred to in its description as a possible deserted village, but the description also suggests this site is the cropmark of a single enclosure. [1] There are Domesday and taxation records for Littleworth but not for a settlement at Thrupp. There are census records for Littleworth and Thrupp. Identified by the NMR.

name: Oare
e179_last: 1587-8 subsidy
description_snippet: Evidence from an air photograph of 1946 suggests that earthworks of tofts and crofts once existed north of the road between the church and Roean Cottage at Oare, although subsequent photographs suggest they have been levelled, perhaps remaining as crop/grass marks.
description_full: Evidence from an air photograph of 1946 suggests that earthworks of tofts and crofts once existed north of the road between the church and Roean Cottage at Oare, although subsequent photographs suggest they have been levelled, perhaps remaining as crop/grass marks. [1, 2] Rocque’s map of 1761 suggests that settlement at Oare was formerly more extensive (if somewhat dispersed in pattern) with buildings depicted at the east and west ends of the village that had disappeared by the time of the 1808 Ordnance Survey drawing. However Rocque’s mapping of the settlement should be treated with some caution as the position of the church (a chapel of Chieveley) seems to be mis-located to the west. The chapel is recorded as one of the chapels of Chieveley in the taxation of 1291, but has no individual amount listed. Identified by the HER and NMR.

name: Odstone
e179_last: 1662-6 Hearth Tax
description_snippet: The probable site of the DMV at Odstone is thought to be situated in a field of 'slightly uneven ground' to the north-west of Odstone Farm at grid reference SU 2691 8618. [1, 2] The field is reported to have contained 'the probable remains of one or two buildings represented by rectangular patches of clunch and sarsen stones' when first ploughed in 1963, [1, 2] and remained under the plough on a further field...
description_full: The probable site of the DMV at Odstone is thought to be situated in a field of 'slightly uneven ground' to the north-west of Odstone Farm at grid reference SU 2691 8618. [1, 2] The field is reported to have contained 'the probable remains of one or two buildings represented by rectangular patches of clunch and sarsen stones' when first ploughed in 1963, [1, 2] and remained under the plough on a further field investigation in 1977. [1] A sketch survey is said to have been made of the site. [3] The documentary evidence confirms the likelihood of a DMV. The vill of Odstone appears to have been reasonably populous, particularly based on the Domesday Book entry and the 84 poll tax payers present in 1381. Although the chronology of subsequent decline has yet to be worked out, by the time of Rocque’s map of 1761 the settlement was reduced to a single farm, and the 1841 census recorded just four inhabited buildings in the tithing. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Peasemore
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Peasemore has been the subject of a recent programme of archaeological and documentary research by the Berkshire Archaeology Research Group.  A series of 19 test pits has been dug in village gardens and adjoining fields, and despite the limited range of medieval pottery present it is possible to reconstruct the story of the settlement’s origin and development.
description_full: Peasemore has been the subject of a recent programme of archaeological and documentary research by the Berkshire Archaeology Research Group. [1] A series of 19 test pits has been dug in village gardens and adjoining fields, and despite the limited range of medieval pottery present it is possible to reconstruct the story of the settlement’s origin and development. Initial settlement, probably dating from the late Anglo-Saxon period seems to have been scattered around the northern and eastern edges of an arable area enclosed by a circular loop of lanes which persists today. The village church was built between 1084 and 1097 at the northern tip of this ‘loop’ and in the twelfth century a planned linear extension to the village was made along what is now the main north-south village street, and perhaps slightly later along Hill Green Lane to the west. This basic village footprint appears to have changed little over succeeding centuries and was still visible on Rocque’s map of 1761. However there are some indications of late medieval shrinkage at Peasemore. Pottery dated to the later fourteenth and fifteenth centuries was poorly represented in the test pit assemblage, and a number of the pits (e.g. west of the main north-south street, and south-east of the church) produced copious medieval pottery but little post-medieval material, suggesting possible limited areas of retraction. Similarly some amorphous or slight earthworks have been identified (but not systematically surveyed) in fields at the south-eastern edges of the village. The likelihood seems to be that depopulation did not deplete any single zone of the village, but instead left a series of gaps in the village plan, as plots were abandoned or amalgamated in the late medieval period. Although the parish is not blessed with plentiful medieval records, the fragmentary survivals also provide support for an element of shrinkage. Indications that the village was experiencing difficulties date from as early as the fourteenth century, when the Nonarum Inquisitiones of 1342 noted that more than 60 acres of arable land was uncultivated within the parish. [2] The vill also had the highest taxation relief within its hundred (85%) in 1352 in the wake of the Black Death, [3] although this may also be related to an unusually high communal tax assessment in 1334. Later medieval manor court entries from 1494 and 1539 citing copyhold tenements in need of repair at Peasemore almost certainly indicate unoccupied properties, [4, 5] and a degree of decline may have continued into the sixteenth century – surveys recorded ten customary tenants in 1522 but only seven in 1547. [6, 7] The post-medieval development of Peasemore is made more difficult to interpret by a fire which destroyed numerous buildings in 1736, although some at least were rebuilt on the same house plots. [8] In general the period seems to have seen a more intensive use of space within the village as well as a limited expansion at the village outskirts (e.g. at Eastley End near the boundary with Leckhampstead from the seventeenth century onwards, and northwards onto Mell Green, starting in 1794 [9]). There were also however some post-medieval losses, including a number in the early nineteenth century which had a significant effect on the village layout. These included the loss of the back lane (perhaps known as Frog Lane) running parallel with the main street to its east, and the loss of the manor house from a site just south-east of Peasemore Manor Farm. Similarly, a row of houses on the north-east side of the Chieveley road heading south-eastwards out of the village is shown depicted in the 1812 Ordnance Survey drawing but had also disappeared by the time of the 1840 Tithe map. Test pits in this location (chosen as the location site for this database) indicate that occupation there extended back to the medieval period. [1] The late medieval settlement retraction at Peasemore, in some cases re-occupied by post-medieval and modern development, is probably not out of the ordinary for villages on the southern Berkshire Downs, and it may well be the case that similar programmes of research would discover evidence for non-permanent shrinkage at neighbouring villages (see the entry for Chieveley for example). Identified by the Berkshire Archaeology Research Group.

name: Petwick
e179_last: c. 1351 'stray'
description_snippet: The first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map has several places with the Petwick name (two Petwick Farms, Lower Petwick, Petwick Cottages (later Petwick Stud Farm)). The site was suggested as a lost village based on the distribution of these names by Gelling,  and listed as a DMV by Brooks.
description_full: The first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map has several places with the Petwick name (two Petwick Farms, Lower Petwick, Petwick Cottages (later Petwick Stud Farm)). The site was suggested as a lost village based on the distribution of these names by Gelling, [1] and listed as a DMV by Brooks. [2] However, with the exception of Lower Petwick (marked as 'Paddock or Padwick Farm' on Rocque's map of 1761), the other places are either absent or differently named on the Rocque map and the Ordnance Survey drawing of 1811. Petwick is found in some medieval documents - it may have been an outlying medieval farm or manor, but the evidence for a village seems very late. The only evidence from aerial photographs appears to be indications of ridge and furrow in the area. [3] Identified by John Brooks.

name: Pingewood
description_snippet: Rocque’s map of 1761 shows buildings scattered around the edge of ‘Pinge wood’ itself, particularly on the north and east sides. These had disappeared by the time Ordnance Survey maps were produced c.1912-24.  Although Pingewood does not appear in the E179 database, the name is of considerable antiquity (perhaps an example of a ‘British’ place-name) and also occurs in medieval documents produced by Reading Abbey.
description_full: Rocque’s map of 1761 shows buildings scattered around the edge of ‘Pinge wood’ itself, particularly on the north and east sides. These had disappeared by the time Ordnance Survey maps were produced c.1912-24. [1] Although Pingewood does not appear in the E179 database, the name is of considerable antiquity (perhaps an example of a ‘British’ place-name) and also occurs in medieval documents produced by Reading Abbey. [2] The pattern of buildings shown in 1761 is that of a ‘common edge’ settlement rather than a traditional nucleated village, but Rocque's depiction of the number and density of buildings (although schematic) is perhaps enough to warrant a possible DMV classification, albeit that we cannot say how much of this wood-edge settlement originated in the medieval period without further research. The area north of the wood is shown under cultivation on modern vertical aerial photos, whilst a gravel extraction lake lies to the south-east. Identified by the HER.

name: Purley Parva
e179_last: 1624-5 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The deserted settlement of Purley Parva is thought to have been situated in the vicinity of Westbury Farm and Springs (formerly Scraces) Farm.  A limited trial trench excavation in 1971 to the west of Westbury Farm found 'a good flint floor butting onto a brick floor...the scant finds suggest a comparatively recent date', and a pit with finds ranging from the 'early medieval' period to the nineteenth century.
description_full: The deserted settlement of Purley Parva is thought to have been situated in the vicinity of Westbury Farm and Springs (formerly Scraces) Farm. [1] A limited trial trench excavation in 1971 to the west of Westbury Farm found 'a good flint floor butting onto a brick floor...the scant finds suggest a comparatively recent date', and a pit with finds ranging from the 'early medieval' period to the nineteenth century. [2] Purley has two entries in Domesday Book, and although not identified by the Phillimore edition, it has been suggested that the small half-hide landholding, with one villein and two bordars could be Purley Parva. [3, 4] Purley Magna and Purley Parva are certainly differentiated in documents of the thirteenth century onwards, [5] with the latter name present in the documents of the E179 database until 1624-5. A correlation between what is assumed to be the manor of Purley Parva and Westbury Farm is made in a Feet of Fine from 1659. [3] The village however is likely to have been depopulated long before, or was always small. Only three tax payers were recorded in the 1327 Lay Subsidy and five in 1332. [6, 7] The 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment for the vill was also below average for accepted DMV sites, and in the 1381 Poll Tax Purley Parva’s 13 taxpayers formed one of the smallest assessments in its hundred. At what point any small village or hamlet effectively ceased to exist is not clear, but Rocque’s map of 1761 shows just the two farms at the site. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Pusey
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Pusey has been suggested as a shrunken or possibly migrated village, [1, 2] no doubt in part because the few houses in the village today are scattered around the southern edge of the mid eighteenth-century parkland associated with Pusey House. This house is thought to have been built between 1746-8, with the grounds initially landscaped at a similar period [3, 4].
description_full: Pusey has been suggested as a shrunken or possibly migrated village, [1, 2] no doubt in part because the few houses in the village today are scattered around the southern edge of the mid eighteenth-century parkland associated with Pusey House. This house is thought to have been built between 1746-8, with the grounds initially landscaped at a similar period [3, 4]. It has also been suggested that the village church was re-built in 1745, [3, 4, 5] and re-sited from a former position near the current house, [5] although conversely Huntingford suggested that the rebuilding may have been somewhat earlier (c. 1720) and carried out at the existing church site, based on the presence of an earlier monument in the churchyard. [6] As such then there is currently little firm evidence that the construction of Pusey House and its grounds caused depopulation at Pusey, although the possibility cannot be ruled out. There is a hint however in the documentary evidence that Pusey may have declined in importance during the medieval period. The percentile rankings for Domesday Book population levels and fourteenth-century tax payers/tax assessments for Pusey suggest the vill was a moderately sized community, but the 12 taxpayers recorded by the 1525 Lay Subsidy gave it a percentile ranking of only 0.15 within Berkshire. The vill’s ranking for the 1801 Census was even lower at 0.075, and this may reflect not just the effect of any displacement by landscaping around Pusey House but also the later eighteenth and nineteenth-century loss of houses, shown by map evidence. In particular a row of houses heading westwards from the vicinity of South Lodge depicted by Rocque in 1761 appears to have largely disappeared by the time of the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing and entirely by the first edition 25 inch Ordnance Survey map surveyed in 1876-7. Identified by John Brooks.

name: Radley
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Radley was initially listed by John Brooks as either a possible migrated or shrunken settlement,  and more recently solely as a migrated village.  The movement apparently envisaged is from the small area of settlement around the church and vicarage at the edge of Radley Park (now occupied by the College) towards the area today known as Lower Radley, about 1km to the east.
description_full: Radley was initially listed by John Brooks as either a possible migrated or shrunken settlement, [1] and more recently solely as a migrated village. [2] The movement apparently envisaged is from the small area of settlement around the church and vicarage at the edge of Radley Park (now occupied by the College) towards the area today known as Lower Radley, about 1km to the east. The latter consists of houses scattered around three sides of a sub-rectangular loop of lanes. The large area of modern settlement around the railway station in between these two foci has mainly grown up over the past century, although a handful of houses are shown in the area on the earliest eighteenth-century maps. Although there is relatively little archaeological evidence from either the ‘church’ site or Lower Radley to help date the respective elements it is clear that both date back to the medieval period. The church itself, although largely re-built, has fourteenth and fifteenth-century elements, [3, 4] whilst the vicarage is also thought to date to the late fifteenth century. [5, 6] At Lower Radley excavation associated with the demolition of a condemned cruck-framed cottage (positioned at the north-west corner of the loop) revealed that occupation of the site dated back to the fourteenth century. [7] The history of settlement at the ‘church’ site needs to be considered alongside that of the adjacent park, which dates back to at least 1262. [8] Radley’s medieval manor belonged to Abingdon Abbey, and it seems some form of manor house was situated within the park, [3] perhaps accounting for the nearby positioning of the church. The park is said to have been ‘disparked’ before 1540 and was apparently once rather larger than its eighteenth-century version. [8] Whether an early creation or expansion of the medieval park caused any settlement displacement is not known, however. The possibility should perhaps also be considered that Radley had a long-standing polyfocal settlement pattern with the fortunes of the various elements not necessarily linked. Identified by John Brooks.

name: Rockley
description_snippet: Rockley has been listed by John Brooks as a doubtful DMV site.  As yet there is no archaeological evidence for a site here, and the documentary record offers relatively little to support the idea of a significant lost settlement.
description_full: Rockley has been listed by John Brooks as a doubtful DMV site. [1] As yet there is no archaeological evidence for a site here, and the documentary record offers relatively little to support the idea of a significant lost settlement. First mentioned as a boundary feature in an Anglo-Saxon charter purporting to be from the tenth century, [2] Rockley is not mentioned in the documents consulted for the E179 database, although it was recorded in the ‘feudal aids’ of 1316 and 1428. [3] Both the 1327 and 1332 Lay Subsidies for Bessels Leigh also mention a Robert (de) Rokele(ye) implying that this tax payer or one of his ancestors once came from this place. [4, 5] The map evidence indicates that Rockley continued to give its name to both a wood and an area of heathland on the first edition 6 and 25 inch Ordnance Survey maps, surveyed in 1876-8. The Rockley Cottages named on this map, just inside the boundary of Cumnor, were however built some time after the 1814 Enclosure map for that parish. [6] Given that the main settlement of Bessels Leigh was once probably near the church (and depopulated, perhaps by post-medieval emparkment – see the entry for that site) another scenario presents itself to explain the ‘loss’ of Rockley. The area of houses now often described on modern maps as Bessels Leigh, immediately south-west of Rockley Copse, along the road leading to Bessels Leigh Farm is shown on maps dating back to Rocque’s plan of 1761, when it was possibly slightly more extensive than in the late nineteenth century. If the medieval settlement pattern in Bessels Leigh parish was polyfocal, might it be that these houses represent the successors to the medieval hamlet of Rockley? Identified by John Brooks.

name: Seacourt
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Seacourt is one of the earliest DMVs to be excavated in Berkshire. Initial excavations in 1937-9 seem to have taken place in the ‘original nucleus’ of the village, finding domestic structures, medieval pits and part of the village church.  The site has also produced Roman pottery implying a farm or hamlet nearby, whilst pottery of the tenth-twelfth century must represent the first stages of the medieval village.
description_full: Seacourt is one of the earliest DMVs to be excavated in Berkshire. Initial excavations in 1937-9 seem to have taken place in the ‘original nucleus’ of the village, finding domestic structures, medieval pits and part of the village church. [1] The site has also produced Roman pottery implying a farm or hamlet nearby, whilst pottery of the tenth-twelfth century must represent the first stages of the medieval village. [2] The village site seems to have been bordered by Marleywood Plantation on the west and Wytham or Seacourt stream on the east. [3] The second phase of excavations in 1958-9, in advance of the construction of the Oxford Western by-pass was focussed on the central area of earthworks. [2] This included the main north-south street that runs along the length of the area given over to the bypass. [2] The 1958-9 excavations revealed evidence of structures no earlier than mid-late twelfth century suggesting that this area was a late twelfth-thirteenth-century extension from the original village core. [2] In 1959 rapid recording was undertaken of the fuller area of the main street uncovered in advance of road construction. [2] Wooden buildings in the village seem to have been replaced by stone-built houses, probably in the first half of the fourteenth century. [2] The site did not reveal evidence of the typical longhouse with animals under the same roof. Instead houses were simple one or two-roomed cottages. [2] The pottery sequence seems to come to an end by the late fourteenth century, suggesting desertion had occurred by c. 1400. [2] The excavations did not manage to locate tenth-twelfth century activity at the site but the presence of pottery supports documentary references to an earlier phase of settlement. [2] Later excavations at the site c. 1988 revealed further settlement remains west of the bypass, [4] whilst analysis of aerial photographs has shown another main north-south hollow way surviving in this area. In total at least nine house platforms have been identified. [4] The documentary evidence suggests that the Domesday vill of Seacourt was reasonably populous, whilst in contrast only three tax payers were recorded in 1327 and 1332, [5, 6] and the vill’s 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment also seems low, perhaps suggesting contraction before the Black Death. The estimated desertion of the site by c. 1400 is supported by a letter dated 1439 which notes that the church had collapsed and only two buildings remained occupied in the village. [1] It has been suggested that Seacourt’s decline could be linked to the rising prosperity of nearby Oxford. [7] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Shalford
e179_last: 1549-52 subsidy ('relief')
description_snippet: No physical remains of a village are known.  The Victoria County History equates the secondary 3.5 hide Domesday Book estate at Brimpton with Shalford (with six villeins, three bordars and six slaves). It also claims that the chapel at Brimpton Manor Farm, some distance away, is the church mentioned in this Domesday entry.  Shalford appears only once in the E179 database.
description_full: No physical remains of a village are known. [1] The Victoria County History equates the secondary 3.5 hide Domesday Book estate at Brimpton with Shalford (with six villeins, three bordars and six slaves). It also claims that the chapel at Brimpton Manor Farm, some distance away, is the church mentioned in this Domesday entry. [2] Shalford appears only once in the E179 database. From 1198 to the dissolution it was the site of a manor belonging to the Knights Hospitallers of St. John of Jerusalem. Dendrochronology has shown the earliest part of Shalford Farm to date to c. 1430. [3] The evidence for a village, as opposed to a medieval manor, seems unproven at present. Rocque's 1761 map does show four sets of buildings at the location, some now lost. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Shaw
depop_text: Possibly medieval, plus post-medieval decline between 1761 and 1808
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces (Shaw cum Donnington)
description_snippet: Shaw was suggested as a shrunken medieval settlement by Copley,  who gave a grid reference just north of Shaw House, perhaps therefore suggesting some form of settlement in this general area prior to the construction of the house, which was completed in 1581.
description_full: Shaw was suggested as a shrunken medieval settlement by Copley, [1] who gave a grid reference just north of Shaw House, perhaps therefore suggesting some form of settlement in this general area prior to the construction of the house, which was completed in 1581. A watching brief in 2000 for a very small trench near the house found a negative feature and four sherds of Kennet Valley ware type B pottery (broadly late twelfth to fourteenth century in date), hinting at earlier occupation in the vicinity. [2] The nearby church of St Mary’s is also isolated from the main later focus of settlement at Shaw. The church is a re-build of 1841-2, [3] although the former medieval church is shown on earlier maps in the same area, and was claimed (based, it seems, on a former round tower) to have been Anglo-Saxon in origin. [4, 5] Archaeological work in 1999 south-west of the current church has found evidence for medieval ‘activity’ in the form of shallow ditches and pits, [6] whilst trenches in advance of a northwards extension of the church in 1994 found a significant ditch containing Kennet Valley ware type B pottery and an associated compacted surface. [7] These probably represent the former graveyard boundary and the road north of it, shown on the 1808 Ordnance Survey drawing. Evidence for settlement shrinkage at Shaw is also said to be held in the MVRG archive, [8] but a search of the Berkshire archive files for the Group held at the NMR produced no information. The documentary evidence for Shaw does suggest a degree of fluctuation in its fortunes. It seems to have been a moderately populous Domesday manor (albeit below average for Berkshire), but the number of tax payers recorded there for the 1327 Lay Subsidy and 1381 Poll Tax gave it a percentile ranking within Berkshire of just 0.11 and 0.13 respectively. However by the 1524 Lay Subsidy this ranking had recovered to 0.56.
