This growth perhaps in part owed something to the fortunes of nearby Newbury, and may have reflected an increase in labourers working in industries such as fulling and tanning mills, parchment making and brick making, all known to have been present at Shaw in the fifteenth or sixteenth centuries. [9] The cartographic evidence suggests that an episode of settlement retraction occurred at Shaw in the post-medieval period. Rocque’s map of 1761 shows rows of buildings along both sides of the eastern part of Church Lane (chosen as the grid reference for this database entry). These buildings had disappeared by the time of the 1808 Ordnance Survey drawing, with the area only being re-developed again in the later twentieth century. Some nineteenth-century growth is also indicated however, as housing expanded further southwards along Shaw Road from the older focus at the northern end near Shaw Bridge. Suggested by G. Copley.

name: Sheffield
e179_last: 1671 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: No physical evidence for a medieval village at this site is known from either earthworks or aerial photographs. Much of the modern landscape in the vicinity is now occupied by water-filled former gravel pits.
description_full: No physical evidence for a medieval village at this site is known from either earthworks or aerial photographs. Much of the modern landscape in the vicinity is now occupied by water-filled former gravel pits. The historic settlement pattern (as shown on Rocque’s 1761 map and named in more detail by the 6 inch Ordnance Survey first edition) seems to have involved an area by the River Kennet (Sheffield Farm and Sheffield Mill) as well as an area on higher ground further south (including Sheffield Bottom and a number of farms). The NMR and HER entries for this site suggest grid reference near the site of Hosehill Farm, [1] or further south, [2] without an obvious explanation. The site has been plotted at the site of Sheffield Farm for this database. Whether the area near the river has been inspected for earthworks is not clear. Sheffield appears as a vill in Domesday Book – its entry records a mill as well as meadowland and woodland, implying a landholding that stretched from the Kennet to higher ground. The 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment is above average for accepted Berkshire DMVs, and combined with the 31 poll tax payers recorded in 1381 is the main evidence for a lost village. However, the possibility of a dispersed medieval settlement pattern in this area should also be considered. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Malton
e179_last: 1648 March 17 monthly assessment for Fairfax's army
description_snippet: The only visible remains at the site are those of a double moated site. A church was recorded from the early thirteenth century, demolished in the early sixteenth century, but then partially rebuilt until final demolition in the eighteenth century.  While there are no physical remains of the village, the documentary evidence does suggest its presence.
description_full: The only visible remains at the site are those of a double moated site. A church was recorded from the early thirteenth century, demolished in the early sixteenth century, but then partially rebuilt until final demolition in the eighteenth century. [1] While there are no physical remains of the village, the documentary evidence does suggest its presence. Malton was not mentioned separately from the village of Orwell until 1200 AD. [2] It continued to be taxed with Orwell in the fourteenth and sixteenth-century tax records which make its true size difficult to plot. In 1463 only 3 residents were recorded at Malton. [1] Malton Farm dates from the fifteenth century and was remodeled between 1509-1511. [3] A date of fifteenth to sixteenth century for desertion would seem apt. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Nosterfield
e179_last: 1283 Jan 20 x Feb 28 thirtieth
description_snippet: There is little evidence to support the existence of the village of Nosterfield. There are no physical remains visible in the area. Field walking by the Havervill and District Archaeological Group located a concentration of pottery close to the site which may suggest some settlement nearby.
description_full: There is little evidence to support the existence of the village of Nosterfield. There are no physical remains visible in the area. Field walking by the Havervill and District Archaeological Group located a concentration of pottery close to the site which may suggest some settlement nearby. [1] To the south of the area is Nosterfield End which may indicate the location of a former settlement, but could also indicate the location of another lost hamlet, Northo. [1, 2] It was mentioned in the appendix in the Domesday Book. [2] It is next mentioned from the 1130s onwards. [3] There is only a single reference to the settlement on the National Records dating from 1283. All the evidence points towards a small hamlet, but no evidence of a sizable settlement. As a whole, the parish of Shudy Camps in which it is located never had many houses, with only 40 recorded from c. 1660s to the early nineteenth century. [3]. It is also possible that Nosterfield was not long lived. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Shingay
e179_last: 1673 March 29 grant of £1,238,750 for supply of extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: Today there are still earthworks visible in the aerial photography, including a substantial moat visible in the surrounding fields, predominantly to the east and west, as well as ridge and furrow.. The village site stood next to the Preceptory of Knights Hospitaller, a large moated enclosure.
description_full: Today there are still earthworks visible in the aerial photography, including a substantial moat visible in the surrounding fields, predominantly to the east and west, as well as ridge and furrow. [1]. The village site stood next to the Preceptory of Knights Hospitaller, a large moated enclosure. Although the Victoria County History records the village as east of the Preceptory there are clear earthworks of at least four tofts and crofts to the west of the moated site. [2] Field survey in 1991 has recorded the complexity of the associated earthworks for the site. [3, 4] The village is first mentioned in 1086 in the Domesday Book, however it was depopulated in the early fifteenth century. [5] The site was one of the earliest preceptories of the Order of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem and dates from 1144 AD. The preceptors carried out a thorough policy of enclosure and by 1452 the village had been mostly cleared and reduced to only a few houses. [6, 7] In June 1381 there was a peasant uprising which badly damaged many of the buildings and required that the site be rebuilt. In 1452 there is mention that ‘the preceptor possessed crofts in which once were houses’. [6] In 1517 there are records of enclosure having taken place in 1504. [8] In April of 1540, the Preceptory was dissolved, however the chapel remained in use, and was still standing in 1643. It was finally demolished in 1697. [6] In the earlier stages of its development, Shingay seems to have had a sizable population, but one that was always overshadowed and dependant on the Preceptory. In the fourteenth-century tax records, the settlement was recorded with Wendy, and we see a healthy population. The decline in the fifteenth century is clear by the sixteenth century with a total range of 8-10 people taxed in 1524-25 and 6 households recorded in 1563. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Werateworde (Wratworth)
description_snippet: The settlement of Werateworde was identified from the Domesday record and at the time of the 1968 Gazetteer was noted as unlocated even though it had been identified by the Place-name survey as the settlement of Wratworth, which later becomes known as Ratford.
description_full: The settlement of Werateworde was identified from the Domesday record and at the time of the 1968 Gazetteer was noted as unlocated even though it had been identified by the Place-name survey as the settlement of Wratworth, which later becomes known as Ratford. [1] The location of the settlement is suggested by a Ratford Close recorded in 1638, near to the present Cobbs Wood and this is where the locator has been placed. [2] The only evidence in this area is a moated site. [2] Field walking to the north of Cobbs Wood has produced evidence of medieval pottery and possible chalk building structures. [3] Another suggestion has placed the location to the south of the parish of Orwell. [4] Wratworth is recorded at Domesday with a minimum population of 32 but had disappeared from the records by 1279 with the lands becoming part of Wimpole. [2, 5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Whitwell
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: No remains of the settlement can be seen on the ground. A pre-enclosure map shows closes to the south of a track.  The area has been heavily ploughed. Apart from at Domesday, Whitwell has always been taxed and mentioned with the settlement at Barton so it is hard to gauge the true population size.  It would seem never to have been a large settlement.
description_full: No remains of the settlement can be seen on the ground. A pre-enclosure map shows closes to the south of a track. [1] The area has been heavily ploughed. Apart from at Domesday, Whitwell has always been taxed and mentioned with the settlement at Barton so it is hard to gauge the true population size. [2] It would seem never to have been a large settlement. Some sources suggest a decline in the fourteenth century when its records are merged with those of Barton. [3, 4] All the fields of the hamlet were engrossed into a single farm unit in the seventeenth century and this is probably the stage at which depopulation was complete. [2] There is a second deserted village named Whitwell in Cambridgeshire in Wimpole parish, which does not appear on the 1968 Gazetteer. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Wimpole
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: A number of areas in the parkland of Wimpole Hall reveal evidence of earthworks of settlement and field systems. These seem to suggest polyfocal settlement in the area. The highest concentration of earthworks is found to the north and south of the church, running along a north-south hollow way. These earthworks have been surveyed on a number of occasions with different interpretations.
description_full: A number of areas in the parkland of Wimpole Hall reveal evidence of earthworks of settlement and field systems. These seem to suggest polyfocal settlement in the area. The highest concentration of earthworks is found to the north and south of the church, running along a north-south hollow way. These earthworks have been surveyed on a number of occasions with different interpretations. [1, 2, 3] The development of the park in the eighteenth and nineteenth century has obscured much of the earthworks. [1] A map by Benjamin Hare of the hall and park in 1638 shows houses close to the church and to the south of the hall. There are also other scatters of houses in other areas of the park. In total there are five clusters of houses around three main routeways. [2] Some of the areas have suffered damage from ploughing, but have produced eleventh-century and later pottery. [2] Since the late 1990s the Cambridge Archaeology Field Group have been undertaking fieldwork and excavations in Wimpole Park, and in 2013 latterly a HLF funded project – Wimpole: silent voices and deserted homes – has been investigating houses seen on the 1638 map. [4] Wimpole is mentioned in Domesday and had a sizable population in the fourteenth-century taxation documents. There was a decline in population by the sixteenth century, but there were still 36 households recorded in 1563. The map of 1638 shows that there was still a sizable population and that the settlements were gradually depopulated in the eighteenth century when the park was laid out. The current settlement at New Wimpole is an estate village outside the park created in the nineteenth century. [5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Brereton
e179_last: 1678 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: No remains of settlement are visible at the site. The church of St Oswald is situated next to Brereton Hall and could possibly have formed part of an early manorial core to the settlement. The extant hall is Elizabethan in date (1585) and the church is perpendicular in style.
description_full: No remains of settlement are visible at the site. The church of St Oswald is situated next to Brereton Hall and could possibly have formed part of an early manorial core to the settlement. The extant hall is Elizabethan in date (1585) and the church is perpendicular in style. [1] However the dispersed nature of settlement in this region, and the number of hamlets within the parish may indicate that no nucleated settlement was located around this core. A settlement at Brereton Green, to the south west of the hall and church appears on the Tithe Map of 1848 and there is now a sizable settlement here. Cheshire HER have suggested a settlement may have been moved to Brereton Green with improvements and parking at the hall. [2] A manor is recorded at Domesday with a medium-sized population, but the lack of fourteenth-century tax records for Cheshire does prove elusive in tracking any changes to this settlement. There is a single appearance on the E179 lists for the Clerical Poll Tax of 1379, then again in the E179 mid-sixteenth century when Cheshire was taxed with the rest of the country for the first time. It then appears regularly through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, but there is no indication of the size of the settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Cholmondeley
e179_last: 1678 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: No remains of this settlement are visible. The isolated chapel in Cholmondeley Park has indicated the existence of a possible settlement along with scant documentary evidence. The extant chapel has evidence of fifteenth-century material, although a chapel was documented from 1285.  A field visit in 1964 found no sign of visible remains in the area.
description_full: No remains of this settlement are visible. The isolated chapel in Cholmondeley Park has indicated the existence of a possible settlement along with scant documentary evidence. The extant chapel has evidence of fifteenth-century material, although a chapel was documented from 1285. [1] A field visit in 1964 found no sign of visible remains in the area. [2] The extensive formal gardens were created in 1688 by Lecocke and the informal park was remodelled in 1777. [1] On the Tithe Map of 1824, a number of buildings are located close to the chapel. Originally in this area stood the Elizabethan Hall which was timber framed with a moat. This was later remodelled in stone in the early 1700s with only a small part still standing. [1] This suggests a manorial core of chapel and hall. A manor is recorded at Domesday, but the lack of fourteenth-century tax records for Cheshire does prove elusive in tracking any changes to this settlement. It first appears in the E179 records in 1549 when Cheshire was taxed with the rest of the country for the first time. It then appears regularly through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, but there is no indication of the size of the settlement. Speede’s map of Cheshire from around 1610 records the settlement and church. The centre of the estate moved in the early nineteenth century with the building of Cholmondeley Castle in 1801. [1] The scant documentary evidence, isolated chapel and presence of the old Hall would support suggestions of a village in the vicinity which has disappeared in the landscaping of the parkland in the seventeenth-eighteenth century. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Shocklach
e179_last: 1678 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: This is a complex area of dispersed settlement which includes the Church of St Edith and a motte and bailey castle.  The grid reference given by this website is to the church. The church has Norman features.  There is only a possibility of medieval settlement close to the church, and the castle and manorial centre are located a distance away to the north.
description_full: This is a complex area of dispersed settlement which includes the Church of St Edith and a motte and bailey castle. [1] The grid reference given by this website is to the church. The church has Norman features. [1] There is only a possibility of medieval settlement close to the church, and the castle and manorial centre are located a distance away to the north. No visible remains were identified by a number of field visits, although they had been recorded by the Ordnance Survey in 1965. [2] Areas of ridge and furrow and former field boundaries can be seen, and investigation of aerial photography in 1984 has suggested that gaps in this ridge and furrow may indicate the area of former settlement. [2] A further deserted medieval settlement has been identified at Castletown to the east of the castle site and this could well be the former settlement of Shocklach. However this would not explain the isolated position of the church. No buildings appear close to the church on the Tithe Map of 1838. A manor is recorded at Domesday but with a small population. The lack of fourteenth-century tax records for Cheshire does prove elusive in tracking any changes to this settlement. It first appears in the E179 records in 1549 when Cheshire was taxed with the rest of the country for the first time. It then appears regularly through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries as the township of Church Shocklack, but there is no indication of its size. Castletown does not appear in the documentary evidence lending weight to the possibility that this township may have contained a number of dispersed settlements and no nucleated centre – as is the case in many areas of Cheshire. There is no indication of a possible reason for desertion of this site. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968. A separate record for Castletown will appear on this website in future editions.

name: Carwether
description_snippet: The site of Carwether is located in Bodmin Moor. There may be prehistoric evidence for the origins of the field systems in this area.  There are clear earthworks of the settlement visible on aerial photography. There is evidence for a number of buildings, including poorly preserved longhouses and several outbuildings.  The site itself is approximately one hectare in size, with a track to the south of the settlement.
description_full: The site of Carwether is located in Bodmin Moor. There may be prehistoric evidence for the origins of the field systems in this area. [1] There are clear earthworks of the settlement visible on aerial photography. There is evidence for a number of buildings, including poorly preserved longhouses and several outbuildings. [1] The site itself is approximately one hectare in size, with a track to the south of the settlement. [1] Some of the buildings have associated garden closes. There is a large set of field systems adjoining the village which may reach around forty hectares and may be an integral part of the settlement. There is very little documentary evidence to help plot the population of the site. A post-medieval date for desertion has been suggested. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Garrow
description_snippet: This site lies in one of the most isolated locations in Cornwall. There is evidence of roads, crofts and buildings.  A platform house on the site has been investigated by excavation.  There are approximately five longhouses among the buildings. The remains of the village can be seen on aerial photographs. There is also an associated field system nearby which may have had links to the village.
description_full: This site lies in one of the most isolated locations in Cornwall. There is evidence of roads, crofts and buildings. [1] A platform house on the site has been investigated by excavation. [2] There are approximately five longhouses among the buildings [1]. The remains of the village can be seen on aerial photographs. There is also an associated field system nearby which may have had links to the village. [1] The excavated evidence shows the buildings to be in use between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries. [2] It has been suggested that the settlement after this date reduced to a single farmstead which was abandoned in the nineteenth century. [3] There is no documentary evidence to help plot the fortunes of the settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Lanyon
description_snippet: There are approximately three buildings that have been identified at the site, just to the north of the pointer on the website.  The area is now very mcuh overgrown but the site was excavated in 1964. [1, 2] The rectangular buildings that have been investigated have been dated from the twelfth century.  Occupation lasted until the late fifteenth or sixteenth century.
description_full: There are approximately three buildings that have been identified at the site, just to the north of the pointer on the website. [1] The area is now very mcuh overgrown but the site was excavated in 1964. [1, 2] The rectangular buildings that have been investigated have been dated from the twelfth century. [2] Occupation lasted until the late fifteenth or sixteenth century. [1] In 1390 there is a record of a chapel at Lanyon but this was located close to the present Lanyon Farm suggesting the focus of settlement had shifted northwards by the late fourteenth century. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Porthillie
description_snippet: The site of the village of Porthillie or Porthilly is now hidden by modern farm buildings. The isolated church is positioned on the edge of the Camel Estuary. In the 1968 Gazetteer the settlement was located around another isolated church to the north (SW 932 772), but the HER and NMR record the settlement at this location, next to the church that is known as Porthilly church and therefore this website has used that...
description_full: The site of the village of Porthillie or Porthilly is now hidden by modern farm buildings. The isolated church is positioned on the edge of the Camel Estuary. In the 1968 Gazetteer the settlement was located around another isolated church to the north (SW 932 772), but the HER and NMR record the settlement at this location, next to the church that is known as Porthilly church and therefore this website has used that reference (SX 938 753). [1] No earthworks are visible at the site. Antiquarian writers from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries recorded the settlement increasing in population but it was depopulated well before 1814 due to shifting sands. [2] Records of building remains and stone coffins revealed by shifting sands have also been recorded in the vicinity but may not be directly related to this location. [1] Due to a lack of documentary evidence recording a settlement at the church and the nature of settlement in this region, this site has been classified as a Deserted Hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Temple
description_snippet: Although listed in the 1968 Gazetteer, there is still a settlement at the site. There are some earthworks that are more likely to do with settlement shrinkage rather than desertion.  The settlement is first recorded in 1200 and named after a settlement of the Knights Templar.  A chapel is recorded as having been built in the twelfth century by the Templars and this is mentioned on a number of occasions.
description_full: Although listed in the 1968 Gazetteer, there is still a settlement at the site. There are some earthworks that are more likely to do with settlement shrinkage rather than desertion. [1] The settlement is first recorded in 1200 and named after a settlement of the Knights Templar. [2] A chapel is recorded as having been built in the twelfth century by the Templars and this is mentioned on a number of occasions. [3] It is unlikely that there was ever a large establishment at the site as the properties of the Templars in Cornwall were relatively poor, and this is more likely a mere property that belonged to the order. With the suppression of the Templars in the early fourteenth century it passed to the Hospitallers, and the chapel and parish continued to be mentioned but the status is indeterminate. [3] There is the possibility that there was never a large settlement at this spot but just an administrative centre with a parish of scattered settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Tresibbet
description_snippet: The village of Tresibbet lies in two sections separated by a hollow way, with a surrounding field system that is at least eight hectares in size, which is thought to have prehistoric origins.  The first section of the village contains around six buildings, three of which have been identified as longhouses.  The second section is a cluster of buildings, with at least two longhouses.
description_full: The village of Tresibbet lies in two sections separated by a hollow way, with a surrounding field system that is at least eight hectares in size, which is thought to have prehistoric origins. [1] The first section of the village contains around six buildings, three of which have been identified as longhouses. [1] The second section is a cluster of buildings, with at least two longhouses. [1] In between these two clusters is located a single longhouse. [2] The location for the settlement in the 1968 Gazetteer (SX 205 750) is incorrect and the monument lies to the north at SX 200 759 which is used by this site. One of the buildings seems to continue in use in the post-medieval period and includes a large stone bread oven. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Treworld
description_snippet: The site of Treworld lies on a steep slope to the south-east of the present hamlet of Treworld. The grid reference for this site has been amended from the original 1968 location (SX 121 905) to correspond to the area of the excavations (SX 123 903). There are no visible remains present and the site has been ploughed.  Excavations in 1963 revealed two phases of occupation at the site.
description_full: The site of Treworld lies on a steep slope to the south-east of the present hamlet of Treworld. The grid reference for this site has been amended from the original 1968 location (SX 121 905) to correspond to the area of the excavations (SX 123 903). There are no visible remains present and the site has been ploughed. [1] Excavations in 1963 revealed two phases of occupation at the site. [2] Initial phases show a succession of turf houses dated between the ninth and twelfth century. These were gradually replaced by two structures, which in the thirteenth century were replaced by stone longhouses. In turn one of these changed use to a barn. [2] These buildings were associated with an enclosed yard. Both houses show clear evidence for subdivision. It is thought these were short lived and the site was abandoned by the fourteenth century. [2] This has been classed as a Deserted Hamlet as there is evidence from the earlier phases of more than one household, although by the thirteenth century it is clearly just a farmstead. There are no documentary references to the settlement so it is difficult to estimate the nature of the population, and it is possible that the name Treworld is a misnomer, as there could have been a medieval hamlet at the present-day settlement to the north-west. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Trewortha
description_snippet: The site of Trewortha has extensive earthworks and building outlines that still can be seen. The grid reference used by this website (SX 226 760) is not the original (SX 239 750) as this was located in error to the south-east. This is the site of one of the earliest excavations of a deserted medieval settlement as it was investigated between 1891-2 by Rev. S. Baring Gould.
description_full: The site of Trewortha has extensive earthworks and building outlines that still can be seen. The grid reference used by this website (SX 226 760) is not the original (SX 239 750) as this was located in error to the south-east. This is the site of one of the earliest excavations of a deserted medieval settlement as it was investigated between 1891-2 by Rev. S. Baring Gould. [1, 2] The site itself had nine or ten oblong buildings and several prehistoric hut circles. The settlement is located on an east facing slope and with associated fields and fits into a larger area of prehistoric field systems and hut circles. [3] The buildings are located along a north-west to south-east street, and it appears to include at least four longhouses and associated outbuildings. All the longhouses run east-west. From the initial excavation, the only suggested date for the site was post-Roman conquest. [2] The few sherds of pottery that could be located in the 1950s were clearly medieval in date and similar to the types excavated at Great Beere in Devon. [4] The date suggested for the occupation of this site is the twelfth century. There has been a lot of damage on the site to the remains from rainfall, cattle and peat cutting, however it is still highly visible from the air. [5] With no further documentary or archaeological evidence it is difficult to plot the development of the site. We have classed the settlement as a Deserted Hamlet due to the likelihood that not more than four households occupied the site at any one time. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Little Brampton
description_snippet: The site is to the northeast of Brampton on the eastern bank of the River Irthing. There is no indication of the name Little Brampton. The isolated church of St Martin has a complex history, with documentary evidence from 1189 onwards..The church is located in the northern most corner of Brampton Old Church Roman fort, and whilst there have been excavations in the area to investigate the Roman period, there is no...
description_full: The site is to the northeast of Brampton on the eastern bank of the River Irthing. There is no indication of the name Little Brampton. The isolated church of St Martin has a complex history, with documentary evidence from 1189 onwards. [1].The church is located in the northern most corner of Brampton Old Church Roman fort, and whilst there have been excavations in the area to investigate the Roman period, there is no evidence for Medieval occupation. Old Church Farm lies to the east of the church, and it is suggested it has Medieval masonry of perhaps a defensive quality. [2] The modern market town of Brampton is located one mile away from the church on the main road between Carlisle and Newcastle, and market grants of 1252 suggest this was the concentration of settlement by this period. [3, 4] Brampton is recorded in the fourteenth-century taxation documents but they refer to this market town. It is unclear if there was ever any sizable settlement located at the church. Further research may uncover more material but at this stage the isolated church does not suggest extensive settlement at this location. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Carlatton

description_full: Carlatton is a place-name that appears at a number of locations, attached to farms and a mill. The grid reference given in the 1968 Gazetteer (NY 530 530) is to the north of this concentration, and the settlement, if it did exist was probably further south (NY 526 518). The grid reference used here has been changed to reflect this. The local farmer in this area has uncovered remains of a stone church or chapel with burials. [1] A decorated grave stone dating from 1344 was recorded in 1907. [2] No features are visible on the aerial photographs. The first place-name evidence for Carlatton appears in the mid-twelfth century. [3] It appears in the taxation records at various points in the fourteenth century and a church is recorded in 1291. The last record on E179 is in 1380 which may indicate a date for the decline of the population. No vicar is recorded after 1380. [4] Carlatton does appear in the census as a hamlet – but its small population reflects the surrounding dispersed farmsteads. There are no clear physical remains of a nucleated settlement. The records indicate a dispersed settlement. It is doubtful whether a truly large settlement ever existed and so the site for the time being is classed as a deserted hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Nether Denton
e179_last: 1662 May 19 hearth tax
description_snippet: The church and vicarage at Nether Denton lie within the remains of a Roman fort. The church was built between 1868-70 and nothing apart from one sculpture remains of the original church.  The Old Vicarage shows evidence of once being a bastle (defended house).  Nether Denton does not appear in the documentary evidence for tax records from the fourteenth or sixteenth countries, although there is a record for Denton.
description_full: The church and vicarage at Nether Denton lie within the remains of a Roman fort. The church was built between 1868-70 and nothing apart from one sculpture remains of the original church. [1] The Old Vicarage shows evidence of once being a bastle (defended house). [1] Nether Denton does not appear in the documentary evidence for tax records from the fourteenth or sixteenth countries, although there is a record for Denton. The Nether Denton place-name only appears from the mid-fifteenth century. [2] Upper Denton is located to the west and has its own church which dates from the twelfth century. [1] Denton Hall and Denton Mill are spread over three kilometres to the south west. It is hard to estimate whether there was ever extensive settlement at Nether Denton, or whether the church was serving a dispersed community over this area. As such it is currently classed as a doubtful DMV. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Great Easby
description_snippet: A cluster of three farm complexes currently exists at Great Easby. Within the 1968 Gazetteer the grid references for settlements at both Great and Little Easby are given as rough estimates, and also at the same location. It is perhaps more likely that Great Easby was located closer to the farm complexes and the grid reference has been altered to reflect this.
description_full: A cluster of three farm complexes currently exists at Great Easby. Within the 1968 Gazetteer the grid references for settlements at both Great and Little Easby are given as rough estimates, and also at the same location. It is perhaps more likely that Great Easby was located closer to the farm complexes and the grid reference has been altered to reflect this. However it is unclear why a settlement has been suggested here. There is very little documentary evidence for settlement in the area, and none specifically for Great Easby until the late sixteenth century, with references to just Easby from the late fourteenth century. [1] No physical evidence is visible on the ground. Ford’s map of 1839 shows simply a settlement at Easby (roughly the position of Great Easby), but other earlier maps show no settlement at all in this area. Whether there was any great concentration of activity at this locale is difficult to ascertain so currently it is listed as doubtful. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Easton
e179_last: 1380 April 4 clerical tenth and poll tax from York province
description_snippet: A chapel was recorded in 1884 but nothing remains in the area now. description_full: A chapel was recorded in 1884 but nothing remains in the area now. [1] The site currently has a large farm complex at the centre, and there are faint areas of ridge and furrow in the vicinity. The area is now known as Chapeltown. Easton is currently located to the north of this area and contains a small scatter of houses. The HER reference places the shrunken settlement at Chapeltown. Easton appears in the Lay Subsidy of 1336 as the subsidiary settlement to Solport. It continues to appear during the fourteenth century in the taxation documents then disappears from the record suggesting either an early desertion or that the settlement amounted to no more than a small cluster of buildings. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Edmond Castle
description_snippet: Edmond Castle is now the site of Hayton Hall, an eighteenth-century house, which was much altered in the nineteenth century.  The hall is set within parkland, and it was here that in the eighteenth century a hamlet consisting of at least four houses was demolished.  The four houses were positioned along a road leading from the old stable block at Hayton Hall, stretching past Home Pond to the edge of the park.
description_full: Edmond Castle is now the site of Hayton Hall, an eighteenth-century house, which was much altered in the nineteenth century. [1] The hall is set within parkland, and it was here that in the eighteenth century a hamlet consisting of at least four houses was demolished. [2] The four houses were positioned along a road leading from the old stable block at Hayton Hall, stretching past Home Pond to the edge of the park. [2] Within the parish registers at Hayton, the local church, baptisms, marriages and burials recorded were from 1628 onwards. The majority of these refer to the Graham family of Hayton Hall, but a small number of other families appear, linked through to the last occupants of those four houses demolished in the eighteenth century. It has also been suggested that Edmond Castle was a peel tower, and there is a possibility that part of the structure is hidden within the present Hayton Hall, but no physical evidence of this has been revealed. [2] The settlement does not appear in any taxation documentation. From the available evidence it would suggest that the settlement was never larger than a hamlet and may just have been in existence from the seventeenth century onwards. The place-name evidence appears from the seventeenth century. [3] If a peel tower had existed there is no evidence of an associated settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Liddel
e179_last: 1357 April 17 x May 5 fifteenth and tenth
description_snippet: Liddel Strength is the location of a motte and bailey castle that has well preserved earthworks. The suggested site of the settlement is in the shadow of these earthworks; however no settlement features are visible from the air. The site of the motte and bailey castle is a Scheduled Ancient Monument and the scheduling would include any evidence of settlement.
description_full: Liddel Strength is the location of a motte and bailey castle that has well preserved earthworks. The suggested site of the settlement is in the shadow of these earthworks; however no settlement features are visible from the air. The site of the motte and bailey castle is a Scheduled Ancient Monument and the scheduling would include any evidence of settlement. The Liddel barony was created in the twelfth century and as it was on the English/Scottish border it came under constant attack. [1] Attacks in 1300 led to the burning of settlements and the death of inhabitants. [1] The first documentary references to the castle appear in 1174, however it disappears from the record in 1399. [2] By 1281-2 the references are to the ‘site of the castle’ and the fourteenth-century references are to a Pele. [2] It remains unclear if there was actually a settlement associated with the castle. A market and fair were granted in 1267. [3] Taxation records exist throughout the early-fourteenth century but nothing later than 1357 suggesting that no more than a small hamlet may have existed close to the castle throughout its period of occupation, but disappeared when the castle went out of use. All documentary references to the castle are concerned with the buildings and structures at the castle and make no mention of any associated settlement. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Alkmonton
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The grid reference for this site (SK 193 375) is different than the one published in the 1968 Gazetteer (SK 186 386). description_full: The grid reference for this site (SK 193 375) is different than the one published in the 1968 Gazetteer (SK 186 386). There are clear earthworks visible at the site, located to the south of modern day Alkmonton, which was a nineteenth-century creation. It is suggested that the earthworks reflect the entirety of the original medieval village core. [1] There are four main streets running from a central green area. A number of house platforms are also visible, and a site of a chapel has been suggested. [2] The site of Alkmonton was first mentioned in the Domesday Book in 1086, with at least fifteen individuals recorded. A hospital for female lepers was founded in 1100. [3] The settlement paid a reasonably high amount for the 1334 Lay Subsidy. The hospital was re-founded in 1406 as it seems it had suffered from the decrease in leprosy. [3] The records for the later taxations do not survive. The VCH records that the hospital and chapel were ‘swept away’ during the reign of Edward VI. [3] In the 1664 Hearth Tax a total of 12 buildings are listed but these may be across a wide area. [4] It is unclear as to whether the settlement was larger than the hospital and its residents in the later periods of its history. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Arleston
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The site is a farm and the remains of the village are no longer visible. Remains had previously been seen in some aerial photographs and ploughing of the site had revealed evidence of buildings and twelfth to thirteenth-century pottery. [1, 2] There is a suggestion that the present farm was the original chapel of the village which was remodelled into a house in the sixteenth century.
description_full: The site is a farm and the remains of the village are no longer visible. Remains had previously been seen in some aerial photographs and ploughing of the site had revealed evidence of buildings and twelfth to thirteenth-century pottery. [1, 2] There is a suggestion that the present farm was the original chapel of the village which was remodelled into a house in the sixteenth century. [3] Arleston appears in the Domesday Book and the 1334 Lay Subsidy records. These documentary sources show that there were at least seven people at the time of the Domesday, and the 1334 tax is an average amount for the area. There is very limited survival of later taxation documents which makes a true assessment of this settlement difficult, and it may never have been very sizable. There are seven buildings listed along with Sinfin in the 1664 Hearth Tax representing buildings across a wide landscape. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Ashe
description_snippet: Slight earthworks of the settlement are visible, and extensive earthworks of field systems can be seen. The grid reference used here is SK 257 333 around modern Ash Farm. name: Ault Hucknall
e179_last: 1661 July 8 free and voluntary present
description_snippet: An isolated church at Ault Hucknall has claims to be the centre of a settlement. In some accounts a village named Griff was located in the vicinity. However this has been dismissed and it is suggested the church was used by a number of surrounding hamlets.  Earthworks visible in the area are most likely caused by mining subsidence.
description_full: An isolated church at Ault Hucknall has claims to be the centre of a settlement. In some accounts a village named Griff was located in the vicinity. However this has been dismissed and it is suggested the church was used by a number of surrounding hamlets. [1] Earthworks visible in the area are most likely caused by mining subsidence. [1] Local residents had reported building foundations being uncovered in the woods but no remains are visible. [1] There is very limited documentary evidence for the site. Ault Hucknall is mentioned in the 1291 tax and the 1563 Diocesan Returns. There is a church that contains elements which have been dated to the eleventh century onwards. [2] The only other record of the settlement is from Diocesan Returns of 1563, and there are no fourteenth or sixteenth-century tax records. This would support the idea that the church has always remained isolated, serving a number of surrounding settlements but was never the focus of settlement itself. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Barton Blount
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The site of Barton Blount was excavated in the late 1960s by Guy Beresford due to the threat from deep ploughing.  This has effectively destroyed the archaeology that was both above and below the surface across a large part of the site.  The settlement lay to the north-east of the hall and church, and spread over a wide area of around 500 metres.
description_full: The site of Barton Blount was excavated in the late 1960s by Guy Beresford due to the threat from deep ploughing. [1] This has effectively destroyed the archaeology that was both above and below the surface across a large part of the site. [1] The settlement lay to the north-east of the hall and church, and spread over a wide area of around 500 metres. There are some property boundaries visible on the aerial photographs close to the Hall, and some features can still be seen in the ploughed areas. The excavations found five possible phases of expansion due to the layout and grouping of the site. The date for the occupation of the site is between the tenth and fifteenth century. The excavations completely investigated four crofts, but there are thought to be about forty-three crofts around the settlement. [1] The historical evidence for the settlement is slight. A high population is recorded at Domesday with a minimum number of 31 people in the area, confirming the early date for settlement development from the archaeological record. It appears in the Lay Subsidy of 1334, but then poor survival of records mean we do not know the fortunes in later periods. A record of 1536 records four tax payers and shows there had been a dramatic decline. [2] A single household is recorded in 1563. At the time of publication Guy Beresford laid the reason for desertion on climate change however this has been challenged. [2] The evidence from the excavated crofts shows a gradual decline – in three of the crofts desertion occurred between the end of the fourteenth century and early fifteenth century, the remaining croft was not deserted until the late fifteenth century – but these refer to just four out of the forty-three crofts. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Birchill
description_snippet: There are no clear visible remains of the settlement on the ground around Birchill Farm. A hollow way has been reported as running from the farm to the A6020.  At Domesday the settlement is mentioned as a berewick of Ashford. Although the entry records 18 people, these are spread over 13 different places. There are no further mentions of the site in the fourteenth-century taxation records.

name: Bupton
description_snippet: Vague features have been reported between Bupton Farm and Hill Top Farm. These include ridge and furrow and a possible moated site, but no conclusive evidence of building plots.  It was reported that field banks and roads had been visible on aerial photographs from the 1940s but had been destroyed by ploughing by the 1970s.  There is little documentary evidence for this settlement.

[3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Callow
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: Remains of the village can be seen on aerial photographs. The grid reference used by the website is SK 267 520 rather than the original one of 1968 (SK 257 512). The one used is located next to Callow Hall and the location of the scheduled remains of the village.
description_full: Remains of the village can be seen on aerial photographs. The grid reference used by the website is SK 267 520 rather than the original one of 1968 (SK 257 512). The one used is located next to Callow Hall and the location of the scheduled remains of the village. The aerial photographs show the moat around Callow Hall, and a number of north-south hollow ways that have enclosures on either side – with at least 10 crofts identified. [1] At Domesday it is mentioned as an outlier of the manor of Wirksworth along with six others – the total population for these outliers is 49 but there is no indication of how this population is distributed. [2] The 1344 Lay Subsidy amount is average, and later records are scarce. It is mentioned in documents into the thirteenth century and is a parish. The later Census shows the parish still well occupied, there are still four properties in the area. The point at which the crofts seen in the aerial photographs were abandoned is unknown. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Catton
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: No clear visible remains have been seen at the site. In 1987 a field survey by the South Derbyshire Archaeological Survey identified three platforms that had been badly damaged although no clear interpretation of these has been given.  The documentary sources include a Domesday reference which suggests around sixteen people. Then there are tax returns for 1291, 1334 and 1524 paying average amounts.
description_full: No clear visible remains have been seen at the site. In 1987 a field survey by the South Derbyshire Archaeological Survey identified three platforms that had been badly damaged although no clear interpretation of these has been given. [1] The documentary sources include a Domesday reference which suggests around sixteen people. Then there are tax returns for 1291, 1334 and 1524 paying average amounts. On the Taxatio of 1291 a chapel is recorded at Catton. [2] This was served by the vicar of Croxall from Norman times. In 1100 Nigel de Albini had granted a church at Catton to the Priory of Tutbury. A Norman font is also present. [3] The building, in the grounds of Catton Hall, was destroyed in 1750 and subsequently rebuilt. [2] The current Catton Hall was built in 1745. [4] It is possible that any settlement evidence was destroyed with emparking activity with this new phase of hall construction. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Chatsworth
e179_last: 1449 Feb 12 x April 1 half a fifteenth and tenth
description_snippet: Chatsworth is today the family seat of the Dukes of Devonshire and famous for its spectacular country house. A lost village of Chatsworth also sat in this area, and this has disappeared with the creation of the house and park, which also affected a number of other settlements in the area.
description_full: Chatsworth is today the family seat of the Dukes of Devonshire and famous for its spectacular country house. A lost village of Chatsworth also sat in this area, and this has disappeared with the creation of the house and park, which also affected a number of other settlements in the area. [1] Staxton’s map of 1577 showed the settlement located on the east bank of the River Derwent but field investigation has found no trace. [2] Conflicting with the map evidence, records of 1448/49 list Chatsworth as ‘devastated and laid waste’. It has also been suggested that the medieval Hall was standing in the 1440s and that a deer park was also created at this point. [3] A survey in the area north of the house has revealed post-medieval features but none securely dated to the medieval period. [3] A map by Senior in 1617 shows only a mill, a grand house and out buildings. [3] There is a mentioned in Domesday Book along with Langley but only seven individuals are recorded. Its absence from the 1334 Lay Subsidy is unexplained, but maybe Chatsworth was always a small settlement. Free tenements are recorded in the village in 1431. [1] The house and parkland were remodelled in the late seventeenth century and it may be at this stage the settlement disappears. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Derwent
e179_last: 1662 May 19 hearth tax
description_snippet: In essence this is not a truly deserted medieval village as it was not abandoned until the 1940s, when the settlement was flooded with the creation of Lady Bower Reservoir. In years of low rainfall remains of buildings can be seen. Excavation in 1990 and 1991 revealed a piece of a pre-Conquest stone cross shaft that had been reused in a nineteenth-century cottage as part of a fireplace surround.

Excavation in 1990 and 1991 revealed a piece of a pre-Conquest stone cross shaft that had been reused in a nineteenth-century cottage as part of a fireplace surround. [1] Derwent is mentioned in 1215, and there are a few records after this. It does not appear in the tax records, however it does appear in the later Hearth Tax and Census Records. The plan of the settlement can be clearly seen on the first edition Ordnance Survey maps published in 1880. Here it was recorded as Derwent Chapel. A church was present, and also recorded was the site of an earlier chapel. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Drakelow

There is a 1334 tax record for the site and on the E179 database it appears regularly into the seventeenth century.
description_full: The site of this settlement was destroyed with the construction of a power station. The place-name evidence for this settlement begins in 942 and continues regularly into the thirteenth century. [1] It is recorded at Domesday with a minimum of six people. A chapel is recorded in 1185. [2] There is a 1334 tax record for the site and on the E179 database it appears regularly into the seventeenth century. By the nineteenth century only Drakelow Hall and Drakelow Mill exist in a landscaped park, and this may indicate what happened to the settlement as the area was emparked. By the 1930s the Hall had been demolished, and by the 1950s the parkland was being developed. Only a small area of the park and the stable block are still visible on the aerial photographs. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Eaton on Dove

No clear evidence of medieval settlement can be seen. At Domesday it is a manor with a minimum of 10 people. In 1334 it pays an average amount of subsidy for the area.
description_full: The grid reference used here (SK 107 361) is not the one on the 1968 Gazetteer (SK 118 363).The site is located to the east of Eaton Wood, in the area where Eaton Hall once stood. No clear evidence of medieval settlement can be seen. At Domesday it is a manor with a minimum of 10 people. In 1334 it pays an average amount of subsidy for the area. Perhaps this suggests a reducing population before this date. The Hall is thought to have dated to the sixteenth century, but was in ruins by 1789 and had been demolished by 1817. [1] The site of Eaton Hall is marked on the first edition the Ordnance Survey map of 1879. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Eaton, Cold
parish_historic: Alsop en le Dale and Eaton
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll

name: Foremark
e179_last: 1663 July 27 four subsidies
description_snippet: A hollow way and ditch have been identified from aerial photography but dense vegetation means they are no longer visible.  The church is still standing and the area is occupied by Foremark Hall. The current church on the site was built in 1662, but was probably on the site of the ruinous chapel that was mentioned from 1271.  The current hall is an eighteenth-century building on the site of an older one.
description_full: A hollow way and ditch have been identified from aerial photography but dense vegetation means they are no longer visible. [1] The church is still standing and the area is occupied by Foremark Hall. The current church on the site was built in 1662, but was probably on the site of the ruinous chapel that was mentioned from 1271. [2] The current hall is an eighteenth-century building on the site of an older one. There is a possibility that the chapel and hall signify the manorial core of the medieval settlement. The area around the two has been landscaped as parkland in the eighteenth century. [3] Foremark is recorded in Domesday as a manor with a minimum of eight people. The settlement is taxed in 1334 and in 1524 and perhaps depopulation occurs after this date, and the ruinous state of the church can be attributed to this. There are five buildings listedin the 1662 Hearth Tax. [4] The census of 1841 records eight inhabited houses and these may form the focus for the settlement to the north-east of the hall. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Gratton
e179_last: 1662 May 19 hearth tax
description_snippet: There are no visible earthworks on the ground, although faint traces have been seen at this location and to the south-east at Dale End in older aerial photographs. There is no consensus as to whether there was substantial medieval settlement in the area.  A chapel is recorded in the twelfth century but no remains are visible.  Domesday records Gratton as a manor with a minimum of six people.
description_full: There are no visible earthworks on the ground, although faint traces have been seen at this location and to the south-east at Dale End in older aerial photographs. There is no consensus as to whether there was substantial medieval settlement in the area. [1] A chapel is recorded in the twelfth century but no remains are visible. [1] Domesday records Gratton as a manor with a minimum of six people. It does not appear in the fourteenth or sixteenth-century taxations, but in the Hearth Tax of 1670 there are 11 buildings recorded. [2] It is possible that this was never a large settlement. Wrightman suggests that the village is not depopulated, but instead the population relocated and moved to Dale End. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Nether Haddon
e179_last: 1606 May 17 six fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The earthworks of the settlement and field system can be seen to the west and south of Haddon Hall. The grid reference used here (SK 230 663) has been refined since the 1968 Gazetteer (SK 235 665) to locate it more accurately at the settlement remains. A hollow way is visible running south-east to north-west following the line of the A6.
description_full: The earthworks of the settlement and field system can be seen to the west and south of Haddon Hall. The grid reference used here (SK 230 663) has been refined since the 1968 Gazetteer (SK 235 665) to locate it more accurately at the settlement remains. A hollow way is visible running south-east to north-west following the line of the A6. This branches off in a number of directions and a number of building platforms and enclosures can be seen in this area. Domesday Book includes Haddon as an outlier of the manor of Bakewell along with a number of others so it is impossible to know how many people are recorded here. The first mention of the site as Nether Haddon is in the mid-thirteenth century, and the smaller settlement of Over Haddon is refered to at this point as well. [1] Haddon though existed before this point. In the twelfth century there is record of settlement, church and fortified manor. [2] It is taxed in 1334, and it appears in the E179 database through the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries but there are no records after the first decade of the seventeenth century. Wrightmen notes that by 1431 there was a single tenant at Nether Haddon. [1] The Scheduled Monument Record for this settlement suggests that it may have been depopulated earlier when a deer park was created in 1330. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Harthill
e179_last: 1606 May 17 six fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The grid reference used by this website (SK 229 647) is different to the 1968 Gazetteer (SK 230 246) as this was located in error. This site of Harthill now lies beneath a seventeenth-century farm house (Harthill Hall) and park land. No earthworks have been spotted and these probably suffered during emparking.
description_full: The grid reference used by this website (SK 229 647) is different to the 1968 Gazetteer (SK 230 246) as this was located in error. This site of Harthill now lies beneath a seventeenth-century farm house (Harthill Hall) and park land. No earthworks have been spotted and these probably suffered during emparking. Harthill was recorded as two separate manors in Domesday and recorded in 1334 with the neighbouring settlement of Winster. The village had disappeared by 1577 as Saxton’s map only shows Harthill Hall with a park. [1] There is little other evidence for the settlement and Wrightman described it as ‘a classic example... of the disappearance through imparking of a small village’. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hazlebadge
description_snippet: There are no clear distinguishable earthworks associated with medieval settlement in this location. Evidence of field systems has been seen, and these features run to the south, but they are very patchy.  There has been a great deal of lead mining in the area which may hide some of the features. This site has very little documentary evidence. There is only a taxation amount for the 1334 Lay Subsidy.
description_full: There are no clear distinguishable earthworks associated with medieval settlement in this location. Evidence of field systems has been seen, and these features run to the south, but they are very patchy. [1] There has been a great deal of lead mining in the area which may hide some of the features. This site has very little documentary evidence. There is only a taxation amount for the 1334 Lay Subsidy. The generally poor survival of documents for Derbyshire may contribute to its absence. The 1334 figure is above average for the area. It does appear through the fourteenth-sixteenth centuries on the E179 database. Wrightman suggests that by 1577 the focus of settlement had moved to Bradwell. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hoon
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: A modern farm is situated at the centre of this site. There are some possible earthworks that can still be seen on aerial photography to the north of the farm, which may represent a hollow way. The place-name Hoon appears at two other locations to the north and it may be the case that there was never a nucleated settlement at Hoon, but instead a number of dispersed farmsteads.
description_full: A modern farm is situated at the centre of this site. There are some possible earthworks that can still be seen on aerial photography to the north of the farm, which may represent a hollow way. The place-name Hoon appears at two other locations to the north and it may be the case that there was never a nucleated settlement at Hoon, but instead a number of dispersed farmsteads. [1] Hoon is potentially mentioned twice in the Domesday Book – once as an outlier, and once possibly as its own manor, however the attribution of this record to Hoon is debated. As such the high number of people recorded at Domesday is not a true reflection of the settlement. In 1334 there is a below average subsidy and by 1525 only three people paid the subsidy. In the 164 Hearth Tax a total of three hearths are recored but no indication of the number of buildings. [2] This evidence would support the suggested dispersed settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hungrey Bentley
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: Earthworks and cropmarks are still visible, which show evidence of several enclosures and hollow ways. An east-west hollow way can be seen to the west of the present farm with enclosures to the north and south. This turns south and a number of enclosures are situated along a north-south hollow way.
description_full: Earthworks and cropmarks are still visible, which show evidence of several enclosures and hollow ways. An east-west hollow way can be seen to the west of the present farm with enclosures to the north and south. This turns south and a number of enclosures are situated along a north-south hollow way. Close to the junction of these two hollow ways there appears to be a later enclosure which overlies the neat line of original enclosures. The 1955 Ordnance Survey map records stone coffins having been found in the area but no further record of these is known. The Domesday record shows that the area was owned by Henry De Ferieres, but is small with no indication of population. It is recorded in the 1334 Lay Subsidy but the lack of late surviving records makes it difficult to plot the fortunes of the settlement. It does appear regularly throughout the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries on the E179 database, so it is difficult to ascertain when the settlement became deserted. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Ireton Parva
e179_last: 1665 Feb 9 royal aid of £2,477,500
description_snippet: Faint linear traces to the north of Ireton Lodge Farm may well be associated with this settlement. No other traces have been seen and it forms part of the extended park of Kedleston Hall. The settlement is primarily recorded as Ireton from the Domesday Book until the late sixteenth century (with a few mentions of Ireton Parva in the early fourteenth century).
description_full: Faint linear traces to the north of Ireton Lodge Farm may well be associated with this settlement. No other traces have been seen and it forms part of the extended park of Kedleston Hall. The settlement is primarily recorded as Ireton from the Domesday Book until the late sixteenth century (with a few mentions of Ireton Parva in the early fourteenth century). [1] It is then recorded as Little Ireton in the seventeenth-century taxation documents. In 1334 it has a below average Lay Subsidy but still has 24 people paying in 1524. The setting out of the parkland around Kedleston Hall began in the 1760s and the village of Kedleston was moved. There is the possibility that a similar fate befell Ireton but there is no documentary evidence to support this. A model farm was constructed in the eighteenth century with the seat of the Iretons having been demolished in 1721. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Kedleston
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The village of Kedleston is now in the parkland surrounding Kedleston Hall. The entire village was moved by Sir Nathaniel Curzon in c. 1760 when he diverted the road away from his house to create the parkland.  The village was located close to the hall and church, and a map from the 1720s shows 13 buildings along the east-west route through the park.  Surveys of the parkland have identified possible house platforms.
description_full: The village of Kedleston is now in the parkland surrounding Kedleston Hall. The entire village was moved by Sir Nathaniel Curzon in c. 1760 when he diverted the road away from his house to create the parkland. [1] The village was located close to the hall and church, and a map from the 1720s shows 13 buildings along the east-west route through the park. [1] Surveys of the parkland have identified possible house platforms. [1] Kedleston is mentioned in Domesday and in the following lay subsidies but appears to have never been that big. It has a below average Lay Subsidy in 1334 and only seven people paid in 1524. In 1664 there are 17 buildings recorded in the Hearth Tax. [2] This is an excellent example of a migrated settlement where the village was moved on one single action. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Kidsley
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: No visible remains are present at the site. Kidsley is mentioned from 1009 and on some occasions is referred to as Kidsleypark.  A deer park was also located in the area. It was mentioned in Domesday as an addition to the margin of the main text. Its true status is unclear but was not a manor but probably an outlier. In the 1334 Lay Subsidy there is a below average amount paid.
description_full: No visible remains are present at the site. Kidsley is mentioned from 1009 and on some occasions is referred to as Kidsleypark. [1] A deer park was also located in the area. It was mentioned in Domesday as an addition to the margin of the main text. Its true status is unclear but was not a manor but probably an outlier. In the 1334 Lay Subsidy there is a below average amount paid. On the E179 database there are records of the settlement up to 1401, then a gap until it reappears in the sixteenth century. This may perhaps suggest that the settlement disappeared in the intervening period, to reappear as the scattered farms that are present today. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Lee
e179_last: 1534 Nov 3 x Dec 18 subsidy
description_snippet: Earthwork evidence of buildings, enclosures and hollow ways are visible at the site. This includes twenty four crofts and building platforms.. A north-south hollow way follows modern field boundaries and the enclosures can be seen mainly on the eastern side of this routeway. It crosses over the modern road from Tissington to Bradbourne in a southwards direction to Lea Hall Farm.
description_full: Earthwork evidence of buildings, enclosures and hollow ways are visible at the site. This includes twenty four crofts and building platforms. [1]. A north-south hollow way follows modern field boundaries and the enclosures can be seen mainly on the eastern side of this routeway. It crosses over the modern road from Tissington to Bradbourne in a southwards direction to Lea Hall Farm. The site is first mentioned in 1215 in the Cartulary of Dunstable Priory. [2] It appears in the lay subsidies in the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries but always with the nearby settlement of Tissington. This makes it difficult to plot the fortunes of the settlement. Enclosure is recorded in 1517 and probably it is around this time that the settlement disappears. [3] The last record on the E179 database is from 1534. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Mercaston
e179_last: 1662 May 19 hearth tax
description_snippet: The site of Mercaston probably formed a linear settlement along Mercaston Lane and a 1760s map of the settlement shows up to 12 buildings.  A number of features have been spotted in the aerial photography which may be related to the settlement.  At Domesday Mercaston is recorded as a manor with a minimum population of 10 people. The Lay Subsidy of 1334 is average for the area, and in 1525 there 16 people taxed.
description_full: The site of Mercaston probably formed a linear settlement along Mercaston Lane and a 1760s map of the settlement shows up to 12 buildings. [1] A number of features have been spotted in the aerial photography which may be related to the settlement. [2] At Domesday Mercaston is recorded as a manor with a minimum population of 10 people. The Lay Subsidy of 1334 is average for the area, and in 1525 there 16 people taxed. There is no clear indication of when the settlement reduced dramatically in size and the map of the 1760s would suggest that the village continued late into the eighteenth century. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Sapperton
e179_last: 1662 May 19 hearth tax
description_snippet: Earthworks of a small settlement had shown in aerial photographs but heavy ploughing of the site has now removed these.  Domesday Book records a manor with at least five people. The Lay Subsidy of 1334 is well below average.
description_full: Earthworks of a small settlement had shown in aerial photographs but heavy ploughing of the site has now removed these. [1] Domesday Book records a manor with at least five people. The Lay Subsidy of 1334 is well below average. There are records on the E179 database for the settlement throughout the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries and there remains the possibility that this was always a small settlement that gradually reduced to a scatter of farms. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Sedsall
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The site of Sedsall is now an isolated farm. Although aerial photographs have suggested settlement features around the farm, it has been suggested the slope would be too steep and unsuitable for buildings. Investigation of the higher, flat area of the farm buildings has not found any evidence of earlier settlement features.  At Domesday Sedsall is recorded as a manor with Eaton.
