Although aerial photographs have suggested settlement features around the farm, it has been suggested the slope would be too steep and unsuitable for buildings. Investigation of the higher, flat area of the farm buildings has not found any evidence of earlier settlement features. [1] At Domesday Sedsall is recorded as a manor with Eaton. The Lay Subsidy of 1334 is below average. It is mentioned into the seventeenth century but may have never been a large settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Sinfin
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The site of Sinfin has now been developed, and is now the site of a superstore. John Hurst visited the site in 1955 and found material had been dumped over much of the area.  Features on aerial photographs may be drainage related.  Sinfin was recorded as a manor in Domesday but with only two villagers. In 1334 it paid below average subsidy. By 1524 only six people paid the subsidy.
description_full: The site of Sinfin has now been developed, and is now the site of a superstore. John Hurst visited the site in 1955 and found material had been dumped over much of the area. [1] Features on aerial photographs may be drainage related. [2] Sinfin was recorded as a manor in Domesday but with only two villagers. In 1334 it paid below average subsidy. By 1524 only six people paid the subsidy. Sinfin continues to appear on the E179 database until the late seventeenth century. In the 1664 Hearth Tax there are seven buildings listed here along with Arleston. [3] It is difficult to plot the downfall of this site, and it is now part of the conurbation around Derby but this has only occurred since the 1970s. On the first edition Ordnance Survey map from 1883 there is Sinifin House, around 6 cottages and a Wesleyan Chapel. The medieval settlement may not have been any larger. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Underwood
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The ridge and furrow of the settlement can be seen to the north and west of the suggested site, but no evidence of the settlement has been identified. Underwood is a late appearance in the landscape, with a first mention of the place-name in 1251.  It has the smallest record for the 1334 Lay Subsidy in the Wapentake. It appears on Saxton’s map of 1577 so must have still been in existence.
description_full: The ridge and furrow of the settlement can be seen to the north and west of the suggested site, but no evidence of the settlement has been identified. Underwood is a late appearance in the landscape, with a first mention of the place-name in 1251. [1] It has the smallest record for the 1334 Lay Subsidy in the Wapentake. It appears on Saxton’s map of 1577 so must have still been in existence. [2] There are no other indications of when the settlement declined. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Badgworthy
description_snippet: The gird reference used by this website is that published by Hall and Hamlin which refined that of the 1968 Gazetteer.  The site of Badgworthy consists of approximately fourteen buildings.  Only foundations remain of these buildings. The earthworks can be clearly seen on aerial photographs.
description_full: The gird reference used by this website is that published by Hall and Hamlin which refined that of the 1968 Gazetteer. [1] The site of Badgworthy consists of approximately fourteen buildings. [2] Only foundations remain of these buildings. The earthworks can be clearly seen on aerial photographs. The layout of the village does not appear to show any kind of system and there are areas above and below which were used for grazing and ploughing. [3] Lynchets are also visible as well as field boundaries which show that there was arable land in use. [2] The site of Badgworthy also known as Badgworthy Water lies in a valley within Exmoor National Park. Origins of this village appear to be in the medieval period. [2] The land was passed to the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem in the twelfth century. [4] The thirteenth century saw the land passed to the Badgworthy family and following this the village grew. There is some mention of expansion in the seventeenth century. [2] However, there is a suggestion that the population decline and desertion was during the fifteenth century. [5, 6] It has been suggested that the cause of the depopulation was a culmination of climate change and the Black Death. [4] The settlement has been associated with the manor of Lacome (Lank Combe) in the Domesday Book, however it does not appear in any of the later taxation documents and may have been included with other of the dispersed settlements of the area. Badgworthy is a well-known deserted medieval village due to its links with R.D. Blackmore’s 1869 novel: Lorna Doone: A Romance on Exmoor. [5] The speculation is that the site is where the Doone family settled after exile from Scotland. [5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Great Beere
description_snippet: The deserted medieval village of Great Beere has very little left that can be seen, war time ploughing destroyed all surface work.  In 1938-1939 excavation work was carried out at the village site.  This was described in 1954 as one of the most thorough pieces of excavation work achieved.  It was also one of the earliest village sites to be excavated.
description_full: The deserted medieval village of Great Beere has very little left that can be seen, war time ploughing destroyed all surface work. [1] In 1938-1939 excavation work was carried out at the village site. [1] This was described in 1954 as one of the most thorough pieces of excavation work achieved. [2] It was also one of the earliest village sites to be excavated. [1] The excavations uncovered the foundations of one house, one barn and two corn-drying kilns as well as trial trenching a number of structures. [3] It is believed that the settlement began in the late twelfth century with its occupation at its peak during the thirteenth century. [3] There are discussions as to whether it existed at Domesday but if it was included it may have been counted as part of the Royal Manor of Tawetona. [3] The settlement does not appear in the later tax records and may have been hidden in the records of other settlements due to the dispersed nature of settlement in the region. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Blackaton
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The site of Blackaton is situated on a low west facing slope; Blackaton Down.  There is evidence of at least seventeen buildings, all of which are situated in or next to crofts.  The remains are still visible today and lie next to a modern farm building. The buildings do form clusters in areas and there is a suggestion that one may have been a chapel.
description_full: The site of Blackaton is situated on a low west facing slope; Blackaton Down. [1] There is evidence of at least seventeen buildings, all of which are situated in or next to crofts. [2] The remains are still visible today and lie next to a modern farm building. The buildings do form clusters in areas and there is a suggestion that one may have been a chapel. [3] This forms a more nucleated settlement than others on Dartmoor and is one of the largest of the deserted settlements in the region. [2] To the south there are some lynchets; which are remains of a much larger strip field system. The first documentary evidence is in 1249. [4] There is evidence of occupation from the thirteenth to the eighteenth century. [1] In the 1332 Lay Subsidy three people are recorded. [5] In 1377 a total of 12 poll tax payers are recorded. There are suggestions that the settlement had been abandoned by the mid-sixteenth century. [6] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Bolt Head
description_snippet: Although initial listings in the 1960s included earthworks at Bolt Head as clear evidence of medieval settlement, this has been overturned in recent years.  There is clear evidence of field boundaries and tentative evidence of prehistoric settlement, but no clear evidence of medieval settlement in the area.
description_full: Although initial listings in the 1960s included earthworks at Bolt Head as clear evidence of medieval settlement, this has been overturned in recent years. [1] There is clear evidence of field boundaries and tentative evidence of prehistoric settlement, but no clear evidence of medieval settlement in the area. A report of medieval pottery is contained within the MVRG archive but this is not enough to confirm a settlement. [2] There is no settlement bearing this name, or Starehole Bottom (the valley in which it is located) in the taxation documents. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Challacombe
description_snippet: The site of Challacombe is located on Dartmoor. There is still earthwork evidence of medieval buildings on the site. A modern farm building still exists within the area of the village. There are the remains of about ten buildings on the site.  These are situated along an old track heading northwards. At least seven crofts are identifiable to the west of this trackway.
description_full: The site of Challacombe is located on Dartmoor. There is still earthwork evidence of medieval buildings on the site. A modern farm building still exists within the area of the village [1]. There are the remains of about ten buildings on the site. [1] These are situated along an old track heading northwards. At least seven crofts are identifiable to the west of this trackway. [2] There is also an east-west track which leads to further earthworks to the east. [3] Many of the building foundations still survive and some of these were used into the post-Medieval period or may indicate the reuse of the site when there was an increase in population in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries due to mining activity. [3] The layout of the settlement appears quite regular and there have been suggestions of this showing evidence of a planned settlement. [2] The field system surrounding the settlement is one of the best examples of strip farming surviving on Dartmoor. [2, 4] The first clear historical data on this site are from 1481. [1] In 1613 five tenements are recorded. [2] There are still references to the site in 1841 when there were the same number of tenements from two hundred years earlier. [1] Earlier documentation such as Domesday with links to Challacombe has been questioned. [1] Lineham postulates that the settlement was never truly deserted but contracted in size at the time when many sites in the region did become deserted. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Little Cordonford
description_snippet: The 1968 Gazetteer records this as Little Cordonford, but a number of later records use Little Corndonford and this is the local spelling on the map, suggesting a misspelling in the original list, which is retained here. The site of Little Corndonford lies within a field of the same name. [1, 2] There are the remains of two, possibly three, buildings as well as evidence of more enclosures and two crofts.
description_full: The 1968 Gazetteer records this as Little Cordonford, but a number of later records use Little Corndonford and this is the local spelling on the map, suggesting a misspelling in the original list, which is retained here. The site of Little Corndonford lies within a field of the same name. [1, 2] There are the remains of two, possibly three, buildings as well as evidence of more enclosures and two crofts. [2] Some of the remains are now covered by vegetation. [1] It is unlikely to have been a sizable settlement in this area. A fifteenth-century desertion is suggested by French and Linehan. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Corndonford
description_snippet: The 1968 Gazetteer records this as Corndonford however the site is most often now referred to as Corndon.  There are some earthwork remains, including what could be field boundaries, which may be linked to the village, however only a single house has been identified.  Corndonford Farmhouse is a listed building dating from at least 1718 from a date stone on the porch.
description_full: The 1968 Gazetteer records this as Corndonford however the site is most often now referred to as Corndon. [1] There are some earthwork remains, including what could be field boundaries, which may be linked to the village, however only a single house has been identified. [1] Corndonford Farmhouse is a listed building dating from at least 1718 from a date stone on the porch. [2] This is situated to the east of the grid reference given for the village. Corndon is listed as a deserted site by Linehan who indicated that its original name is unknown. [3] This would help explain the lack of documentary references to any settlement evidence. It would also appear that the settlement was never of great size, perhaps a single farmhouse although a hollow way has also been suggested. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Cripdon
description_snippet: The site of Cripdon continues in use with a farm and enclosures. One of the earlier buildings is still used by the modern farm. Another four buildings recorded on the Ordnance Survey maps had disappeared by 1963. There are some earthworks that are still visible which may be connected to the village site.
description_full: The site of Cripdon continues in use with a farm and enclosures. One of the earlier buildings is still used by the modern farm. Another four buildings recorded on the Ordnance Survey maps had disappeared by 1963 [1]. There are some earthworks that are still visible which may be connected to the village site. A plan of the site shows the modern farm building incorporating the remains of a longhouse, two separate smaller buildings, and another complex of three buildings situated to the south. [2] All these buildings are situated along an east-west trackway. No documentary evidence exists for this settlement which would suggest that it is much more likely to have been a small hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Ford
description_snippet: There are two sites that lie close to each other in Cornwood parish - Ford Waste and Ford Barn.  Ford Waste is the site associated with the grid reference given in 1968, however both sites have clear earthwork evidence. Ford Barn will appear in a later edition of this website. At Ford Waste there is evidence of two longhouses and several other buildings, as well as enclosures.
description_full: There are two sites that lie close to each other in Cornwood parish - Ford Waste and Ford Barn. [1] Ford Waste is the site associated with the grid reference given in 1968, however both sites have clear earthwork evidence. Ford Barn will appear in a later edition of this website. At Ford Waste there is evidence of two longhouses and several other buildings, as well as enclosures [1]. Documentary evidence for this site does not exist, although Ford appears in a Lay Subsidy roll in 1330. [2] This could be referring either to this or the settlement at Ford Barn. Ford Waste could be an off shoot of Ford Barn. [1] Much of what survives is hidden beneath dense vegetation and therefore cannot be seen on aerial photographs, although field boundaries can be seen. It is worth noting that there is much dispersed settlement in this region and this one similarly may not have been a nucleated settlement. Instead it appears more like a series of hamlets within a parish. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hayne
description_snippet: The site of Hayne consists of the remains of six buildings and enclosures.  A modern house currently uses the enclosures.  The site has been recorded as having excellent standing remains, but little work has been carried out on the site.  Little if any documentary evidence survives for this site.
description_full: The site of Hayne consists of the remains of six buildings and enclosures. [1] A modern house currently uses the enclosures. [1] The site has been recorded as having excellent standing remains, but little work has been carried out on the site. [2] Little if any documentary evidence survives for this site. With at least six buildings present this would suggest a sizable concentration of settlement compared with some of the other deserted settlements in this area of Dartmoor. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hound Tor
description_snippet: The site of Hound Tor is probably one of the most well known in Dartmoor. The grid reference used here is SX 746788 which places the locator over the village. The originally published grid reference (SX 748796) placed the locator away from the evidence to the north. The village itself consists of about eleven buildings located within an enclosure.
description_full: The site of Hound Tor is probably one of the most well known in Dartmoor. The grid reference used here is SX 746788 which places the locator over the village. The originally published grid reference (SX 748796) placed the locator away from the evidence to the north. The village itself consists of about eleven buildings located within an enclosure. [1, 2] Earthworks reveal the remains of these buildings on aerial photographs. Full excavation of the site was completed between 1961 and 1975. [2] The location of the village is between Hound Tor and Greater Rocks lying on a gentle slope. [1, 2] Hound Tor Farmstead lies three hundred and forty yards to the north west of the village. [2] It includes one house and two barns. [2] The foundations of the buildings can also be seen on the ground and the site is publically accessible and managed by Dartmoor National Park on behalf of English Heritage. The village would appear to consist of eight houses and three corn drying barns. [2] Three of the houses are clear longhouses with cross passage ways. One of the buildings has a single entrance way to the south-east but is similar in dimension to the longhouses. The remaining four buildings are smaller and may represent smaller houses or out buildings. The buildings are clustered together and have small enclosures, possibly gardens close to the longhouses. There is no discernible plan to the settlement and it is suggested that although there is evidence of rebuilding, the settlement plan reflects the original layout of the settlement. [2] The site of Hound Tor village appears to have had periodic settlement since the Bronze Age, with cultivation of the land also in evidence. [1, 2] Excavation also uncovered some evidence of seventh and eighth-century activity in the area of the village. [2] The medieval village itself seems to have developed in the middle of the thirteenth century and then became deserted in the middle of the fourteenth century. [2] More recent pottery analysis has suggested that the settlement was still occupied into the late fourteenth or maybe early fifteenth century. [3] Unlike other deserted sites on Dartmoor, documentary evidence exists for Hound Tor including an entry in the Domesday Book with a population of six recorded. Hound Tor or its residents appear in documents throughout the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. [2] The reasons for desertion are not completely clear but there is evidence to suggest this was due to climate change. [2] As Hound Tor was one of the highest villages above sea level on Dartmoor, there is a claim that the changing climate would have affected these sites earlier and more deeply [2]. There is evidence for bad harvests but there are also good harvests mixed in with those years. Climate change was slow as was the desertion of the site. [2] Pollen analysis does show a change from arable to pastoral activity in the fourteenth century. [4] Whatever the reason for the desertion of Hound Tor, it is one of the best sites to view the remains of settlement activity. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: North Rowden
description_snippet: The site of North Rowden is probably indicative of a small hamlet or farmstead typical of this region of Dartmoor. There is evidence for four buildings, though parts of them date to the eighteenth century.  At least one of the structures is a typical longhouse. The site is located just north of an unclassified side road, down a track which is now fenced off and it would seem to be a self-contained settlement.
description_full: The site of North Rowden is probably indicative of a small hamlet or farmstead typical of this region of Dartmoor. There is evidence for four buildings, though parts of them date to the eighteenth century. [1] At least one of the structures is a typical longhouse. The site is located just north of an unclassified side road, down a track which is now fenced off and it would seem to be a self-contained settlement. [2] The aerial images show evidence of possible industrial work. The documentary evidence for activity is absent. It is clear that the farmhouse was still occupied in the mid-nineteenth century so may never have become deserted in the true sense in earlier periods. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The site of South Rowden is also known as Hutholes. The medieval name for the settlement is unknown, however it may have been the manor of Drewton recorded at Domesday. [1] There are the ruins of at least six buildings that have been linked to the deserted medieval settlement. [1, 2] The site is well preserved and the remains can be seen clearly on aerial photographs. The site was excavated between 1964-5 by E. Marie Minter. There are at least three longhouses and one of the smaller buildings contains a corn drying kiln in the later occupation of the site. The buildings are located within a large enclosure. There is only a single subdivision in the interior of this enclosure, suggesting that all buildings operated as one unit, rather than as separate households. [1] Excavations revealed a range of turf-built structures later replaced in stone. [1] The excavators originally identified this as an earlier phase of settlement from the early-eleventh century but this has been recently re-evaluated and dismissed. [3] One of the longhouses was re-excavated and two phases of activity identified, with no evidence for the turf-built initial phase. [3] The settlement’s peak of occupation was in the thirteenth century and experienced gradual desertion until final abandonment by the mid-fourteenth century. [1, 3] The reasons for desertion have been linked to climate change which included a number of bad harvests. [1] There was no continuation of use as has been seen at other sites such as North Rowden and the Tithe Map of 1843 records the area as waste. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: North Thorne
description_snippet: The village earthworks of North Thorne are well preserved, with much of it observable on aerial photographs. It is located to the south-east of the present farm building. There are remnants of nine buildings and intersecting hollow ways.  Excavations in 1959 and 1960 found traces of a building and pottery dated to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.  The building has cob walls on a footing of undressed stone.
description_full: The village earthworks of North Thorne are well preserved, with much of it observable on aerial photographs. It is located to the south-east of the present farm building. There are remnants of nine buildings and intersecting hollow ways. [1] Excavations in 1959 and 1960 found traces of a building and pottery dated to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. [2] The building has cob walls on a footing of undressed stone. [2] Later excavations in 1992 revealed a more complex history as pottery from the fourteenth to the seventeenth centuries was uncovered. [3] There is no documentary reference to this settlement. It would appear to go out of use in the fourteenth century – a similar pattern that is seen in other settlements in the area. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Treable
description_snippet: The site of Treable has no remains of a deserted settlement. The first mention of a ‘Tryfebel’ is in 1242.  The ‘Tre’ part is Celtic for a village.  Although the area has been reviewed on a number of occasions no settlement evidence has been located.  It does appear in a number of documents through the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries but it is unclear whether it was ever larger than a farm.

name: Afflington
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: Afflington is located around a mile to the south-east of Corfe Castle.  The surviving earthworks include hollow ways, house platforms, a pond and a field system. An east-west hollow way forms the main street of the settlement.  There are a number of enclosures but part of the site has been damaged by the construction of a lake.
description_full: Afflington is located around a mile to the south-east of Corfe Castle. [1] The surviving earthworks include hollow ways, house platforms, a pond and a field system. An east-west hollow way forms the main street of the settlement. [2] There are a number of enclosures but part of the site has been damaged by the construction of a lake. It is mentioned in the Domesday Book, but recorded under the name, ‘Alvrontone’, it has also been recorded as ‘Alfrington’ and ‘Addlington’. [2] At 1086 there is a minimum population of 10. In 1334 it pays a well below average Lay Subsidy. In the sixteenth century there are still a number of people at the settlement with 14 people taxed in 1525 and 10 are taxed in 1544. There are still accounts of up to twenty houses being inhabited right up to the seventeenth century. [1, 3] During the 1700s the site had become a single farmstead. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: West Bexington
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: The village of West Bexington is located near Chesil Beach and lies around 200m to the south-southeast of West Bexington Farm. [1, 2] A field investigation in 1955 which re-evaluated historical accounts dating from the 1730s and 1770s.  Visible earthworks included square banked platforms, hollow ways and scarps.
description_full: The village of West Bexington is located near Chesil Beach and lies around 200m to the south-southeast of West Bexington Farm. [1, 2] A field investigation in 1955 which re-evaluated historical accounts dating from the 1730s and 1770s. [1] Visible earthworks included square banked platforms, hollow ways and scarps. Excavation of the site of the church in 1984 revealed a graveyard containing human remains and pottery sherds dating from the twelfth to fourteenth century. [3, 4] The area of the church had been heavily damaged in the 1940s and many of the burials disturbed. [4] Much of the area has since been developed and little earthworks are now visible. It is clear the area had started to be encroached upon from the 1960s Ordnance Survey maps. The first record of the village appears in 1042-66 during the reign of Edward the Confessor. In Domesday there is a minimum population of 20 at both East and West Bexington. Around 1439-40, both the village and its chapel were burnt by French invaders and the villagers held to ransom. [1, 2] This event was instrumental in the start of the depopulation of the village and by c. 1625, the village was reported deserted. [1, 2] A single house is recorded in the 1664 Hearth Tax. [5] After the village became deserted, the site was converted into a farm and remained as such until the end of the First World War. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Blackmanston
description_snippet: The site spans two fields and is divided by a stream.  The site is characterised by several house platforms, banks and ditches and hollow ways.  Much of these features have suffered from plough damage. Excavations have revealed a midden containing quantities of oyster shells and medieval pottery as well as collapsed walls.  The village of Blackmanston is recorded in the Domesday Book.
description_full: The site spans two fields and is divided by a stream. [1] The site is characterised by several house platforms, banks and ditches and hollow ways. [2] Much of these features have suffered from plough damage. Excavations have revealed a midden containing quantities of oyster shells and medieval pottery as well as collapsed walls. [1] The village of Blackmanston is recorded in the Domesday Book. Unfortunately there is a lack of detailed later taxation records which makes it difficult to plot the fortunes of the settlement. It is possible this was an early desertion. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Brockington
description_snippet: The deserted medieval village of Brockington lies immediately to the north of Brockington Farm. The remains include two well defined hollow ways, which are bounded by perhaps nine or ten distinct enclosures accompanied by low banks and scarps which may represent individual houses. [1, 2] One hollow way runs north-west to south-east. At its northern end it is met by a south-west to north-east hollow way.
description_full: The deserted medieval village of Brockington lies immediately to the north of Brockington Farm. The remains include two well defined hollow ways, which are bounded by perhaps nine or ten distinct enclosures accompanied by low banks and scarps which may represent individual houses. [1, 2] One hollow way runs north-west to south-east. At its northern end it is met by a south-west to north-east hollow way. The settlement is just to the north of the deserted settlement and church of Knowlton. Brockington is recorded in the Domesday Book, however there are few later tax records for the village and therefore it is impossible to determine the population or the time and cause of desertion. [1,2] It is recorded in a number of other documents and appears on Saxton’s map in 1575 which suggests it still existed at this point. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Bryanston
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: The original village of Bryanston was located in close proximity to its church, now known as the Portman Chapel.  Bryanston House and Portman Chapel are both of nineteenth-century date and possibly the landscaping and construction of the House and its predecessors have destroyed the remains of the settlement. In Domesday Book Bryanston is mentioned with a minimum population of 28.
description_full: The original village of Bryanston was located in close proximity to its church, now known as the Portman Chapel. [1] Bryanston House and Portman Chapel are both of nineteenth-century date and possibly the landscaping and construction of the House and its predecessors have destroyed the remains of the settlement. In Domesday Book Bryanston is mentioned with a minimum population of 28. A total of 23 tax payers are recorded in 1333, however the population quickly declined. In 1543 there were eight tax payers and by 1664 there were only six households remaining. [1, 2] On a map of 1765 there are no houses in the area of the church. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Frampton
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: The modern village of Frampton was once known as Northover (north bank of the River Frome) and Southover (south bank of the River Frome).  The current village was built during the seventeenth century along with Frampton Court which was built in 1740 and stood on the site of the Frampton Priory before being demolished during the Second World War.  The rebuilt settlement sits partially over the remains of Southover.
description_full: The modern village of Frampton was once known as Northover (north bank of the River Frome) and Southover (south bank of the River Frome). [1] The current village was built during the seventeenth century along with Frampton Court which was built in 1740 and stood on the site of the Frampton Priory before being demolished during the Second World War. [1] The rebuilt settlement sits partially over the remains of Southover. These remains are those identified as Frampton and stretch intermittently westwards for approximately half a mile from the site of the old priory. [1] Earthworks are present along the south bank of the river consisting of a series of banks, enclosures and scarps, included in these remains are: a suspected farm, a mill and several buildings. [2, 3] The earthworks are all very much reduced by modern cultivation. [3] Frampton is recorded at Domesday and is a large manor with a minimum population of 57. In 1334 it pays an average Lay Subsidy. When the settlement shifted focus to the north bank is not known. It has been classed here as a shrunken settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Frome Belet
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: The grid reference has been altered from that of the 1968 Gazetteer (SY 715 895) to an area around Stafford House (SY 722 899) as recorded by the NMR and Good. description_full: The grid reference has been altered from that of the 1968 Gazetteer (SY 715 895) to an area around Stafford House (SY 722 899) as recorded by the NMR and Good. [1, 2] The settlement of Frome Belet or Frome Billet has not been securely located but slight earthworks have been spotted to the south and south-west of Stafford House, and the church was located to the west of the house. There are nineteenth-century reports of bones and stone work having been unearthed in this area. [3] In 1278, there is mention of the parochial church and again in 1470 when the village was united with West Stafford. [4] At Domesday there was a minimum population of nine and a mill recorded. It pays a below average Lay Subsidy in 1334 and 18 people paid the 1381 Poll Tax, but it does not appear in later taxation documents. With the church still mentioned in 1470 it suggests that there was still a settlement here. A single building was recorded in the 1673 Hearth Tax. [5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Fryer Mayne
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: The remains of Fryer Mayne or ‘Friarmayne’ are located in close proximity to the settlement of Broadmayne. [1, 2] Hutchins suggested that the site was a commandary of the Knights Hospitaller built before 1305 but this has been disputed, as it is hard to distinguish if the Mayne recorded in this context is Fryer Mayne or Little Mayne. [1, 3, 4] The remains of the village had been ploughed and destroyed by 1963.
description_full: The remains of Fryer Mayne or ‘Friarmayne’ are located in close proximity to the settlement of Broadmayne. [1, 2] Hutchins suggested that the site was a commandary of the Knights Hospitaller built before 1305 but this has been disputed, as it is hard to distinguish if the Mayne recorded in this context is Fryer Mayne or Little Mayne. [1, 3, 4] The remains of the village had been ploughed and destroyed by 1963. [2] The main features noted prior to this were a main hollow way running south-west to north-east, bounded on either side by multiple house platforms, to the east of the site of the chapel. [3] Houses to the north end of the hollow way were raised upon platforms. The walls of the houses were leveled and exposed by ploughing, their presence indicated by spreads of cob and stone rubble. [3] Field walking of the area recovered potsherds which dated from the fourteenth century. [3] There is no clear mention of Friar Mayne in the Domesday Book, but the two manors at Mayne probably relate to either Little Mayne, Fryer Mayne or Broadmayne suggesting in all likelihood Fryer Mayne was one of these small manors. The first mention of Fryer Mayne is in the mid-thirteenth century. [5] In 1334 it is taxed along with East Stafford and they pay a less than average amount. A water mill was recorded in 1338. [4] In 1381 there are 55 people taxed with East Stafford. The only later record of the settlement is the five people taxed in 1545. This would suggest that the settlement had already started to decline by the sixteenth century. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Gotowre
description_snippet: Gotowre appears on the 1968 Gazetteer and is a site that has been, in some ways, disputed. It was identified by Beresford and Joseph as the site of a new town that was planned by Edward I.  The place-name only appears in this context in the thirteenth century as Gotowre super Mare, now identified as the area of Goathorn in Poole Harbour.
description_full: Gotowre appears on the 1968 Gazetteer and is a site that has been, in some ways, disputed. It was identified by Beresford and Joseph as the site of a new town that was planned by Edward I. [1] The place-name only appears in this context in the thirteenth century as Gotowre super Mare, now identified as the area of Goathorn in Poole Harbour. [2] At the location plotted by this website the remains of a number of buildings have been recorded but these have now been identified as later in date, probably seventeenth-century fisherman’s houses. [3, 4] Beresford and St Joseph removed this site from the second edition of their book as there was so little evidence for the site. [5] There are no tax records for a settlement here and the place-name evidence of Goathorn Pier and Point suggest a name for an area of landscape rather than settlement. However it is mentioned in the plans of Edward I in 1286. [4, 6] It is stated that the plan was ‘to lay out with sufficient streets and lanes, adequate sites for a market and church, plots for merchants and others in a new town with a harbour in a place called Gotowre’, however it is not clear to what extent the order was ever carried out. [1, 3] Four months later a charter was granted to the burgesses of Nova Villa (Newtown) for a weekly market. After this though, no further references are found to the Gotowre or Newton. [1] It is suggested that if this settlement was ever established, then it was probably located half a mile to the east of the area of Goathorn. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hanford
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: The site of the settlement lies to the north of Hanford House and church. There are no clear remains currently visible, but the RCHME have noted a range of features. The main hollow way identified is orientated north-east to south-west, with five rectangular closes divided by low scarps and banks. To the west there was a collection of irregular hollows, mounds and scarps.
description_full: The site of the settlement lies to the north of Hanford House and church. There are no clear remains currently visible, but the RCHME have noted a range of features. The main hollow way identified is orientated north-east to south-west, with five rectangular closes divided by low scarps and banks. To the west there was a collection of irregular hollows, mounds and scarps. [1] First mentioned in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of eight. It is granted a market and fair in 1241. [2] In 1334 it pays a very low payment in the Lay Subsidy. In 1428, the total subsidy paid indicated no more than 10 inhabitants. [1] Only two tax payers are recorded in 1543. A single house is recorded in the 1664 Hearth Tax. [3] This was Hanford House, built between 1604 and 1623 and the landscaping of the grounds around the house probably hides the settlement remains. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hemsworth
e179_last: 1340 April 3 two ninths and fifteenths and tax on wool

description_full: One area of earthworks can be seem to the north of the building now known as Hemsworth Farm. These earthworks are focused on a hollow way running south-east to north-west with a number of enclosures on either side of the route. [1] It does not appear in the later taxation documents and the last mention on the E179 database is 1340 suggesting that this settlement was deserted early on in its history. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Holworth
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: Clear earthworks are visible at the site. The central feature is an east-west hollow way with seven tofts and crofts to the north, and a number of enclosures to the south. A trial excavation in 1936 uncovered pottery and stone work and one of the tofts was excavated in 1958.
description_full: Clear earthworks are visible at the site. The central feature is an east-west hollow way with seven tofts and crofts to the north, and a number of enclosures to the south. A trial excavation in 1936 uncovered pottery and stone work and one of the tofts was excavated in 1958. [1] This uncovered pottery dating from the twelfth to the fifteenth century and a longhouse was revealed that was divided into three parts with rubble floors. [1] Holworth was first mentioned in 933 AD during the reign of King Athelstan. [1, 2] At Domesday Holworth is recorded as part of the Milton Abbey estate with a minimum population of 13. In the 1333 Lay Subsidy 14 individuals were taxed. [2] It does not appear in the later sixteenth-century tax records but four houses are recorded in the 1664 Hearth Tax. [3] The pottery evidence and documentary evidence would suggest that the settlement was depopulated in the late fourteenth to fifteenth century. The excavation report suggests climatic deterioration as the cause for desertion. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Knowlton
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: The remains of the settlement have been damaged through drainage and quarrying but still remain recognizable within the landscape. The location used by this website is that of the church, but the clear settlement remains can be seen to the north-west. The settlement runs to the south and parallel to the River Allen and to the west of the road to Brockington.
description_full: The remains of the settlement have been damaged through drainage and quarrying but still remain recognizable within the landscape. The location used by this website is that of the church, but the clear settlement remains can be seen to the north-west. The settlement runs to the south and parallel to the River Allen and to the west of the road to Brockington. [1] It is made up of a series of twelve roughly rectangular enclosures and platforms and areas of disturbance produced pottery dating from the twelfth to the seventeenth century. There are further disturbed areas of ground to the north-east of the Brockington Road indicating further closes and raised platforms. [1] The church stands to the south of this area, located within a Neolithic henge monument. The settlement remains on the south side of the river directly opposite those of the deserted settlement of Brockington. The relationship between these two settlements is unknown but they fall in different parishes. There are records of two manors at Domesday but one of them is included with a number of other large manors and so a population estimate is not possible. An average amount is paid in the 1334 Lay Subsidy. There is evidence of additions being made to the church in the fifteenth century suggesting a sizable population still existed. [2] By 1525 only three people are taxed and the church fell into disuse in 1650. [2] This evidence would suggest depopulation during the sixteenth century. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Lazerton
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: The remains of the settlement survived until 1962 when they were destroyed.  Prior to its destruction, the village lay in two parts. The northern section contained a roughly rectangular area with a complex series of scarps, banks and ditches and a rectangular platform which is recorded as the position of the church.  During the destruction a limestone coffin-lid was uncovered as well as flat, unglazed roof tiles.
description_full: The remains of the settlement survived until 1962 when they were destroyed. [1] Prior to its destruction, the village lay in two parts. The northern section contained a roughly rectangular area with a complex series of scarps, banks and ditches and a rectangular platform which is recorded as the position of the church. [1] During the destruction a limestone coffin-lid was uncovered as well as flat, unglazed roof tiles. The southern section comprised seven closes defined by low banks and fragmentary platforms characteristic of buildings. [1] At the time of Domesday, Lazerton was an independent parish and recorded as one of the ‘Iwernes’ with a minimum population of seven. [1] In the twelfth century, the church was so poor that it was released from all payments. [1] In 1334 is pays a well below average amount along with the neighbouring hamlet of Ash. In 1428, the Parish was not taxed due to having fewer than 10 inhabitants, and finally in 1431, the church was declared destitute of a chaplain due to small profits and joined with the parish of Stourpaine. [2] It does not appear in the sixteenth-century tax records and no returns were made for the 1664 Hearth Tax. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Lewcombe
description_snippet: There are no physical remains of the settlement of Lewcombe. The church is recorded in the twelfth century, rebuilt in the sixteenth century and then renovated during the eighteenth century.  It stands isolated to the north of Lewcombe Manor which is late eighteenth century in date and the landscaping of the area may have altered the remains of the settlement.
description_full: There are no physical remains of the settlement of Lewcombe. The church is recorded in the twelfth century, rebuilt in the sixteenth century and then renovated during the eighteenth century. [1] It stands isolated to the north of Lewcombe Manor which is late eighteenth century in date and the landscaping of the area may have altered the remains of the settlement. [2] There are no clear documentary records associated with this settlement which makes any estimation of size hard to judge. It is however recorded as a place-name from 1251. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Little Mayne
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: The remains lie in the area to the north, south and south-west of Little Mayne Farm.  The main features include a well-defined hollow way to the north of the farm. It is orientated north and runs between two banks, their crests marked at intervals with protruding sarsen stones.
description_full: The remains lie in the area to the north, south and south-west of Little Mayne Farm. [1] The main features include a well-defined hollow way to the north of the farm. It is orientated north and runs between two banks, their crests marked at intervals with protruding sarsen stones. [1] While it has been suggested that these have a prehistoric origin, possibly an avenue leading to the stone circles located nearby, it is thought more likely that they are medieval in date. [1] Along this hollow way lie several scarped closes. There is a record of a chapel of St Stephen’s, the remains of which were destroyed in 1960 and a section overlaid by cattle pens. [2] The first documentary mention of Little Mayne or ‘Parva Maene’ seems to be in 1201-2. [1] There is some confusion in the Domesday Book as there is reference to a village of ‘Maine’ which has been attributed to three separate villages, Broadmayne, Friar Mayne and Little Mayne. Which one to chose is unclear, but may indicate settlement at this time. The earliest rector of the chapel is recorded in 1326 and the last recorded in 1491. [1] Hutchins describes the village as an ancient manor and hamlet. [3] Although there is clearly evidence for the settlement, in terms of the physical remains, the documentary evidence is seriously lacking which may suggest Little Mayne being ‘hidden’ in the record, or for example taxed with another village. The only tax record for the settlement is in 1545 when two people are taxed. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Melcombe Horsey
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: The remains are located in ‘Chapel Close’, north-west of Higher Melcombe House. The village lay in close proximity to the village of Bingham’s Melcombe which is also deserted.  It is recorded as Melcombe from Domesday, as Up Melcombe, Over Melcombe and West Melcombe in the thirteenth century and Melcombe Horsey in the sixteenth century.
description_full: The remains are located in ‘Chapel Close’, north-west of Higher Melcombe House. The village lay in close proximity to the village of Bingham’s Melcombe which is also deserted. [1] It is recorded as Melcombe from Domesday, as Up Melcombe, Over Melcombe and West Melcombe in the thirteenth century and Melcombe Horsey in the sixteenth century. [1] The principal features span an area of approximately 10 acres and include a hollow way running south-east to north-west flanked by several roughly rectangular closes, characterized by low banks and ditches. [2] To the south of the closes lay incomplete building sites and an irregular circular mound. Much of these remains have been destroyed through quarrying. [2] Melcombe Horsey also had a chapel whose foundations, according to Hutchins, were still surviving in the late eighteenth century but which subsequently disappeared and the location of which was lost. [3] Sherds of medieval pottery were retrieved from mole-hills to the south-west of the site during field investigations. [4] Due to its proximity and close relationship with its neighbour, Bingham’s Melcombe, their populations have always been recorded together and therefore it is impossible to distinguish one from the other. At Domesday there is a mention of a manor at ‘Melcombe’ with a minimum population of 36. This is identified by the Philimore edition as Melcombe Horsey but by the English Place-Names Society as Bingham’s Melcombe. [1, 5] In 1334 Melcombe paid an average amount of tax. In 1525 15 people paid the Lay Subsidy for Melcombe. It is possible to track a gradual decline until the mid-1600s with population and tax reductions in 1333 and 1435. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Melcombe, Bingham
e179_last: 1662 May 19 hearth tax
description_snippet: The remains of Bingham’s Melcombe can be found in close proximity to the village of Melcombe Horsey or Higher Melcombe, which is also deserted. To distinguish the two settlements, this site has been known as Nether and East Melcombe in the thirteenth to fifteenth century, with Bingham’s Melcombe first appearing in the fifteenth century.
description_full: The remains of Bingham’s Melcombe can be found in close proximity to the village of Melcombe Horsey or Higher Melcombe, which is also deserted. To distinguish the two settlements, this site has been known as Nether and East Melcombe in the thirteenth to fifteenth century, with Bingham’s Melcombe first appearing in the fifteenth century. [1] The site of Bingham’s Melcombe lies immediately to the south of the Church of St Andrew and covers a meadow know as Town Hayes spanning approximately 10 acres. [2] The site itself is divided by a hollow way, orientated west to east with a series of more than ten closes of rectangular shape and four level platforms set on terrace-ways. Strip lynchets are visible on the north and north-east slopes surrounding the village. Although now destroyed, aerial photography showed that there existed around 30 acres of strip fields surrounding Bingham’s Melcombe’s House. [2] This house is located to the north-east of the church and settlement. The House probably overlies the original manorial centre which was contemporaneous with the settlement, and recorded in the early thirteenth century although there is no record of when it was constructed and by whom. It was rebuilt and remodelled in the fourteenth, sixteenth and seventeenth century, only a small fragment of walling remains from the thirteenth century. [2] Due to its proximity and close relationship with its neighbour, Melcombe Horsey, their populations have always been recorded together and therefore it is impossible to distinguish one from the other. At Domesday there is a mention of a manor at ‘Melcombe’ with a minimum population of 36. This is identified by the Philimore edition as Melcombe Horsey but by the English Place-Names Society as Bingham’s Melcombe. [1, 3] In 1334 Melcombe paid an average amount of tax. It is possible to track a gradual decline until the mid-1600s through population and tax reductions in 1333 and 1435. In 1525 15 people paid the Lay Subsidy for Melcombe. Nine houses were recorded in the 1664 Hearth Tax, but three of these are recorded as demolished or very poor, five houses are recorded in the 1673 Hearth Tax. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Milborne Symondeston
description_snippet: Milborne Symondeston is recorded from the thirteenth century. Although given a grid reference in the 1968 Gazetteer there is uncertainty about its true location. The location used in 1968 is recorded (although at the wrong grid reference) by the RCHME as evidence of settlement remains but identified as Milborne Deverel.
description_full: Milborne Symondeston is recorded from the thirteenth century. Although given a grid reference in the 1968 Gazetteer there is uncertainty about its true location. The location used in 1968 is recorded (although at the wrong grid reference) by the RCHME as evidence of settlement remains but identified as Milborne Deverel. [1] In 1774 Hutchins records Milborne Symondeston’s location as entirely unknown, but possibly between Milborne St Andrew and Milborne Churchstone. [2] It is recorded as lost in the place-names volume. [3] Good suggests it may be the un-named settlement identified by the RCHME as earthworks, but it is unclear to which of the three areas identified he links the settlement. [4] For the current time it cannot be identified with any certainty, and there is a possibility that this was just another name for one of the other Milborne settlements. It does not appear in the tax records. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Milton Abbas
e179_last: 1663 June 20 or later - July 23 four clerical subsidies
description_snippet: The remains of the former village or town of Milton Abbas cover approximately 25 acres and lie south of the Abbey Church and Milton Abbey House.  The whole area is divided by Milborne Brook. Towards the north end of the site, there are the fewest surviving remains as a result of garden landscaping which occurred in the late 1700s. Outside the gardens, the remains are extensive and better preserved.
description_full: The remains of the former village or town of Milton Abbas cover approximately 25 acres and lie south of the Abbey Church and Milton Abbey House. [1] The whole area is divided by Milborne Brook. Towards the north end of the site, there are the fewest surviving remains as a result of garden landscaping which occurred in the late 1700s. Outside the gardens, the remains are extensive and better preserved. [1] A complex grid of streets and side lanes are visible as clearly defined hollow ways, however, house sites tend only to be visible as shallow hollows with only a few exceptions. Field investigations and aerial photography has established that there are other hollow ways, banks and scarps which continue south but which have been disturbed by a fishpond. Extensive quantities of twelfth to eighteenth-century pottery have been discovered across the whole site. [1] In 1769-1771, before the village was destroyed, William Woodward created a map of the village. The plan subsequently drawn during investigations carried out by the RCHME, highlights remains which Woodward did not include suggesting that they were already abandoned prior to the demolition of the village. [1] Another plan of roughly the same date as that of William Woodward also shows fewer houses suggesting the settlement was in decline. [2] Milton Abbas is a fascinating example of deliberate destruction of an established and flourishing town for the purpose of ‘improving’ the landscape. In the mid-tenth century, the founding of the Benedictine Abbey allowed the village to thrive and by Domesday the village had become one of the largest settlements in central Dorset, with its own fair and market. [3] A minimum of 53 people are recorded. In 1333, as many as 104 tax payers are listed. [3] It pays a well above average Lay Subsidy in 1334. The stability of the town was such that the dissolution of the monastery in 1539 had little effect on its prosperity which continued throughout the seventeenth century. [3] 137 people signed the Protestation Returns of 1641–2. [3] In 1752, the estate was purchased by Joseph Damer and he commissioned the construction of a new manor house whilst retaining the church and Abbot’s Great Hall. [1] Wishing to empark a larger area of his estate, Damer began to purchase leases and holdings and subsequently succeeded in also demolishing the town allowing for the creation of landscape gardens and an ornamental fishpond in around 1780. [3] More than one hundred homes, three inns and a school were all relocated, to ensure an uninterrupted view from his new home. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Orchard (Rew)
description_snippet: The village of Orchard is more commonly referred to as Rew or Winterbourne Rew.  The settlement remains consist of a long narrow stretch of approximately one quarter mile of banked and scarped closes. It is suggested that the name ‘Rew’ derives from this alignment or ‘row’ of enclosures.
description_full: The village of Orchard is more commonly referred to as Rew or Winterbourne Rew. [1] The settlement remains consist of a long narrow stretch of approximately one quarter mile of banked and scarped closes. It is suggested that the name ‘Rew’ derives from this alignment or ‘row’ of enclosures. [2] At the western end of this alignment and separated by a hollow way running in a northerly direction, are several large enclosures which may have been part of a manorial complex. Closes to the east are defined by steep banks, however portions have been destroyed by ploughing and it is suspected that this destruction may account for the complete lack of building platforms or houses. [2] There are nine rectangular crofts identified with a north-west to south-east hollow way to the north and at the western end a north-east to south-west hollow way. [3] The settlement was not recorded as Rew until 1283 but it is probably much older. [2] It is unclear where the name ‘Orchard’ used in the gazetteer derives from, but was recorded in an unpublished text on Dorset villages by P. Lock. [4] There are no tax records for this settlement and perhaps it was never seen as a separate settlement or known as another Orchard. An estate map of 1768 shows the settlement deserted. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Polingston (Pulston)

There are remains of three more closes to the south and other enclosures can be seen in the area.  To the south-east the area has been ploughed but contained further closes and when ploughed produced flint rubble and twelfth to fifteenth-century pottery.
description_full: The remains of the settlement can be seen centred on the remains of Pulston Barn. To the north there are at least four enclosures. [1] There are remains of three more closes to the south and other enclosures can be seen in the area. [1] To the south-east the area has been ploughed but contained further closes and when ploughed produced flint rubble and twelfth to fifteenth-century pottery. [1] Pulston is directly recorded at Domesday but probably forms part of the entries for Cerne. [2] It is suggested that in 1333 it is included with Forston where 11 tax payers are recorded. [1] In 1334 they both pay a slightly below average amount. In the 1381 Poll Tax 35 people were taxed with Forston. A chapel was present and is last recorded in 1411. [1] In 1545 there are seven people taxed. There are no houses recorded in the seventeenth-century hearth taxes so it is suggested desertion was complete by this point. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Puddle, Little (Little Piddle)
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships

description_full: The grid reference used by this website (SY 719 966) is refined since the 1968 Gazetteer to place its location over the visible remains. The physical remains of Little Piddle are located across a valley bottom straddling the River Piddle and in close proximity to Little Puddle Farm on the west bank of the river. [1] The remains cover approximately 32 acres and the whole area was most likely enclosed by a boundary bank although the overall quality of preservation of the site is variable. On the eastern bank of the river there are several long rectangular closes which may have once been the crofts belonging to houses situated in the valley bottom. To the west of the site, the presence of the farm, surrounding buildings and water meadows have destroyed much of the archaeology though there is a small number of shortened banks which protrude from the boundary bank. [1] Little Piddle was divided into two manors, Combe Deverel, to the north in the parish of Piddlehinton and Little Piddle, to the South in the parish of Puddletown. First recorded as these two manors in Domesday, with a minimum population of 19, there is no clear evidence of the settlement being physically divided into the separate manors. [1] By 1333 there was already sign of decline in the Little Piddle manor with the number of tax payers having fallen to seven. In 1334 a below average amount is paid to the Lay Subsidy. It was deserted by 1529 as the Musters Roll of that year showed the total population being two. [1] In 1664 only two households are recorded. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Ringstead (West)
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: The physical remains at this location are usually referred to as West Ringstead. The remains are characterized by enclosures and hollow ways. Additionally building remains are visible in banks with protruding stonework. There has been some damage as the area was flooded and used as water meadows.  To the north of the site lies the location of the church and cemetery.
description_full: The physical remains at this location are usually referred to as West Ringstead. The remains are characterized by enclosures and hollow ways. Additionally building remains are visible in banks with protruding stonework. There has been some damage as the area was flooded and used as water meadows. [1] To the north of the site lies the location of the church and cemetery. The church was converted into Glebe Cottage in the eighteenth century. Directly to the south of this are four house sites, and a further four less-defined house sites can also be seen. [1] Prior to the fifteenth century Ringstead was an independent parish containing four separate ‘Ringsteads’, East, West, Middle and Up Ringstead. [1] The significance of this is that in documentary evidence all four villages were taxed together as a parish rather than individually. ‘West’ Ringstead was first recorded in conjunction with East Ringstead in 1285. [2] Ringstead is first recorded in 1086 with a minimum population of 19. The first record of the church was in 1227. [1] In the Lay Subsidy Roll of 1327, seventeen individuals are taxed, and by 1333 this has fallen to thirteen. A below average payment is made in the 1334 Lay Subsidy. In 1428, there were still more than ten individuals but by 1488, the rectory was joined with the vicarage of Osmington due to the poverty of both parishes. Despite there being no mention of Ringstead as a separate tithing later than this, there was a record in the Dorset Hearth Tax Assessment in 1664, with three houses remaining. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The physical remains of the village of East Shilvinghampton lie approximately 400m east from its neighbour, West Shilvinghampton. [1] The 1968 Gazetteer has both these sites located at the same grid reference. This has been kept for East, but the grid reference for West has been refined to SY 625 844. Although visible in aerial photography the remains at East Shilvinghampton are very disturbed and are not extensive. They only include two small rectangular closes which are probably building platforms. [1] Situated immediately north-east of East Shilvinghampton Farm, the remains cover an area of around 8 acres which is entirely given over to pasture. [2] It is first mentioned at Domesday as Shilvinghampton with a minimum population of nine. In 1334 the two settlements together paid a well below average subsidy. In 1545 there are only three people taxed in Shilvinghampton. Only three houses were recorded in Shilvinghampton in the 1664 Hearth Tax. [3] In 1774 East Shilvinghampton was described as a small hamlet consisting of two farmsteads. [4] The settlement remains indicate that at some point prior to this, the hamlet had been larger, but maybe never extensive. [5] It has been classified here as a deserted hamlet. There is the possibility that there was a larger settlement here if the two settlements were in fact part of the same village. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

[2] By 1774 West Shilvinghampton was described as having been reduced to a single farmstead. [3] It seems never to have been large and is described here as a hamlet. name: Stanton St. Gabriel
description_snippet: The only clear evidence visible at the site is the ruins of the Chapel of St Gabriel. The current ruins incorporate medieval elements including a fourteenth-century doorway.  While the village appears in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of 16, there is no clear indication of the village’s development from that time onwards.
description_full: The only clear evidence visible at the site is the ruins of the Chapel of St Gabriel. The current ruins incorporate medieval elements including a fourteenth-century doorway. [1] While the village appears in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of 16, there is no clear indication of the village’s development from that time onwards. The lack of records during the fourteenth century may suggest that this was the period in which it was deserted and its subsequent reappearance in the mid-1500s may be indicative of the new and shifted settlement, although only five tax payers are recorded in 1525. There are 15 houses recorded in the 1664 Hearth Tax. [2] In 1774 Hutchins notes that the chapel is in disrepair. [3] Stanton St Gabriel, is an example of a shifted and subsequently deserted village. Once a fishing village, it is thought the reason for its desertion was due to its proximity to the coast which caused its inhabitants to relocate to a more accessible area inland. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Steepleton Iwerne

description_full: There are no clear visible remains of the settlement, however the Church of St Mary which has elements that dated to around the late eleventh century still survives. [1] The village was deserted by 1662 and the site is now occupied by Stepleton House and its gardens and ornamental lake. [1] The House dates from the seventeenth century. [1] The only surviving evidence of the village is some slight disturbance to the east of the house which may suggest other old buildings. [2] Steepleton Iwerne is mentioned in Domesday as the manor known as ‘Werne’ with a minimum population of 14. In 1334 a below average amount is paid. Subsequently, the village disappears from records only to reappear in the 1801 and 1841 census records under the name of Steepleton Iwerne or Preston. It possibly suffered from emparking in the seventeenth century, but may have already been small as it does not appear in the seventeenth-century records. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.
