description_snippet: East Shefford follows a common pattern for putative DMVs in Berkshire, with a mismatch between the archaeological and documentary evidence. The settlement’s Norman church still stands, and next to it was the medieval moated manor house, known as Hug Ditch Court, apparently destroyed in 1871.  East Shefford House is thought to date from the seventeenth or eighteenth century.
description_full: East Shefford follows a common pattern for putative DMVs in Berkshire, with a mismatch between the archaeological and documentary evidence. The settlement’s Norman church still stands, and next to it was the medieval moated manor house, known as Hug Ditch Court, apparently destroyed in 1871. [1] East Shefford House is thought to date from the seventeenth or eighteenth century. [2] Apart from Wickfield Farm in the south of the historic East Shefford parish it would appear the medieval population was largely concentrated near the River Lambourn. The most likely location for a nucleated village was near the church and former manor, and a small number other buildings are situated in the more general vicinity. However no physical remains of a DMV are known. [3, 4] In contrast the the Domesday Book and 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment do suggest that the vill may have been reasonably populated with percentile ranks within Berkshire of 0.37 and 0.35 respectively, although the eight taxpayers in 1327 give a somewhat lower rank of 0.18. [5] By the 1524/5 Lay Subsidy East Shefford’s six tax payers made it the joint smallest vill within Kintbury and Eagle Hundred, and with a Berkshire percentile rank of just 0.04. Close to the suggested DMV site lies an early Anglo-Saxon cemetery. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Shinfield (Green)
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces (Shinfield)
description_snippet: This site at the southern end of what was Shinfield Green is said by the East Berkshire HER to represent the former site of Shinfield manor house (demolished in the late eighteenth century or perhaps c.1804), an associated moat and a series of earthworks of a possible associated settlement.
description_full: This site at the southern end of what was Shinfield Green is said by the East Berkshire HER to represent the former site of Shinfield manor house (demolished in the late eighteenth century or perhaps c.1804), an associated moat and a series of earthworks of a possible associated settlement. [1, 2] The site appears to be east of the Shinfield Road (in line with the HER’s grid reference but not its description) and has been subject to a number of archaeological interventions. A sketch of the earthworks shown on an aerial photograph of 1964 has been made, and excavations in 1989 north of the earthworks and west of the former moat produced medieval (thirteenth/fourteenth-century) and post-medieval pottery, as well as two post holes and a medieval pebbled surface. [1] A geophysical survey in 1994 identified high resistance anomalies associated with the earthworks, perhaps including garden features [1] whilst an archaeological watching brief of an adjoining housing developing in 2006 found evidence for the surviving remains of the moat. [3] The area further south appears to have been disturbed in recent years by works to create a new roundabout, but without finds relevant to the site. Taken together the archaeological evidence hints at the possibility that the post-medieval manor house had some sort of medieval precursor here, and perhaps even an associated hamlet, although given the dispersed settlement pattern in the wider Shinfield Green area, a former village seems unlikely. This dispersed settlement pattern also means that documentary evidence about the vill or parish of Shinfield is not especially informative about the past status of this site. Map evidence such as Rocque’s 1761 plan and the 1809 Ordnance Survey drawing show only a single farmstead or small hamlet in the vicinity – the post-medieval manor house was it seems replaced with the building of Duckett’s Farm in the nineteenth century. Identified by the HER.

name: Shottesbrooke
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Although no evidence has been identified on the ground or in aerial photographs for a deserted settlement at Shottesbrooke,  some of the documentary evidence suggests a modest medieval community of some form probably once existed here.
description_full: Although no evidence has been identified on the ground or in aerial photographs for a deserted settlement at Shottesbrooke, [1] some of the documentary evidence suggests a modest medieval community of some form probably once existed here. The vill appears to have been relatively populous at the time of Domesday Book and the 1334 Lay Subsidy is fairly high compared to other accepted DMVs, although only seven tax payers were recorded in the 1327 Lay Subsidy and only five in 1332. [2, 3] Shottesbrooke was the site of a foundation of a monastic college in 1337, and its current church seems to have been built at about this time (presumably replacing the church referred to in Domesday Book). [4] The college is thought to have been situated south of the church but no evidence of its buildings is known to remain. [5] The chronology of Shottesbrooke’s depopulation is puzzling. By the time of the 1524/5 Lay Subsidy the small number of tax payers (seven in one assessment) was already the lowest in the medieval Hundred of Cookham and Bray. Nevertheless Beresford and Hurst suggested that depopulation at Shottesbrooke occurred as a result of seventeenth/eighteenth-century emparkment. [6] Shottesbrooke House is thought to date originally from the sixteenth century, with eighteenth and nineteenth-century re-modelling. [4] Its associated parkland is shown in Rocque’s map of 1761, although this map also appears to show that elements of the village still persisted. On the road heading southwards from the church Rocque depicts an odd line of nine offset buildings, which seems to have disappeared by the 1809 Ordnance Survey drawing. Rocque also seems to show further buildings adjoining the network of lanes south of Shottesbrooke Park, some of which seem to have subsequently disappeared. Whether buildings in this area were once part of a medieval village is unclear and depends on how tightly nucleated it was. The parish of Shottesbrooke does have several outlying farms, some of which may have been settled in the medieval period (see for example Smewin's Farm with its moat and late Tudor house). [7] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Southcote
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Upper Circourt Farm represents the site of the medieval village known as ‘Southcote’, the modern name being a relatively recent corruption.  Some physical traces of the medieval village remain, with a hollow way on the east side the farm probably the former village street and an area of uneven ground further east of the farm perhaps representing former dwellings.
description_full: Upper Circourt Farm represents the site of the medieval village known as ‘Southcote’, the modern name being a relatively recent corruption. [1] Some physical traces of the medieval village remain, with a hollow way on the east side the farm probably the former village street and an area of uneven ground further east of the farm perhaps representing former dwellings. The modern farm buildings may also occupy some of the medieval village ‘footprint’. [2] A sketch survey is said to be present in the MVRG archive, but was not found in the site file. The medieval documents, including the 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment and 1381 Poll Tax (32 residents assessed) also make it clear that Circourt must once have been much more populous than a single farm or hamlet. The medieval vill was usually assessed individually, but during the second half of the seventeenth century it was often grouped with Goosey. Beresford and Hurst estimated a period of desertion c. 1450-1700, which would tally with this. Rocque’s map of 1761 shows ‘South Cutt’ having just three buildings, perhaps already a single farm. Identified by the NMR and place-name evidence.

name: Sparkmoor Cottage, nr Tidmarsh
description_snippet: Sparkmoor Cottage is marked on the first edition 25 and 6 inch Ordnance Survey maps (surveyed in 1877-8) on the north side of an east-west lane that formerly marked the southern parish boundary of Tidmarsh. Rocque’s 1761 map shows four buildings (but perhaps schematically representing two farmsteads or house plots) along the north of this lane, forming a row that may possibly have edged a small area of common.
description_full: Sparkmoor Cottage is marked on the first edition 25 and 6 inch Ordnance Survey maps (surveyed in 1877-8) on the north side of an east-west lane that formerly marked the southern parish boundary of Tidmarsh. Rocque’s 1761 map shows four buildings (but perhaps schematically representing two farmsteads or house plots) along the north of this lane, forming a row that may possibly have edged a small area of common. It has been suggested that an aerial photograph of 2003 may show further crofts to the south, [1] but there is little beyond this to suggest that the settlement was ever more than a hamlet, and no medieval references to the name have been published, suggesting that the settlement might be post-medieval in origin. Sparkmoor Cottages are mentioned in sale particulars of the late 1930s, [2, 3] but seem to have been abandoned by c. 1941 and were last mapped by the Ordnance Survey in 1960. [1] Identified by the HER.

name: North Standen
e179_last: 1549-52 Subsidy ('relief')
description_snippet: The case for a DMV at North Standen remains uncertain. The West Berkshire HER suggests the site was accepted by the Medieval Village Research Group on the basis of aerial photographic evidence, although no settlement earthworks were identified by a recent National Mapping Programme in Berkshire.
description_full: The case for a DMV at North Standen remains uncertain. The West Berkshire HER suggests the site was accepted by the Medieval Village Research Group on the basis of aerial photographic evidence, although no settlement earthworks were identified by a recent National Mapping Programme in Berkshire. [1] The Medieval Village Research Group archive for Berkshire does not contain any information on the site, although the Wiltshire archive has yet to be checked. The vill is probably recorded in Domesday Book as one of two ‘Standens’ in the Kinwardstone Hundred of Wiltshire, although it has also been suggested this entry may refer to Chute Standen. [2] A separate vill of North Standen is found in the E179 database as early as 1269, and the settlement had a chapel from at least the thirteenth century, thought to have survived within a barn to the north-east of the main house. [3] The fourteenth-century documentary evidence for the status of North Standen is ambiguous. Usually the vill is grouped alongside [South] Standen and sometimes Froxfield. In the 1377 Poll Tax North Standen appears separately, with 19 taxpayers, although it is unclear whether this entry might also have included Standen and Froxfield, which do not otherwise appear. In 1379 North Standen appears to have been subsumed, perhaps within the entry for Charnham Street/Charlton. The settlement is recorded with Charleton Strete in 1525, and this may also include South Standen but this is unclear. The vill does not appear in the E179 database beyond the mid-sixteenth century, suggesting that if it was ever a village it had by then been reduced to a manorial site. The earliest phase of North Standen House is thought to be sixteenth-century. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Stanford Wick
description_snippet: The evidence for a DMV at Stanford Wick, identified by John Brooks  close to the main village of Stanford in the Vale, comes from an air photo showing 'numerous irregular plots separated by shallow ditches and the whole enclosed by broad hollow ways which also demarcate the edge of rig-and-furrow cultivation'.  The area has also produced twelfth-century pottery.
description_full: The evidence for a DMV at Stanford Wick, identified by John Brooks [1] close to the main village of Stanford in the Vale, comes from an air photo showing 'numerous irregular plots separated by shallow ditches and the whole enclosed by broad hollow ways which also demarcate the edge of rig-and-furrow cultivation'. [2] The area has also produced twelfth-century pottery. [3] An area of narrow rectilinear fields nearby is known as ‘Wick Closes’ prompting the suggested name of ‘Stanford Wick’ for the site, although it is not clear if this name appeared in any medieval documentation. Certainly the name does not appear in any of the E179 records, suggesting any population was recorded under the main village. This lack of documentary evidence means it is hard to pin down a period of desertion. Certainly the 1761 map of John Rocque shows no settlement in the area. It has been suggested that the ‘Wick Closes’ could have resulted from early enclosure for dairying, [3] although whether this can be connected to the existence or decline of any satellite settlement of Stanford in the Vale is uncertain. Identified by John Brooks.

name: Steventon
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Steventon is a large village which experienced significant late medieval shrinkage, some of which was subsequently obscured by post-medieval growth. As such the village provides a good example of the dangers of placing too much confidence in the interpretation of village plans shown on post-medieval maps.
description_full: Steventon is a large village which experienced significant late medieval shrinkage, some of which was subsequently obscured by post-medieval growth. As such the village provides a good example of the dangers of placing too much confidence in the interpretation of village plans shown on post-medieval maps. Originally assumed to have been a linear planned ‘row’ settlement, the more complex history of Steventon’s medieval fortunes has been revealed by careful study of manorial documents and local topography by C.R.J. Currie. [1] Currie postulates that Steventon may have originated as two small settlement nuclei, one located at the far western end of the village, near the church, manor house, and Steventon Mill, with a second at the far eastern end of the present village. Both nuclei – and those cottages that grew up in between – fringed the southern edge of what would once have been a larger Steventon Green. The early focus of settlement along this Green edge also provided easy access backing onto the Mill Brook, and was linked by a narrow lane (now only intermittently marked by field boundaries) running roughly parallel with the brook and later known as the Twychen. The Causeway at Steventon is judged by Currie to be a secondary element in the village plan, cutting across the Green, added as a planned element to the village, perhaps shortly after the Priory of Pré acquired the manor in 1121. The later medieval manorial records produced during Westminster Abbey’s ownership from 1399 onwards have allowed Currie to demonstrate the scale and pattern of late medieval settlement shrinkage. Between 1380 and 1560 a conservative estimate indicates the loss of between 67 and 77 houses from the village (although there was some rebuilding during this period). Whilst there was some loss of buildings and amalgamations on the Causeway, the majority of the retraction occurred in the southern part of the village, as mapped by Currie. [2] It seems that this more southerly area became less attractive for settlement or re-building because of a number of factors, including less ease of access to the open fields, the smaller size of house plots compared to the Causeway, and potentially from the 1430s onwards pollution of the brook by the tanning industry. Ironically then, although being the later element in the settlement plan, over time the Causeway became the main village street, with an unusually large number of medieval and Tudor period timber-framed buildings surviving to the present day. The timing of the medieval depopulation at Steventon has also been explored by documentary references in the manorial records to taxation payments by incomers and (sometimes oblique) references to empty house plots. It seems that the village had a flourishing cloth-finishing industry from the 1390s onwards, and decline did not set in until after the early 1430s, when pollution by tanners may have had an impact on the cloth industry. [3] The national taxation evidence appears to support this picture. Steventon was always one of Berkshire's more populous vills, having a percentile ranking within Berkshire of 0.93 for individuals enumerated at Domesday. Steventon’s 1334 Lay Subsidy communal assessment (made at a tenth) is unusually low, but the 47 taxpayers present in the 1327 Lay Subsidy confirm the vill was still one of Berkshire’s largest, with a percentile ranking of 0.94. Steventon had exactly the same ranking for the 1381 Poll Tax (0.94, 171 taxpayers). A decline is however indicated by the 32 taxpayers present at the 1524 and 1525 Lay Subsidies, giving a ranking of 0.67 and 0.66 respectively, with only a slight recovery by the 1801 Census (101 inhabitants, ranking 0.73). The village’s post-depopulation post-medieval layout showed little change from Rocque’s 1761 map through to the late nineteenth century, but modern building has now altered the balance of the village, adding new housing to the north, and repopulating some of the southern parts of the village. Identified by C. Currie.

name: Straight Lane, nr Eastbury
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces (Eastbury)
description_snippet: Two small earthwork platforms (perhaps building platforms) on the north side of Straight Lane outside Eastbury were noted and sketched by Julian Richards in 1976.  These are located several hundred metres outside the main core of Eastbury, and may represent the remains of a former separate farmstead or hamlet.
description_full: Two small earthwork platforms (perhaps building platforms) on the north side of Straight Lane outside Eastbury were noted and sketched by Julian Richards in 1976. [1] These are located several hundred metres outside the main core of Eastbury, and may represent the remains of a former separate farmstead or hamlet. However the site has been classed as shrinkage at the edge of Eastbury, on the basis that Rocque’s 1761 map shows buildings in the south-eastern part of the village that were lost by the time of the 1812 Ordnance Survey drawing. These lost buildings were mainly along the south side of the Newbury Road, eastwards from its junction with Straight Lane, but some houses also seem to have been lost along Straight Lane itself, perhaps even around the sharp bend leading towards this site. The site of the building platforms was presumably deserted at some point before the 1750s, although the first edition 6 inch and 25 inch Ordnance Survey maps (surveyed 1878) did still show a small paddock at this location, perhaps marking a former boundary of the house plots. Identified by the HER.

name: Stroud
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: No evidence has been identified on the ground for a DMV at Stroud, but documentary evidence does point to a late medieval reduction in settlement in this area, part of which may have been focussed in the floodplain of the Thames.
description_full: No evidence has been identified on the ground for a DMV at Stroud, but documentary evidence does point to a late medieval reduction in settlement in this area, part of which may have been focussed in the floodplain of the Thames. Pottery of twelfth or thirteenth century date has been reported from the river bank at Pinkhill Lock Marina, [1] and settlement of some form may have existed in this vicinity and west of Stroud Copse. The documentary evidence confirms the likelihood of some river-side settlement, with tax payers at Stroud in the 1327 Lay Subsidy including Alice and Isabell ‘atte Flodyate’, Thomas and Roger ‘atte Strode’ (the name comes from a marshy area with brushwood) and John ‘atte Ware’ (i.e. Weir). [2] This lay subsidy recorded 20 taxpayers in all, [3] implying a reasonable population and the 1334 Lay Subsidy was also slightly above average for accepted DMVs. However one difficulty in interpreting the documentary evidence for Stroud is that the name was applied to a tithing within Cumnor parish in both the medieval and post-medieval periods. Consequently some of the population recorded is likely to have been dispersed in areas away from the riverbank. Evidence for a late-medieval population decline comes from the Abingdon Abbey dissolution accounts, showing that customary rents from the vill were paid by 7 tenants, holding 20 former tenements between them, including nine messuages and 10 tofts. [2] The 1524/5 Lay Subsidies probably also reflect this decline, with 13 and 11 taxpayers respectively. By the time of the seventeenth-century Hearth Tax 10 houses were recorded at Stroud, [2] but one suspects the majority of these may have been found dispersed around the tithing. As a comparison, the 1841 Census recorded 12 inhabited dwellings for the tithing, but by this stage none seem to have been by the river near Stroud Copse, and indeed this area must have been deserted before Rocque’s map of 1761. One probable focus of post-medieval population within the tithing is at Farmoor, which appears to have been a more substantial settlement in 1761 compared to the two farms shown on the 1814 Enclosure map [4] and late nineteenth-century Ordnance Survey map. Whether Farmoor was occupied in the medieval period is uncertain – Gelling’s survey found no medieval references to the place-name. [5] The modern landscape around Stroud has altered radically with Farmoor Resevoir occupying much of the landscape to the south, and new housing occupying the north side of the reservoir. Beresford and Hurst suggested a seventeenth or eighteenth-century date for depopulation at Stroud, [6] but as noted above, this seems rather late for the assumed riverside settlement of Stroud itself, and indeed it remains unclear whether any such medieval settlement was substantial enough to be considered a village. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Sugworth
e179_last: c. 1200 carrucage
description_snippet: As early as 1813 it was recognised by Lysons that Sugworth had 'once been a considerable hamlet'.  The main evidence for a DMV at Sugworth is a series of earthworks to the south of Sugworth Farm, extending over perhaps 100m or more and described as 'an ordered system of rectilinear platforms and plots defined by ditches, with ‘units’ whose average dimensions are 60m x 48m'.
description_full: As early as 1813 it was recognised by Lysons that Sugworth had 'once been a considerable hamlet'. [1] The main evidence for a DMV at Sugworth is a series of earthworks to the south of Sugworth Farm, extending over perhaps 100m or more and described as 'an ordered system of rectilinear platforms and plots defined by ditches, with ‘units’ whose average dimensions are 60m x 48m'. [2] These earthworks were planned by the National Mapping Programme, but had already been identified as building platforms and village plots in a field investigation of 1963. [2] It would appear some of the earthworks have been lost to ploughing and, in the western part, to the construction of the A34 dual carriageway. [3] A further complication may be that at least part of the area is marked as a golf course on Ordnance Survey maps of 1914 and 1922, so it is possible some earthworks could relate to any associated landscaping for the course. The documentary evidence for a DMV at Sugworth is more ambiguous; indeed were it not for the archaeological evidence the site would probably be classified as a manorial or hamlet site. Sugworth appears in Domesday Book, but details of its estate are grouped with landholdings in Sunningwell and Kennington. The manor was held in the medieval period by Abingdon Abbey, and it appears in the E179 database only once, in an Abbey carrucage list of c. 1200. Sugworth is recorded in the 1316 Nomina Villarum, albeit grouped with three other places, and it appears in the 1428 Feudal Aid for a quarter of a knight’s fee, where curiously the vill is said to have previously been called 'Saucers'. [4] The dissolution accounts for Abingdon Abbey record that John Audelett and his wife held a 26 year lease for 'Sugworth, Sawcers and Borrowleys' and various lands, whilst a widow, Katherine Audelett was also recorded as a lessee of Sugworth. [5] This entry might suggest that any medieval settlement at Sugworth had been reduced by the sixteenth century, falling into the hands of one or two families, along with other lands in the area. By 1761 John Rocque’s map shows a single un-named building in the area of Sugworth Farm, whilst the 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing actually names the building as 'Radley Farm'. The name ‘Sugworth Farm’ appears on late nineteenth-century Ordnance Survey maps. Indentified by the NMR.

name: Swallowfield
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Although neither the local HER nor the NMR classes Swallowfield as such, it may be a potential candidate for a shifted village, based on the isolation of its church from the main village focus 0.5km to the west. The church is perhaps twelfth century in origin,  and sits on the opposite bank of the Blackwater River from the main village street, a pattern that can be seen clearly as far back as Rocque’s map of 1761.
description_full: Although neither the local HER nor the NMR classes Swallowfield as such, it may be a potential candidate for a shifted village, based on the isolation of its church from the main village focus 0.5km to the west. The church is perhaps twelfth century in origin, [1] and sits on the opposite bank of the Blackwater River from the main village street, a pattern that can be seen clearly as far back as Rocque’s map of 1761. Although no archaeological evidence for abandoned areas of settlement has been discovered, this may reflect a lack of archaeological investigation. The influence of Swallowfield Park on possible local settlement shift or desertion also needs further consideration. The park’s history dates back to the fourteenth century, with subsequent post-medieval re-modelling [2, 3]. Both the main village street and the church can be found at the edge of the park, which also extends into part of the landscape between the two elements, raising the possibility that it may have had a role in creating the disjuncture between village and church. Identified during Beresford's Lost Villages Project.

name: Swinford
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Swinford was listed as a DMV in 1981 by the Medieval Village Research Group, however the NMR entry states tersely that it is 'not accepted as a deserted village'.  The site is not listed by the local HER. Although there is no mention of physical evidence for a DMV here (and it is perhaps unlikely to be found as the site is now dominated by a waterworks), the documentary sources are suggestive of a decline.
description_full: Swinford was listed as a DMV in 1981 by the Medieval Village Research Group, however the NMR entry states tersely that it is 'not accepted as a deserted village'. [1] The site is not listed by the local HER. Although there is no mention of physical evidence for a DMV here (and it is perhaps unlikely to be found as the site is now dominated by a waterworks), the documentary sources are suggestive of a decline. The 1334 Lay Subsidy assessment for Swinford was just below average for Hormer Hundred, whilst by 1525 just one tax payer was listed. On Rocque's map of 1761 four buildings are shown in the area, which seems to have acted as a ferry crossing point on the Thames. Further research on the medieval documentation may be useful. Identified by the MVRG.

name: Thrupp
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Thrupp today consists of only a main house and (two) cottages but the documentary evidence in particular suggests that this hamlet was more significant in the medieval period, if always relatively small. Only limited archaeological work has taken place, with some small trenches in gardens to the east of Thrupp Cottages producing thirteenth-century gullies and c. 500 sherds of medieval pottery.
description_full: Thrupp today consists of only a main house and (two) cottages but the documentary evidence in particular suggests that this hamlet was more significant in the medieval period, if always relatively small. Only limited archaeological work has taken place, with some small trenches in gardens to the east of Thrupp Cottages producing thirteenth-century gullies and c. 500 sherds of medieval pottery. [1] Thrupp is not mentioned in Domesday Book, contrary to some sources which appear to confuse it with the village of the same name near Kidlington in Oxfordshire. However the settlement may have existed by the late Anglo-Saxon period. It is mentioned as a ‘wick’ in the Abingdon Chronicle in an entry concerning alterations to the channel of the Thames in the 1050s or 1060s. [2] Other chronicle entries detail renders of cheese and eels owed to the Abbey from Thrupp. [3] The early description of Thrupp as a ‘wick’ might suggest a small settlement perhaps specialising in dairying, although the description could be applied to larger settlements too. The place-name ‘Thrupp’ itself suggests a description of a small hamlet or farm. [4] By the fourteenth century some of the taxation evidence for Thrupp suggests that, although still relatively small, it had perhaps grown to resemble a small village. Eight taxpayers were listed in the 1327 Lay Subsidy giving a percentile ranking of 0.18 within Berkshire, [5] although the 1334 communal subsidy figure had a lower percentile ranking of 0.06. In 1352 Thrupp received an 87% relief on its 1334 tax quota, [5] suggesting that the settlement had suffered disproportionately in the Black Death. For a relatively small place this may have caused a significant episode of depopulation from which it never fully recovered. However, the statement that after 1352 'no more is heard of it' [6] is not correct. Thrupp continued to be recorded, often separately, in medieval taxation records. In the Lay Subsidies of 1524/5 Thrupp was grouped with nearby Wick and had five taxpayers listed, the majority of whom perhaps lived at Thrupp, since Wick was said to contain only one messuage in 1538. [7] The Dissolution Accounts of Abingdon Abbey confirm the picture of a small hamlet persisting at Thrupp, with three tenants each holding a messuage and a fourth tenant having 6 ‘former holdings’ which included four messuages and two tofts. [5] Although these ‘former’ holdings might have been sub-let, they may also reflect settlement contraction. By the time of the seventeenth-century Hearth Tax Thrupp contained only four houses. Rocque’s 1761 map shows two small groups of buildings, perhaps still present into the nineteenth century, but the southerly buildings, which were situated south of the disused railway line, have since been lost. The modern landscape surrounding the former settlement has been affected by gravel extraction. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Trunkwell, nr Little Copse
e179_last: 1624 three fifteenths and tenths (Trunkwell)
description_snippet: Possible ditches and enclosures on aerial photographs, but could be drainage or old field boundaries.  Close to medieval vill of Trunkwell (Farm) but documents suggest this is likely to have been a hamlet rather than a village. The 1524/5 references are to Beech Hill (which perhaps included Trunkwell). The field immediately surrounding the Farm may be of more interest.
description_full: Possible ditches and enclosures on aerial photographs, but could be drainage or old field boundaries. [1] Close to medieval vill of Trunkwell (Farm) but documents suggest this is likely to have been a hamlet rather than a village. The 1524/5 references are to Beech Hill (which perhaps included Trunkwell). The field immediately surrounding the Farm may be of more interest. In 1334 the settlement is recorded as Trucwell and has been identified by Glasscock as Beech Hill. [2] This identification is continued by Fenwick for the Poll Taxes. [3] Identified by the HER.

name: Tubney
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The earthwork remains of the DMV of Tubney have been identified and mapped by John Brooks in a field immediately north of Tubney Manor Farm. Various hollow ways and banks were identifiable, suggesting a site 'limited in extent', but almost certainly the DMV. [1, 2, 3] Further evidence of the former settlement south of the farm may have been ploughed out.
description_full: The earthwork remains of the DMV of Tubney have been identified and mapped by John Brooks in a field immediately north of Tubney Manor Farm. Various hollow ways and banks were identifiable, suggesting a site 'limited in extent', but almost certainly the DMV. [1, 2, 3] Further evidence of the former settlement south of the farm may have been ploughed out. [1] The current Tubney Manor Farm is thought to have been built in the early seventeenth century, [4] but the site is partially moated and may have been the medieval manorial site. The site of Tubney chapel or church, referred to in twelfth century documents, [5] is marked about 100m to the south-west of Tubney Manor Farm on the Ordnance Survey first edition 6 inch map of 1883. The landscape to the south of Tubney Manor Farm has also been affected by modern quarrying, and excavation in advance of extraction in this area has also identified Anglo-Saxon and medieval ditches. [6] The documentary evidence for Tubney provides some clues to its former size and date of depopulation. The 1327 Lay Subsidy records 21 tax payers, making it a fairly populous vill, [7] although its 1334 tax quota was only roughly the norm for a Berkshire DMV, perhaps reflecting a relative lack of taxable wealth. The vill received no post-Black Death taxation relief and still had 27 taxpayers present in 1381, suggesting that a sustainable if relatively small village probably still existed. An extent of 1394 confirmed that the manor still had 20 tenants, although some holdings were unoccupied and a degree of shrinkage had apparently occurred since the earlier fourteenth century. [1] The major period of depopulation at Tubney seems to have taken place in the fifteenth century. Brooks has noted some enclosure (of uncertain degree but perhaps including one of the major open fields) had taken place by 1445. [1] The vill was not recorded in the 1524/5 Lay Subsidies, implying desertion was complete by this stage, whilst John Leland, passing through in c. 1540, noted that Tubney was a lost village, with a derelict Manor House 'now clene downe' and a surviving church. [8] The church, which had a graveyard, is thought to have disappeared entirely by 1806 [1] – it is not clear if Rocque’s map of 1761 shows it or a nearby cottage. The post-medieval period also seems to have seen new settlement growth in the south of the parish, where the modern village has taken hold, separated from the medieval village site by the expanse of Tubney Wood. Possibly most of the nine houses recorded in the 1663/4 Hearth Tax [3] were by then in this southern part of the parish. Tubney House seems to date from the early seventeenth century, [9] whilst Tubney Warren House dates from c. 1730-40. [10] St Lawrence’s Church was built between 1844-7, [11] whilst the majority of settlement along the Fyfield-Abingdon Road dates from the nineteenth century or later. Although medieval precursors for the farms shown on Rocque’s 1761 map in this area cannot be ruled out, Brooks has suggested that the lack of 1524/5 tax returns may indicate an ‘empty parish’ that was later re-populated by the new farms to the south. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Tulwick
description_snippet: Although Tulwick does not appear in the medieval taxation record, there is good archaeological evidence for a medieval settlement, probably a village, to the north of Tulwick Farm. [1, 2] The earthworks of the site were surveyed in 1963 by Reading University and again c. 1976 by C.J. Bond showing a village plan of a north-south hollow way and an area of ‘green’ towards the north.
description_full: Although Tulwick does not appear in the medieval taxation record, there is good archaeological evidence for a medieval settlement, probably a village, to the north of Tulwick Farm. [1, 2] The earthworks of the site were surveyed in 1963 by Reading University and again c. 1976 by C.J. Bond showing a village plan of a north-south hollow way and an area of ‘green’ towards the north. Bond’s survey identified 'some house sites and croft boundaries'. [3, 4] The earthworks had been disturbed by later clay pits and the southern part of the site has been ploughed. The site was excavated by the Wantage & District Field Club between 1962-6 apparently finding medieval structures as well as pottery from the twelfth to the early sixteenth century. [1] Tulwick Farm itself is thought to be seventeenth-century. [5] A handful of buildings (mainly barns) shown on Rocque’s 1761 map and the nineteenth-century Ordnance Survey maps at the edges of the site have subsequently been lost. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Ufton Green (Ufton Nervet)
e179_last: 1679-80 (Ufton Nevet) - grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The settlement of Ufton Green contains the former site of St John the Baptist’s church, first recorded in a presentment of 1297. [1, 2] St John the Baptist was the parish church for Ufton Nervet, one of the two main manors in the Ufton area, and the hamlet of Ufton Green may formerly have been regarded as the main village of Ufton Nervet Parish, perhaps bearing that name.
description_full: The settlement of Ufton Green contains the former site of St John the Baptist’s church, first recorded in a presentment of 1297. [1, 2] St John the Baptist was the parish church for Ufton Nervet, one of the two main manors in the Ufton area, and the hamlet of Ufton Green may formerly have been regarded as the main village of Ufton Nervet Parish, perhaps bearing that name. The modern settlement is probably a contraction of the medieval settlement. The church was converted into a private dwelling sometime after the parish merged with Ufton Robert in 1434-5, and only a wall now survives. [1, 2] The representation of this settlement on Rocque’s map of 1761 appears to show a larger settlement footprint than the modern Ufton Green, but the schematic nature of the map makes interpretation difficult. The documentary evidence either refers to just 'Ufton' or Ufton Nervet. Identified by the HER.

name: Ufton Robert
e179_last: 1625 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The church of St Peter’s is a Victorian (1862) rebuild of an earlier church, which was considered to be the parish church for Ufton Robert,  one of the two main manors in the Ufton area. These two manors are probably the successors of the two Domesday Book manors of Ufton, and originally Ufton Nervet and Ufton Robert each had their own parish churches.
description_full: The church of St Peter’s is a Victorian (1862) rebuild of an earlier church, which was considered to be the parish church for Ufton Robert, [1] one of the two main manors in the Ufton area. These two manors are probably the successors of the two Domesday Book manors of Ufton, and originally Ufton Nervet and Ufton Robert each had their own parish churches. The two parishes were merged in 1434-5, [1] and St Peter’s became the main church for the new parish which was usually known as Ufton Nervet. It is not clear whether any substantial medieval settlement existed around Ufton Robert’s parish church. The medieval manorial centre was probably at the moated site situated 350m to the south-west of the church. [2] Possibly other medieval settlement was dispersed throughout the parish. On Rocque’s map of 1761 buildings still seem to be indicated in the vicinity of the moated site, but only one building is shown next to the church. The settlement that now surrounds the (rebuilt) church seems to be largely late nineteenth or twentieth-century growth, and confusingly this settlement is now marked on Ordnanec Survey maps as ‘Ufton Nervet’. The documentary evidence either refers to 'Ufton' or Ufton Nervet. Identified by the NMR.

name: Wadley
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Wadley has been identified as a DMV by John Brooks.  The NMR has no details on any archaeological remains for this site and it is not listed by the Oxfordshire HER. Wadley first appears in the E179 database in the Lay Subsidy of 1523-5, although this was not published by Sheail.
description_full: Wadley has been identified as a DMV by John Brooks. [1] The NMR has no details on any archaeological remains for this site and it is not listed by the Oxfordshire HER. Wadley first appears in the E179 database in the Lay Subsidy of 1523-5, although this was not published by Sheail. [2] It does however appear as a manorial centre in other medieval records, and a park may have been created either there, or at nearby Wicklesham, in 1365. [3, 4]. The earliest phase of Wadley House itself is sixteenth century. [5] Identified by John Brooks.

name: Wawcott
description_snippet: The place-name (originally 'Walcot') is recorded from at least the thirteenth century,  but may have earlier origins, perhaps referring to a 'British' (native) settlement. There is however no firm evidence that it should be considered as a former medieval village. Identified from place-name evidence.
description_full: The place-name (originally 'Walcot') is recorded from at least the thirteenth century, [1] but may have earlier origins, perhaps referring to a 'British' (native) settlement. There is however no firm evidence that it should be considered as a former medieval village. Identified from place-name evidence.

name: Weston
e179_last: 1624 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: Classed as a deserted settlement on the West Berkshire HER, with no firm supporting evidence.  Perhaps more appropriately classed as a shrunken village. Areas of housing shown on Rocque's 1761 map (including to the south-west of the village) appear to have been subsequently lost.
description_full: Classed as a deserted settlement on the West Berkshire HER, with no firm supporting evidence. [1] Perhaps more appropriately classed as a shrunken village. Areas of housing shown on Rocque's 1761 map (including to the south-west of the village) appear to have been subsequently lost. The lost areas may have been occupied in the medieval period, but it is not clear if any contraction can be dated to then as well as the post-medieval period. The 1334 Lay Subsidy was below average for all Berkshire vills, but slightly above the average of accepted DMVs. However only five tax payers were recorded here in 1327, giving a Berkshire percentile ranking of 0.08. [2] Identified by the HER.

name: Whatcombe
e179_last: 1677 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: Whatcombe was identified as a lost settlement in the 1870s, when Walter Money noted building foundations south-west of the old Manor House.  A century later Julian Richards observed earthworks at the site forming a 'complex of house platforms, banks and a hollow-way.'  The site was subsequently scheduled, although a significant proportion of the earthworks are thought to have been ploughed level.
description_full: Whatcombe was identified as a lost settlement in the 1870s, when Walter Money noted building foundations south-west of the old Manor House. [1] A century later Julian Richards observed earthworks at the site forming a 'complex of house platforms, banks and a hollow-way.' [2] The site was subsequently scheduled, although a significant proportion of the earthworks are thought to have been ploughed level. [2] Evidence of potential tofts and crofts and perhaps one building platform towards the west of the scheduled area are thought to be visible on aerial photographs. [3] The documentary evidence suggests Whatcombe was only a small medieval settlement, both at the time of Domesday and the 1334 Lay Subsidy, its assessment for the latter being easily the smallest of the 11 vills within Eagle Hundred. Nevertheless, the settlement possessed a church by the twelfth century, and within this sparsely populated part of the Berkshire Downs Whatcombe formed a parish that may have persisted until the early sixteenth century. By 1596 entries for Whatcombe were found in the Fawley Parish Registers. [4] Beresford and Hurst estimated that desertion at Whatcombe took place between 1450 and 1700; [5] certainly by 1761 the settlement was shown on Rocque’s map as just a farm. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Whistley Green
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: Whistley Green has been suggested as a shrunken medieval village, on the basis of fieldwalking evidence for a medieval pottery scatter near the settlement (EBAS scatter no. 17, to the east). [1, 2] Medieval pot and tile is known from just north of the settlement,  whilst medieval features (ditches, pits, ridge and furrow) and pottery have also been found during evaluation works further to the south-west in Whistley...
description_full: Whistley Green has been suggested as a shrunken medieval village, on the basis of fieldwalking evidence for a medieval pottery scatter near the settlement (EBAS scatter no. 17, to the east). [1, 2] Medieval pot and tile is known from just north of the settlement, [3] whilst medieval features (ditches, pits, ridge and furrow) and pottery have also been found during evaluation works further to the south-west in Whistley Park. [4] Two watching briefs of works immediately south of Whistley Green found no archaeological deposits. [5, 6] Although Whistley is found in Domesday Book and was a late Anglo-Saxon property of Abingdon Abbey, the location of the earliest settlement is uncertain – the former site of Whistley Park Mansion has been suggested as a possibility. [7] The eleventh-century chapel referred to in the Abingdon Chronicle may either be lost, or perhaps a reference to the church site at Hurst. [8] Nevertheless it seems likely that Whistley Green is actually a later, secondary settlement focus in the local area (in common with many medieval ‘green’ suffix settlements). [9] As such the village would likely represent (at least initial) settlement expansion on an area of common waste or pasture, perhaps developing within a generally dispersed settlement pattern. Whether the medieval surface finds surrounding Whistley Green genuinely represent a significant episode of later medieval or post-medieval settlement contraction (as opposed to intensive manuring activity, for example) would require further research to establish. Identified by the HER.

name: Whitley
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The archaeological remains of the DMV of Whitley are thought to be located in fields to the east of Whitley Copse. A field investigation in 1963 reported that 'the sites of approximately eight buildings are visible as patches of stone in ploughed fields' at c. SP 443 047, with thirteenth-century pottery also found at the site.
description_full: The archaeological remains of the DMV of Whitley are thought to be located in fields to the east of Whitley Copse. A field investigation in 1963 reported that 'the sites of approximately eight buildings are visible as patches of stone in ploughed fields' at c. SP 443 047, with thirteenth-century pottery also found at the site. [1] More recent analysis of remaining earthworks at this location and further west towards the copse as part of the Thames Valley NMP has identified at least two 'polygonal enclosures' and further field boundaries. [1] The HER reports a tradition that the field with former stone buildings was called 'the graveyard' or the 'churchyard'. [2] It would appear based on this evidence that Upper Whitley Farm and Lower Whitley Farm originated as post-medieval farmsteads rather than either forming a remnant of the medieval village. They are shown as East and West 'Wheatley' Farm respectively on Rocque’s map of 1761 (with the latter seemingly having a significant number of ancillary buildings or cottages) and the current farmhouses are thought to date from the early/mid seventeenth century (Upper) and mid seventeenth century (Lower). [3, 4] The documentary evidence for Whitley suggests it may have become depopulated in the decades following the Black Death. Ten tax payers at Whitley were wealthy enough to pay the 1327 Lay Subsidy, [5] suggesting that a village existed, although oddly in 1334 Whitley’s tax quota was one of the smallest in the county. In 1351 Whitley was granted 100% relief on this already modest tax quota, [5] presumably because of the effects of the plague. By the 1524/5 Lay Subsidy only two tax payers were recorded, whilst the Abingdon Abbey dissolution accounts show only one free tenant with a single messuage and lands (including rented demesne) and a lessee renting six closes, but with no mention of a messuage. [5] The five houses recorded in the seventeenth-century Hearth Tax presumably included the post-medieval farms and any associated cottages, and by the 1841 Census only three buildings were inhabited within Whitley tithing. Identified by the ER and NMR.

name: Wickfield
description_snippet: Wickfield was classed by John Brooks as ‘doubtfully deserted’,  and there seems to be little evidence that this place was ever more than a farmstead or small hamlet. No earthworks of former settlement remains are recorded on the NMR or HER, although cropmarks of former field banks and lynchets of unknown date have been identified from fields to the north-west of Wickfield Farm.
description_full: Wickfield was classed by John Brooks as ‘doubtfully deserted’, [1] and there seems to be little evidence that this place was ever more than a farmstead or small hamlet. No earthworks of former settlement remains are recorded on the NMR or HER, although cropmarks of former field banks and lynchets of unknown date have been identified from fields to the north-west of Wickfield Farm. [2] Wickfield was not recorded as a separate vill in the E179 taxation records, although the earliest record of the place-name identified by Margaret Gelling dates from a feet of fine of 1199 concerning one and a quarter virgates of land in Wickfield. [3, 4] Gelling notes that the place-name does not seem to be linked to a lost ‘Wick’ place, [3] and the name may perhaps have originally been coined in reference to nearby Wickham in Welford parish. Wickfield appears on Rocque’s 1761 map as a single farmstead and it may be that along with nearby Oakhanger, a dispersed settlement pattern has existed in the immediate local area since the medieval period. Identified by John Brooks.

name: Wicklesham
description_snippet: The NMR records that 'earthworks resembling a deserted medieval village have been identified from 1969 aerial photographs at Wicklesham',  whilst the Oxfordshire HER notes a description of the site that includes '2 linear fishponds, [a] raised roadway, and several building earthworks'.
description_full: The NMR records that 'earthworks resembling a deserted medieval village have been identified from 1969 aerial photographs at Wicklesham', [1] whilst the Oxfordshire HER notes a description of the site that includes '2 linear fishponds, [a] raised roadway, and several building earthworks'. [2] There is seemingly nothing in the documentary evidence to suggest that Wicklesham was a village rather than a medieval manorial centre or hamlet. Part of the area of earthworks seems to have been occupied by a now grubbed out area of Wicklesham Copse in the nineteenth century, but this wood is not shown on Rocque’s 1761 map. A possible site, but further evidence is needed on its date and extent before it could be classed as a DMV. Wicklesham Lodge is shown on Rocque’s map, whilst a medieval park may have been created here (or at Wadley) in 1365. [3] Identified by the NMR and HER.

name: Willington
description_snippet: Willington has been suggested as a doubtful DMV site,  of uncertain location. The place-name appears in Domesday as a reasonably populous vill with a church, thought to have possibly encompassed the western part of Long Wittenham parish,  and perhaps some or all of Didcot.  An Anglo-Saxon charter for Appleford (from c. 1200, but claiming to be from c.
description_full: Willington has been suggested as a doubtful DMV site, [1] of uncertain location. The place-name appears in Domesday as a reasonably populous vill with a church, thought to have possibly encompassed the western part of Long Wittenham parish, [2] and perhaps some or all of Didcot. [3] An Anglo-Saxon charter for Appleford (from c. 1200, but claiming to be from c. 895) includes a boundary clause indicating part of Willington bordered Appleford. [4] The oldest known specific location using the vill’s name appears to be the house now called the Manor, west of Long Wittenham church in the heart of that village, but formerly named as Willington’s Farm on the first edition 6 and 25 inch Ordnance Survey maps surveyed in 1875-7. This house, which may date back to the seventeenth century, [5] has been used as the location for the database entry, although any ‘lost settlement’ is presumably mooted for the western half of Long Wittenham parish. However, two houses in that area using the Willington name appear to be relatively recent. Willington’s Down Farm (at SU 541 919) is said by its listed building entry to be early eighteenth century, [6] but is absent from Rocque’s 1761 map and the 1809 Enclosure map for Long Wittenham, [7] therefore probably only being built sometime before 1875-7. Wigbald (Farm) at SU 539 923 is more recent still, not appearing on Ordnance Survey maps until the 1920s or 1930s. The modernity of these buildings suggests we should be highly cautious in adopting Gelling’s suggestion [2] that they provide further evidence that Willington covered the western part of Long Wittenham. Willington is absent from the E179 database taxation documents, although other documentary references to the place continue until at least 1205. [2] The earliest reference to Didcot documented by Gelling dates from 1206, [8] and given the apparent close association of the manorial history of both places, the possibility that Didcot supplanted Willington as the usual name for at least part of the former Domesday vill may be worth exploring. However this still leaves the puzzle of the name appearing in the middle of Long Wittenham village. Taken together with the lack of archaeological evidence for any obvious location of a lost settlement, Willington is certainly best classified as a doubtful site, albeit one worthy of further research. Identified by John Brooks.

name: Old Windsor
e179_last: 1679 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: A series of excavations took place at Old Windsor between 1953 and 1958, with only limited details published.  Taken together with later excavations on this scheduled site, there is evidence for occupation in the Roman and early-mid Anglo-Saxon periods, with a higher status settlement present from at least the ninth century, if not earlier.
description_full: A series of excavations took place at Old Windsor between 1953 and 1958, with only limited details published. [1] Taken together with later excavations on this scheduled site, there is evidence for occupation in the Roman and early-mid Anglo-Saxon periods, with a higher status settlement present from at least the ninth century, if not earlier. A tenth and eleventh-century phase seems to include a royal ‘palace’ complex used by late Anglo-Saxon and early Norman kings. Old Windsor hosted a royal court in 1107 after which this function was supplanted locally by Windsor Castle. It is thought that the royal vill included an associated settlement, probably accounting for the 95 hidage mentioned in Domesday Book. Evidence for this settlement has emerged in the form of tightly dated eleventh and twelfth-century occupation remains from two areas, ‘The Paddock’ and ‘The Manor’. [2] The 1950s excavations found evidence of a thirteenth to fourteenth-century ‘Grange’ building, but it seems possible that the substantive settlement had already been abandoned during the twelfth century. Nevertheless Old Windsor still gave its name to a wider parish and the dispersed settlement in this larger area no doubt accounts for some of the taxpayers recorded in the vill throughout the medieval period. The area south of the scheduled site of Kingsbury has seen substantial twentieth-century housing development. Identified through fieldwork.

name: Woodhill
e179_last: 1352 three fifteenths and tenths (schedule of reductions)
description_snippet: Woodhill has been identified by John Brooks as the site of a DMV,  although no evidence was found of settlement earthworks on aerial photographs by the Lambourn Downs NMP.  Woodhill was a medieval settlement, although perhaps more likely to have been a hamlet or merely a farm, and can be found in the 1316 Feudal Aid.
description_full: Woodhill has been identified by John Brooks as the site of a DMV, [1] although no evidence was found of settlement earthworks on aerial photographs by the Lambourn Downs NMP. [2] Woodhill was a medieval settlement, although perhaps more likely to have been a hamlet or merely a farm, and can be found in the 1316 Feudal Aid. [3] It appears in only one document in the E179 database, although this instance may lend some limited support to the case for a DMV. The document is a schedule of taxation reliefs from 1352 to take account of the effect of the Black Death. Woodhill is listed with a reduction of 18s 1d. [4] Woodhill does not appear in the 1334 Lay Subsidy list, but this reduction alone would count for nearly one fifth of the quota for ‘Challow’ (presumably including both East and West Challow). Although we do not know how large a population contributed to Woodhill’s original share of the quota, a case could theoretically be made for Woodhill being more than a single farm before the Black Death, but whether it was a hamlet, small village or part of a dispersed pattern is difficult to say. The farm is depicted on Rocque’s map of 1761. Identified by John Brooks.

name: Woolley
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The remains of Woolley DMV have been identified in a field immediately south of Woolley Park and south-west of Woolley Farm. Traces of the village are said to have been observed c. the 1920s and fragmented earthworks of the settlement are thought to be shown on aerial photographs of 1955 and 1964.
description_full: The remains of Woolley DMV have been identified in a field immediately south of Woolley Park and south-west of Woolley Farm. Traces of the village are said to have been observed c. the 1920s and fragmented earthworks of the settlement are thought to be shown on aerial photographs of 1955 and 1964. [1] This field has also been identified as the site of Woolley Chapel, which existed by the twelfth century but had disappeared before 1759. [2] About 200m west of the village site in Mitchell Copse a possible ‘ringwork’ has been identified, accompanied by surface finds of twelfth-century pottery. [3] The vill of Woolley is recorded in Domesday Book, and seems to have been reasonably populous by the high medieval period. An extent of 1291 records 24 tenants (one free, 23 customary), whilst 12 people qualified to pay the 1327 Lay Subsidy tax. [4] The vill’s 1334 tax quota was below average for accepted DMVs, but it received only a modest 20% relief in 1352. The decline of Woolley is more likely to be linked to the process of late medieval enclosure. The enclosure inquests of 1517 heard that the landlord of Woolley, the Nuns Minoresses of London, had enclosed a total of 80 acres in 1493 and 1497 in ‘Chaddleworth’, evicting 12 people, with a further 120 acres in Woolley (perhaps of demesne land) converted from arable to sheep pasture in 1509. [5, 6] Although the 1493/7 enclosures are said to have taken place in ‘Chaddleworth’ it seems likely that these accusations also refer to land and messuages in the Woolley part of the parish. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Woolstone
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The evidence for settlement shrinkage at Woolstone comes in the form of earthworks, (originally mapped from aerial photographs and surveyed in 1974) that can be found to the south-west of the village, in the fields immediately west of the church and either side of the road towards Woolstone Hill.
description_full: The evidence for settlement shrinkage at Woolstone comes in the form of earthworks, (originally mapped from aerial photographs and surveyed in 1974) that can be found to the south-west of the village, in the fields immediately west of the church and either side of the road towards Woolstone Hill. [1, 2, 3] The loss of settlement from this area might explain why the church (the earliest fabric of which is thought to be c. 1200) and Manor Farm occupy such a peripheral position within the current village.[4] Evidence of probable medieval ridge and furrow earthworks has also been observed from aerial photographs to the north-east and to the west of the village, perhaps in part reflecting a reduction in arable farming at some stage. [5] The map evidence suggests that the loss of some of the buildings in the area of these earthworks, particularly along the road to Woolstone Hill took place in the post-medieval period, after Rocque’s map of 1761. It is also noticeable that Woolstone appears to have had a large population in the Domesday Book, but was a below average ranked vill at the time of the 1334 Lay Subsidy, although whether this reflects genuine change in the status or size of the village is unclear. Identified by the NMR and HER.

name: Wyld Court
e179_last: 1624 three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: No archaeological remains of a DMV at Wyld are known, but the documentary evidence confirms that it was a medieval settlement, albeit probably always relatively small. In 1334 and 1381 the settlement has been incorrectly identified as Wellhouse. Only two tax payers qualified to pay the 1327 Lay Subsidy,  and Wyld’s 1334 tax quota was also below average for accepted DMVs in Berkshire.
description_full: No archaeological remains of a DMV at Wyld are known, but the documentary evidence confirms that it was a medieval settlement, albeit probably always relatively small. In 1334 and 1381 the settlement has been incorrectly identified as Wellhouse. Only two tax payers qualified to pay the 1327 Lay Subsidy, [1] and Wyld’s 1334 tax quota was also below average for accepted DMVs in Berkshire. The settlement received only a 19% tax relief in 1352, [1] and 12 poll tax payers were recorded in 1381. Wyld was most likely affected by late medieval depopulations for enclosure, and two episodes were reported to the inquest of 1517. In 1513 40 acres were enclosed with five persons evicted, whilst the following year another 50 acres were enclosed displacing four persons from labour. [2] These alleged acts may have been enough to deplete significantly the sustainability of a small settlement such as Wyld. Certainly by 1761 Rocque’s map shows only a single farm in the area. Some areas adjoining this farm have subsequently been built upon in the twentieth century. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Wytham
e179_last: 1679-80 grant of supply to pay and disband the armed forces
description_snippet: The likelihood of a degree of post-medieval settlement shrinkage is suggested at Wytham by the fact that a number of buildings shown along lanes at the northern and western outskirts of the village by Rocque’s 1761 map do not appear on the subsequent Ordnance Survey drawing of 1811 nor the 1814 Enclosure map.
description_full: The likelihood of a degree of post-medieval settlement shrinkage is suggested at Wytham by the fact that a number of buildings shown along lanes at the northern and western outskirts of the village by Rocque’s 1761 map do not appear on the subsequent Ordnance Survey drawing of 1811 nor the 1814 Enclosure map. [1] Whether any of these lost settlement areas had their origins in the medieval period is not known, but the documentary evidence does hint that Wytham may have experienced a relative decline in status since the fourteenth century. The vill’s percentile ranking within Berkshire for its number of 1327 tax payers and 1334 communal assessment was 0.79 and 0.66 respectively, [2] but the ranking for tax payers had fallen to 0.41 in 1525 and remained 0.38 for population in the 1801 Census. Identified during Beresford's Lost Villages Project.

name: North Wytham
description_snippet: ‘North Wytham’ is listed as a possible DMV by the NMR, originally based on its inclusion by Brooks as a doubtful site in a list for the Medieval Village Research Group. [1, 2] The name ‘North Wytham’ appears to be a modern appellation for the site; it is not found in the E179 database.
description_full: ‘North Wytham’ is listed as a possible DMV by the NMR, originally based on its inclusion by Brooks as a doubtful site in a list for the Medieval Village Research Group. [1, 2] The name ‘North Wytham’ appears to be a modern appellation for the site; it is not found in the E179 database. The suggestion for a DMV at this site appears to originate in an article in the 1804 edition of the Gentleman’s Magazine, where it is stated that the village of Wytham was previously situated further north than the current village, near Wytham Mill. In this area it is said 'the plough has frequently been hindered by small masses of rubble stone and other signs of foundations'. [3] As such it seems that a medieval migration from this site to Wytham was envisaged, and the site has been classed as such for this database. A few houses are shown scattered along the southern half of the lane leading from Wytham to the mill on nineteenth-century maps (e.g. The 1811 Ordnance Survey drawing, the 1814 Enclosure map and the first edition 6 inch and 25 inch Ordnance Survey maps) and perhaps on Rocque’s 1761 map too. [4] Whether any settlement previously existed along the northern half of this routeway might merit further investigation. The northern and western parts of Wytham village proper do also show elements of shrinkage themselves between 1761 and the early nineteenth century (see separate entry). Identified by the NMR and John Brooks.

name: Ackhampstead
description_snippet: There are no visible remains at the site. The ruins of an isolated chapel are present in a clump of trees to the south-east. These were recorded as low flint walls in 1912, and reported to be a rectangular structure with lancet windows.  The farmhouse, another house and an outbuilding have been dated to the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.  The first recorded evidence of the place-name is in 1199.
description_full: There are no visible remains at the site. The ruins of an isolated chapel are present in a clump of trees to the south-east. These were recorded as low flint walls in 1912, and reported to be a rectangular structure with lancet windows. [1] The farmhouse, another house and an outbuilding have been dated to the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. [1] The first recorded evidence of the place-name is in 1199. [2] There is a manorial history of Ackhampstead from the mid thirteenth century until the late fifteenth century, when it is presumed it is sold. [3] The chapel was recorded from at least 1241 but was noted as in disrepair in the late sixteenth century. [3] In the eighteenth century there were still occasional services at the chapel, but it was taken down in 1849. [3] There are no early taxation records, and those from the Poll Taxes in the fourteenth century do not survive. In essence this would suggest that there was never a great population located here and in fact may never have been much larger than the few farms and houses present today. It is not recorded on either the NMR or local HER record, suggesting that it is not viewed by others as a deserted settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Addingrove

description_full: The location of the site in the 1968 Gazetteer and used here is located just to the north of the modern Addingrove Farm. However this is a more recent addition, and on the first edition Ordnance Survey map of 1885 Addingrove Farm and Little Aggingrove Farms are located about 400m to the north. Ridge and furrow is visible around the whole area and the HER has reported possible house platforms close to the old Addingrove Farm. [1] A possible moated site is visible to the south-east of the present farm. There is a Domesday reference for Addingrove with a minimum population of 10. The NMR suggest a desertion between 1350-1450, however no reason for why is given. [2] It does not appear in later taxation records. A chapel is occasionally recorded, first mentioned in the twelfth century and still present in 1318. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Aston Mullins
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: The grid reference used here is a slightly amended version (SP 762 087) of the original 1968 Gazetteer. The location is now to the north-west, in the area of a moated site where settlement remains had been seen before the area was ploughed.
description_full: The grid reference used here is a slightly amended version (SP 762 087) of the original 1968 Gazetteer. The location is now to the north-west, in the area of a moated site where settlement remains had been seen before the area was ploughed. [1] The village was recorded as Aston in the thirteenth century, on some occasions as Aston Bernard after the holder of the manor in the twelfth century, and then Aston Mullins after the family who held the manor in the fourteenth century. [2] Aston Mullins is not clearly mentioned at Domesday but may have been included with Ilmer, with which it is included in the fourteenth and sixteenth-century tax records. [2] This would suggest a settlement around the manorial centre at the moated site. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_snippet: Nothing is clearly visible on the ground at the site, however possible features have been spotted from aerial photographs. description_full: Nothing is clearly visible on the ground at the site, however possible features have been spotted from aerial photographs. There is a manorial history but with little suggestion of a large population at the site and perhaps it was more a hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Boarstall
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: Earthworks of the settlement are visible to the south of the manorial complex at Boarstall. This manorial centre is still present, and includes the church and a moated site. The earthworks to the south include a north-south hollow way, with ridge and furrow to the west and four tofts to the east. Further settlement evidence may have been ploughed out further east.
description_full: Earthworks of the settlement are visible to the south of the manorial complex at Boarstall. This manorial centre is still present, and includes the church and a moated site. The earthworks to the south include a north-south hollow way, with ridge and furrow to the west and four tofts to the east. Further settlement evidence may have been ploughed out further east. [1] This is confirmed by map evidence with a map of the late sixteenth/early seventeenth century showing houses on each side of the road. [2] During a field visit to the area of the settlement, thirteenth to fifteenth-century pottery was recovered. [2] Boarstall does not appear at Domesday as until at least 1213 it was part of the manor of Brill. [3] The church is recorded in the 1291 Taxatio. There are no clear lay taxation records until the sixteenth century. In 1524 36 people were taxed and in 1563 22 households are recorded. Gray noted three open fields present in 1449, but there is evidence of the land being enclosed before 1639. [4] The end of the settlement can be clearly dated. This area of Buckinghamshire was close to Royalist strongholds during the Civil War of the mid seventeenth century, and as such was an area where fortified houses were garrisoned. Boarstall House housed a Royalist garrison until late 1643 when it was abandoned and taken over by the Parliamentarians. [5] It was soon again in Royalist hands. The village and church being so close to the manorial centre were used several times in blockading the forces inside the garrison and so in 1645 the order was set out to clear the village and church. The houses were burnt within two days and the church had been demolished before 26 July. [5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Boycott

description_snippet: There are no visible remains at the location which is now landscaped on the outskirts of the park land of Stowe. It is recorded at Domesday and pays a lower than average amount in 1334. It is not mentioned in the sixteenth-century records. It is said to have been destroyed by 1735, and in 1755 recorded as a decayed hamlet.  Boycott developed as one of four villages in the parish of Stowe.
description_full: There are no visible remains at the location which is now landscaped on the outskirts of the park land of Stowe. It is recorded at Domesday and pays a lower than average amount in 1334. It is not mentioned in the sixteenth-century records. It is said to have been destroyed by 1735, and in 1755 recorded as a decayed hamlet. [1] Boycott developed as one of four villages in the parish of Stowe. Each of these settlements were separate nucleated settlements unlike other parishes in the same area which saw a single village develop but with dispersed areas of nucleation often called ends. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Burston
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths  (Upper Burston)
description_snippet: The deserted village of Burston is located in a valley, which is overlooked by a high ridge to the north. The remains of the site can be seen clearly from the air. The main feature of the site is the hollow way which crosses the site from the south-east to north-west.  Halfway along this hollow way, a smaller one leads northwards.
description_full: The deserted village of Burston is located in a valley, which is overlooked by a high ridge to the north. The remains of the site can be seen clearly from the air. The main feature of the site is the hollow way which crosses the site from the south-east to north-west. [1] Halfway along this hollow way, a smaller one leads northwards. To the west of the main hollow way, enclosures can be seen, with possible house positions. To the east of the hollow way and on either side of the second hollow way there are further tofts which are focussed on this secondary routeway rather than the main one. Ridge and furrow can be seen surrounding the settlement and the earthworks close to Lower Burston Farm may represent later gardens and landscaping. [2] Fifteenth-century carved stonework has been found in the farmyard. [3] Burston is recorded at Domesday and there is a minimum population of 15. The Lay Subsidy of 1334 is above average but also includes another settlement. It does not appear in the sixteenth-century records, and it is last recorded on the E179 in 1624. In 1488 the free holder of the land evicted 60 people and converted it into pasture. [2, 4] This was commented on by Leyland in 1517. [5] In 1526 the manor of Burston was granted a royal licence to empark its lands. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Caldecote in Newport Pagnell
e179_last: Not recorded
description_snippet: This site is located on the edge of Newport Pagnell. Two moated sites are in the area. There is a Domesday record of Caldecote with a minimum population of 12 but it does not appear in the other records on this site. It does however have a manorial history.
description_full: This site is located on the edge of Newport Pagnell. Two moated sites are in the area. There is a Domesday record of Caldecote with a minimum population of 12 but it does not appear in the other records on this site. It does however have a manorial history.
