[2, 3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Caldecote in Weston Turville
e179_last: Not recorded
description_snippet: There is some confusion about the true identification of the name of the site at this specific location. There are two lost hamlets in the area noted as Caldecote and Bedgrove. The 1968 Gazetteer records this as Caldecote. However the area has also now been shown to be Bedgrove, and Caldecote has yet to be located.
description_full: There is some confusion about the true identification of the name of the site at this specific location. There are two lost hamlets in the area noted as Caldecote and Bedgrove. The 1968 Gazetteer records this as Caldecote. However the area has also now been shown to be Bedgrove, and Caldecote has yet to be located. At present the record for this website records both settlements, but in a later version of the website, two separate records will be created. This location has been developed in the latter half of the 1960s, therefore the remains have been destroyed. [1] Areas were excavated ahead of the damage. [2] One house platform was excavated and areas of cobble spread were also uncovered. [2] The excavations suggested a settlement that developed by the late tenth century and deserted after the fourteenth century. [2] Bedgrove is mentioned in the Domesday Book. There are limited later tax records surviving for Bedgrove. The manor of Caldecote is also mentioned in a number of records. [3] It is mentioned in Domesday but does not appear in the later taxation records. This lack of substantial later records is partly what hampers distinguishing between both sites. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Chetwode
e179_last: 1663 July 27 four subsidies
description_snippet: The site of Chetwode has a variety of cropmark and earthwork remains visible. However there is some debate about whether these are associated with a settlement or the priory at the site.  A small house of Austin Cannons was founded in 1245.  Chetwode is mentioned from 949 AD.  The Domesday record for Chetwode includes a minimum population of 15 people.
description_full: The site of Chetwode has a variety of cropmark and earthwork remains visible. However there is some debate about whether these are associated with a settlement or the priory at the site. [1] A small house of Austin Cannons was founded in 1245. [2] Chetwode is mentioned from 949 AD. [3] The Domesday record for Chetwode includes a minimum population of 15 people. The settlement paid a just below average Lay Subsidy in 1334, and by the sixteenth century seven people paid the Lay Subsidy in 1524 and seven households are recorded in 1563. In 1603 there were 18 communicants. [4] There is evidence of the area being enclosed around 1480. [5] There is a dispersed settlement pattern in the area today. Although the NMR claims that there are no visible remains at the site, the documentary evidence would allude to a settlement in the area. Whether this was nucleated or dispersed is unknown. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Middle Claydon

The area in the gardens around the house may well indicate depopulation due to emparking.
description_full: The house that currently occupies the site dates to around the eighteenth century. [1] There was also evidence of a church in the area from the thirteenth century. [1] A small hamlet still exists to the north. There are faint traces of settlement evidence between the house and the hamlet. The area in the gardens around the house may well indicate depopulation due to emparking. The Domesday Book records a minimum population of 21 at Middle Claydon, and a just below average Lay Subsidy is paid in 1334. There is still a substantial population in the sixteenth century with 33 people taxed in 1524, and 25 households recorded in 1563. In 1603 a total of 100 communicants are recorded. [2] There is evidence of enclosure around 1657. [3] It is recorded that the villagers were moved during emparking in the mid eighteenth century. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Cottesloe

name: Creslow
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: There are clear earthworks at Creslow. To the north of the road are a number of possible tofts and building platforms. description_full: There are clear earthworks at Creslow. To the north of the road are a number of possible tofts and building platforms. name: Cublington
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: This site was located around a motte and bailey castle called The Beacon to the west of the present village. [1, 2] An east-west hollow way is present with earthworks surrounding this – at the western edge of this is the castle site.  Much of the earthworks have been damaged in recent times. Excavations in 1925 located the site of the church and a number of burials.  At Domesday there was a minimum population of 21.
description_full: This site was located around a motte and bailey castle called The Beacon to the west of the present village. [1, 2] An east-west hollow way is present with earthworks surrounding this – at the western edge of this is the castle site. [3] Much of the earthworks have been damaged in recent times. Excavations in 1925 located the site of the church and a number of burials. [1] At Domesday there was a minimum population of 21. In 1283 there were around 39 households. [3] By the 1334 Lay Subsidy an above average amount was paid. The village was abandoned sometime after 1341 amidst increasing poverty. [1, 3] The decay had started before the Black Death with reports of land lying fallow and uncultivated, and that the tenants had left. [4] A site just to the east was then repopulated in 1400. [1, 4, 5, 6] The church was also rebuilt in 1400 in the new village, with the burial of John Dervyle in 1410 marked as ‘the first rector of the present church’. [4] By 1519 the Bishop of Lincoln noted that the former churchyard was being desecrated. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Denham

description_full: The grid reference used by this site has been refined from the original 1968 Gazetteer (SP 758 205) and is now SP 753 206 over the scheduled remains. There is the deserted medieval settlement, Denham Lodge and an enclosed deer park. [1] Denham Lodge moated site lies to the south, with a north-south hollow way to the north with a number of tofts, surrounded by ridge and furrow. Further earthworks are present to the west of Denham Lodge. Denham Lodge was built around 1620 over the old Denham Manor, and so confuses the medieval settlement remains. [1, 2] The place-name evidence starts in the early thirteenth century. [3] There is evidence of enclosure in around 1514 according to Beresford, but according to Leadam this is another Denham. [4, 5] There are no further documentary references to the settlement. The settlement never seems to have been large so has been classed here as a hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Doddershall

name: Eythrope
description_snippet: The site of Eythrope lies on low lying land to the north bank of the Thame.  The site is now part of Waddesdon Park.  There is evidence of at least nine enclosures and ridge and furrow to the south-east of the hall.  The grid reference has been refined since the 1968 Gazetteer (SP 770140) to place it over these earthworks. A hollow way runs roughly east-west with the enclosures to the north.
description_full: The site of Eythrope lies on low lying land to the north bank of the Thame. [1] The site is now part of Waddesdon Park. [1] There is evidence of at least nine enclosures and ridge and furrow to the south-east of the hall. [1] The grid reference has been refined since the 1968 Gazetteer (SP 770140) to place it over these earthworks. A hollow way runs roughly east-west with the enclosures to the north. A number of other enclosures have also been seen in the surrounding area. At the time of the Norman Conquest Eythrope was part of the manor of Waddesdon Park. During the twelfth century the Darches Family took ownership and it became a separate manor. [1] In 1334 it pays an average for the Lay Subsidy but with un-named members. In the sixteenth century 19 people paid the 1524 Lay Subsidy. From around the seventeenth century there were a number of ownership changes and the land became emparked. [1] It is probably depopulated at this point. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Fleet Marston
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions

The Domesday Book records a minimum population of 12. There were 15 families recorded in 1332.
description_full: House platforms and hollow ways were once visible at the site, but ploughing and road realignment has removed the majority. The Domesday Book records a minimum population of 12. There were 15 families recorded in 1332. [2] The 1334 Lay Subsidy is below average for the area. There are still 12 tax payers in the early sixteenth century but by 1543 this has reduced to three and there are three households recorded in 1563. In 1603 there are 11 communicants recorded. [3] The area was enclosed c.1510-1551 along with depopulation. [2] Over 45 people were displaced in the early stages of the enclosure. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Foxcote
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions

The church lies in isolation and the area to the north of this has been heavily landscaped as part of the gardens of the manor house. name: Fulbrook

description_full: There are clear earthworks visible at the site. The current Fulbrook manor house was built in the sixteenth century, with alteration in the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries. To the north and east of the manor site there is evidence of an east-west hollow way, running along the line of the modern road with tofts to the north and south. Fulbrook is not recorded at Domesday. The first mention of the place-name is in 1197. [2] In 1334 it is recorded with the neighbouring deserted settlement of Hogshaw and combined they paid an average amount. In 1524 there are 15 people taxed at both of these settlements and they pay an above average amount. There is a record of early enclosure with at least 60 people displaced in the two settlements in 1498. [3] It would seem this brought an end to the settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Gayhurst

There are no clear signs of settlement in the area, although some ridge and furrow is present. In Domesday there is a minimum population of 12 recorded. In 1334 it is taxed above average for the area, but is recorded with Little Linford.
description_full: The village of Gayhurst was situated close to Gayhurst House and church. It was moved north in 1725 when the area was landscaped for George Wrighte. It would seem that there was still a population living close to the house before the new village was constructed. In 1603 there are 70 communicants recorded. [4] There was a dispersed distribution of cottages on a map of 1711. [5] In essence this is a migrated settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Grove

name: Hallinges

description_full: The grid reference given for this site in the 1968 Gazetteer (SP 838 095) is very similar to that for the deserted settlement of Stoke Mandeville (SP 837 095). This has caused some difficulties in distinguishing the two settlements. It has now been concluded that the settlement at this location is Stoke Mandeville and that Hallinges was probably located at SP 825 108, which has been used here. [1] However there is still a debate on this location. Mawer and Stenton dismiss the link between Hallinges and the present name of Hall End. [2] There are no clear visible remains at the site but medieval pottery has been recovered from the area of Hall End and Jeffrey’s map of 1788 shows a cluster of cottages here. [1] The MVRG archive has recorded this settlement as Hall End and have it at this new location. Further evidence is needed to confirm this association between the two names of Hallinges and Hall End. The first place-name evidence for Hallinges is in 1200, with mentions into the fourteenth century. [2] However there is very little information on this site, and it would appear to be a small hamlet, perhaps always over shadowed by Stoke Mandeville. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Great Hampden
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: The gird reference is located next to Hampden House and the church of Great Hampden. No remains are visible on the site. Hampden House has elements that can be dated back to the fourteenth century.  Medieval trusses are present in houses in the present village at Great Hampden.
description_full: The gird reference is located next to Hampden House and the church of Great Hampden. No remains are visible on the site. Hampden House has elements that can be dated back to the fourteenth century. [1] Medieval trusses are present in houses in the present village at Great Hampden. [1] At Domesday there is a minimum population of six recorded for Hampden but it is not clear whether this is Little or Great Hampden, although the VCH claims it is likely to be Great Hampden. [2] The distinction between Little and Great appears in the mid thirteenth century. [3] The church was in place by at least 1291. In 1334 a below average is paid for the Lay Subsidy. In 1543/5 22 people pay the Lay Subsidy and 34 households are recorded in 1563. In 1603 80 communicants were recorded. [4] The area around Hampden House has been landscaped and it could be a case that the village was moved outside the park. Without evidence of a forced move this is currently classed as shifted. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: There are two separate sites on the 1968 Gazetteer and these are probably two parts of a polyfocal settlement. Hardmead I is the northernmost of the areas of the settlement, and hence given the name here North End. Please note that in 1971 Beresford termed this the East End, but this seems to be in error. [1] Until the 1960s there were upstanding earthworks but the area has been heavily ploughed. These earthworks represented a range of crofts around a village green. [2] A moated site was situated to the east which is suggested to be the main manor house site. [2] A survey and watching brief took place at the site between 1973-4 during levelling of the earthworks, and a number of trial trenches were also excavated. [2] Pottery from the site dated from the twelfth to nineteenth century. [2] The church of Hardmead is located between the two sites. Hardmead is recorded in Domesday with a minimum population of 36. This is a large population for the area and the size of landholding is greater than the surrounding area. It has been suggested that a dependant village is also included within this assessment. [2] In 1344 the settlement pays an average amount. By 1524 there are 22 people paying the Lay Subsidy and in 1603 80 communicants are recorded. [3] A 1638 estate map shows that after enclosure there were many small tenant holdings that were scattered and probably uneconomic. [2] The northern area of Hardmead appeared to shrink but then remain occupied until the mid nineteenth century. [2] In 1802 there are three farms, an old rectory and ten cottages in the parish. Five of the cottages were on the green, presumably here at the northern end of the site. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Helsthorpe

Crafton did not appear on the 1968 Gazetteer and will feature on a future release of this website. The NMR record for Helsthorpe is really the detail from the Crafton site. [1] Helsthorpe was recorded in Domesday Book with a minimum population of seven. In the 1334 Lay Subsidy it is recorded with Drayton Beauchamp. It does not appear in the later records, and probably was subsumed in Drayton Beauchamp. In 1388 there was a chapel, but it is unknown when this disappears. There are reports of stones being uncovered. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hogshaw
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: There was a perceptory of the Knights of the Hospitallers with an associated settlement at Hogshaw. which existed from 1180 to around 1470.  The site has previously been a nunnery of the Sisters of St. John which was moved to Buckland.
description_full: There was a perceptory of the Knights of the Hospitallers with an associated settlement at Hogshaw. which existed from 1180 to around 1470. [1] The site has previously been a nunnery of the Sisters of St. John which was moved to Buckland. [1] The main visible earthworks at the site are a moated site and fish ponds and it is believed that the village stood to the south although there were some suggestions to earthworks to the east as well. [1] A church on the site was still in use in 1650 but by the end of seventeenth century the church was no more than ruins. [1, 2] The church site is marked on early maps as just south of the moat. During a watching brief in 2003 the remains of eight buildings were seen. [3] The buildings were orientated north-east to south-west and fronted onto the main road. The pottery recovered dated from the late twelfth century to the early sixteenth century. [3] Hogshaw is recorded at Domesday with a minimum population of eight. There are 20 families recorded in 1327. [4] In 1334 it is recorded with the neighbouring deserted settlement of Fulbrook and combined, they paid an average amount. In 1524 there are 15 people taxed at both of these settlements and they pay an above average amount. There is evidence of early enclosure with at least 60 people displaced at both of these settlements by 1498. [5] This seems to have brought an end to the settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hughenden

In the sixteenth-century lay subsidies 20 people pay. In 1603 there are 250 communicants. [4] This pattern would seem to confirm that this is a dispersed settlement, and that if there had been a settlement at the site, it is hard to distinguish from the available records. name: Lenborough
e179_last: 1641 May 13 two subsidies
description_snippet: The grid reference that appears in the 1968 Gazetteer was placed at a place called Lenborough Farm on the first edition Ordnance Survey map of 1880. description_full: The grid reference that appears in the 1968 Gazetteer was placed at a place called Lenborough Farm on the first edition Ordnance Survey map of 1880. However there are clear earthworks to the north-west at Manor Farm (SP 699 313) and it is this site which is recorded as Lenborough by both the HER and NMR, and is therefore used by this website. Much of the area has been affected by later quarrying, but some earthworks are still visible. The area of Manor Farm would appear to be the centre of the settlement. There are extensive areas of ridge and furrow surrounding the area. To the east of Manor Farm there would appear to be a north-south hollow way, and this could meet another hollow way, now the main route through the farm. A more recent interpretation of the north-south hollow way sees this feature as associated with the quarrying activities at the site and not with the medieval settlement. [1] Lenborough is recorded in Domesday Book with a minimum population of 12. In 1334 it pays a slightly above average Lay Subsidy. By the sixteenth century there had been a decline. There are five tax payers in 1524, and only two households are recorded in 1563. There are records of enclosure in 1500 with 60 acres having been enclosed and two people displaced. [2, 3] This would seem to suggest that the population was in decline at this point in time, or that the recorded enclosure in 1500 was the start of the enclosure process which saw the rest of the village population displaced. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Lillingstone Dayrell
description_snippet: The site of the deserted medieval village of Lillingston Dayrell is situated to the north and south of the church that has been dated to the thirteenth century and earlier.  Field walking to the south of the church during the Whittlewood Project uncovered pottery with evidence of pre-1000 activity.  There are earthworks of house platforms to the north and east.
description_full: The site of the deserted medieval village of Lillingston Dayrell is situated to the north and south of the church that has been dated to the thirteenth century and earlier. [1] Field walking to the south of the church during the Whittlewood Project uncovered pottery with evidence of pre-1000 activity. [2] There are earthworks of house platforms to the north and east. Another village street is also suggested to the south of this. [2] The settlement is recorded at Domesday with a minimum population of 11. In 1334 an average payment was made for the Lay Subsidy. In 1535 only three people paid the Lay Subsidy and in 1563 there are four households recorded. There is clear evidence for early enclosure and depopulation. Glebe terriers in the early seventeenth century record memory of the depopulation and in 1517 the local inquiry into enclosure laid the blame at the feet of Thomas Dayrell in 1491. [3] The inquiry recorded 40 people had been displaced and that this was the total population. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Linslade
e179_last: 1671 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: Linslade is located on the border of Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire. Historically it was in Buckinghamshire but is now included in Bedfordshire. description_full: Linslade is located on the border of Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire. Historically it was in Buckinghamshire but is now included in Bedfordshire. This deserted settlement is known as Old Linslade as the settlement shifted position south to the area that is now Linslade. The settlement is thought to have lain to the south and west of the church and medieval pottery has been found in the area. [1] At Domesday the manor is extensive with a minimum population of 33. In 1334 an average amount is paid. The historical evidence for the settlement shows a thriving settlement of borough status. In the late thirteenth century the settlement became a market town with a market and fair granted in 1251. [2] A holy well at Linslade was attracting pilgrims, but by 1299, a ban was issued by the Bishop of Lincoln due to false miracles, and this affected the town. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Liscombe

[1, 2] It paid an average amount in the 1334 Lay Subsidy but along with Creslow. It has a single tax payer in 1524 and for the later records it is probably recorded with Stewkley. In 1494 there is record of enclosure and 24 inhabitants being displaced. Then a further eight tenants were evicted in 1507. description_full: Earthworks are clearly visible at the site. The size of some of these suggests they may have acted as paddocks, but others were probably tofts and crofts. [2] Moreton was not directly recorded in Domesday Book but it is suggested that it may have been included with West Wycombe. [3] The first place-name evidence is in the early thirteenth century. [4] It paid an above average amount in the 1334 Lay Subsidy with West Wycombe but does not appear in later records, and has little documented history. The village was certainly depopulated by the time of a 1660 map. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Okeney

[2] The 'villiata de Ekeney' is recorded in 1262 when it was fined, and various lawsuits at the end of the thirteenth century recorded at least seven families. [3] It is suggested that the settlement was deserted by 1340 or by 1459. [2, 4] A survey of 1473 records four cottages, but many are derelict. [5] The chapel was demolished by 1560. [1] The settlement was not mentioned after 1619. [6] It may never have been very large and is recorded as a hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Olney Hyde
description_snippet: Nothing can be seen at the site but field walking and excavation have uncovered buildings and at least 14 pottery kilns, with the centre of evidence located 500m north of the farm. [1] The settlement is to the north of the medieval market town of Olney and forms a completely separate settlement. [1] An area in Olney Hyde was emparked in 1374 and it is suggested that this could have covered most or all of the open fields of the settlement. [1, 2] In 1411 there were 12 tenants as well as freemen and cottagers suggesting the settlement continued and this is evidenced by the continuation of the pottery industry that does not go out of action until the fifteenth century. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The site was listed in Beresford’s 1954 ‘Lost Villages of England’ and appears in the 1968 Gazetteer. [1] However in the intervening years, in 1957, in a listing of DMVs in Buckinghamshire, there is a note that the site has been removed from the list. [2] The debate on the site surrounds whether there was ever a settlement here or whether it was just a manorial centre. Petsoe Manor still exists as a ruin and the hamlet of Petsoe End still exists to the west. There is a question about whether Petsoe was ever more than this dispersed settlement. However Chibnall has produced convincing evidence of a settlement and so has been classed as a DMV here. [3] A chapel is documented but no evidence of it exists on the ground but on a map of 1643 it is marked south of the manor house. [4, 5] In 1967 it was reported that much stone and roof tile was visible when the area was ploughed. [6] The first mention of Petsoe is in 1151. [7] In 1231-2 a dine is imposed on the 'villata de Pettesho'. [3] In around 1460 it is suggested that it comprised a manor house, seven farms, five cottages and a distant residence. [3] It does not feature in the fourteenth-century tax records. There is evidence of enclosure in the late-fifteenth century or early sixteenth century. In 1561 there is a record that there was no church and no population. [8] In 1563 a single household is recorded. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Putlowes

name: Quarrendon I
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: The grid reference for this site has been refined since it was published in 1968 to more accurately locate it over the earthworks that are known as Quarrendon I. description_full: The grid reference for this site has been refined since it was published in 1968 to more accurately locate it over the earthworks that are known as Quarrendon I. There are three separate areas of earthworks in this area which have been given the identifications of I, II, and III. They probably all represent the dispersed settlement of Quarrendon within a regional mixture of villages, ‘ends’, hamlets and farmsteads. [1] There is also extensive evidence of a sixteenth and seventeenth-century country house and landscape gardens in between Quarrendon I and II, which is recorded as partly pulled down in 1666. [1] Close to this area is located the remains of the church of St Peter’s. This is known from at least the twelfth century, but has a potential earlier origin perhaps back to the seventh century. [1] Quarrendon I is the eastern most part of the settlement evidence. It is linked with Quarrendon II via an east-west hollow way. The remains are clear and can be seen from the air and on the ground. Survey work at the site has shown that the settlement was perhaps four or five farmsteads clustered around a green. [1] At Domesday Quarrendon is recorded with a minimum population of 28. It is assessed with an average payment in 1334. In 1524 there are 20 tax payers but by 1543 and 1563 there are only four households recorded. The survey work at the site seemed to show that the settlements had been deserted by the time the country house is constructed in the mid sixteenth century. [1] As part of the depopulation of the settlement at Quarrendon I there seems to be one large property. [1] There is evidence of conversion of much of the arable to pasture. By 1540 there had been created 960 acres of pasture. [1] In 1636 Quarrendon was described as ‘anciently enclosed and depopulated’. [1] This website has continued the use of three separate areas at Quarrendon, although they should be considered as all part of the same settlement. It continues calling them DMVs as they are clear evidence of a deserted medieval settlement of a size larger than a hamlet, but they should all be considered as one settlement site. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

There is evidence of conversion of much of the arable to pasture. By 1540 there had been created 960 acres of pasture [1] In 1636 Quarrendon was described as ‘anciently enclosed and depopulated’. [1] This website has continued the use of three separate areas at Quarrendon, although they should be considered as all part of the same settlement. It continues calling them DMVs as they are clear evidence of a deserted medieval settlement of a size larger than a hamlet, but they should all be considered as one settlement site, with Quarrendon III being a distant outlying element to the settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Saunderton

description_full: By the 1870 Ordnance Survey map there was only a church, farm complex and a couple of other buildings at the site. The documentary record suggests two settlements, close together, Saunderton St Nicholas and Saunderton St Mary. The evidence at the site includes a moated site, an upstanding church and the possible remains of a further church. There are no clear signs of medieval village remains. Excavations on the moated site in the 1950s revealed twelfth and thirteenth-century pottery, as well as a selection of Roman material associated with a settlement to the north. [1] At Domesday two manors are recorded at Saunderton with a minimum population of 38. By 1215 two separate parish churches were in existence – St Mary’s and St Nicholas’. The present church is on the site of St Mary’s, but the site of St Nicholas’ is now lost. Both manors were amalgamated in 1452, and only a single church continued after this date. [1] Burials and material have been found at Church Farm to the west of the moated site and it is suggested that these are associated with St Nicholas. [1] This would mean both parishes churches were in close proximity. In the 1334 Lay Subsidy there is a payment from Saunderton that is average for the area. By 1377 there is a distinction in the tax record between St Mary and St Nicholas and 42 pay at Saunderton St Nicholas and 43 at Saunderton St Mary. By the time of the sixteenth-century tax records, it is back to a single record of Saunderton with 18 people paying in 1524. In 1603 there are 60 communicants recorded. [2] With both settlements being so close it may have been the case there was never a physical distinction between the two. The amalgamation of the two manors from 1452 explains the reduction to one church. There is no indication when the settlement declines. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The site of Stantonbury has been destroyed by quarrying in the 1950s and 1960s. [1] A watching brief was undertaken but by this point much of the village had been destroyed. Today a few house platforms, the garden of a seventeenth-century manor house, and the ruins of a church survive. [1] Excavations in 1955 investigated the church and found a tower at the west end. [1] The watching brief undertaken during the destruction of the site located pottery from house platforms suggesting occupation from the twelfth to fourteenth centuries. [1] The early aerial photographs from the site and the watching brief suggest settlement to the north of the church with two streets running east-west with tofts between. [1] The excavations also found a number of sherds of Saxon pottery suggesting an early origin and there is suggestion of an early church structure at the site. [1] At Domesday a minimum population of 14 is recorded. In the 1334 Lay Subsidy a slightly below average payment is made along with Bradwell. There are no sixteenth-century tax records. The village was enclosed and depopulated by Nicholas Vaux in the early sixteenth century, with 40 people displaced. [2, 3] In 1603, in the list of communicants, Stantonbury is listed but the entry is left blank. [4] Only four houses are recorded in the parish in 1736. [1] It is clear that enclosure had affected the population of this village. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: There has in the past been some confusion over this site and that at Hallinges. A parish church was on the site from the twelfth century and was in use until 1886 and it was finally demolished in 1966. [1] A moated site had also been present but all sign of this and any associated settlement has been ploughed out. Pottery dating from the eleventh to thirteenth century has been collected from the field to the south of the church. [2] Some signs of settlement could be seen in earlier photographs including a north-west to south-east hollow way. At Domesday a large manor is recorded with a minimum population of 45, although some of these were based on the lands of Aylesbury Church. It pays an above average Lay Subsidy in 1334, and there are more than 47 tax payers in 1379. There are still 27 tax payers in 1524. Stoke Mandeville exists today to the north of the site, and this is a case of a village that has shifted but when and why is unknown. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The area of the settlement of Stowe has been heavily landscaped and no above ground features are visible. The present Stowe House was initially constructed in 1676, and then much modified and enlarged. [1] The settlement of Stowe was depopulated in the seventeenth century when Peter Temple enlarged the deer park surrounding the earlier house. [2] Some of the villagers appear to have been relocated to Dadford. [2] Unfortunately no map of the village exists before its destruction and it is assumed it was located close to the parish church to the south-east of the Hall. [2] Stowe is mentioned at Domesady with a minimum population of three. It pays an average Lay Subsidy in 1334 along with Lamport. By 1524 there are 32 tax payers, and 20 households are recorded in 1563. There were still over 18 tenants at Stowe in 1620. [2] By 1637 enclosure was underway when the common land in Stowe and neighbouring Lamport was enclosed. [2] It is suggested that between seven and 12 houses were depopulated by 1653. [2] This was the first move to create a large landscaped garden around the house, which went through a number of stages of construction through the later seventeenth and early eighteenth century. A few buildings may have remained until the later phases of landscape construction. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The site of Tattenhoe has been encroached upon by Milton Keynes. The church and a moated site still exist with faint traces of the settlement to the south. There are reports that much of the site has been ploughed. [1] Before ploughing a hollow way ran south of the church and split into two branches. [2] A series of at least eight crofts were aligned to this hollow way and on initial identification it would appear that they contained building platforms. However on excavation it was found that buildings were located in negative hollows rather than the platforms. [2] Two series of excavations have been carried out on the site. In 1988 evaluation trenches were places across the entirety of the site and in 1990 three large areas were excavated. These excavations identified evidence of activity from the late eleventh century when two separate foci of settlement are suggested. In the thirteenth century there is clear evidence of a nucleated village when the crofts develop. However by the early sixteenth century the settlement was abandoned. [2] Tattenhoe is not recorded in Domesday but a church is recorded by 1291. The place-name first appears in the second half of the twelfth century. [3] In the 1334 Lay Subsidy an average amount is paid along with Shenley End. By 1524 there are only two tax payers. It is enclosed by 1585. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Badlingham

description_snippet: There is no physical evidence of the village at this location. Today the only remains on the site are of Badlingham Farm, now known as Badlingham Manor/Hall. description_full: There is no physical evidence of the village at this location. Today the only remains on the site are of Badlingham Farm, now known as Badlingham Manor/Hall. The farmhouse was in use during the early sixteenth century by Sibton Abbey, in Suffolk, as a grange. At some point between 1500 and 1599, the farmhouse underwent major renovations and was converted into a private residence. Subsequently, it was renamed Badlingham Hall and thereafter, Badlingham Manor. [1] The building itself is positioned within a rectangular-shaped moated site which is often indicative of twelfth to fifteenth-century activity. [2] The moated site surrounding Badlingham Manor would suggest that this was originally a ‘manorial core’ for the village of Badlingham. Field walking and trial trenching in the area revealed no evidence for medieval activity. [3] Badlingham is recorded from 1086 onwards. In 1334, the Lay Subsidy returns came to a total of 432p. In 1377, there were a total of 37 individuals who contributed to the Poll Tax. [4] Earlier records have Badlingham taxed with Chippenham. By 1279, the two settlements between them housed 163 landholders. [5] This is, relatively speaking, a significant number of households. It would seem that the two settlements must have at some point divided and Badlingham, the smaller of the two, declined in population and prosperity. By 1327, Badlingham hamlet had the much lesser total of 12 tax payers, compared to 47 at Chippenham. [5] This total did increase in 1377, but by the fifteenth century it would seem that the settlement was starting to struggle. The settlement of Badlingham was relieved of 19 percent of its tax burden in 1432-3 and 28 percent in 1489. [6] One of the final records of the village prior to its decline was in 1659, where a total of nine cottages were recorded. [4] The settlement seems to have declined gradually, but may never have been a settlement of any great size. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Barham

description_snippet: Any physical evidence of the village has disappeared in the modern landscape. In the Domesday Book it contained a minimum of 20 people and by 1279, there were 70 tenants.
description_full: Any physical evidence of the village has disappeared in the modern landscape. Aerial photographs show some features to the south east of Barham Hall, but they are hard to interpret and may not indicate medieval settlement. [1] Barham is first mentioned in 1050. [2] In the Domesday Book it contained a minimum of 20 people and by 1279, there were 70 tenants. [3] This suggests a settlement of considerable size, unlike Beresford’s description of a hamlet. [4] At this point it is also recorded in its own right and the settlement gained a market and fair in 1282. [5] It is unclear whether the market was ever successfully established. In the early-thirteenth century a chapel was founded in Barham but was later taken over when a house of Crutched Friars was established in 1293. [3] This site became Barham Hall after the suppression in 1539-40. [3] From 1316 onwards the tax records become less definite and the settlement was amalgamated with Linton which comprised Great and Little Linton. It subsequently became deserted. [6] This means that it is difficult to distinguish the tax and population records of each individual village in the later records. The history of the landholding of Barham Manor may indicate the fate of the settlement. In 1279, the estate amounted to 32 acres and in 1323 an extra 52 acres were added for the purpose of farming sheep. By 1532, the sheep fold of 120 sheep had fallen into disuse. [3] Here we clearly see the change to sheep farming and even an abandonment of this activity by the sixteenth century. This once prosperous settlement, with the potential of a market and a fair and a religious establishment, seems to show evidence of land enclosure from the fourteenth century onwards and then a rapid decline. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Castle Camps
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The grid reference used by the website has been refined from that published in the 1968 Gazetteer (TL 630 425) to place the marker over the earthworks at the site. The village of Castle Camps originally developed as a direct consequence of the construction of the castle, Castle Camps, sometime before 1100.
description_full: The grid reference used by the website has been refined from that published in the 1968 Gazetteer (TL 630 425) to place the marker over the earthworks at the site. The village of Castle Camps originally developed as a direct consequence of the construction of the castle, Castle Camps, sometime before 1100. This motte and bailey castle, recognized as the largest in the county, was built by Aubrey De Vere shortly after the Norman Conquest. [1] The remains of the village of Castle Camps are situated on the exterior of the outer bailey and to the north-east of the castle. [1] All that remains of the village now are small areas of earthworks, although they were once more extensive and pottery scatters would suggest settlement over a wider area. [1] The main feature of the site is a large hollow way which bisects the village area running north-south. At each end of the hollow way are the remains of what appear to be houses. In addition to these residence sites, there are earthworks representing perimeter and inner plot demarcations, leveled building platforms and tracks and spoil mounds. [2]. Between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries a park was recorded as attached to the castle, and its increase in size over the period, may be one reason for declining settlement at the site. [3] There was a sizable population recorded at Domesday (although this included Shudy Camps), and the fourteenth-century taxations also show a similar picture. The Victoria County History suggests that there was never a great nucleated settlement, but that the area consisted of scattered hamlets and farmsteads. [3] Castle Camps has also appeared in documents titled as Great Camps (in 1236, 1271 and 1314) and as Earl’s Camps (in 1086). [4] By the sixteenth century there had been a decline in the number of people taxed, but this was against a background of changes to the settlement structure in the area and the development of a new ‘Castle Camps’ settlement. The current village of Castle Camps is located to the north east of the castle site and is the amalgamation of two of these hamlets, Camps Green and Camps End and these names only appear in the 1820s. [3, 4] The parish church is still situated at the isolated location of the castle and village site. The eventual decay of the settlement at the castle has been attributed to the decline of the castle itself whose importance dwindled towards the end of the medieval period. It would seem that there is no record of the actual size of the village or the final date of its desertion. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Caxton
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: Two areas of settlement remains are visible to the east of the current village of Caxton. The location given by this website lies between these two areas. They have been built over in recent times but a roughly east-west hollow way still exists as a farm track linking the church to Ermine Street.
description_full: Two areas of settlement remains are visible to the east of the current village of Caxton. The location given by this website lies between these two areas. They have been built over in recent times but a roughly east-west hollow way still exists as a farm track linking the church to Ermine Street. A further hollow way has been identified to the south of this and it is suggested that there are closes between these two which may be part of the former village. [1] To the north of this area tofts can still be seen aligned along the east side of St Peter Street and a moated site and manorial complex are positioned on the western side of the road. This moated site had gone out of use by 1750. [1] Pottery has been collected from these areas of former settlement and are dated no later than the late thirteenth century. [2] Caxton is recorded in the Domesday record and has a minimum population of 35. It is suggested that after a market was granted in 1248 the focus of the settlement shifted from this location to along Ermine Street where the focus of the village is still today. [2, 3] There is no indication of decline at the settlement. In 1334 it pays an above average Lay Subsidy and 131 people are taxed in 1377. Although there is a slight reduction in the number taxed in the sixteenth century there is still a sizable population. By 1662 37 people are listed in the Hearth Tax. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Childerley, Great and Little
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: Although these appeared to be actually two separate settlements, particularly in the early years, they were treated together by the 1968 Gazetteer and this is continued here. After 1279 they were usually taxed together so can be hard to separate as two settlements in their own right. They both had chapels, and were also parishes until they were united in the 1500s.
description_full: Although these appeared to be actually two separate settlements, particularly in the early years, they were treated together by the 1968 Gazetteer and this is continued here. After 1279 they were usually taxed together so can be hard to separate as two settlements in their own right. They both had chapels, and were also parishes until they were united in the 1500s. [1] The remains of both settlements are located within the park of Childerley Hall. The remains of Great Childerley are situated to the east and the south-east of the hall. The village complex was made up of several hollow ways, a cobbled street, a church called St Mary’s, a manor house site, various buildings and house platforms, fishponds and several quarry areas. [2] The remains follow a complex grid of varying sized hollow ways. Overall the various features of the village follow the direction of the main hollow way which runs east to west. [2] Excavations were carried out at Great Childerley in 1961 and 1962 by J. Alexander and volunteers of the Extra Mural Department of Cambridge University. [2, 3] The excavations revealed many features including a cobbled surface which was thought to have been part of a yard. This contained fourteenth-century pottery and showed evidence for two separate phases of medieval occupation with artefacts such as a whetstone and a quern stone. [3] Excavation also revealed that ploughing had damaged several house platforms but there were several twelfth to thirteenth-century platforms which remained unharmed. [2] Little Childerley was situated to the north-west of the hall. Until the 1950s, the earthworks of the village were still visible, but were unfortunately destroyed by ploughing between 1955 and 1959. [4] The area is now covered by a plantation of trees. A faint trace of an east-west hollow way can be seen to the north-east of the hall, with ridge and furrow present to the south and this may be a continuation of the main hollow way in the settlement, now lost. The RCHME reports that old photographs and accounts show the main feature of the settlement as a track which ran straight with an east-west orientation with a patchy cobbled surface, indicating a street. [2] Flanking the track were rectangular platforms with ridge and furrow abutting the exterior of the platforms. Eleventh to thirteenth-century pottery was discovered associated with these features. [2] In 1991, an archaeological watching brief was undertaken prior to the installation of a pipeline which ran from Boxworth to Childerley. An investigation at Little Childerley revealed two cobbled surfaces and these were considered to be medieval trackways. It was also established that the area had high potential for preservation of organic materials due to its waterlogged remains. Finds included Saxo-Noman pottery, animal bone and a copper alloy pin. [5, 6] Both villages are listed separately as different manors in the Domesday Book, with a minimum population of 14 for Great Childerley and 11 for Little Childerley. By 1279 the total number of tax payers had nearly doubled to 25 inhabitants for Great Childerley and 20 inhabitants for Little Childerley. [4] From that point onwards, Great and Little Childerley began to be assessed together. In 1327, between the two villages there were 22 inhabitants, but 76 paying the Poll Tax by 1377. From the early fifteenth century we start to see a decline. In 1411, Great Childerley is recorded as having 15 tenants. By 1524 there was a single tenant and two hired labourers. [4] In 1563 there were 3 households, and between 1639 and the 1670s the only house inhabited in the parish was the hall. [4] Depopulation was gradual with early enclosures recorded at Little Childerley which disappeared by 1500. [1, 7] It is supposed that the final depopulation of Great Childerley took place when the fifth Sir John Cutts extended the park in the seventeenth century. [7] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Chilford

description_full: There is no physical evidence for settlement in the vicinity of Chilford Hall. The Victoria County History has suggested that Chilford Hall, constructed in 1841, had no connection with earlier Chilford manor. [1] The only suggestion of a settlement was the name itself, which would suggest a village. [2, 3] Chilford is also the name of one of the hundreds in Cambridgeshire and a hundred meeting place has been suggested, but its location is unknown with a suggestion it was on the Linton boundary at a ford due south of Little Chilfords. [4] Apart from the hundred name there are very few references to Chilford or Little Chilfords, namely in 1279, 1298, 1600 and 1662. [4] Chilford manor is mentioned in 1547 and 1600 but there is no indication of settlement or earlier existence. [1] As such there is no firm evidence that a settlement ever existed at this location and for the present it is classed as doubtful. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Clopton
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll.
description_snippet: Earthworks of the village are still visible to the north of the cluster of modern farm buildings. While many of these features are clearly defined, more than half of the village’s 33 acre extent has been destroyed through various means. [1, 2] During the Second World War some of the fields were ploughed, destroying what archaeology remained.
description_full: Earthworks of the village are still visible to the north of the cluster of modern farm buildings. While many of these features are clearly defined, more than half of the village’s 33 acre extent has been destroyed through various means. [1, 2] During the Second World War some of the fields were ploughed, destroying what archaeology remained. [1] This also spread the earthwork profiles so that it is difficult to carry out effective surveying. Today, the field is used as permanent pasture. Other factors affecting the preservation of the village include, quarrying, coprolite mining and military exercises such as machine-gun range targeting and trenching. [1] Features still visible today include a number of hollow ways, boundary ditches and to the south of the main settlement evidence of a small rectangular moated site. The remains are connected by four separate wide-sweeping hollow ways running east to west, north-east to south, south-east to east and west to north. Orientated around these ‘roads’ were four principal sites namely, a church, a mill, a number of house sites and fish ponds. [2, 3] Excavations took place between 1960 and 1964 carried out by J. Alexander of Cambridge University. The excavations revealed that there were three main areas containing house platforms associated with cobbled surfaces and pottery, and some Roman to Late Saxon and thirteenth to sixteenth century-sherds. [3] Excavations on the church in 1964 established the actual structure, tiled floors, roof and glazed windows and that it was probably destroyed around the seventeenth century. [3] Over 100 burials were also uncovered. [3] Alexander concluded that the settlement reached it final form in the thirteenth century. [3] The village of Clopton is sometimes also known as Clapton. [1] First recorded in 1086 with a minimum population of 18, there are substantial fourteenth-century tax records with 104 tax payers in 1377. There was a market in the thirteenth century, but this declined in the later middle ages. From c.1495 there is evidence the land was undergoing enclosure by John Fisher when he acquired the estate. Final depopulation and enclosure occurred between 1500-1518. [1, 4, 5] A total of 6 people paid the Lay Subsidy in 1524 and only a single person was recorded the Diocesan Return of 1563. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Croxton
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll.
description_snippet: The village of Croxton has a complex history, becoming deserted in several stages. The monument as a whole is extremely well preserved and clearly visible in the well preserved remains where both the medieval earthworks and hollow ways survive alongside the subsequent landscape.. Croxton probably had two foci, one to the south of the current village, and one close to the church.
description_full: The village of Croxton has a complex history, becoming deserted in several stages. The monument as a whole is extremely well preserved and clearly visible in the well preserved remains where both the medieval earthworks and hollow ways survive alongside the subsequent landscape. [1]. Croxton probably had two foci, one to the south of the current village, and one close to the church. [2] The main concentration of earthworks is seen close to the church and in the grounds of Croxton Park. On the enclosure map of 1811, the layout of the park looks somewhat different to later depictions. [3] The whole area is shown to be occupied by several houses and attached gardens and the two principal remains, two hollow ways appear to be streets. In early nineteenth-century depictions of the park, a fish pond has been constructed and the houses have been removed. This coincides with the enlargement of the park. This final stage of emparkment represents the completion of a gradual desertion. On a survey conducted in the 1990s a clear north-south hollow way can be seen running from the church. A number of building platforms are visible on either side. [4] The second focus is close to the late medieval buildings of Westbury Farm, probably originally moated, and the Manor House. [3] On more recent aerial photography there is the possibility of a number of tofts and crofts aligned along the driveway to the park, along the western side and could be a continuation of the present settlement in this area. The name Westbury for this area may indicate an outlier to the main settlement. [2] The 1990s survey also shows these earthworks and highlights that the documentary history may indicate two separate tenurial units, one at Croxton (the earliest) and one at Westbury. [5] The settlement is recorded from Domesday onwards and has a sizable population with 118 tax payers in 1377. This was reduced in the sixteenth century to 38 in 1524 and 23 in 1563. However after this there was an upturn in population. [2] Croxton Park house dates to 1761, but may contain elements of an earlier building. [3] To the south of the current extent of Croxton village is the Manor House which is a well preserved example of a late medieval hall. [3] The complex evidence from this site would suggest a shifted settlement, not a deserted one and this is how it has been classed by Oosthuizen. [5] This is also a good example of polyfocal settlement perhaps, never having a clearly nucleated centre. [4] The inhabitants resident in the park were gradually cleared to the north by the 1820s. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Henny
description_snippet: Overall, there is very little evidence for the village of Henny in Soham. As for physical remains there are no visible features in RAF aerial photographs.  The settlement was recorded in the Domesday Book but then appears never to have attained a separate mention in any tax records.  It is mentioned in papers concerning Pembroke College, Cambridge until 1490, but the nature of any settlement is unknown.
description_full: Overall, there is very little evidence for the village of Henny in Soham. As for physical remains there are no visible features in RAF aerial photographs. [1] The settlement was recorded in the Domesday Book but then appears never to have attained a separate mention in any tax records. [2] It is mentioned in papers concerning Pembroke College, Cambridge until 1490, but the nature of any settlement is unknown. [2] It is believed to have been located around TL 557 752. [3] The Domesday reference refers to Hainey being only half a hide and that it does not give tax and did not give tax in the time of Edward. [4] It was also described as an island in Domesday. [4, 5] In all there is doubt over whether a settlement actually existed at this site, or whether it was simply a landholding. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The isolated position of Stonehouse Court and St Cyril’s church to the southwest of the present settlement of Stonehouse has suggested that this was once the location of the village. No earthworks associated with medieval settlement have been recorded at the site. [1] Stonehouse is recorded in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of 34. In 1327 14 people are assessed. [2] In 1334 an above average is paid in the Lay Subsidy and 47 people pay the Lay Subsidy in 1524. In 1563 52 households are recorded and there are 284 communicants in 1603. [3] The VCH suggests that although the name of the parish was taken from the presumably early manor house site which became Stonehouse Court, the settlement developed along the road to Gloucester. [4] The place-name evidence would suggest that a stone-built house had been in place from the Saxon period. [4] The church had been built close to this manorial centre by the late twelfth century. [4] There is no firm evidence that there was extensive settlement around this manorial core. The settlement of Stonehouse has not seen any dramatic decline in population or a shift from its original development and as such is classed as doubtful on the available evidence. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Sudeley

description_full: Sudeley Castle and church possibly indicate the location of the village of Sudeley. The castle has a long developmental history with elements dating back to the fifteenth century along with a fifteenth-century great barn. [1] Excavations in 1875 by Canon Lysons reportedly revealed foundations of a house, road and stone walls of the former manor house to the east of Sudeley Castle. [2] To the south of the castle are a number of earthworks that could be related to the settlement but have more recently been interpreted as garden features. [3] Sudeley is recorded in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of 40. In 1327 16 people are assessed. [4] In 1334 it pays a below average amount to the Lay Subsidy, and in 1381 35 people pay the Poll Tax. There has been a reduction by 1525 when only 18 pay the Lay Subsidy and by 1563 10 households are recorded. It is unclear whether the settlement lay close to the castle and church, but it would now seem that all trace has been removed by later developments. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Taynton Parva
description_snippet: Taynton Parva is an excellent example of a number of different medieval landscape elements including a ringwork, motte and bailey, moated site and fishponds, a church, swannery as well as the settlement evidence.  The castle site is the most distinct feature in the centre of the site, with the moated site to the east and the location of the church to the southeast.
description_full: Taynton Parva is an excellent example of a number of different medieval landscape elements including a ringwork, motte and bailey, moated site and fishponds, a church, swannery as well as the settlement evidence. [1] The castle site is the most distinct feature in the centre of the site, with the moated site to the east and the location of the church to the southeast. The site is surrounded to the south and east by a defensive earthwork constructed during the Civil War when Royalist Troops were garrisoned at the site. [2] The evidence of the village is less clear and some of the features are covered by trees so are hard to interpret from the air, but presumably lay around these sites. [2] The site has been surveyed but the remains are still open to interpretation. [3] At Domesday a minimum population of six is recorded. In 1327 nine people are assessed. [4] In 1334 a below average Lay Subsidy is paid. By the sixteenth century there is only a record for Taynton and it is not subdivided into Magna and Parva. The church was in existence by 1134 but burnt down by Royalists in 1643. [3, 5] This has been confirmed in recent years by the discovery of metalwork in the area, particularly lead from the church. [6] It has been suggested that the village was abandoned by 1485, but there is insufficient evidence to be sure. [1, 3] In 1285 the landowner was granted a charter to use his lands at Taynton as a hunting chase and warren. [3] It is perhaps this that signifies the start of a slow decline. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Upcote
description_snippet: The grid reference used in the 1968 Gazetteer places this site to the south of Thorndale Farm. description_full: The grid reference used in the 1968 Gazetteer places this site to the south of Thorndale Farm. It has now been revealed that the settlement of Upcote was located 800m to the south at Upcote Farm. The earthworks at Thorndale Farm represent the settlement of Thorndon and this will appear as a separate record on the website when the list of deserted settlements is reviewed. [1] Within this parish there are a number of small settlements recorded including Upcote and Thornden which belonged to the main manor and held lands in Withington open fields. [1] The earthworks at Upcote Farm indicate at least three building platforms and a possible hollow way. [2] Upcote rarely appears in the taxation record and was probably always subsumed into Withington. One of the holdings at Withington in the Domesday Book has been identified as Upcote. [3] Upcote was the centre of a freehold estate, but the only suggestion of size comes with a mention in 1288 as a vill. In 1510 Upcote was described as a manor with two houses and by 1687 there was only one farmstead. [4] It is likely that this was never more than a manorial centre but on the presence of the earthworks there may have been a small associated settlement so has been classed as a deserted hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Upton
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The earthworks of Upton are located to the east and north of Lambs’ Cottage. A possible nine crofts are visible to the north and south of the line of the valley. A number of house platforms are located in these crofts and positioned near the central valley area.  To the east are further building platforms. The entire settlement seems to be demarcated by stone banks at the back of the crofts.
description_full: The earthworks of Upton are located to the east and north of Lambs’ Cottage. A possible nine crofts are visible to the north and south of the line of the valley. A number of house platforms are located in these crofts and positioned near the central valley area. [1] To the east are further building platforms. The entire settlement seems to be demarcated by stone banks at the back of the crofts. At least 27 buildings have been suggested across the site with one situated outside the main settlement interpreted as a possible sheepcote. [1, 2] The site was excavated between 1959 and 1968. This evidence suggests the number of structures is probably greater than 27 as a single earthwork may hide a number of structures. [3]. The excavation concentrated on a building complex at the centre of the site. [1, 3] This revealed a series of stone buildings focused around two separate longhouses which expanded and were adapted over time, preceded by timber structures. [1, 3] During excavation Roman material was discovered suggesting earlier occupation in the area. [1] It is suggested that the main building phases are later twelfth to fourteenth century. Only a handful of finds can be dated to the fifteenth century and are nothing more than indications of people walking across the site. [1] In 1973 a number of trenches were excavated across the site to improve the water supply. [4] A watching brief conducted at the time recorded 49 features, including some that are not visible on the earthwork plan of the site, as well as buildings outside the core of the settlement. [4] Upton was part of the large Blockley estate of the Bishop of Worcester. [1] Upton is first mentioned in a land dispute in 897. [1] By the thirteenth century Upton was favoured for its pasture with in 1299 pasture for 500 wethers (male sheep) – the highest recorded in the manor that year. [1] However the population in this period was also rising. In 1275 11 paid the Lay Subsidy, although their contribution was low. [1] In 1327 eight people are taxed. [1] By 1332-3 only four people are taxed showing at this point the decline had begun. [1] By 1334 Upton was now recorded with Blockley. A number of accounts for the manor of Blockley from 1383-4 do not include Upton, and the only mention of it was the lord of the manor paying the Lay Subsidy suggesting there was no-one else left in the village to pay. [1] Much of the manor of Blockley was increasingly used in this period as the main pasture ground for the flocks of the Bishops of Worcester. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: No clear earthworks of medieval settlement are visible in the area, and some features that have been indentified are probably field boundaries. description_full: The site of Williamstrip has not been firmly located. No clear earthworks of a deserted settlement can be seen in Williamstrip Park to the north. [1] One of the holdings of Hatherop in the Domesday Book has been identified as that which becomes Williamstrip from the late thirteenth century adopting the name of the manorial lord. [2, 3] In Domesday a minimum population of 12 is recorded. In 1327 ten people are assessed. [4] There is also an assessment of 28 people in Eastleach Turville and Williamstrip. [4] In 1381 open fields are recorded, but several inclosures had been made by 1713 and it had been completely enclosed by 1754. [5] In 1775 the population of Williamstrip is put at 48. [5] If the settlement was located in Williamstrip Park, landscaping began in 1754 and may have disguised any remains. [6] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Wormington Dastyn
e179_last: 1606 May 17 six fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: Two different locations for this site have been given. The 1968 Gazetteer places the site at Berry Wormington (SP 053340) and a review of deserted settlements placed it 900m to the north (SP 053349).  Neither of these locations has visible earthworks suggesting settlement evidence and both areas show ridge and furrow over much of the area in the 1947 air photographic coverage.
description_full: Two different locations for this site have been given. The 1968 Gazetteer places the site at Berry Wormington (SP 053340) and a review of deserted settlements placed it 900m to the north (SP 053349). [1] Neither of these locations has visible earthworks suggesting settlement evidence and both areas show ridge and furrow over much of the area in the 1947 air photographic coverage. This site, and that of Wormington Parva also on the Gazetteer, are hard to locate and distinguish from each other and from the surviving settlement of Wormington and Wormington Grange. In the Domesday Book only a single manor is recorded simply at Wormington with a minimum population of eight. Later in the records, a manor of Wormington Daston is distinct from that of Wormington, the Daston or Dastyn signifying the manorial lord. There had been a suggestion that Daston was the same as Wormington Magna but Glasscock notes that the separate taxation of Daston and Magna in 1334 shows they were two separate manors. [2, 3] In this 1334 Lay Subsidy a below average is paid along with Littleton. In the slightly earlier 1327 Lay Subsidy it is Wormington Parva that is recorded with Littleton which may suggest that it is Wormington Parva that is the same as Wormington Daston. Eighteen people paid the Poll Tax in 1381 at Daston again with Littleton. Rudder notes that anciently a separate manor in Wormington was held by the Daston family. [4] There are few fifteenth-century taxation records for Daston, but it does appear on the E179 database through the sixteenth century. Until the documentary evidence can be fully reviewed there is the possibility that a distinct Daston settlement may not have been present, although a distinct manor did. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Wormington Parva
e179_last: 1610 Feb 9 x July 23 subsidy

However the HER records a note that the documentary evidence is clear that Wormington Grange should be equated with Wormington Magna.  However the evidence for this is a single mention in deeds from 1621-1657 of the manor of Wormington Magna called Wormington Grange.
description_full: Wormington Parva has been equated by some authors with Wormington Grange and it is here that the 1968 Gazetteer places the site. However the HER records a note that the documentary evidence is clear that Wormington Grange should be equated with Wormington Magna. [1] However the evidence for this is a single mention in deeds from 1621-1657 of the manor of Wormington Magna called Wormington Grange. [2] In the area of Wormington Grange no features of medieval settlement have been identified in aerial photographs. In the Domesday Book only a single manor is recorded simply at Wormington with a minimum population of eight. In 1334 there are three separate records for Wormington: Wormington Magna, Wormington Parva and Wormington Dastyn – suggesting three distinct settlements being taxed. At this point Wormington Dastyn is taxed along with Littleton. In 1327 there are only two settlements recorded – Parva and Magna and it is Parva at this point which is taxed with Littleton with a total of 19 people listed. [3] Glasscock has equated Wormington Parva with Wormington Grange that appears in later records. [4] Parva at this point pays an average amount. In the 1381 Poll Tax again there are three separate records for Wormington: Wormington, Wormington Daston and Wormington Parva (again associated with Wormington Grange). [5] In Parva 32 people pay the Poll Tax. By 1524 the Lay Subsidy paid is well below average suggesting that decline had begun. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Stinsford
e179_last: 1661 July 8 free and voluntary present
description_snippet: Despite field investigations and aerial photographic analysis being carried out, there are no visible remains of the medieval settlement.  The church still stands and dates mostly from the thirteenth century.  The grid reference used by this site has been refined since the 1968 Gazetteer to locate it closer to the location of the church (SY 711 910).
description_full: Despite field investigations and aerial photographic analysis being carried out, there are no visible remains of the medieval settlement. [1] The church still stands and dates mostly from the thirteenth century. [2] The grid reference used by this site has been refined since the 1968 Gazetteer to locate it closer to the location of the church (SY 711 910). Stinsford is recorded in Domesday with a minimum population of eight. [1] The village is mentioned again in the 1334 Lay Subsidy with an average return. There are no further records and the only account derives from 1774. [3] Hutchins recounts that the manor of Stinsford was in its final throes of depopulation, that there only remained the church, the vicarage, a farmhouse and a small cluster of cottages. [3, 4] The manor house was rebuilt during the 1700s and it would seem that the village remnants were destroyed with the construction of the park around the house. [4] In the 1801 and 1841 Census, Stinsford reappears with a significant population but this is explained by the establishment of the new Stinsford which still exists today a few miles to the west of the Kingston Maurward Park. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Whitcombe
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: The physical remains of the village are located to the north and east of the present hamlet of Whitcomb. The remains are centred around the church and include a hollow way and house platforms.  Once a large hamlet, Whitcomb is an example of a shrunken settlement. description_full: The physical remains of the village are located to the north and east of the present hamlet of Whitcomb. The remains are centred around the church and include a hollow way and house platforms. [1] Once a large hamlet, Whitcomb is an example of a shrunken settlement. Whitcomb Farm is flanked by large seventeenth-century barns and sits on the edge of a large village green. [2] Whitcomb appears in Domesday with a minimum population of 14. The church is recorded in 1291 and in the 1334 Lay Subsidy the settlement paid a well below average amount. During the fourteenth century, the village disappears from all documentary record and only reappears in the 1545 Lay Subsidy when 13 people paid. 15 houses are recorded in the 1664 Hearth Tax. [3] A late eighteenth-century map records 10 dwellings. [1] This would seem to suggest periods of depopulation and recovery, and as such this has been classed as a shrunken settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Wimborne All Saints
description_snippet: This site is recorded as Wimborne All Hallows in several documents. On the first edition Ordnance Survey map of 1889 the main building on the site is All Hallows Farm, but to the south of this, is marked the site of All Hallows Church. No clear earthworks are visible at the site and much of the area has been affected by the creation of watercress beds.
description_full: This site is recorded as Wimborne All Hallows in several documents. On the first edition Ordnance Survey map of 1889 the main building on the site is All Hallows Farm, but to the south of this, is marked the site of All Hallows Church. No clear earthworks are visible at the site and much of the area has been affected by the creation of watercress beds. Wimborne All Hallows is located just to the north-east of Wimborne St Giles. The church at All Hallows was the mother church of this settlement. The area of All Hallows was originally named after the family who owned the estate with the name variant of Wimborne Karentham in the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries. [1] Wimborne All Saints and All Hallows occur from the late thirteenth century onwards. [1] Wimborne is mentioned in a number of places in the Domesday Book but these have been identified with Wimborne Minster and Wimborne St Giles, although the reference to Opewinburne is suggested to include All Hallows. [2] In the 1525 Lay Subsidy six people paid the tax, and three paid in 1545. The church was destroyed when the parish was joined to Wimborne St Giles in 1733. [3] By 1774 it was no longer standing. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.
