description_full: The area of Winterborne Came is now occupied by Came House, a mid eighteenth-century mansion. The village was said to be located to the north of the house and west of the church. [1] The earliest elements in the church are fourteenth century. [2] No earthworks of the settlement are visible and may well have been disturbed by the emparking around the House. Winterborne is recorded over 30 times in the Domesday record but it has not been possible to identify which Winterborne is specifically recorded in each entry. [3] This Winterborne is clearly seen in place-name evidence from the early twelfth century and is distinguished as Came from the late thirteenth century. [4] It does not appear in early tax records. Two houses are recorded in the 1664 Hearth Tax. [5] In 1774 Hutchins records it as almost depopulated with three or four houses. [6] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Winterbourne Farringdon
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: The physical remains of Winterbourne Farringdon are located 500m to the west of Winterbourne Came. The earthworks are divided into two blocks. The western block includes a complex of hollow ways, with a north-south route having two arms running east-west. These are surrounded by irregular platforms but also include the remains of the fourteenth-century St German’s church.
description_full: The physical remains of Winterbourne Farringdon are located 500m to the west of Winterbourne Came. The earthworks are divided into two blocks. The western block includes a complex of hollow ways, with a north-south route having two arms running east-west. These are surrounded by irregular platforms but also include the remains of the fourteenth-century St German’s church. [1] At least eight building platforms have been suggested. [1] The eastern block of earthworks is suggested to be incomplete and includes at least four enclosures possibly crofts. It has been suggested that the eastern part of this site could be part of the remains of Winterbourne Came. [2] The village of Winterbourne Farringdon may be one of the many Winterbourne’s in the Domesday Book. The settlement appears as Winterborne Germain from the mid-thirteenth century, and Winterborne Farringdon is recorded from the mid-fifteenth century. [3] In 1428 the village was excluded from taxation on the basis that that there were too few inhabitants. [1] The village continued its slow decline and by 1650 there were only three inhabitants recorded. [1] By 1774 Hutchins described the village as ‘entirely depopulated and has been so beyond the memory of man'. [4] Winterbourne Farringdon has in general, a lack of taxation records. This may be due to the village being subsumed into nearby settlements. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The only remains at Witherston or Wytherston are the farm and the complex of farm buildings. name: Wolfeton
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: Wolfeton is located in the parish of Charminster which was divided in two by the River Cerne. On the east bank of the Cerne lay a number of small medieval settlements each with a length of river bank and a long strip of land stretching north-east away from the water’s edge.  Wolfeton occupied one of these strips.
description_full: Wolfeton is located in the parish of Charminster which was divided in two by the River Cerne. On the east bank of the Cerne lay a number of small medieval settlements each with a length of river bank and a long strip of land stretching north-east away from the water’s edge. [1] Wolfeton occupied one of these strips. The hamlet of Wolfeton lay immediately to the west of Wolfeton House and covered an area of approximately 15 acres. The remains are now mostly destroyed, with only a few indistinct scarps and banks remaining. Prior to 1962, the remains were more complex with at least five long closes aligned along the road to the house. [1] To the south of the area is extensive evidence for water meadows. Wolfeton House was built in the sixteenth century over the site of an earlier fifteenth-century building, however it is only a small part of this structure, with much of the house being destroyed in the nineteenth century. [1] Wolfeton is not listed in Domesday although it may be recorded under the name of ‘Cerne’ along with several of the neighbouring villages. [1] In 1327 a population of two is recorded. [1] The village appears in the 1334 Lay Subsidy with a well below average payment. In the 1381 Poll Tax six people paid. It also appears in the 1545 Lay Subsidy when three individuals were taxed. In the 1664 Hearth Tax only the one house is recorded. [2] The village is thought to have been entirely deserted by 1772. This seems to have always been a small settlement and is best recorded as a deserted hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Woodsford
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: There are no clear physical remains at the site, although these were recorded in 1970.  The area has been damaged by ploughing. Woodsford is also known as Woodsford Strangways and the remains lie immediately to the east of the Woodsford Castle, a fourteenth-century structure.  The remains are characterized by hollow ways and enclosures.
description_full: There are no clear physical remains at the site, although these were recorded in 1970. [1] The area has been damaged by ploughing. Woodsford is also known as Woodsford Strangways and the remains lie immediately to the east of the Woodsford Castle, a fourteenth-century structure. [1] The remains are characterized by hollow ways and enclosures. Finds of flint, worked chalk blocks and thirteenth to fourteenth-century pottery were recovered along the northernmost hollow way. [1] Field investigations in 1981 discovered that the majority of the earthworks had been destroyed through ploughing. [2] Woodsford was first surveyed in the Domesday Book as two separate parts: an eastern section owned by the Cerne Abbey and the site of the current village of Woodsford; and the western section which is represented by Woodsford Castle. [1] Originally the western manor was owned by the Belet family. In 1335 a licence to crenellate the manor house was granted to William de Whitefield. [1] The village remains stretch between both manors and it may have been one contiguous settlement. [3] At Domesday the western manor records a minimum population of nine. The later tax records do not clearly distinguish between two manors. In the 1334 Lay Subsidy a well below average is paid. Only two people pay the 1544 Lay Subsidy. Four houses were recorded in the 1664 Hearth Tax, two houses in 1673. [4] With a cluster of buildings still occupied, partly in the area of East Woodsford, this is more a shrunken settlement than deserted and is classed as such by the NMR. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: There are no clear remains at the site with the present buildings being a manor house and farm. The RCHME believe it may have never been any bigger than this, with the settlement of Woodyates being at East Woodyates which survives today. [1] West Woodyates Manor House is seventeenth-century in date but may include some earlier elements. [1] A chapel is recorded at the site. [2] Woodyates is recorded in the ninth century. [3] All of the tax records refer to Woodyates and this is most likely East Woodyates. Although according to the English Place-Name Society the distinction of East and West Woodyates does not appear until the eighteenth century, there is a record of West Woodyates in 1525 with seven people taxed. [3] It has been classed as a deserted hamlet for the present. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Woolcomb Maltravers
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships.
description_snippet: There is no physical evidence for the village of Woolcomb Maltravers.  However gaps in the ridge and furrow along the current road may indicate the area of settlement. The location of the site given in the 1968 Gazetteer and by the NMR is just to the north of High Woolcomb Dairy. There are also other Woolcomb places in the area which have been highlighted by Good as possible locations for the settlement.
description_full: There is no physical evidence for the village of Woolcomb Maltravers. [1] However gaps in the ridge and furrow along the current road may indicate the area of settlement. The location of the site given in the 1968 Gazetteer and by the NMR is just to the north of High Woolcomb Dairy. There are also other Woolcomb places in the area which have been highlighted by Good as possible locations for the settlement. None of them bear the name Maltravers. [2] One is Woolcombe Farm to the east (ST 596 052) and the other is Redford Farm to the west (ST 607 057). The current cluster of cottages bearing the name Woolcomb is situated at ST 600 051. In the early documentation only Woolcomb is recorded. In the Domesday Book, two separate Woolcomb’s are identified. The one relating to this site can be traced by ownership to a John Mautravers, hence the name. [3] In the 1334 Lay Subsidy Woolcomb pays a well below average contribution. In 1524 nine people pay the Lay Subsidy and 16 people are taxed in 1563. Woolcomb Matravers (slightly different spelling) was described by Hutchins in 1774 as a tything, manor and hamlet with a chapel. [2] The site of the chapel has not been established. [1] 13 houses are recorded in the 1664 Heath Tax. [4] These later tax records probably refer to the scatter of farmsteads bearing the name as outlined above and this may reflect a dispersed area of settlement. The earlier records may well suggest a nucleated village in the area. It was never very large, and then it may have declined before becoming a dispersed settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Little Burdon
description_snippet: There are faint features still seen surrounding Little Burdon Farm. To the north there are a number of low banks at the edge of the ridge and furrow. There have been a number of different interpretations of these banks. These include that the ridge and furrow is later in date than the settlement remains, but the banks more likely signify the edge of the ridge and furrow.
description_full: There are faint features still seen surrounding Little Burdon Farm. To the north there are a number of low banks at the edge of the ridge and furrow. There have been a number of different interpretations of these banks. These include that the ridge and furrow is later in date than the settlement remains, but the banks more likely signify the edge of the ridge and furrow. [1] If they are the edge of the ridge and furrow then any settlement in the area may be hidden in the area of the present farm which sits in this area. Some earthworks that had previously been seen in the area have been infilled. [1] Little Burdon is mentioned in 1183. [2]. From the thirteenth to the early sixteenth century some land is owned by Neasham Priory and they take tithes from Little Burdon. [3] It is unclear the extent of any settlement at this site and is classed as a hamlet by this website. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Castle Eden

description_snippet: There are no clear remains at the site, but areas of ridge and furrow can be seen in the surrounding area. The area of the settlement has been landscaped and ploughed. description_full: There are no clear remains at the site, but areas of ridge and furrow can be seen in the surrounding area. The area of the settlement has been landscaped and ploughed. It is suggested that the settlement was located between The Castle and the church to the south. In 1775 an Anglo-Saxon burial was discovered in this area. Further excavations were carried out in 1974 when the site was under threat from development. [1] Ten trenches were excavated down to the first archaeological features, but not fully excavated. [1] These revealed a north-south hollow way and suggested houses to either side forming two rows. [1] Pottery uncovered dated from the twelfth to sixteenth century. [1] The first mention of Castle Eden is in pre-conquest documents, recording the place-name. There is evidence of the settlement through the medieval period. The church is recorded in 1291. There are three households recorded in 1563. In the 1666 Hearth Tax a total of 18 people are listed. [2] The estate was bought in 1758 by Rowland Burdon who landscaped the area around a new house ‘The Castle’ that he built in c. 1765. [1] This development also included ‘The Village’ a settlement of two rows on the road to the church which was built to replace the medieval settlement that had been lost before the early nineteenth century. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The remains of the village of Thrislington have been badly damaged during quarrying activity, but rescue excavations were undertaken in 1973-1974. [1] The east-west track present in the 1970s signified the medieval routeway through the settlement and on either side of this were enclosures which backed onto ridge and furrow. [1] These enclosures seemed to represent tofts with building platforms to the front of them. [1] The excavations suggested the manor house was constructed in the twelfth century and abandoned in the early fourteenth century. [1] Excavation of buildings in the tofts suggests they appear in the thirteenth century and some disappear by the middle of the fifteenth century, while others continue until the sixteenth century. [1] Due to Thrislington being a secular freehold, there is little record of its development. It is recorded in 1208 as a holding of Roger de Thurstanton, tenants are mentioned in 1262, but then do not appear again until the mid-fourteenth century. [1] By the end of the sixteenth century all the landholdings at Thrislington were in the hands of one family and this seems to signify the final desertion of the village. [2] The earliest mention of Ulnaby comes in the form of a marriage settlement in the twelfth century. [1] By 1629 the settlement is still recorded but it has reduced to three cottages. [1] There continues to be the reduced population into the nineteenth century when eventually only the Hall and associated buildings remain. description_full: The identity of this settlement has been somewhat debated. It was given the name Yoden by antiquarian writers but has since been identified as Horden. Excavations in 1884 proved the medieval date of the remains uncovering what were described as ‘foundations of the rudest descriptions, consisting entirely of mere shapeless masses of un-hewn stone’. [1] The area of the site is surrounded by the modern settlement of Peterlee, and the earthworks themselves have suffered damage over the years. Yoden is mentioned from the twelfth century, however these are reporting accounts of earlier activity back to the tenth century. [2] It should be noted though that there is no concrete evidence that Yoden mentioned in these documents is represented by the earthworks visible at this site. [2] The evidence does point to these remains being the village of Horden which is mentioned in documents from the fourteenth century. [2] Horden Hall is located 500m to the north of the site. A valuation of 1431 suggests at this time there were eight crofts at the site. [2] Documents have suggested the site was abandoned by 1435. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: This is a complex place to understand. More usually referred to as Belchamp St Ethelbert this settlement was close to Belchamp Otten and Belchamp St Paul’s. At one time it was its own parish but all record of this has disappeared. Added confusion about this settlement has crept in with the church at Belchamp Otten being dedicated to St Ethelbert, and this site sometimes referred to as St Albrights. Through the thirteenth and fourteenth century there are references to Belchamp St Ethelbert and Belchamp St Albrights. [1] Rodwell records the church as long ago demolished. [2] However the church is located at a distance (TL 8052 4326) from the grid reference in the 1968 Gazetteer (TL 770 420). As all records point to the former grid reference it has been adopted here. There are reports of pottery and stone work being seen in the area, and the field name on the Tithe Map of the area is Chapel Field. [3] The VCH in its transcription of Domesday Book identified one of the Belchamp records in the lands of Count Eustace in Essex as Belchamp St Ethelbert. [4] However this has not been followed by either the Phillimore edition of the Domesday Book or the English Place-Name Society. [1, 5] There is a lack of documentary evidence supporting a large settlement here and the best that can be suggested at the present time is a deserted hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Little Birch
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: There are no clear remains of settlement in the area of the ruined church at Little Birch. This is situated close to the site of the now demolished Little Birch Hall, built on the site of the old manor house.  The parish of Little Birch was once separate to the neighbouring parish of Great Birch. Little Birch is recorded at Domesday with a minimum population of 19.
description_full: There are no clear remains of settlement in the area of the ruined church at Little Birch. This is situated close to the site of the now demolished Little Birch Hall, built on the site of the old manor house. [1] The parish of Little Birch was once separate to the neighbouring parish of Great Birch. Little Birch is recorded at Domesday with a minimum population of 19. Unfortunately in later taxation records it is always included with other settlements which makes it impossible to establish the size of population. The church at Little Birch existed by the eleventh century but at various points in the seventeenth century the church is described as derelict and in need of repairs. [2] This all suggests a limited population by this point. In 1607 the parishioners attend services at Great Birch due to the ruinous state of the church, in 1664 parishioners are once again recorded as attending other churches and by 1684 the three families of the parish attend Easthorpe Church. [2] By 1768 the church had been mainly demolished, although there is still considerable standing material today. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Great Braxted
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The HER and NMR have records of earthworks of a village to the south of the church but also record that no clear earthworks are now visible. [1, 2] Braxted is mentioned at Domesday, but the name Great Braxted first appears in 1206.  There are two separate holdings in Domesday Book which may reflect the later division into Great and Little Braxted. The church contains twelfth-century features.
description_full: The HER and NMR have records of earthworks of a village to the south of the church but also record that no clear earthworks are now visible. [1, 2] Braxted is mentioned at Domesday, but the name Great Braxted first appears in 1206. [3] There are two separate holdings in Domesday Book which may reflect the later division into Great and Little Braxted. The church contains twelfth-century features. [4] Great Braxted pays an average Lay Subsidy in 1334, and 52 people pay the Lay Subsidy in 1524. In the 1670 Hearth Tax there are 58 households taxed. [5] It is suggested the village was deserted after Braxted Park was extended around 1832. [1, 6] That there was a medieval population in the area can be clearly seen from the medieval taxations but it is unclear whether there was ever a nucleated settlement close to the church, or if there was a settlement at the manorial centre, now under Braxted Park. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Faulkbourne
e179_last: 1671 March 6 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: The church at Faulkbourne stands at the edge of the park land surrounding Faulkbourne Hall. There are no clear earthwork remains close to the church. On the 1838 Tithe Map the area around the church is marked as ‘Park Lands’.  Faulkbourne is mentioned in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of 11. The main structure of the church is twelfth century in date.
description_full: The church at Faulkbourne stands at the edge of the park land surrounding Faulkbourne Hall. There are no clear earthwork remains close to the church. On the 1838 Tithe Map the area around the church is marked as ‘Park Lands’. [1] Faulkbourne is mentioned in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of 11. The main structure of the church is twelfth century in date. [2] In the 1377 Poll Tax 27 people were taxed and in 1525 30 people paid the Lay Subsidy. It continues to appear in the census. Faulkbourne Hall dates from the fifteenth century. [2] Sir John Montgomery was granted licence to crenellate his house in 1439. [3] The settlement does not appear in the 1670 Hearth Tax returns but a certificate of exemption was issued in 1671. [4] A small cluster of houses still exists to the north of the church. This might be a relocated settlement arising from emparking, but it is more likely there never was a nucleated settlement around the church. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Snoreham
e179_last: 1571 May 29 or earlier clerical subsidy
description_snippet: Although the site is listed as the village of Snoreham in the Gazetteer of 1968, on some records such as the NMR and HER it is recorded as the deserted medieval village of Latchingdon. [1, 2] Latchingdon still exists but to the south is located Snoreham Hall Farm. There are no visible earthworks in the area of Snoreham Hall Farm.
description_full: Although the site is listed as the village of Snoreham in the Gazetteer of 1968, on some records such as the NMR and HER it is recorded as the deserted medieval village of Latchingdon. [1, 2] Latchingdon still exists but to the south is located Snoreham Hall Farm. There are no visible earthworks in the area of Snoreham Hall Farm. The church of St Peter’s once stood in the area and there is some suggestion that a rectangular area to the south of Snoreham Hall marks its location. [3] There are place-name references to Snoreham from 1238 to 1552. [4] Elements of the current Snoreham Hall Farm date from the sixteenth century. Snoreham only appears in clerical taxations. It does not appear separately in Domesday Book but may be one of the four references to Latchingdon. There are no secular taxations to help plot the site of any settlement. Snoreham does not appear in the 1670 Hearth Tax but Latchingdon does appear with 19 households recorded. [5] There is no clear evidence of a substantial settlement here. For the present it is classed as a deserted hamlet and may have been hidden in the documentary record with Latchingdon. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Stanway
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The grid reference used here (TL 952 220) is an edited version of that provided in the 1968 Gazetteer (TL 952 206) which placed the site in the same general location as Little Birch. The site is now covered by Colchester Zoo, with only the ruins of All Saints church and Stanway Hall remaining. The church dates from the late thirteenth century but has been in ruins since the early eighteenth century.
description_full: The grid reference used here (TL 952 220) is an edited version of that provided in the 1968 Gazetteer (TL 952 206) which placed the site in the same general location as Little Birch. The site is now covered by Colchester Zoo, with only the ruins of All Saints church and Stanway Hall remaining. The church dates from the late thirteenth century but has been in ruins since the early eighteenth century. [1] The hall was constructed in the middle of the sixteenth century. [2] Early in the seventeenth century the church was converted to a private chapel, suggesting that the population had faded by this point. [1] Stanway is mentioned from c. 1000, and in some of these early references it is recorded as Stanways. [3] Later reference is made to two hamlets, Great and Little Stanway, and this plural reference may be an indicator that it was always two settlements. [3] The settlement of Little Stanway has continued, located 2.5km to the north of the current site, and had its own chapel that is now the parish church. The centre of modern Stanway is situated to the east of this area. The area of Stanway Hall and All Saints was the centre of Great Stanway. [3] The settlement has always been recorded as Stanway and that makes it difficult to see the true size at Great Stanway – and whether this ever had any nucleated settlement could be in doubt. It is clear that settlement has always been dispersed throughout the parish. [4] At Domesday Stanway is recorded with a minimum population of 75. In the Poll Tax of 1377, 99 people were taxed and in 1524, 37 paid the Lay Subsidy. Stanway appears in the 1670 Hearth Tax with 54 households recorded. [5] At present this has been classed as a deserted hamlet as there is no clear evidence for a nucleated settlement in the area. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Thunderley
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: No clear remains of a settlement can be seen apart from the moated site around Thunderley Hall. The site of Thunderley church is recorded to the south on Ordnance Survey maps. Faint traces have been spotted on aerial photographs.  The farmer has reported building debris in the area of the church, but not from other areas.  Field walking in 1967 recovered twelfth to fourteenth-century pottery.
description_full: No clear remains of a settlement can be seen apart from the moated site around Thunderley Hall. The site of Thunderley church is recorded to the south on Ordnance Survey maps. Faint traces have been spotted on aerial photographs. [1] The farmer has reported building debris in the area of the church, but not from other areas. [1] Field walking in 1967 recovered twelfth to fourteenth-century pottery. [2] There are references to Thunderley from Domesday through to the fourteenth century. [3] At Domesday a minimum population of 17 is recorded. In 1334 it pays a well below average Lay Subsidy suggesting this was never a large settlement. The parish of Thunderley was combined with Wimbish in 1425, when the church was recorded as ruined. [1, 4, 5] The parish is exempt from taxation as there are fewer than ten parishioners in 1428. [6] Thunderley does not appear in the 1670 Hearth Tax returns. [7] It is mentioned in the census with Wimbish. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Wickham Bishops
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The site of the old Saint Bartholomew’s Church (sometimes referred to as St Peter’s) stands next to the flood plain of the River Blackwater. This site is located 2km to the southwest of the modern settlement and church of Wickham Bishops. Essex HER records a collection of pottery recovered from the area of the old church by Rev. Gibbons between 1899-1907. This included a range of medieval and post-medieval pottery.
description_full: The site of the old Saint Bartholomew’s Church (sometimes referred to as St Peter’s) stands next to the flood plain of the River Blackwater. This site is located 2km to the southwest of the modern settlement and church of Wickham Bishops. Essex HER records a collection of pottery recovered from the area of the old church by Rev. Gibbons between 1899-1907. This included a range of medieval and post-medieval pottery. [1] No features of medieval settlement are visible apart from the church. The name Wickham Bishops (instead of just Wickham) appears from the late thirteenth century and is associated with the Bishops of London. [2] Wickham however appears from c.940. [2] The church dates from the late eleventh century. [3] The RCHME also records a fifteenth-century cottage close to the church. [3] Wickham is recorded in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of 14. In the Poll Tax of 1377, 53 people were taxed. The settlement is absent from the sixteenth-century taxations used by this website but appears throughout this period on the E179 database. In the 1670 Hearth Tax returns 32 households are recorded. [4] It is clear that there has always been a population at Wickham Bishops. Whether it has always been a dispersed settlement, with an isolated church, or whether the settlement has shifted locations over time is not currently discernible and for this reason at the moment the settlement has been classed as a doubtful DMV. This site has been added and removed from the list of deserted medieval villages a number of times by the Medieval Settlement Research Group, highlighting the uncertainty about this settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Abloads Court

description_full: There is only limited evidence for a settlement around Alkington Farm although it is the name of the parish. There is a moated site 330m to the southwest of the farm. No clear earthworks are visible. Alkington is referred to in the Domesday Book as one of the outliers of Berkeley, so although the record suggests a large population, there is no way of knowing the figure at Alkington rather than the other separate outliers. In 1327 45 people pay the Lay Subsidy. [1] Along with Hilton it pays an above average Lay Subsidy in 1334. In the sixteenth century an above average payment is made in 1524 and records continue into the nineteenth-century census. This would appear to have always been an area of dispersed settlement. The site has been classified as a deserted hamlet as if there was a manorial centre as suggested by the moated site, there may have been a small associated settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Ampney St. Mary
description_snippet: There are two sites that have been classed as a deserted settlement at Ampney St. Mary. The church of St Mary stands isolated, close to Ampney Brook at SP 075 015. The church contains twelfth-century elements.  On the HER and NMR this is recorded as the deserted medieval village of Ampney St. Mary and the settlement is confirmed by the Bristol and Gloucestershire Archaeological Society.
description_full: There are two sites that have been classed as a deserted settlement at Ampney St. Mary. The church of St Mary stands isolated, close to Ampney Brook at SP 075 015. The church contains twelfth-century elements. [1] On the HER and NMR this is recorded as the deserted medieval village of Ampney St. Mary and the settlement is confirmed by the Bristol and Gloucestershire Archaeological Society. [2, 3, 4] The current settlement of Ampney St. Mary is also known as Ashbrook. Close to this location a field visit in 1988 noted areas of limestone rubble. [5] The Gazetteer had the settlement based at this site. It has been decided to assign the settlement at the church site, not the one given by the Gazetteer. Ampney St. Mary is recorded in Domesday with a minimum population of 18. The church is recorded in 1291. There is no record in the fourteenth-century taxations. In 1525 13 people are taxed and the settlement continues to be recorded into the census periods. It is suggested that the settlement was relocated when it was deemed that the ford was too dangerous and the coach road was diverted. [2] It is unknown at exactly which time this happened. This in essence is a migrated settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Aston
e179_last: 1606 May 17 six fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: There are no clear earthworks of house plots or routeways but a small number of linear features have been identified to the northeast of Aston Farm. [1, 2] The area to the north of Aston Farm has been disturbed by the construction of Aston Down airfield. Aston, along with another deserted settlement, Lowesmore, formed a detached section of Avening parish. Aston is not recorded in the Domesday Book.
description_full: There are no clear earthworks of house plots or routeways but a small number of linear features have been identified to the northeast of Aston Farm. [1, 2] The area to the north of Aston Farm has been disturbed by the construction of Aston Down airfield. Aston, along with another deserted settlement, Lowesmore, formed a detached section of Avening parish. Aston is not recorded in the Domesday Book. At Lowesmore and Aston there were 15 tenants in the late twelfth century. [3] In 1327 11 people paid the Lay Subsidy in Aston, and they paid an average amount in 1334. [4] In 1381 there are still eight tax payers, unlike Lowesmore where no-one paid the tax. By the eighteenth century there were only two houses in Aston and Lowesmore. [3] It would seem that Aston was deserted at a later date than Lowesmore but the records are unclear when this happened. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Aylworth
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: A number of different earthworks can be seen to the south of Aylworth Farm. The area of earthworks has been sliced through by a railway line. Features to the south of the railway line have been ploughed.  A number of building platforms have been plotted. The settlement was situated in an area of a number of springs.  A minimum population of 11 is recorded in the Domesday Book.
description_full: A number of different earthworks can be seen to the south of Aylworth Farm. The area of earthworks has been sliced through by a railway line. Features to the south of the railway line have been ploughed. [1] A number of building platforms have been plotted. The settlement was situated in an area of a number of springs. [2] A minimum population of 11 is recorded in the Domesday Book. In 1327 only three people were assessed. [3] By 1341 it is recorded that ‘many tenants left their holdings and left them vacant and uncultivated’. [4] In 1344 a very low amount is paid in the Lay Subsidy. In 1381 only six people paid the Poll Tax. The VCH suggests that this may not be complete depopulation but redistribution of the population through the area, hence the six people recorded in 1381. [2] This seems to have always been a small settlement, perhaps with dispersed elements and has been classed here as a deserted medieval hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Bidfield
e179_last: 1662 May 19 hearth tax
description_snippet: Earthworks were visible to the west of Bidfield Farm but were partly destroyed in road widening in 1966.  Excavations at the time of the road widening revealed evidence of five or six houses as well as Roman pottery and a circular structure but the records from this work have been lost.  A small number of earthworks can still be seen, but some of these may be later in date.
description_full: Earthworks were visible to the west of Bidfield Farm but were partly destroyed in road widening in 1966. [1] Excavations at the time of the road widening revealed evidence of five or six houses as well as Roman pottery and a circular structure but the records from this work have been lost. [1] A small number of earthworks can still be seen, but some of these may be later in date. [1] Bidfield emerged as a detached portion and separate unit of Bisley parish by 1270. [2] Only four people were assessed in 1327, it pays a below average amount in 1334 and by 1381 it was recorded as uninhabited. [2, 3] A record of open fields exists in 1370 but there are no further mentions. [2] It is suggested that this settlement was deserted in the 1370s or 1380s. [4] There is no evidence for a sizable settlement here and it has been classed as a deserted medieval hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Boxwell
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: There are no clear features of buildings or houses, though field boundaries and enclosures have been plotted.  Boxwell Court House and St Mary’s Church are situated in the centre of the site. The church includes thirteenth-century elements. Boxwell Court belonged to St Peter’s Abbey, Gloucester until the Reformation, and elements of the current building date to the fifteenth century.
description_full: There are no clear features of buildings or houses, though field boundaries and enclosures have been plotted. [1] Boxwell Court House and St Mary’s Church are situated in the centre of the site. The church includes thirteenth-century elements. Boxwell Court belonged to St Peter’s Abbey, Gloucester until the Reformation, and elements of the current building date to the fifteenth century. [2] Boxwell was mentioned in Domesday with a minimum population of 21. In 1327 four people are assessed. [3] By 1334 a below average Lay Subsidy is paid. In 1524 17 people are assessed along with Leighterton. For the time being this has been classed as a deserted medieval village but there is a possibility that it acted as the manorial centre for an area of dispersed settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Brickhampton
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: There are no clear settlement remains at the site. The site has now been landscaped as part of a golf course. A scatter of medieval pottery was recorded during the construction of the golf club house.  Six trenches were excavated close to Brickhampton Court Farm but this did not reveal evidence of medieval settlement but areas of ridge and furrow were recorded.
description_full: There are no clear settlement remains at the site. The site has now been landscaped as part of a golf course. A scatter of medieval pottery was recorded during the construction of the golf club house. [1] Six trenches were excavated close to Brickhampton Court Farm but this did not reveal evidence of medieval settlement but areas of ridge and furrow were recorded. [2] Brickhampton is first recorded in the mid-twelfth century. [3] In 1327 five people are assessed. [4] In 1334 a below average Lay Subsidy is paid. It does appear in some of the later sixteenth-century lay subsidies, but not in the ones used by this website. This would never seem to have been a big settlement and has been classed as a hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Castlett Farm
e179_last: 1606 May 17 six fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: A slightly refined grid reference (SP 089 259) has been used to locate the site over the features. description_full: A slightly refined grid reference (SP 089 259) has been used to locate the site over the features. At least 14 house platforms have been plotted at the site, along a northwest-southeast running hollow way although these are not clear on aerial photography. [1] Medieval pottery was reported during construction work. [1] An evaluation in 2005 revealed a ditch in-filled in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. [2] Pottery at the site seems to decline in the fifteenth century. [2] Castlett is recorded in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of four. In 1327 five people are assessed. [3] In 1334 a below average Lay Subsidy is paid. In 1381 four people paid the Poll Tax. By 1504 it had been converted to pasture. [4] Although the earthworks at the site may suggest more extensive settlement, the documentary evidence would suggest a small settlement and it has been classed as a hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Charlton
description_snippet: The 1968 Gazetteer has the site located at Charlton Down House, 700m to the west of the deserted settlement of Elmestree. There are some traces of ridge and furrow close to Charlton Down House, but no evidence of settlement can be seen. This had been called Elmestree Farm and it is more likely that the settlement of Charlton was located just to the west of Tetbury at Charlton House, rather than at this location.
description_full: The 1968 Gazetteer has the site located at Charlton Down House, 700m to the west of the deserted settlement of Elmestree. There are some traces of ridge and furrow close to Charlton Down House, but no evidence of settlement can be seen. This had been called Elmestree Farm and it is more likely that the settlement of Charlton was located just to the west of Tetbury at Charlton House, rather than at this location. [1] The gird reference used here has been modified to place it at this new location (ST 880 932). The Cotswold NMP recorded building platforms and a trackway at this site. [2] Charlton is recorded as a hamlet of Tetbury from the mid-thirteenth century. [3] Charlton does not appear directly in the Domesday record but is suggested to be part of the members of the manor of Westbury. [4] In 1327 nine people are assessed. [5] It pays an average Lay Subsidy in 1334 and 26 people paid the Poll Tax of 1381. There had been a reduction by 1525 when eight people pay the Lay Subsidy. Of the four hamlets of Tetbury, Charlton is the only one surviving into the seventeenth century. [6] In 1672 there were 11 households assessed for the Hearth Tax. [6] By 1824 Charlton consisted of the manor house and a few cottages. [6] Although the physical evidence does not suggest a large settlement, the documentary evidence would indicate a larger settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Upper Coberley
e179_last: 1662 May 19 hearth tax
description_snippet: The grid reference used here has been refined to SO 973 158 over the evidence of earthworks mapped at the site. The earthworks have been recorded to the west of current Westbury and Lower Farm. They include a trackway and at least ten building outlines.  These earthworks are 500m to the east of the evidence of the shrunken settlement at Coberley.
description_full: The grid reference used here has been refined to SO 973 158 over the evidence of earthworks mapped at the site. The earthworks have been recorded to the west of current Westbury and Lower Farm. They include a trackway and at least ten building outlines. [1] These earthworks are 500m to the east of the evidence of the shrunken settlement at Coberley. In Domesday Book a single hide is recorded at Upper Coberley as part of the manor of Northleach. In later records Upper Coberley is recorded with Northleach, apart from 1327 when it is recorded separately and seven people are assessed. [2] In 1334 they pay an above average amount of Lay Subsidy. At least 24 people were taxed in 1381. It continues to be recorded through the sixteenth century. [3] The earthwork evidence clearly shows a more extensive settlement than the three farms now present. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Combe End
description_snippet: The grid reference has been refined to place it over the earthwork evidence at SO 983 115. The area is now ploughed and planted with trees but features had been spotted on earlier aerial photographs suggesting field boundaries and building platforms to the north and east of Combend Manor.  There was no clear structure to any settlement. A field visit to the site saw an area of ploughing.
description_full: The grid reference has been refined to place it over the earthwork evidence at SO 983 115. The area is now ploughed and planted with trees but features had been spotted on earlier aerial photographs suggesting field boundaries and building platforms to the north and east of Combend Manor. [1] There was no clear structure to any settlement. A field visit to the site saw an area of ploughing. No pottery was discovered but areas of building rubble were encountered. [1] The Phillimore Domesday translation places the land noted as Colesbourne at Combend, rather than the settlement of the same name. [2] The place-name appears from the early thirteenth century. [3] Our main historical evidence comes from the seventeenth century onwards. A hamlet is in existence in 1630, but by 1710 there were only four houses, the settlement had grown again by the early nineteenth century, but a single house was there by 1883. [1] Until there is clearer evidence of a medieval settlement at the site it has been classified as doubtful. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Daylesford
domesday_ref: GLOS E27. E29. EvA121. EvC41. EvN5. WoB7. WoC6
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: A number of features have been plotted at Daylesford around the church. These include boundaries, rectilinear enclosures and building platforms.  The church was rebuilt in the nineteenth century replacing a Norman structure.  A moated site to the north was probably the site of the manor house. At the site around the church there are a number of buildings built from the early nineteenth century as an estate village.
description_full: A number of features have been plotted at Daylesford around the church. These include boundaries, rectilinear enclosures and building platforms. [1] The church was rebuilt in the nineteenth century replacing a Norman structure. [2] A moated site to the north was probably the site of the manor house. At the site around the church there are a number of buildings built from the early nineteenth century as an estate village. The old houses were pulled down as the new ones were constructed. [3] Daylesford is recorded from the eighth century. [4] It appears in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of 12. In 1334 it is recorded in Worcestershire with an average payment to the Lay Subsidy. In 1525 six people pay the Lay Subsidy. Its absence in other records makes it hard to plot the maximum size of this settlement. The earthworks suggest a larger settlement than is currently present and this has been classified as a shrunken settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Didcot
e179_last: 1695 Nov 22 or later aid of four shillings in the pound for one year
description_snippet: The settlement evidence can be found to the east of Didcot Farm, surrounded by areas of ridge and furrow. A hollow way and five tofts have been plotted.  Didcot is first mentioned in the eleventh century. At Domesday a minimum population of 12 is recorded. In 1327 ten people were assessed.  In 1334 an average Lay Subsidy was paid.
description_full: The settlement evidence can be found to the east of Didcot Farm, surrounded by areas of ridge and furrow. A hollow way and five tofts have been plotted. [1] Didcot is first mentioned in the eleventh century. At Domesday a minimum population of 12 is recorded. In 1327 ten people were assessed. [2] In 1334 an average Lay Subsidy was paid. There was a chapel of Tewksbury Abbey until the sixteenth century, but the settlement was mostly depopulated in the late fifteenth century when the area was inclosed, and 30 people were evicted in 1491. [3] The settlement was reduced to a single farm by the seventeenth century. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Lower Ditchford
description_snippet: The earthworks of Lower Ditchford can be clearly seen to the north of Ditchford Mill, to the northwest of the Knee Brook. description_full: The earthworks of Lower Ditchford can be clearly seen to the north of Ditchford Mill, to the northwest of the Knee Brook. There were three Ditchfords recorded in documents, Upper, Middle and Lower, all of which continued as a separate farm. The history of these sites is complex as they formed a detached part of Worcestershire, within Gloucestershire, at various points of time. [1] The complex set of earthworks includes a number of tofts on either side of a sinuous hollow way and wide green. [2] At least 12 building enclosures and at least eight buildings have been identified. [3] Surrounding the settlement is a number of fields which were probably seasonally flooded water meadows. [3] A number of building structures are possibly post-desertion structures. [4] There is not always a clear division into separate settlements in the records. Ditchford was recorded in the Worcestershire section of the Domesday Book with a minimum population of five. In 1334 Upper and Middle Ditchford are recorded in the Lay Subsidy but Lower Ditchford is absent. The villages at Ditchford were noted as ruinous in 1491 by John Rous, a priest of Warwick. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

Upper Ditchford pays an average Lay Subsidy in 1334 and is recorded in Worcestershire. The villages at Ditchford were noted as ruinous in 1491 by John Rous, a priest of Warwick. [1] The value of the tithe-corn in Upper Ditchford had halved in value between 1384-1419 and the end of arable farming is signaled when it ceased completely in about 1475 [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Frocester
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: This site has been identified due to the presence of St Peter’s Church 1.5km to the west of the present settlement of Frocester. The church has been mainly destroyed, but areas have been excavated which show evidence of a Roman villa, followed by a Norman church constructed on the site.  The area surrounding the church shows no evidence of settlement remains, but ridge and furrow is present.
description_full: This site has been identified due to the presence of St Peter’s Church 1.5km to the west of the present settlement of Frocester. The church has been mainly destroyed, but areas have been excavated which show evidence of a Roman villa, followed by a Norman church constructed on the site. [1] The area surrounding the church shows no evidence of settlement remains, but ridge and furrow is present. There has been extensive excavation and fieldwork carried out in the parish enabling a detailed understanding of settlement development from the pre-Roman period onwards. [2] Frocester was recorded in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of 18. A church is recorded in the 1291 Taxation. In 1327 12 people were assessed. [3] In the sixteenth century at least 40 households are recorded and in 1603 210 communicants are recorded. [4] Antiquarian reports suggested the village around the church had been burnt down and moved to a dryer location. [5] A sizeable settlement still exists and bears the name Frocester but this is to the east. It has been suggested that this has always been the location of the settlement. [6] The location of the church could be explained as being placed in between Frocester and Coaley, both of which it served. [6] It has also been shown that the parish of Frocester included a number of small dispersed settlements, many of which were abandoned in the thirteenth century. [7] There is no clear evidence of settlement in the area of St Peter’s Church and therefore the site has now been classified as doubtful. [2] However when the deserted settlements of Gloucestershire are reviewed in the future, a number of the small dispersed settlements that have been identified in the parish may then appear in the new gazetteer. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Gawcombe

It is suggested that the settlement disappeared when Gawcombe Wood was emparked in 1246.
description_full: This settlement identified as Gawcombe in the 1968 Gazetteer is connected with the settlement of Combe Baskerville, which later becomes Westcote. House sites were said to be present in c. 1700 in Gawcombe Wood but only minimal earthworks are now present. [1] These include one possible house platform, lynchets and a hollow way. [2] It is suggested that the settlement disappeared when Gawcombe Wood was emparked in 1246. There is no direct reference in Domesday Book but Combe Baskerville is possibly the manor recorded as Combe with a minimum population of 22. [1] A chapel is suggested in some early documents. [1] As Westcote is referred to by several different names up until the sixteenth century, it becomes difficult to distinguish clearly if any records relate to this settlement in the woods. [1] Gawcombe does not appear in any of the taxation records used by the website, and Combe Baskerville only appears on three records in the E179 section of the National Archives – once in 1294 and two in 1340. It would appear from the evidence that there may have been a small settlement in the woods, and the VCH records this as possibly the earliest settlement in the parish, but it disappeared early on. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Harford
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: This village is more often referred to as Lower Harford. description_full: This village is more often referred to as Lower Harford. The remains of the settlement can be seen to the east of the River Windrush, with two hollow ways running southwest to northeast ending at the river. At least 11 building platforms can be discerned. [1] It is suggested that only a few of these were actual domestic dwellings with the rest being used for agricultural purposes. [2] There is also evidence of water management features close to the river. [3] It is suggested that Harford was the earliest settlement in the parish, located at the ford, with the settlement of Naunton, the newer settlement. [4] At Domesday there is a minimum population of seven. In 1327 two people are assessed. [5] By 1341 it is suggested that the settlement was largely deserted and a well below average Lay Subsidy is paid in 1334. [4, 6] By 1381 it is no longer distinguished from Naunton in the tax records. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hilcot
e179_last: 1606 May 17 six fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The earthworks of the settlement of Hilcot (sometimes referred to as Upper Hilcot) are visible to the east of Upper Hilcot Farm. description_full: The earthworks of the settlement of Hilcot (sometimes referred to as Upper Hilcot) are visible to the east of Upper Hilcot Farm. The grid reference has been slightly refined to place it over the earthworks. They include an east-west hollow way and two house platforms to the south. The NMP suggests that this might be more likely a farmstead rather than a settlement, however Dyer suggests there was once possibly up to six houses. [1, 2] Medieval pottery has been recovered from molehills and an excavation by an unknown party is said to have been conducted. [3] A sheepcote was constructed over the remains of the settlement. [2] Hilcot is often recorded with Withington. [4] At Domesday it is recorded as one of the lands in Withington. It pays a below average amount in 1334. By 1381 it is recorded separately but no people were taxed. It is suggested that the settlement was abandoned between the 1370s-1380s. [5] Due to the small size of the earthworks and the suggested small size from the documentary evidence it has been classed here as a deserted hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hullasey

description_full: Extensive earthworks of the village of Hullasey are now engulfed in Hullasey Grove, which has preserved the remains, some which stand to 1m high. [1] They include a north-south hollow way with a shorter east-west section at the southern end. A survey in 1981-2 recorded 30 buildings and a possible five others. [2] There is evidence of Bronze Age and Roman activity at the site as well. [1] A chapel existed by 1349 and was still there in the eighteenth century but by this time it was used as a barn. [1] Excavations in 1907 revealed two houses and a large building which was suggested as the manor house, but this has more recently been described as four separate buildings. [2, 3] The excavations also located the chapel. [3] Hullasey was recorded in Domesday with a minimum population of eight. In 1327 27 people are assessed in Coates, Tarlton, Trewsbury and Hullasey. [4] The last mention on the E179 database is 1415. From both the archaeological and historical evidence it would suggest this settlement was deserted in the fifteenth century. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Lancaut
e179_last: 1621 March 4 - 23 three clerical subsidies
description_snippet: The remains of medieval settlement are located on a peninsula formed by a meander in the River Wye, close to the ruins of St James’ church. The earliest part of the church dates to the late twelfth century, but a lead font dating to 1130-1140 from the church is now on display in Gloucester Cathedral. description_full: The remains of medieval settlement are located on a peninsula formed by a meander in the River Wye, close to the ruins of St James’ church. The earliest part of the church dates to the late twelfth century, but a lead font dating to 1130-1140 from the church is now on display in Gloucester Cathedral. The church was remodeled in later periods but has been in ruins since c. 1865. [1] The lack of fine architectural detail and small size of the church suggests it served a small parish. [1] The remains of the deserted settlement can be seen to the north and west of the church. A geophysical survey in 1994 identified linear features but no discernible buildings. [2] The modern settlement of Lancaut is situated further to the north on the higher ground. Place-name evidence suggests that a church at least may have been present on the peninsula since the seventh century. [1] There is no clear taxation history for the settlement but the manor of Tidenham had ten tenants at Lancaut in 1306. At Lancaut in 1551 there were 19 communicants and five households were recorded in 1563. [3] By 1710 four families are recorded and this had decreased to two inhabited houses by 1750. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Lark Stoke
e179_last: 1695 Nov 22 or later aid of four shillings in the pound for one year
description_snippet: Earthwork remains of the settlement of Lark Stoke can be seen on either side of a stream to the south of Lower Lark Stoke. At least ten crofts have been identified.  There is also evidence of a number of hollow ways.
description_full: Earthwork remains of the settlement of Lark Stoke can be seen on either side of a stream to the south of Lower Lark Stoke. At least ten crofts have been identified. [1] There is also evidence of a number of hollow ways. [1] It is suggested that the manorial complex for the settlement is located close to the modern Lower Lark Stoke Farm, and excavations in 1995 to the south of the current house revealed stone wall footings and nine possible burials, suggesting the location of a chapel. [2] Pottery recovered from the excavation mainly dates between the twelfth and fifteenth centuries. The area has also been surveyed as part of the Admington Survey Project by Professor Christopher Dyer. Field walking finds suggest that the open fields of the village were still in operation after the village was deserted. [3] Lark Stoke is recorded in Domesday with a minimum population of ten. In 1327 six people were assessed. [4] It pays an average Lay Subsidy in 1334. In 1381 25 people pay the Poll Tax, but by 1525 the settlement is being taxed with Admington. A rental of 1447 recorded ten tenants, but five were absent, suggesting only five households by this point. [1] It is suggested the village went into decline in the later fifteenth century. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: There are a number of earthworks visible to the south of the church and Lasborough Manor but these have been described as not a distinctive deserted medieval settlement. [1] The Cotswold National Mapping Programme has reviewed all the available aerial photographic sources and plotted boundary banks and a hollow way. [1] Lasborough is recorded in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of 13. In 1327 five people are assessed. [2] In 1334 it pays an average Lay Subsidy. The only surviving taxation record for the fourteenth century records that nobody paid the Poll Tax in 1381. Three people paid the Lay Subsidy in 1525 and two households were recorded in 1563. It is suggested that the settlement was deserted between 1370s-1380s, but had never been larger than a small village. [3, 4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Upper Lemington
e179_last: 1695 Nov 22 or later aid of four shillings in the pound for one year
description_snippet: Extensive earthworks are visible between Upper Lemington (now just Lemington) and Lower Lemington. The grid reference has been slightly refined from that in the 1968 Gazetteer (SP 222 341) to place it centrally over these earthworks. It is suggested that these are the remains of the settlement of Lemington and formed a larger single settlement rather than two separate places.
description_full: Extensive earthworks are visible between Upper Lemington (now just Lemington) and Lower Lemington. The grid reference has been slightly refined from that in the 1968 Gazetteer (SP 222 341) to place it centrally over these earthworks. It is suggested that these are the remains of the settlement of Lemington and formed a larger single settlement rather than two separate places. [1] The earthworks to the north of Lemington Manor are those traditionally called Upper Lemington, and these run northwards to the church at Lower Lemington. There are further earthworks to the north of the church. As such this would be quite an extensive settlement. Some of the earthworks appear to be overlain by ridge and furrow suggesting an early date for abandonment. A hollow way runs from Lower Lemington Manor south along the current hedge line. Both settlements were simply recorded as Lemington up until the sixteenth century lending support to the idea of one continuous settlement. [2] At Domesday there are two entries for Lemington, with the one identified as Upper Lemington being an outlier of the large manor at Deerhurst. Lemington pays an average Lay Subsidy in 1334. In 1524 a below average amount is paid, and seven households are recorded in 1563. Throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries there has been a steady population recorded at Lower Lemington. There were around 20 households in 1650 but only six paid the Hearth Tax in 1672. [2] The distinguishing of Lower and Upper Lemington may just be a result of two different manorial descents and land holdings. [2, 3] This settlement is now considered to be evidence of a shrunken settlement, rather than a deserted village. This website has continued to use a single record for Lemington, instead of splitting this into two separate records for Lower and Upper Lemington as has happened in other lists of deserted settlements. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Lowsmoor
e179_last: 1606 May 17 six fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: Very faint earthworks have been seen directly to the north of Lowesmoor Farm. To the northeast of the farm are the earthwork remains of stone quarrying. Across the entire site there has been much ploughing so that no clear pattern can be seen, with only one, possibly two, house platforms suggested.  At Lowsmoor and neighboring Aston there were 15 tenants in the late twelfth century.
description_full: Very faint earthworks have been seen directly to the north of Lowesmoor Farm. To the northeast of the farm are the earthwork remains of stone quarrying. Across the entire site there has been much ploughing so that no clear pattern can be seen, with only one, possibly two, house platforms suggested. [1] At Lowsmoor and neighboring Aston there were 15 tenants in the late twelfth century. [2] At least six people were assessed in 1327. [3] In 1334 Lowsmoor pays an above average amount in the Lay Subsidy but by 1381 no-one was taxed. By the eighteenth century there were only two houses. [2] It has been suggested that Lowsmoor was never much larger than very few of properties and has been classed here as a deserted hamlet. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Manless Town
description_snippet: The remains of a medieval settlement and a Roman site can be seen on either side of the Climperwell to Caudle Green road.  In 1962 trial trenches were placed across the site to test for remains below the surface.
description_full: The remains of a medieval settlement and a Roman site can be seen on either side of the Climperwell to Caudle Green road. [1] In 1962 trial trenches were placed across the site to test for remains below the surface. [2] These revealed a range of features including stone walls and rubble surfaces however there has been disagreement over interpretation with the original excavator favouring an interpretation in the Roman period. [2] In 1973/74 the creation of a reservoir did reveal evidence of a Roman quarry and burial, however the walls from the earlier excavation are most likely medieval in date. [2, 3] In 1992 the remaining earthworks were plotted and field walking was undertaken in the ploughed fields. [1] The field walking produced medieval pottery dating to the twelfth to thirteenth centuries as well a range of Roman material. [1] The survey of the earthworks found that there had been disturbance from quarrying and topsoil dumping over the area. A hollow way can be identified running parallel, in part, to the modern road. At least three building platforms are visible along this hollow way. To the east are two more distinct building earthworks, one of which Dyer has interpreted as a sheepcote overlying the remains of the village. [4] The first reference to this field as Manless Town was in 1622. [5] The settlement has also been recorded as Haywick, Munley Towne, Old Mondley, Longlorn Town and Keywich. [6] It is unclear as to the original name of the settlement, and hence there are no taxation records available. The name Manless would suggest a deserted settlement and local legends would seem to confirm this, but it has also been suggested that the place-name originates from a manorial name. [7] In 1731 a survey map includes the text ‘A patch of Plumb Hey within the ruins of Old Mondley formerly a Market Town and a Roman Station was Sacked and Burnt in the Wars of King John...’. [6] On a ‘Survey of Lands in Brimspfield’ dating to the late eighteenth century a note records ‘stood Longlorn Town, which was destroyed in the reign of King John, then and still traces of Foundations to be seen and it has since that Time been called Manless Town’. [6] In 1779 it is recorded as a hamlet by Samuel Rudder but with the caveat ‘if a place can be called so with no house in it’. [8] He also mentions that the original name for this area was Haywick, the location where a weekly market was held in the reign of Edward III, but the men of the settlement were all killed and since then it has been known as Manless Town. [8] The evidence of a sheepcote suggests that after the site was deserted the area was used as pasture, and perhaps a more mundane fate occurred with a reduction in settlement with increased pasture as happened in other local settlements. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Naunton
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: There are gaps in the ridge and furrow around Naunton Farm. Earthworks that had been suggested as signs of medieval settlement are in fact hut emplacements and an access road built during the Second World War.  Nevertheless the documentary evidence does suggest that a village was once located here. Naunton is recorded in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of five.
description_full: There are gaps in the ridge and furrow around Naunton Farm. Earthworks that had been suggested as signs of medieval settlement are in fact hut emplacements and an access road built during the Second World War. [1] Nevertheless the documentary evidence does suggest that a village was once located here. Naunton is recorded in the Domesday Book with a minimum population of five. For much of the taxation record Naunton is included with the neighbouring deserted settlement of Frampton. In 1327 15 people are assessed at Naunton and Frampton. [2] They pay an average amount to the Lay Subsidy in 1334. In 1381 43 people are taxed at both sites, and another record for Naunton may include a further 15. This extensive population had reduced by 1525 when six people paid the Lay Subsidy at both settlements. In 1466 Henry Tracey was accused at the manorial court of keeping a flock of 1400 sheep on pasture at Frampton and Naunton, so it would seem by this point much of the land of both settlements had been turned over to pasture. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Newington
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll

Slight traces of earthworks may suggest a settlement or a farmstead.  Newington is recorded as one of the many outliers of Berkeley in the Domesday Book along with a number of properties and so a clear minimum population cannot be given to this particular holding.
description_full: An isolated church and motte are visible at Newington Bagpath and so it has been suggested that a settlement was also present. Slight traces of earthworks may suggest a settlement or a farmstead. [1] Newington is recorded as one of the many outliers of Berkeley in the Domesday Book along with a number of properties and so a clear minimum population cannot be given to this particular holding. In 1327 15 people are assessed in Newington Bagpath and Ozleworth. [2] In 1334 they both pay an above average amount. In 1563 24 households are recorded in the parish. It is possible that this has always been a dispersed settlement, but the earthworks suggest that there may have once been a village. name: Northwick
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll

description_full: Earthworks are present to the south of Northwick Park, and the grid reference has been refined to place the locator over these features (SP 163361). These are mainly ridge and furrow but investigation in 1966 suggested the presence of a castle earthwork. [1] Northwick Park has a seventeenth-century core to a building that has been adapted over many years. [2] Northwick does not appear in the Domesday Book. In 1334 a below average Lay Subsidy is paid. Twelve people are recorded as paying the Lay Subsidy in 1524, but there are two Northwicks in this hundred, with only one appearing in this subsidy and there is a possibility that this is the wrong Northwick. There is a possibility that there was never a substantial settlement here apart from the manorial settlement. So for now it has been classed as doubtful. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Norton, Burnt

Dyer has mapped the slight earthworks and suggested that they may represent two households.  He suggests this settlement may have originated as the settlement of a tenant acting as a woodward, or one that has been assarted on the edge of a wood.

[1] It is more likely that this is the centre of the manor mentioned in Domesday as Norton with a minimum population of 21, rather than has been suggested by the Phillimore Domesday as Burnt Norton. In Norton sub Edge 18 people are assessed in 1327. [2] By 1334 an above average Lay Subsidy is paid, and in 1381 36 people pay the Poll Tax. There are no guild members recorded after 1440. [3] By the sixteenth century there are no records on the 1524 and 1525 Lay Subsidies, however there are records in later years. The only record on the E179 database for Lower Norton is in 1662, however Norton sub Egge is recorded up until 1607. A sizable population is suggested by the earlier taxation history, and was probably the main nucleated settlement in the area. [4]. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Oldbury

The church itself sits within a circular churchyard which, it has been suggested, was an earlier camp defined by a ditch, however this has more recently been interpreted as levelling of a natural knoll. [2] In 1334 it pays a slightly above average Lay Subsidy. In 1524 21 people pay the Lay Subsidy and there are 70 households recorded in 1563. There is no clear evidence for a settlement at the church site itself which might have served dispersed places in general. If there ever was a permanent settlement it must be elsewhere in the parish. [3] It has therefore been classed as doubtful. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

Poulton Court is a Tudor farmhouse, and to the south a moated site signifies the location of an earlier manor house. No clear settlement earthworks have been plotted at the site. From the documentary evidence it appears that Poulton was the site of a manor in the early middle ages but was later incorporated into the Hagloe Estate. [3] The absence of any taxation record does not support the idea of a large settlement. The area was characterised by scattered farmsteads and the records of tenants would seem to represent this dispersed settlement and it has therefore been classed as doubtful. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Roel
e179_last: 1678 March 20 act for raising money by a poll
description_snippet: The village of Roel has been the subject of in-depth study combining the archaeological and documentary evidence to good effect.  Part of the settlement is still visible with a row of at least six crofts aligned to the east of a north-south hollow way with another fainter three crofts to the south.  To the west of the hollow way the modern farm complex sits over the site of the manor house, church and vicarage.
description_full: The village of Roel has been the subject of in-depth study combining the archaeological and documentary evidence to good effect. [1] Part of the settlement is still visible with a row of at least six crofts aligned to the east of a north-south hollow way with another fainter three crofts to the south. [1] To the west of the hollow way the modern farm complex sits over the site of the manor house, church and vicarage. [1] The locator used by the website is placed over this location, however this is not the entirety of settlement evidence for the village of Roel as further crofts, located 2km to the south, to the north of Hawling village at SP 067 233 have now been identified as part of Roel settlement, named Roelside. [1] It is suggested that Roel developed as a secondary settlement of Hawling, originating as a woodland hamlet. [1] The church is recorded as a subordinate of Hawling in 1174. [1] Domesday records a minimum population of 21. In 1294 28 tenants are recorded as owing services with 31 tenanted yardlands. [1] In 1327 13 people are assessed. [2] In the fourteenth-century taxations it is included with Hawling. A below average amount is paid in 1334. The documentary evidence suggests there may have been as many as 30 households in the early fourteenth century, however the physical evidence at Roel Farm does not suggest many more than nine house plots and hence the further settlement evidence to the north of Hawling. The documentary evidence has confirmed this area once formed part of Roel village, named Roelside. [1] Further analysis of the documentary evidence shows that the split between the two areas of settlement, always recorded singularly as ‘Roel’ saw around a quarter of the population located at Roel and three quarters at Roelside. [1] The village declines in the later middle ages, with 15 tenants recorded in 1355. [1] As the number of tenants decreased, land was engrossed into larger units, but these were not successful and the tenants left. [1] By the 1460s the last tenants relinquished land. [1] Roel and Roelside seemed to decline at the same time. The decrease in the number of tenants appears as a result of outward migration, possibly due to poor yields, rather than forced eviction. [1] In the future development of this website a separate record will be created for the Roelside area of settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Sennington
description_snippet: The earthwork remains of a settlement known as Old Sennington can still be seen from the air. These include at least two north-south hollow ways, and a number of indistinct croft boundaries. A report of coins having been discovered was published in 1889 which also suggested that the original chapel of Sevenhampton may have been located at the settlement.
description_full: The earthwork remains of a settlement known as Old Sennington can still be seen from the air. These include at least two north-south hollow ways, and a number of indistinct croft boundaries. A report of coins having been discovered was published in 1889 which also suggested that the original chapel of Sevenhampton may have been located at the settlement. [1] The present church at Sevenhampton is located 800m to the southeast. Unpublished excavations at the site in 1936 revealed stone walls as well as twelfth and thirteenth-century pottery. [2, 3] Sennington would appear to be a variant of the place-name Sevenhampton, with other variants including Senhampton and it is suggested that this is indicative of seven settlements. [4] Many small hamlets and farmsteads become deserted in the parish in the fourteenth century. [5] No separate settlement of Sennington is recorded and it is possible that these earthworks were one of the smaller settlements of Sevenhampton, or it could have been an extension of the settlement of Nash to the west. It has been classed as a hamlet due to the small size and lack of documentary evidence. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Shipton Solars
