description_full: Shipton Sollers is the name given to the western end of the long linear settlement of Shipton, with the eastern end given the name Shipton Oliffe. Both were separate parishes but were united in 1871. [1] A slightly refined gird reference (SP 028185) has been used by the website to place the marker directly over the location of the visible earthworks. A hollow way is visible running nearly parallel to the modern road in a southeast-northwest direction. To the west of this hollow way at least six croft divisions can be seen. Three possible house platforms have been recorded. [2] The present settlement of Shipton Solers contains the manor house and church as well as a number of modern buildings. Six separate estates are recorded at Shipton in the Domesday Book although by the fourteenth century the village is recorded as a single unit. In some records the different estates are signified by different village names such as Solers reflecting the ownership of the estate. [1] Shipton Solers had also been recorded as Shipton Champfleur in the 1230s and Shipton Tyrel in the late thirteenth century. [1] Although Shipton Solers and Shipton Oliffe signified two separate villages with their own fields, the boundary between the two has not been clearly identified and the recording of both as Shipton in the fourteenth century may suggest there was no physical boundary or gap between them. At Domesday the holding that has been identified with Shipton Solers has no recorded population. In 1327 11 people are assessed in Shipton with Hampen and they pay an above average Lay Subsidy in 1334, and 40 people are taxed in 1381. [3] From the later records of the settlement it is clear that although there have been fluctuations in population, Shipton Soler has remained as an active settlement. [1] In 1603 there are 24 communicants recorded. [4] The earthworks probably represent the extended medieval settlement of Shipton Solers, with a complex relationship with its neighbour, and that this should be classed as evidence of a shrunken settlement rather than a deserted village. The VCH does suggest that the earthworks may represent the settlement of Frogmarsh that was inhabited until the late thirteenth century. This is based on the present fieldname. [1] This would associate the earthworks with Frogmill to the south, instead of Shipton Solers to the east. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Slad
description_snippet: Earthworks of a possible medieval settlement are visible to the southeast of Jones Slad Farm. They represent linear earthworks, possible field boundaries but no distinctive house plots. A round mound in this area of earthworks has been postulated as a round barrow, but the stony nature of this could also suggest a more recent date and a decayed building structure.
description_full: Earthworks of a possible medieval settlement are visible to the southeast of Jones Slad Farm. They represent linear earthworks, possible field boundaries but no distinctive house plots. A round mound in this area of earthworks has been postulated as a round barrow, but the stony nature of this could also suggest a more recent date and a decayed building structure. [1] There is no direct documentary evidence for a settlement at this location. Documentary evidence does exist of a possible estate known as Cliveshale which may have been located at Thougham Slad to the east of the earthworks, but again there does not seem to have been an extensive settlement associated with these records. [2] With the nature of the earthworks not directly indicating settlement and the lack of records this has been classed as a doubtful deserted medieval settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Argam
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax
description_snippet: A set of well preserved earthworks marks the location of this site to the south of Argham Grange Farm. The earthworks are thought to represent the majority of the medieval village and have twice been surveyed producing differing interpretations of the village layout. An initial survey suggested a layout of discrete farmsteads formed by accretion, lacking a manor site.
description_full: A set of well preserved earthworks marks the location of this site to the south of Argham Grange Farm. The earthworks are thought to represent the majority of the medieval village and have twice been surveyed producing differing interpretations of the village layout. An initial survey suggested a layout of discrete farmsteads formed by accretion, lacking a manor site. [1] A further survey concluded that the layout began as a planned two-row village, succeeded by a number of farmsteads and a manor house. [2] The western end of the village is marked by a bank which partly coincides with the prehistoric Argam dyke linear earthwork. Argam is recorded as a berewick in Domesday. It possessed a church, taxed in 1291, and apparently forming its own parish from 1269 onwards. [3] Appointments to the church living continued into the early seventeenth century, but by 1632 the church had been largely removed and its precise layout forgotten. The settlement then consisted of 'a cottage where a shepherd and his wife lived'. [4] Although not listed in the poll tax or 1524/5 Lay Subsidy returns, Argam was routinely listed in other lay taxation returns from the late thirteenth to the late seventeenth century. However the continuing presence of farms within the parish and the fact it was usually grouped with Bartindale (another deserted site) and later Grindale, means that the circumstances of desertion are still uncertain. Further documentary research or archaeological investigation would be required to narrow down its precise period of depopulation, assumed to be for sheep farming some time in the fifteenth or sixteenth century. Beresford noted that 'the ruins [of the village] were finally removed in 1819-39'. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Arram
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax
description_snippet: A field investigation of this site, as marked on the 1854 6 inch first edition Ordnance Survey map north of Arram Hall, concluded that although 'a few minor hollows and ground swellings were visible...nothing exists to establish any general pattern'.  Other areas surrounding Arram Hall appear to be under cultivation on modern aerial photographs.
description_full: A field investigation of this site, as marked on the 1854 6 inch first edition Ordnance Survey map north of Arram Hall, concluded that although 'a few minor hollows and ground swellings were visible...nothing exists to establish any general pattern'. [1] Other areas surrounding Arram Hall appear to be under cultivation on modern aerial photographs. Recorded in Domesday as a manor, Arram is typically grouped in lay taxation records with the village of Bewholme to the north and another deserted site at Nunkeeling 1.5km to the east, detracting from the value of this evidence for the chronology of depopulation. Arram Hall is thought to have been built in the early seventeenth century, [1] and by the mid eighteenth century was the only building in the area. [2] The 1854 Ordnance Survey map shows Arram as a hamlet of Atwick parish, forming a western extension of the parish that takes in Arram Hall, Little Arram (a farm built between 1828 and 1854 [2]) and, at its northern edge, the supposed site of the deserted village. The hamlet is joined to the main, coastal part of Atwick parish by a thin strip of land, perhaps suggesting former independence for Arram before it was joined with Atwick proper. Beresford noted the documentary evidence showing land in the parish was acquired by Meaux Abbey in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries; in 1340 there were 11 ‘bovate-holders’, all tenants of the Abbey.[3] The desertion presumably dates from between the late fourteenth and mid-eighteenth century, and the settlement may always have been on the small side. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Arras
e179_last: 1678 Act of 1677 to raise money to build 30 ships
description_snippet: An aerial photograph taken in 2000 of the ploughed fields presumed to be the site of this deserted village showed spreads of chalk interpreted as buildings with back plots along a single street of 280m from SE 9234 4173 to SE 9207 4164. Elements of this arrangement are possibly discernable from recent vertical photographs. Previous field investigation had failed to find visible evidence on the ground.
description_full: An aerial photograph taken in 2000 of the ploughed fields presumed to be the site of this deserted village showed spreads of chalk interpreted as buildings with back plots along a single street of 280m from SE 9234 4173 to SE 9207 4164.[1] Elements of this arrangement are possibly discernable from recent vertical photographs. Previous field investigation had failed to find visible evidence on the ground. Fieldwork in 2004-05 to the west of the farm found a large quantity of pottery dating from the twelfth to fifteenth centuries. [2] It also potentially located the position of the chapel. Beresford noted a documentary reference to the village in 1368, [3] and the settlement was separately recorded in lay taxation records from the early fourteenth century onwards with 35 tax payers in the 1377 Poll Tax. Arras continued to be listed in some lay taxation returns in the fifteenth and sixteenth century, but Beresford observed that the local landscape was being converted from arable to pasture in the early sixteenth century, although at least five tofts and crofts survived in 1526. [3] Sir Robert Constable purchased part of Arras in 1531 and completed the conversion to pasture. [2] The land around Arras forms a distinct easterly tongue of Market Weighton parish, perhaps once the chapelry. By the seventeenth century the majority of lay taxation records mentioning Arras grouped it with Market Weighton. Although the broad period of depopulation seems clear, the origins of the settlement are less so. Beresford suggested that the village might represent a migration from the site of ‘Old Arras’ during the medieval period. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Old Arras
description_snippet: This site was identified by Beresford from earthworks shown on an aerial photograph just to the east of Arras Belt plantation. He describes the site as 'a small group of houses – not much more than a hamlet – but with a clear definition. In layout and size they resemble Holme Archiepiscopi or Raventhorpe in Leconfield'.
description_full: This site was identified by Beresford from earthworks shown on an aerial photograph just to the east of Arras Belt plantation. He describes the site as 'a small group of houses – not much more than a hamlet – but with a clear definition. In layout and size they resemble Holme Archiepiscopi or Raventhorpe in Leconfield'. [1] The plantation has since been removed and the fields in the vicinity have recently been under cultivation. The identification of this site as Old Arras or ‘Ald Erghes’ derives from a fourteenth-century reference to a vill of this name in Etton parish where the bounds of Etton, Gardham, Arras and Helesskew met. Beresford suggested this settlement was a precursor to the settlement of Arras, itself subsequently deserted. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Auburn
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax
description_snippet: Beresford noted that the site of this coastal deserted site, shown on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map in 1854, was eroding into the sea by 1952. He observed that 'a section of the street can be seen now in the cliff face'.  A field survey in 1966 found that three small tofts were still visible as earthworks.
description_full: Beresford noted that the site of this coastal deserted site, shown on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map in 1854, was eroding into the sea by 1952. He observed that 'a section of the street can be seen now in the cliff face'. [1] A field survey in 1966 found that three small tofts were still visible as earthworks. [2] Auburn chapel (also shown on the 1854 map) appears to have been situated slightly away from the main site, to the south of Auburn Farm at TA 1673 6262. Beresford’s statement that the chapel site had also been eroded appears to be erroneous. It was apparently in use in 1650 [3] and was excavated in 1948 revealing stone foundations, a child’s skeleton, roofing slabs, glass and a knife. [4] Auburn was a small township within Carnaby parish in the nineteenth century. Auburn is recorded as a manor at Domesday but with a very small holding. It is recorded independently in lay taxation returns from the thirteenth to the sixteenth century, although the majority of seventeenth-century references group it with nearby Fraisthorpe village. Although the village was granted a substantial 55% relief on its post-black death tax obligations in 1354 [1], the village still had 32 tax payers in the 1377 Poll Tax. However by the 1525 Lay Subsidy the entire settlement paid only the paltry sum of 6d, suggesting that major depopulation had occurred by this stage. By 1731 the settlement consisted of just three houses. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Barthorpe
e179_last: 1677 Act to raise money for building ships
description_snippet: Beresford noted that this site was represented on maps by Barthorpe Grange and Barthorpe Bottoms (a valley).  To this we can add Barthorpe Lodge, and set over a kilometre away, Barthorpe House. Not far south of Barthorpe House, centred at SE 769 604, earthworks and cropmarks of possible crofts have been identified on an air photo of 1946.
description_full: Beresford noted that this site was represented on maps by Barthorpe Grange and Barthorpe Bottoms (a valley). [1] To this we can add Barthorpe Lodge, and set over a kilometre away, Barthorpe House. Not far south of Barthorpe House, centred at SE 769 604, earthworks and cropmarks of possible crofts have been identified on an air photo of 1946. [2] This is the grid reference used by this website instead of the 1968 Gazetteer reference (SE 770 595). Barthorpe was listed individually in most fourteenth-century lay taxation records, although it appears to have two headings in the 1381 Poll Tax return, one with 10 tax payers, the other (which is listed with its original spelling of ‘Barkthorp’) with 32. [3] This seems incongruous alongside the 12 tax payers recorded in 1377. The settlement received a considerable 91% relief on its post-Black Death taxation requirement in 1354 [1], but the combined 1381 figures suggest the settlement was then still of reasonable size. By the taxation returns of 1453 Barthorpe was grouped with the nearby village of Leppington. Taxation entries of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries also consistently group Barthorpe with Leppington (the entry sometimes erroneously reading ‘Carthorpe’), but from the mid-sixteenth century onwards, in addition to this entry, Barthorpe is also listed twice further in many documents. This seems to result partly from part of the settlement once being taxed as an ecclesiastical liberty, but may also suggest that the settlement pattern had by this stage become dispersed, perhaps as a result of depopulation, although possibly settlement had always been dispersed or polyfocal in the vicinity. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Bartindale
e179_last: 1625 Three fifteenths and tenths levied in 1624
description_snippet: The earthworks of this site are preserved in pasture directly to the east of Bartindale Farm , stretching east-west over about 180m. Rectangular tofts and at least seven house platforms can be discerned running either side of a single, sunken street, with field systems to the north and south.  The earthworks have been mapped by the Ordnance Survey, with a revision in 1969.
description_full: The earthworks of this site are preserved in pasture directly to the east of Bartindale Farm [1], stretching east-west over about 180m. Rectangular tofts and at least seven house platforms can be discerned running either side of a single, sunken street, with field systems to the north and south. [2] The earthworks have been mapped by the Ordnance Survey, with a revision in 1969. [3] To the north-west of the site is a rectangular earthwork interpreted as a medieval or post-medieval pastoral enclosure, perhaps associated with the site, although more likely to be Georgian in date. [4, 5] Although not mentioned in Domesday Book, the settlement is referred to in Kirby’s Inquest of 1285 and is said to have had a chapel in the thirteenth century. [2] In 1297 three people paid the Lay Subsidy. [6] Bartindale was usually accounted for in lay taxation returns with the nearby deserted site of Argam. Although Bartindale (like Argam) is absent from the 1524/5 survey it is found in other taxation records of the later sixteenth century. However whereas references to Argam continue throughout the seventeenth century, Bartindale is last mentioned in the lay taxation records in 1625. Bartindale may always have been a relatively small settlement, and whilst the major period of depopulation cannot be pinned down without further work, perhaps by the early seventeenth century the settlement had entirely disappeared or shrunk to a size that did not merit inclusion in taxation returns. The current Bartindale Farmhouse is said to have been built ‘by 1810’ [7], so it is not clear if the site was ever entirely deserted. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Battleburn
e179_last: 1547 [?] Subsidy granted in 1545
description_snippet: A set of earthworks including tofts, crofts and hollow ways is preserved in a pasture field between the village of Kirkburn to the west and the deserted site of Eastburn to the east. The Ordnance Survey maps show a probable village street as a hollow way running SW-NE and turning east towards Eastburn. The modern road makes a dog leg around the north of the field containing these earthworks.
description_full: A set of earthworks including tofts, crofts and hollow ways is preserved in a pasture field between the village of Kirkburn to the west and the deserted site of Eastburn to the east. The Ordnance Survey maps show a probable village street as a hollow way running SW-NE and turning east towards Eastburn. The modern road makes a dog leg around the north of the field containing these earthworks. The field immediately east of the site, dividing it from Eastburn, is under cultivation. The nearby fields have produced evidence of Roman, and Anglo-Saxon activity, as well as a possible medieval post-mill. [1] The site is apparently also known as ‘Low Battleburn’ [2] and, as Beresford noted, is almost contiguous with Kirkburn to the west and perhaps Eastburn to the east. [3] In addition to its probable small late medieval size, this proximity to Kirkburn might explain why the settlement appears so rarely in records of lay taxation, appearing only once in the E179 database in a document of c. 1547, grouped with Kirkburn. Consequently it is difficult to pin down the period of major depopulation. Beresford noted that a rental of 1300 listed 24 ‘bovate-holders’, 'each with 12 acres in the field and a toft-and croft of half an acre. The position of the crofts is described.' [1] A small number of cottages are mentioned in 1672 and 1740. [4] The 1841 census recorded just three houses at Battleburn. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Belby
e179_last: 1692 Quarterly poll tax for one year
description_snippet: Although Beresford noted in 1952 that Belby House (Hall) stood in isolation,  there are today a small number of other buildings scattered slightly further afield, some of which were present on the 1854 6 inch Ordnance Survey map and were associated either then or now with the Belby place-name (including the site of Little Belby Cottages, labelled simply ‘Belby’ in 1854).
description_full: Although Beresford noted in 1952 that Belby House (Hall) stood in isolation, [1] there are today a small number of other buildings scattered slightly further afield, some of which were present on the 1854 6 inch Ordnance Survey map and were associated either then or now with the Belby place-name (including the site of Little Belby Cottages, labelled simply ‘Belby’ in 1854). 'Ground irregularities' identified to the SE of Belby Hall at SE 7725 2879 have been interpreted as ponds, drains and watercourses, possibly of post-medieval date. [2] Most of the fields beyond the immediate vicinity of Belby Hall are now under cultivation. Belby was recorded individually for lay taxation in the fourteenth and fifteenth century and appears to have been of a moderate size in 1379 when 52 residents were recorded (36 of whom were taxed). The settlement received a modest tax relief of 11% in the fifteenth century. [1] Some of the sixteenth-century lay taxations grouped Belby with other settlements including the deserted site of Thorpe (Lidget), the shrunken settlement of Balkholme and Kilpin. However Belby was again taxed individually in most of the seventeenth-century records. The township had 11 houses in 1841, albeit scattered. In the absence of earthwork evidence it is hard to pin down a date of depopulation, or indeed to be certain that the settlement pattern was not always dispersed to some degree. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Belthorpe
e179_last: 1692 Quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: As Beresford noted, this site is represented by Belthorpe House, surrounded by a medieval moat.  A series of earthworks survives in a field immediately west of the moat, but suggestions that these are connected with the DMV  have been disputed on the grounds they overlay medieval ridge and furrow and are therefore most likely post-medieval.
description_full: As Beresford noted, this site is represented by Belthorpe House, surrounded by a medieval moat. [1] A series of earthworks survives in a field immediately west of the moat, but suggestions that these are connected with the DMV [2] have been disputed on the grounds they overlay medieval ridge and furrow and are therefore most likely post-medieval. [3] A number of cropmarks of enclosures and a possible settlement have been noted in the wider area to the west and south, although these are assumed to be prehistoric or Roman. [4] Belthorpe is recorded in both Domesday Book and the 1377 Poll Tax, where its 19 tax payers suggests a fairly small settlement. The settlement was allowed a modest 8% tax relief in the mid-fifteenth century. [1] Although the village does not appear in the 1524/5 or 1543 Lay Subsidies it is recorded in other lay taxation documents throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, usually accounted for individually, and on some occasions recorded twice since part of the settlement fell within an ecclesiastical liberty. On one occasion, in the 1662 Hearth Tax, the settlement was grouped with Bishop Wilton. The settlement was also grouped with Bishop Wilton for the 1801 and later census returns. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: East Benningholme
e179_last: 1692 Quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: Beresford noted earthworks around the site of both Benningholme Hall (TA 126 387) and Benningholme Grange (1km to the west), suggesting that there were two small vills here, perhaps ‘East’ and ‘West’ Benningholme (although these names rarely seem to be used).
description_full: Beresford noted earthworks around the site of both Benningholme Hall (TA 126 387) and Benningholme Grange (1km to the west), suggesting that there were two small vills here, perhaps ‘East’ and ‘West’ Benningholme (although these names rarely seem to be used). [1] The existence of these earthworks on aerial photographs and on the ground was subsequently questioned; those around the Hall were said to be 'very slight and unintelligible'. [2] The majority of the fields surrounding the site are now under cultivation. These two sites appear here as two records but may have been a single settlement. Benningholme was listed as one vill in the majority of lay taxation documents and had a sizeable population in 1377. The earliest recording of East Benningholme is in 1240. [3] A number of documents of the sixteenth and seventeeth century however do group Benningholme with South Skirlaugh, and sometimes both ‘Benningholme’ and ‘Benningholme Grange’ are named. Without further research it is hard to know whether the settlement pattern may always have been dispersed to some degree, but given the enclosure of 1517 noted by Beresford [1] and the nature of the sixteenth-century taxation records it seems likely some depopulation took place between the late fourteenth and early sixteenth century. The current Benningholme Hall is thought to date from the 1820s. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

[1] The existence of these earthworks on aerial photographs and on the ground was subsequently questioned. The majority of the fields surrounding the site are now under cultivation. Cropmarks south-west of Benningholme Grange have been interpreted as Iron Age or Roman ditched enclosures. [2] West Benningholme is first recorded in 1221-35 in documents from Meaux Abbey. [3] Benningholme was listed as one vill in the majority of lay taxation documents and had a sizeable population in 1377. A number of documents of the sixteenth and seventeeth century however do group Benningholme with South Skirlaugh, and sometimes both ‘Benningholme’ and ‘Benningholme Grange’ are named. Without further research it is hard to know whether the settlement pattern may always have been dispersed to some degree, but given the enclosure of 1517 noted by Beresford [1] and the nature of the sixteenth-century taxation records it seems likely some depopulation took place between the late fourteenth and early sixteenth century. name: Bewick
e179_last: 1572 Collection of Subsidy of May 15th 1571
description_snippet: This site is now represented by Bewick Hall farmhouse and the medieval moat. Cropmarks of possible former fields and a roadway have been suggested in the surrounding fields, but no physical evidence for a deserted site has been put forward.
description_full: This site is now represented by Bewick Hall farmhouse and the medieval moat. Cropmarks of possible former fields and a roadway have been suggested in the surrounding fields, but no physical evidence for a deserted site has been put forward. [1] The surrounding fields are now largely cultivated and ploughing is thought to have removed the suggested foundations of an earlier Bewick Hall to the south-west of the moat, marked on the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1855. Bewick is rarely recorded in lay taxation records, perhaps because it was always a small settlement, maybe never more than a hamlet or manor complex. It was recorded as a berewick of Aldbrough at Domesday. The 1377 Poll Tax lists nine tax payers, in 1543/4 just four were recorded. In other taxation records of the 1540s and 1550s Bewick is grouped with Great and Little Cowden, in 1571/2 it was grouped with Aldbrough. The current farmhouse dates from the seventeenth century. [2] If a ‘depopulation’ can be said to have occurred on such a small site perhaps it was between the late fourteenth and early sixteenth centuries. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Birdsall
e179_last: 1692 Quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: Beresford identified the likely location for this deserted site from the ruined Norman church next to Birdsall House. He believed that the earthworks of the deserted site existed between the House and the modern road (built after 1855), including former roads.
description_full: Beresford identified the likely location for this deserted site from the ruined Norman church next to Birdsall House. He believed that the earthworks of the deserted site existed between the House and the modern road (built after 1855), including former roads. [1] A further review of the aerial photographs and a site visit in 1974 was more pessimistic, claiming that the area was covered by ridge and furrow, but 'apart from an isolated irregular shaped amorphous platform, occasional banks and sunken ways there are no remains of the medieval village.' [2] Nevertheless the medieval taxation records do show a substantial population at Birdsall, with 138 recorded in 1377, even if the population totals will no doubt include outlying settlements in the wider parish. Beresford identified the most likely cause of depopulation as emparkment, with a new church built further north in 1823. [3] Birdsall House itself is thought to date to the late sixteenth century, [4] and the origins of the park have been ascribed by one source to 1598-1602. [5] A late sixteenth or early seventeenth-century date for ‘depopulation’ at this site therefore seems most likely, although further research is needed to establish the chronology of the wider settlement pattern in the parish. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Bonwick
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year.
description_snippet: The two farms of High and Low Bonwick are situated almost 1km apart. The site NGR is derived from the latter, more northerly site. Beresford referred only to the documentary evidence for this site, and the land surrounding and between both farms is now under cultivation.
description_full: The two farms of High and Low Bonwick are situated almost 1km apart. The site NGR is derived from the latter, more northerly site. Beresford referred only to the documentary evidence for this site, and the land surrounding and between both farms is now under cultivation. Bonwick, as Beresford noted, was taxed as a single named vill in the fourteenth and fifteenth century, [1] although the 1377 Poll Tax and 1524/5 Lay Subsidy returns grouped it with Dunnington. The E179 database shows examples of Bonwick being taxed separately into the seventeenth century but by then it was more commonly grouped with Dunnington. On one mid-sixteenth century return it was grouped with Brandesburton. Given the lack of physical evidence from the two sites, and indeed the considerable distance between them, it is perhaps not surprising this site is not classified as a DMV on the NMR. However, the 1334 and 1543 Lay Subsidy returns hint at a population that was larger than the two farms which survive today. Whether this consisted of lost isolated farms, or a hamlet sized settlement at one or both of High and Low Bonwick is not known. Whilst certainly not a classic ‘DMV’, it seems unwise to jettison the site from the list of potential sites without further research, so it has been classed as a deserted hamlet for the time being. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Bracken
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: Bracken appears to have been a sizeable village, although much of the physical evidence for the site seems to have been lost. The settlement consisted of one main farm by the nineteenth century. East and south-east of the farm (and north of the road) some earthworks survive, thought to represent 'small fields, with only one possible building steading', a possible hollow way, and an area of ridge and furrow.
description_full: Bracken appears to have been a sizeable village, although much of the physical evidence for the site seems to have been lost. The settlement consisted of one main farm by the nineteenth century. East and south-east of the farm (and north of the road) some earthworks survive, thought to represent 'small fields, with only one possible building steading', a possible hollow way, and an area of ridge and furrow. Further small fields were visible north-west of the farm. The main area of earthworks was probably south of the road, marked as ‘foundations’ on the 1855 6 inch Ordnance Survey map, but field investigation in 1973 noted these had been destroyed by ploughing and 'do not merit survey action'. [1] A close named Chapel Garth marks the site of a chapel which was demolished by 1573. [2] A refined grid reference is used by this website instead of the 1968 original (SE 981 505). The main guide to Bracken’s former extent is therefore the documentary evidence. The fourteenth-century village was evidently sizeable, with an above average tax assessment in 1334 and 78 tax payers recorded in the 1377 Poll Tax. Although it received a mid-fifteenth-century tax relief of 27% Beresford noted that the settlement’s assessment was 'still considerable for that district'. [3] He suspected a ‘sheep depopulation’, and the 1543 record of just nine tax payers suggests significant depopulation may have occurred by then. The settlement was separately taxed through the period covered by the lay taxation database (until the late seventeenth century). At least half a dozen families are present in the early 1660s. [2] This much reduced settlement continued until at least the end of the seventeenth century. Enclosure did not lead to total depopulation. [2] By 1801 the population of the township was just 14. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Brackenholme
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll tax for one year
description_snippet: Beresford included this site in his list of lost Yorkshire villages, whilst recognising that, since there was no evidence of earthworks to be seen on aerial photographs, Brackenholme and its surrounding hamlets were probably never nucleated. Certainly the settlement consisted of just a couple of farms in the mid-nineteenth century.
description_full: Beresford included this site in his list of lost Yorkshire villages, whilst recognising that, since there was no evidence of earthworks to be seen on aerial photographs, Brackenholme and its surrounding hamlets were probably never nucleated. Certainly the settlement consisted of just a couple of farms in the mid-nineteenth century. Beresford does imply that Brackenholme, along with two other settlements - Babthorpe and Bowthorpe – had been reduced in size since their appearance in Domesday Book, [1] although we should perhaps not rule out the possibility that these settlements were no more than manor houses or small hamlets at that time. The treatment of the hamlets in this area by medieval taxation records may provide some useful evidence and would repay closer inspection. Brackenholme paid £1 15s 7d in the 1334 Lay Subsidy and had 67 residents listed (46 were taxed) in the 1379 Poll Tax, both figures which would normally mark it out as a moderately sized village. However neither the 1334 nor the 1379 returns provide figures for the hamlets of Hagthorpe (adjacent to Brackenhome and itself present in Domesday Book), Babthorpe (about 1 km to the west, also in Domesday Book) and Woodhall. It seems likely that these three places were included in the 1334 and 1379 tax assessments, [2] and indeed the Lay Subsidies of 1524/5 and 1543 spell out that all four settlements were grouped. Other taxation returns of the sixteenth and seventeenth century saw inconsistent groupings of the various hamlets. If the 1379 Poll Tax and 1543 Lay Subsidy returns covered a similar range of settlements they might still imply some late medieval loss of population from one or more of the four sites. The site of Woodhall, with the possible banks shown on the 1854 6 inch Ordnance Survey map and an area given over to parkland, could merit further research in this context. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Buckton
description_snippet: A limited collection of earthworks have been observed at this site from aerial photographs and field visits. There are possibly two small areas of earthworks on both sides of Settrington Beck to the south of Settrington village, close to Kirkhill and Buckton Garths.
description_full: A limited collection of earthworks have been observed at this site from aerial photographs and field visits. There are possibly two small areas of earthworks on both sides of Settrington Beck to the south of Settrington village, close to Kirkhill and Buckton Garths. [1] They include a small number of building platforms, some of which are thought to be a post-medieval farm, three or four ditches that could be toft boundaries, a hollow way, the possible dams of former mill ponds, and evidence of ridge and furrow. [2, 3] Although no physical evidence is recorded, the 1890 25 inch Ordnance Survey map marks the former site of a church just east of Kirk Hill Farm, which perhaps owes its name to the church. Buckton is not recorded in the lay taxation documents of the E179 database, perhaps partly because of the site’s proximity to Settrington, forming part of that manor. An Inquisition Post-Mortem of 1304/5 recorded 38 cottages and two mills in the village, [2] suggesting a moderately sized settlement no longer reflected by the limited earthwork survival. The village survived the Black Death in some form, since ‘messuages, land and rent’ at Buckton are referred to in an Inquisition Ad Quod Dampnum of 1363/4. [4] By the time of a survey of Settrington Manor in 1600 it appears the site was entirely depopulated, surviving only in the field name ‘Buckton Garths’. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Burdale
e179_last: 1625 Three fifteenths and tenths levied in 1624
description_snippet: Although only a single farm in the nineteenth century this site seems to have extended into the valley floor where ‘white marks’ – perhaps visible on aerial photographs but apparently not intelligible on the ground – are thought to represent the banks of house platforms and tenement boundaries. An excavation nearby produced both medieval and Roman pottery.
description_full: Although only a single farm in the nineteenth century this site seems to have extended into the valley floor where ‘white marks’ – perhaps visible on aerial photographs but apparently not intelligible on the ground – are thought to represent the banks of house platforms and tenement boundaries. An excavation nearby produced both medieval and Roman pottery. [1, 2] As Beresford observed much of the site is likely to have been destroyed by the creation of the railway line, now disused. [3] Fourteenth-century taxation returns suggest Burdale was of a reasonable size, both before and after the Black Death, although it received a 30% tax relief in 1354. In 1377 Burdale had twice as many tax payers (63) as its more famous neighbour, Wharram Percy (30). The catalogue of lay taxation returns provides some indication of the chronology of depopulation for the village. Burdale was always taxed separately, but was omitted from the early sixteenth-century returns (including those of 1523/4), albeit reappearing from 1540 onwards. The last return to feature Burdale was collected in 1625, and by 1650 the reduced population prompted a survey of livings to suggest annexation with Fimber. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Burstwick, Bond
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: Bond Burstwick was included in Beresford’s original list of East Riding DMVs based on the possibility it once represented a separate settlement from Burstwick.  The early documentary evidence is ambiguous.
description_full: Bond Burstwick was included in Beresford’s original list of East Riding DMVs based on the possibility it once represented a separate settlement from Burstwick. [1] The early documentary evidence is ambiguous. Beresford noted that the two names were accounted for separately in a document of 1259, whilst Poulson suggests that Bond Burstwick may have been considered a sub-manor during the reign of Edward III, although perhaps originally deriving its name from an area of Burstwick manor allocated to bond tenants. [2] Confusingly however, in some documents ‘Bondburstwick’ appears to have been used as an alternative name for Burstwick – for example the 1297 Lay Subsidy returns (which uses one name for a list of tax payers and the other for tax collectors) [3] and the 1377 Poll Tax. The statistics for documents in the E179 database combine both names, although ‘Burstwick’ is more common and was often grouped with the conjoined settlement of Skeckling. The NMR and grid references in this database entry are to a set of earthworks, isolated to the north-west of Skeckling and Burstwick, and believed to have been a medieval castle, moat and fishponds and possible head site of the fourteenth-century manor of Burstwick. The manor is thought to have been a valued royal holding in the first half of that century. [4] The detachment of this site from the main settlement invites further research into the local settlement pattern – if the castle was effectively the main medieval manor house, might ‘Bond Burstwick’ have sometimes been used as a name for the larger settlement to the south? Could the site effectively be a lost manorial centre rather than a deserted village? Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Burton Constable
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: Despite this site’s afterlife as a landscaped park the village layout is apparently visible on aerial photographs, including the former windmill, mentioned in a document of 1293.  This includes earthworks to the north and west of the Hall.
description_full: Despite this site’s afterlife as a landscaped park the village layout is apparently visible on aerial photographs, including the former windmill, mentioned in a document of 1293. [1] This includes earthworks to the north and west of the Hall. Burton Constable was routinely grouped with nearby West Newton (and occasionally Tunstall and Tansterne) in the lay taxation returns, but the depopulation of the site must have been responsible for the decrease from 105 tax payers in 1377 to 26 tax payers in 1543/4, the majority of the latter probably based in West Newton. Beresford listed the evidence from medieval extents, which gave figures for Burton Constable alone and show it once to have been a 'substantial village'. [1] In 1293 there were 15 cottagers and 21 bovate holders. In 1326 similar numbers were recorded: 15 bondsmen, 22 cottagers and 1 free tenant. A tax relief of one third after the Black Death suggests some fallback of population, but many of the 105 tax payers in 1377 must have lived in Burton Constable. A deed of 1438 shows the settlement still persisted, so it seems likely that the ‘depopulation’ said to have taken place between 1488 and 1517 marked the most significant, perhaps final, step towards desertion. [2] The village nevertheless continued to be named in lay taxation returns and in c. 1570 the current country house was constructed, [3] with the park first laid out in the late seventeenth or early eighteenth century and remodelled according to plans by Capability Brown between 1769 and 1782. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Camerton
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: Present in Domesday Book as a berewick of Burstwick, the isolated nineteenth-century site of Camerton Hall was said by Beresford to represent a 'small site',  although it is not clear whether Beresford believed the site to contain earthworks.
description_full: Present in Domesday Book as a berewick of Burstwick, the isolated nineteenth-century site of Camerton Hall was said by Beresford to represent a 'small site', [1] although it is not clear whether Beresford believed the site to contain earthworks. The NMR does not record Camerton as a DMV and the grouping of the settlement with nearby Ryhill in lay taxation records means it is difficult to estimate from this source whether it was ever more than a manorial centre. The NGR reference is to the surviving outbuildings of the Hall. It has been suggested that the site lay on the south side of the Hull Road. There were five houses in the seventeenth century but only the Hall was present by the nineteenth century. [2] In 1288 there were nine bovates of demesne land as well as nine tenants who had 15 bovates. [2] This does indicate a small settlement, and perhaps it was always small as it was recorded as Ryhill with Camerton. There is no indication of when it declined. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Cavil
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: Beresford noted that a single farm represented this settlement, and that the ‘site’ lay north-east of it,  although it is not clear what this was thought to consist of. There was a moat, visible (but not named) on the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map and 1948 air photograph, but the site is said to have been recently ‘bulldozed and ploughed’ before John Hurst visited it c. 1958.
description_full: Beresford noted that a single farm represented this settlement, and that the ‘site’ lay north-east of it, [1] although it is not clear what this was thought to consist of. There was a moat, visible (but not named) on the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map and 1948 air photograph, but the site is said to have been recently ‘bulldozed and ploughed’ before John Hurst visited it c. 1958. [2] The eighteenth-century hall itself was demolished in 1969. The 1854 6 inch Ordnance Survey map does show some features, including wells, to the north west of the hall, but these may have been post-medieval drainage or ‘extraction’ features. [3] The farm buildings of Caville Hall are now surrounded almost entirely by cultivated land. Caville is mentioned in Domesday Book as a berewick of Howden, and its 1334 and 1377/9 taxation returns (with 37 people listed and 25 taxed in 1379) suggest the site was more than a single farm in the medieval period. The settlement received only a modest 10% post-Black Death relief in 1354. [1] Caville was taxed separately in the fourteenth century, but first grouped in taxation records with the neighbouring moated site of Burland in 1453. In 1525 and 1543/4 it was additionally grouped with Portington, preventing direct comparison with earlier statistics, although the 14 tax payers at the three sites in 1543/4 suggest that Caville had experienced a degree of depopulation by that stage. Caville was still taxed separately in some returns in the later sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Caythorpe
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: The scheduled earthworks situated east and west of the house at Low Caythorpe seem to represent the manorial complex and village referred to in medieval documents as simply ‘Caythorpe’ (the ‘Low’ prefix is presumably more recent and to distinguish the settlement from High Caythorpe 2 km to the north).
description_full: The scheduled earthworks situated east and west of the house at Low Caythorpe seem to represent the manorial complex and village referred to in medieval documents as simply ‘Caythorpe’ (the ‘Low’ prefix is presumably more recent and to distinguish the settlement from High Caythorpe 2 km to the north). The earthworks east of the house appear to be those of a former manorial complex and include remains of a moat and a series of fishponds. Excavations here between 1962 and 1966 revealed a late Saxon building rebuilt in the twelfth and fourteenth centuries and abandoned in the sixteenth century. [1, 2, 3] The fish ponds and gardens features in this area may date from c. 1513 when the Constable family built a large house at the eastern end of the modern farmyard. The earthworks west of the house are thought to be those of the village of Caythorpe and include 'house platforms, crofts, trackways and quarries', along with signs of ridge and furrow to the south. The village is believed to have had an east-west alignment along a central trackway. [2] Caythorpe appears in the Domesday Book as a manor, and by 1296 had at least 10 houses, a windmill and a water mill. [4] The fourteenth-century tax assessments suggest it was likely to have been a small village, but typical in size for those that were later deserted. The village had received a substantial 40% tax relief just after the Black Death in 1354. Depopulation at the site was reported in 1517 with 20 residents and five houses removed as a result of the enclosure of 300 acres for sheep pasture. [4] In 1525 Caythorpe was jointly assessed with the nearby manor of Thorpe, the low assessment suggesting a depleted but not abandoned settlement. Two families are thought to have still occupied the site in 1600, [1] suggesting a drawn out process of population reduction. Although Caythorpe had been separately assessed in taxation returns from the late thirteenth to early sixteenth centuries, it was increasingly grouped with Rudston and Thorpe in the later sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Cleaving
description_snippet: The surviving earthworks are those of the moat, said to be of the site of Cleaving Hall, although the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map and air photographs make clear they were formerly more extensive, including fishponds and ditched enclosures.
description_full: The surviving earthworks are those of the moat, said to be of the site of Cleaving Hall, although the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map and air photographs make clear they were formerly more extensive, including fishponds and ditched enclosures. The place-name ‘Cleaving Garths’ north of the moated site may be of significance, although the possibility that the eleventh-century and later settlement was always small, perhaps little more than a hamlet or large manor complex should be borne in mind. Beresford noted a reference to a toft at the settlement in 1301 as evidence that there was formerly 'more here than the ‘Hall’ and Moats''. [1] Cultivation has removed some of the earthwork evidence, but the moat itself is scheduled. Cleaving was recorded in Domesday Book as a manor, but does not feature in any of the medieval taxation returns of the E179 database. It may be an unusual case of a medieval settlement abandoned at an early stage and succeeded by a moated site, said to have been a manor of the Knight’s Hospitallers. [2, 3, 4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Cleeton
description_snippet: In 1952 Beresford was able to sum up the evidence for Cleeton in a single word: “Drowned”.. Certainly this is where the evidence pointed at that time. The first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map marked the spot on the coast where the 'supposed site of the village of Clayton' was thought to have succumbed to the sea.
description_full: In 1952 Beresford was able to sum up the evidence for Cleeton in a single word: “Drowned”. [1]. Certainly this is where the evidence pointed at that time. The first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map marked the spot on the coast where the 'supposed site of the village of Clayton' was thought to have succumbed to the sea. Writing in 1841 George Poulson reported that Cleeton 'stood south-east of Skipsea, it is now entirely depopulated; foundations of houses were formerly often ploughed up, no doubt a great part of it has gone into the sea'. [2] The implication that the settlement had been deserted some time prior to its assumed erosion into the sea may be significant. Cleeton was the pre-eminent vill in its locality in Domesday Book, incorporating the sokes of Dringhoe and Upton (both subsequently deserted). However it does not appear in the records of medieval lay taxation, having been superseded by the new settlement of Skipsea (the castle was founded in the late eleventh century, Skipsea Brough probably c. 1160, and the village of Skipsea perhaps sometime in the late eleventh or twelfth century). [3] Nevertheless the Manor of Cleeton is well documented from the thirteenth to the nineteenth century. [4] The medieval manor house may have been south of Skipsea in the field called ‘Hall Garth Hill’, [3] where the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map shows the ‘Site of Hall’ and ‘foundations’. Documentary evidence suggests the house was occupied in the thirteenth and fourteenth century and abandoned by the sixteenth century. [3]. Excavation of the moat and island at this site produced evidence of fourteenth-century pottery, [5] although the main range of material appears to date from c. 1450-1650. [6] Manorial records suggest the demesne of Cleeton manor was worked by between seven and 13 men in the late thirteenth and fourteenth century, but the tenanted land was farmed by tenants from Skipsea and Newhithe. [3] This might imply that there was no longer a substantial village at Cleeton even by this early stage, although further study of the medieval and post-medieval manorial records would perhaps clarify this. In this context the 2004 geophysical survey and excavations conducted for the ‘Time Team’ television programme in fields west of Skipsea Grange are particularly relevant. The geophysical survey revealed a site (centred at c. TA 174 539) of at least six hectares with a 'dense concentration of ditch and pit type anomalies'. [7] An initial assessment of the medieval pottery assemblage from the trial trenches showed that the site seems to have been abandoned by the mid-thirteenth century. [7] Although the theory is not favoured by the evaluation report, the television broadcast speculated that this site might be the medieval village of Cleeton. This theory would have the advantage of explaining why men from Skipsea and Newhithe were farming the tenanted land of Cleeton’s medieval manor, although the stories of Cleeton’s loss to the sea would still require explanation. Perhaps the considerable lapse of time since the abandonment of the site led to confusion over its former location. The land once assumed to have been the site of the village is thought to have been lost to the sea c. 1800, [3] but Poulson’s assertion that it was already under the plough means that the assumed site could have been erroneous. To add a further layer of complication to the picture, it seems that the name ‘Cleeton’ was applied to features over a fairly wide area, perhaps a reflection of the extent of its manor. Modern Ordnance Survey maps mark an eastern area of Skipsea village with the name, and the lane heading east out of the village was marked as ‘Cleeton Lane’ on the 1892 25 inch map. However the 6 inch 1854 map suggests that the (empty) plots of land in this part of the village were formerly known as ‘East Garths’ – perhaps themselves an area of settlement shrinkage. A farm towards the southern end of the parish ‘Far Grange’ was also formerly known as Clayton Grange Farm. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Cotness
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll tax for one year
description_snippet: The 6 inch Ordnance Survey map shows just the site of Cotness Hall, Manor Farm, and a few other buildings. South-east of the modern Hall are two ditches marked on the modern Ordnance Survey map as a moat, although field investigation in 1962 suggested the features were more likely to be 'ornamental'.  400m further north along Cotness Lane there is another moated site marked on modern Ordnance Survey maps.
description_full: The 6 inch Ordnance Survey map shows just the site of Cotness Hall, Manor Farm, and a few other buildings. South-east of the modern Hall are two ditches marked on the modern Ordnance Survey map as a moat, although field investigation in 1962 suggested the features were more likely to be 'ornamental'. [1] 400m further north along Cotness Lane there is another moated site marked on modern Ordnance Survey maps. The fourteenth-century lay taxation returns make clear that Cotness was once a larger place (even allowing for some possible dispersal of settlement), with 69 tax payers recorded in 1377. In 1379 60 people are listed with a total of 40 people taxed. Cotness was taxed separately during the fourteenth and fifteenth century, but was occasionally grouped with Saltmarshe and Metham in the sixteenth and seventeenth century. In the mid-fifteenth century the settlement received only a small taxation relief of 6%. [2] By 1543/4 the assessment for Cotness, grouped with Saltmarshe and Metham, was 34 tax payers, suggesting a degree of depopulation had occurred by this stage. By 1841 there were only nine inhabited buildings in the township. Although no evidence has been noted for earthworks of tofts and crofts, the length of Cotness Lane might theoretically have served as a village street and could be a worthwhile focus for further research. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Cottam
e179_last: 1692 quartetly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: The well preserved village earthworks surrounding Cottam House led Beresford to describe Cottam as 'one of the finest sites in the Wolds'.  The layout of the village, and possibly even some phasing of settlement is discernable and described in detail in the Scheduled Monument Entry report.
description_full: The well preserved village earthworks surrounding Cottam House led Beresford to describe Cottam as 'one of the finest sites in the Wolds'. [1] The layout of the village, and possibly even some phasing of settlement is discernable and described in detail in the Scheduled Monument Entry report. [2] Notable features include a main street, building platforms, numerous tofts and a few crofts, and an area around the church (rebuilt in the late nineteenth century but since disused) which may have been the earliest (Anglo-Saxon?) focus of the village. A potential medieval manorial site has also been identified opposite Cottam House west of the former main street. The village is also surrounded by medieval cultivation terraces, which in places are overlain by late medieval or post-medieval sheep enclosures. The documentary evidence for Cottam allows a fairly detailed picture to be built up of a prolonged depopulation, something which is probably common elsewhere but not always demonstrable. The 1334 Lay Subsidy return suggests Cottam was of above average size for those vills which would later be deserted. It paid almost as much tax (85%) as neighbouring Langtoft, of which it probably formed a chapelry. The Black Death was particularly severe on Cottam, resulting in a 54% relief granted in 1354. [1] For the 1377 Poll Tax Cottam recorded 50 tax payers, still a moderately sized village, but only half the number of tax payers found at Langtoft. In 1515 Cottam was grouped in a lay taxation return for the first time, with Langtoft. For the rest of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries it would sometimes be grouped and sometimes recorded separately (perhaps because it continued to exist as a separate township). In the 1525 Lay Subsidy the total tax paid by Cottam (5s 9d) suggests further shrinkage, paying less than a third of the tax assessment at Langtoft. Beresford noted contradictory evidence on enclosure from 1569, including one survey which suggested the township had already been largely enclosed. [1] By 1706 just nine cottages still stood in the village, further reduced when permission was granted for the demolition of 'all but four cottages' by the Dean and Chapter of York (presumably acting as manorial landlords). [2] Only one family is said to have lived in Cottam by 1743. The 1801 census recorded 16 inhabitants in the township and there were just two inhabited buildings in 1841. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Little Cowden
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: The medieval site of Little Cowden has apparently been entirely lost to the sea, although it seems to have been depopulated long before. According to Poulson, writing in 1840 its chapel (presumably that mentioned in the 1291 Taxatio) was lost to coastal erosion c. 1690 ('about a century and a half since').  (Beresford attributed Poulson’s statement to the chapel of Great Cowden, seemingly in error ).
description_full: The medieval site of Little Cowden has apparently been entirely lost to the sea, although it seems to have been depopulated long before. According to Poulson, writing in 1840 its chapel (presumably that mentioned in the 1291 Taxatio) was lost to coastal erosion c. 1690 ('about a century and a half since'). [1] (Beresford attributed Poulson’s statement to the chapel of Great Cowden, seemingly in error [2]). An area of earthworks visible on air photographs (of the 1940s) has since been lost to the sea, but was thought to show a possible moat, platforms and hollow ways. [3] Beresford suggested they represented the ‘hamlet’ of Little Cowden. [2] A refined grid reference is used by this website instead of the 1968 original (TA 242 420). Although it possessed a church of its own, it appears that Little Cowden was, as its names suggests, always smaller than Great Cowden. In 1297 Little Cowden recorded one tax payer to Great Cowden’s four [4]. The great majority of lay taxation returns group Great and Little Cowden, and it seems likely there was a reduction in population between the 1377 Poll Tax and the 1543/4 Lay Subsidy at one or both sites. In 1428 Little Cowden was one of only two East Riding parishes excused taxation on the grounds that it had fewer than ten households. [2, 5] Whether this indicates depopulation at Little Cowden or just the continuance of a small community is hard to say, but Beresford noted the eviction of 24 people reported in 1517 (presumably as a result of enclosure), [2] which must have removed the bulk of the remaining population. For the 1543-4 Lay Subsidy only five people paid at Little Cowden compared with 22 at Great Cowden. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Cowlam
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll tax for one year
description_snippet: Described by Beresford in 1952 as 'a worthy twin to its neighbour, Cottam',  Cowlam has sadly seen a different fate in the late twentieth century, its earthworks being ploughed level. The layout of the village is shown on the 25 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1890 with two main streets heading east-west and north-south, and building platforms and tofts shown north of one street and east of the other.
description_full: Described by Beresford in 1952 as 'a worthy twin to its neighbour, Cottam', [1] Cowlam has sadly seen a different fate in the late twentieth century, its earthworks being ploughed level. The layout of the village is shown on the 25 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1890 with two main streets heading east-west and north-south, and building platforms and tofts shown north of one street and east of the other. Aerial photography showed at least 12 crofts to the north of the east-west route, ten to the south and a further 12 to the east of the north-south route. [2] A rescue excavation was conducted in 1971-2 in advance of ploughing, uncovering four structures within the area of one croft. [2] This croft has shown evidence of a courtyard farm and the excavations showed that this had been creates by the merger of two croft units towards the end of the medieval period. [2] Three of the structures were typical longhouses with chalk footing walls. Pottery from the site suggestesd this farm was occupied until the late seventeenth century. [2] A field visit in 1975 still found discernable earthworks in the north whilst the southern parts had been ploughed. By the late 1990s air photographs show the whole site to have been ploughed level, albeit that some features are still visible as cropmarks. [3] The features suggest some element of planning to the settlement and perhaps the eastern row was a later extension. [2] A late Anglo-Saxon strap end in Hull Museum is said to be from Cowlam, [4] and the settlement and a chuch were present in Domesday Book, supporting two manors, one belonging to the King, the second, waste in 1086, belonging to the Archbishop of York. Like Cottam, Cowlam seems to have suffered considerably as a result of the Black Death, with a 65% tax relief granted in 1354. [1] Oddly however, the village, which had rendered only half the amount of tax as Cottam in 1334 had slightly more tax payers (54) by 1377, a figure which suggests a viable village had survived. In the 1524/5 Lay Subsidy Cowlam paid 14s 2d, more than twice Cottam’s contribution. In the Hearth Tax of 1674 at least 14 houses still exisited. [2] Analysis of parish records suggests that desertion occurred around 1680 when baptisms disappear from the record. [2] Cowlam appears to have been taxed separately throughout the period covered by the E179 database, including the seventeenth century. By the early eighteenth century the village had become almost entirely deserted. Beresford noted the ruination of the church and that by 1735 the parish was 'depopulated not any inhabitants save two shepherds'. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Croom
e179_last: 1661-2 'Free and voluntary present'
description_snippet: The scheduled earthworks of crofts and building platforms of the medieval village of Croom surround Croome House. The layout appears to have been a simple two row arrangement along an east-west street. In addition to peasant longhouses and crofts an area of possible higher status enclosures has been suggested.
description_full: The scheduled earthworks of crofts and building platforms of the medieval village of Croom surround Croome House. The layout appears to have been a simple two row arrangement along an east-west street. In addition to peasant longhouses and crofts an area of possible higher status enclosures has been suggested. [1] To the north-west of the village are a well preserved set of medieval or earlier cultivation terraces also included in the scheduling. [2] Croom featured in Domesday Book, split between several manors and seems to have been an average sized vill in 1334 and above average for those that would subsequently be deserted. Like its neighbours Cowlam and Cottam, Croom must have suffered in the Black Death, receiving a 50% tax relief in 1354. [3] The village was not mentioned in the 1377 or 1381 Poll Tax returns, but was recorded in taxation documents of the fifteenth century. In the 1524/5 Lay Subsidy Croom was grouped with its parochial village of Sledmere, perhaps suggesting depopulation by this time, although later sixteenth and early seventeenth-century records still record Croom separately. It was again grouped with Sledmere from 1628 to 1661, at which point it disappears from view in the E179 taxation database. (The statements in [1] and [4] that Croom is last mentioned in 1585 appear to be an over-interpretation of a document quoted by Beresford in [3]). Perhaps the most likely scenario is that the village was seriously depleted by a combination of the Black Death and fifteenth/sixteenth-century enclosure, but a handful of buildings survived into the seventeenth century. Croom House, which overlies part of the medieval village, is thought to date from the late eighteenth century. [5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_snippet: The scattered settlement of Danthorpe is mainly laid out along two parallel east-west lanes, which are a continuation of the lanes forming the focus of Elstronwick to the immediate west. Although there are some signs of settlement shrinkage at Danthorpe, it is not clear whether it ever formed a nucleated village.
description_full: The scattered settlement of Danthorpe is mainly laid out along two parallel east-west lanes, which are a continuation of the lanes forming the focus of Elstronwick to the immediate west. Although there are some signs of settlement shrinkage at Danthorpe, it is not clear whether it ever formed a nucleated village. Aerial photographs show some evidence of 'field boundaries, with no evidence of house platforms' between the two parallel lanes at TA 238 235, and these might represent former village tofts or crofts. [1] Danthorpe Hall itself is thought to be late seventeenth century in date. [2, 3] A windmill is shown at the western end of the township on the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map and may be a successor to medieval and post-medieval mills mentioned in documentary evidence. [3] With the exception of the 1297 Lay Subsidy and seventeeth-century Hearth Tax Danthorpe was routinely grouped in taxation records with Elstronwick, providing few clues to former levels of population in the vill. The evidence that does exist suggests Danthorpe was always a thinly populated vill. Beresford noted that at least four tofts existed in 1299, 1367 and during the reign of Elizabeth I. [4] In 1297 only two tax payers were assessed above the 9s threshold, [5] but in 1303, when the property of John of Danthorpe was divided, the vill contained at least eight separate tofts as well as the capital messuage. Perhaps these might have formed a hamlet or small village, although we cannot be sure how scattered the plots were. [6]. In 1672 eight buildings were assessed for the Hearth Tax, and the same number were inhabited in 1841. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: Although no earthwork evidence has yet been suggested for a village at this site, there is some reason to believe the vill experienced depopulation. It was mentioned as a manor in Domesday Book, and had a modest 20s Lay Subsidy assessment in 1334. In 1354 a tax relief of 50% was allowed, suggesting the settlement was badly affected by the Black Death. [1] Perhaps because of a decline in population the vill was grouped with another deserted site, Everthorpe, for the 1377 Poll Tax and early sixteenth-century lay subsidies. These figures suggest a small population in 1377 possibly reduced further by the mid-sixteenth century at one or both of these vills. Drewton continued to be recorded separately in the 'tenth and fifteenth' taxation records, but was otherwise grouped with Everthorpe in records continuing into the seventeenth century. The vill was apparently further depopulated in 1672 [2], and by the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map in 1855 was no more than a scatter of buildings including the main manor house. The manor house is also said to have been a findspot for various Roman artefacts. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: The well-preserved earthworks at Eastburn indicate that a sizeable village once existed on this site, with house plots, tofts and hollow ways visible. [1, 2] The documentary evidence supports this picture: Eastburn was recorded in Domesday Book as a berewick of Driffield, and judging by its above average tax assessment in 1334 was by then a substantial village. Although the 69 tax payers recorded in 1377 is slightly below the average for villages in Harthill wapentake, [3] it still betokens a substantial settlement, and Beresford noted that 40.5 bovates of land were recorded attached to the settlement in both 1358 and 1401. [3] The 13 tax payers recorded in 1543/4 suggests that the settlement was by then significantly depleted, albeit that desertion was not inevitable. By the early seventeenth century a case before the diocesan courts remarked upon the fact that Eastburn 'did anciently consist of a great many messuages, cottages and dwelling houses...'. [3] Whether this reference should be taken as evidence for a complete depopulation is not clear however. Eastburn was bought by John Heron in 1664-6 who is reported to have converted the entire township to pasture and pulled down all the houses. [4] A case was heard against Heron at the archbishop's court in 1682. [4] The township of Eastburn was always separately taxed, but by the early nineteenth century it consisted of just a single farm. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Easthorpe
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: In the early 1950s Beresford described the earthworks of Easthorpe village as 'clearly visible on the ground near the stream with a complex of fishponds' and accorded them a ‘two star’ rating.  A field visit 20 years later was more pessimistic, interpreting some of the ‘old banks’ marked on early Ordnance Survey maps as a hollow way leading to a chalk pit and another as a field bank.
description_full: In the early 1950s Beresford described the earthworks of Easthorpe village as 'clearly visible on the ground near the stream with a complex of fishponds' and accorded them a ‘two star’ rating. [1] A field visit 20 years later was more pessimistic, interpreting some of the ‘old banks’ marked on early Ordnance Survey maps as a hollow way leading to a chalk pit and another as a field bank. [2] These banks were shown by the 1854-5 6 inch Ordnance Survey map surrounding Easthorpe Farm, although modern Ordnance Survey maps show the site of the village further west near the site of ‘Chapel Hill’ and the string of fish-ponds running through Londesborough Park. These ponds are now thought to be associated with the Park rather than the village. The Park was designed between 1676 and 1680 and extended between 1721 and 1753. [3, 4] A soil mark - possibly thought to be associated with the former settlement - has been noted north-west of Easthorpe Farm, in one of a number of fields near the farm now under cultivation. [2] The documentary evidence confirms that Easthorpe may have once been populous enough to be considered a village. The vill supported two manors in Domesday Book and it had a sizeable tax assessment in 1334, although the 24 tax payers in 1377 suggest a below average sized village by that stage. There were 13 tax payers in 1543, suggesting a small settlement survived, assuming the population was concentrated in one place. The point at which Easthorpe was finally abandoned is not clear although presumably it is before the early eighteenth-century expansion of the Park. Easthorpe was usually taxed separately in the E179 database records, except in 1671 when it was grouped with Londesborough. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Easton
e179_last: 1677 Act to raise money to build ships
description_snippet: 'Settlement traces' are said to be visible in aerial photographs of the area north and south of Easton Farm,  presumably as cropmarks since most of the surrounding fields are now under cultivation. description_full: 'Settlement traces' are said to be visible in aerial photographs of the area north and south of Easton Farm, [1] presumably as cropmarks since most of the surrounding fields are now under cultivation. There are few other obvious signs of the former village, although possibly a field boundary shown on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map running parallel with the main road to the north could have represented the back of village plots. Nevertheless, the documentary evidence suggests that Easton (presumably named from its position relative to Boynton) was once a small village, assuming that the medieval population recorded in tax returns was concentrated on one site. The vill had a modest five tax payers in 1297 [2] and a below average tax assessment for its wapentake in 1334. The village had a small (15%) relief for the effects of the Black Death in 1354, [3] and 10 poll tax payers were recorded in 1377. The vill was taxed separately throughout the fifteenth century but by the early sixteenth century it was grouped for the first time with Bessingby. Later sixteenth and early seventeenth-century tax records again recorded Easton separately, although it was again commonly grouped with Bessingby in the later seventeenth century. Depopulation seems most likely sometime in the fifteenth or early sixteenth century. By 1841 the township contained just two farms, suggesting the site is better classed as a ‘DMV’ (rather than a ‘shrunken village’, as suggested by the NMR record). Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Eddlethorpe
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: The existence of a DMV seems doubtful. Beresford noted that it was 'now shrunken to a straggle of farm-buildings',  but there is as yet no firm evidence that a nucleated medieval village existed. The settlement pattern shown on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance map is widely dispersed, and no evidence for village earthworks is yet known from any of the farms or buildings within the township.
description_full: The existence of a DMV seems doubtful. Beresford noted that it was 'now shrunken to a straggle of farm-buildings', [1] but there is as yet no firm evidence that a nucleated medieval village existed. The settlement pattern shown on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance map is widely dispersed, and no evidence for village earthworks is yet known from any of the farms or buildings within the township. [2] The site of Manor Farm, named as Eddlethorpe on the 6 inch Ordnance map at SE 773 661 is perhaps the most likely site for the medieval manor based simply on the place-name (Eddlethorpe Hall is a late addition). Moreover it is not clear from the documentary sources whether Eddlethorpe saw medieval depopulation on any scale, since the vill is usually grouped with North Grimston and Firby in lay taxation returns. The individual assessments in 1297 (with two tax payers) [3] and 1524/5 suggest the township was never very populous. In one of the 1662 Hearth Tax returns Eddlethorpe and Eddlethorpe Grange are listed separately. Possibly the township has always had a dispersed settlement pattern. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Enthorpe
e179_last: 1301 Fifteenth
