Beresford noted that the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map showed 'foundations' in a field east of the house,  a field which also contained a draw well. A field visit in 1972 concluded that the foundations marked in this area were likely to be those of an old field bank, and that 'there are no other apparent remains normally associated with depopulation'.
description_full: The case for a DMV at Enthorpe seems rather weak. Beresford noted that the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map showed 'foundations' in a field east of the house, [1] a field which also contained a draw well. A field visit in 1972 concluded that the foundations marked in this area were likely to be those of an old field bank, and that 'there are no other apparent remains normally associated with depopulation'. [2] Beresford also suggested that Enthorpe was recorded in Domesday Book, [1] but it is not clear which entry he had in mind. Possibly he was linking it with an unattributed ‘thorp’ in Weighton hundred, which some modern translations identify with Thorpe-le-Street. [3] Aside from this Enthorpe is mentioned just once in the E179 database of lay taxation records – as one of a number of granges in a document of 1301-2 (perhaps belonging to the Bishop of Durham). [4] It is possible a settlement fell out of use here in the century or two following Domesday Book, but otherwise the evidence for a former village looks rather flimsy. Neave suggests the village was never large enough to merit separate taxation. [5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Eske
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: The earthworks marking the medieval village of Eske surround Eske Manor House to the south and west. Beresford was able to unpick the topography of the village from an aerial photograph, with the village 'centred around a road to the ford' containing 'a number of two and three-roomed cottages'.
description_full: The earthworks marking the medieval village of Eske surround Eske Manor House to the south and west. Beresford was able to unpick the topography of the village from an aerial photograph, with the village 'centred around a road to the ford' containing 'a number of two and three-roomed cottages'. [1] A site visit in 1962 found that the earthworks were more difficult to interpret on the ground, noting that 'the remains of this village are poorly defined and little of the detail visible on the A.P. can now be identified'. [2] The fields surrounding the deserted village show up as ridge and furrow in the photograph printed in [1], although these areas are now again under cultivation. The complex history of this site has been thoroughly investigated in the 1980s. This showed the replanning of the site which occurred in 1300. [3] Field walking produced a range of thirteenth to sixteenth-century pottery, but all the later fifteenth-century sherds were fine tablewares indicating that just the leading tenants remained in residence. [3] A north-south street with a number of tofts and sunken yards is visible. The tofts to the east of the hollow way appear to have no crofts. To the south of this area is an east-west hollow way leading to the River Hull. This is suggested as the original focus of the settlement with the area to the north as a planned expansion sometime before the late thirteenth century. [3] Eske is mentioned in Domesday Book, amongst the properties of the Archbishop of York, and the vill was then more populous than neighbouring Tickton. Eske seems to have been only just below an average sized settlement based on the 1297 and 1334 subsidies (with only three tax payers recorded for the former). [4] A charter of c. 1280 notes at least 10 tofts, [5] whilst 63 tax payers were recorded in 1377 – again indicating a just below average, but certainly sustainably, sized village. There is no evidence of tax relief during the fifteenth century. In 1458 at least seven messuages survived, [5] but by the 1524/5 Lay Subsidies Eske was grouped with Routh in the taxation records, as it was again in the later seventeenth century. It has been suggested that depopulation accompanied the enclosure of Eske’s common fields in the sixteenth or seventeenth century, [6] but the final decline of the settlement appears to have been a drawn out process. The present Manor House is thought to date from c. 1680, probably a re-build of the nine-hearth house present in the Hearth Tax of 1672. The year before five one-hearth dwellings survived in addition to the manor house. [6] In 1786 the manor contained just three farms, reduced to two by 1788, and the township had only three buildings in the 1841 Census. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Etherdwick
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: The earthwork remains of a former small settlement have been identified from aerial photographs in the area between Etherdwick’s two surviving farms. Beresford noted that this area was named as ‘Old Garths’ on the tithe map.  A field visit in 1974 identified ‘disturbed hummocky ground...consistent with depopulation’ in this area, but was unable to discern a coherent layout.
description_full: The earthwork remains of a former small settlement have been identified from aerial photographs in the area between Etherdwick’s two surviving farms. Beresford noted that this area was named as ‘Old Garths’ on the tithe map. [1] A field visit in 1974 identified ‘disturbed hummocky ground...consistent with depopulation’ in this area, but was unable to discern a coherent layout. [2] However an aerial photograph taken in 2000 is now thought to have shown up tofts divided by east-west hollow ways, centred around a central north-south track. [2] The north of the area, still under grassland, has traces of ridge and furrow which presumably bounded the medieval settlement. The documentary evidence on the size and decline of Etherdwick is limited, mainly because it was almost always grouped with Flinton in lay taxation records. The 85 tax payers in 1377 noted by Beresford in fact relate to both Flinton (itself a shrunken village) as well as Etherdwick. The two places were separately taxed in 1297, when Flinton had four tax payers and Etherdwick just one, [3] hinting that it may have been the less populous of the two vills and was perhaps always on the small side. Etherdwick’s common fields were enclosed by agreement in 1651 when there were five freeholders of common land, [4] although these need not all have resided in the settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: East Flotmanby
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: In the mid ninteenth century, as today, Flotmanby consisted of just two farmhouses, East Flotmanby (now Manor Farm) and West Flotmanby, separated along a track by about 550m. Beresford noted 'signs of houses and crofts in crop marks west of East Flotmanby, and on the ground around West Flotmanby house', presumably from aerial photographs.
description_full: In the mid ninteenth century, as today, Flotmanby consisted of just two farmhouses, East Flotmanby (now Manor Farm) and West Flotmanby, separated along a track by about 550m. Beresford noted 'signs of houses and crofts in crop marks west of East Flotmanby, and on the ground around West Flotmanby house', presumably from aerial photographs. [1] It would appear that Beresford envisaged that this was formerly a single, small village, although East and West Flotmanby are listed separately in the 1968 Gazetteer, which is continued here. The area was bulldozed in 1957 and there was evidence of scattered remains of chalk buildings and thirteenth to fifteenth-century pottery. [2] Certainly the medieval taxation records always refer to a vill simply named as ‘Flotmanby’, and it appeared to suffer in the Black Death, with 100% tax reliefs granted in 1353 and 1354. Nevertheless the 88 tax payers recorded in 1377 would still be consistent with a small village. A confirmation charter of property here to Rievaulx Abbey also mentioned a toft in addition to land. [3] In the 1524/5 taxation Flotmanby was grouped with Folkton, perhaps implying it was then regarded as a very small settlement. The majority of the area between the two farms remains under cultivation on modern vertical aerial photographs. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Fosham
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: The suggestion of a deserted village at Fosham was first made in 1841 by George Poulson, who noted that one of the three extant farm houses, Fosham Garth was formerly surrounded by a moat and that the settlement formerly had a mill (perhaps south-east of Low Fosham in the area known as Mill Fields, and perhaps the windmill mentioned in documents of 1577-8).
description_full: The suggestion of a deserted village at Fosham was first made in 1841 by George Poulson, who noted that one of the three extant farm houses, Fosham Garth was formerly surrounded by a moat and that the settlement formerly had a mill (perhaps south-east of Low Fosham in the area known as Mill Fields, and perhaps the windmill mentioned in documents of 1577-8). [1, 2] Fosham Garth was subsequently demolished in the late nineteenth century, [2] and aerial photographs of 1946 are thought to show 'ditches and house platforms' in the area. [3] Whether these represent a former village rather than the remains of the farm is not certain however. The refined grid reference is used here compared to the 1968 original (TA 209 388). Fosham is recorded as a berewick of Aldbrough at Domesday. The later documentary evidence is unhelpful, since Fosham was routinely grouped with Marton and Carlton in the medieval taxation records, although this itself may suggest that Fosham was never a large settlement. The classification of Fosham as a DMV is therefore somewhat uncertain and may be difficult to resolve since the earthworks had been destroyed by ploughing by the time of a field visit in 1974 and the area remains under cultivation. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Gardham
e179_last: 1624 Three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1854-5 gives a detailed depiction of the earthworks or foundations of the lost village of Gardham, situated in an area known as Old Gardham Field with house plots either side of an east-west road. The site was subsequently ploughed, showing as soilmarks on an aerial photograph of 1971, although nothing was visible on the ground by 1972 and the site remains under cultivation.
description_full: The 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1854-5 gives a detailed depiction of the earthworks or foundations of the lost village of Gardham, situated in an area known as Old Gardham Field with house plots either side of an east-west road. The site was subsequently ploughed, showing as soilmarks on an aerial photograph of 1971, although nothing was visible on the ground by 1972 and the site remains under cultivation. [1] Beresford suggested that the current hamlet of Gardham, about 1.2km to the north-east was originally called Newton in Domesday Book, but adopted the name of Gardham when the old village was depopulated, perhaps a deliberate move to a better environment. [2] The identification of Newton as Gardham has also been adopted by the Phillimore editions of the Domesday Book. Beresford also thought the depopulation of Gardham may have been caused by the Black Death, and he noted the 75% tax relief granted in 1354. The 1379 Poll Tax certainly suggests that Gardham, already small in 1334 had become one of the least populous vills in the area with 26 people listed, and 19 taxed. It is not clear however when ‘Newton’ finally adopted the name of Gardham. Both vills are recorded in Domesday Book and a feudal aid dated to 1346/7, whilst Beresford noted a sixteenth-century petition naming both places. The name ‘Gardham’ occurs in tax assessments until 1624. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Garrowby
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: Although Garrowby appears at first sight to have a dispersed settlement pattern there is a case to be made for a former village, centred around Home Farm (formerly Garrowby House). Earthworks surrounding the house include a sunken trackway, banks, ditches, and possible house platforms. description_full: Although Garrowby appears at first sight to have a dispersed settlement pattern there is a case to be made for a former village, centred around Home Farm (formerly Garrowby House). Earthworks surrounding the house include a sunken trackway, banks, ditches, and possible house platforms. [1, 2] A refined grid reference to the farm is used by this website instead of the 1968 original (SE 795 574). Garrowby is recorded as a manor at Domesday. The tax assessment of Garrowby for 1334 would be consistent with a small village and Beresford noted a 1332 reference to tenements. By 1381 the vill had the joint lowest taxed population in Buckrose Hundred, implying some depopulation may have resulted from the Black Death (a 35% tax relief was granted in 1354). Certainly the depopulation must have taken place long before 1584 when the existence of Garrowby was disputed in a tithe suit. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Little Givendale
e179_last: 1671 subsidy for the king's extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: Although identified by Beresford as a potential deserted site on the documentary evidence,  it seems that the DMV Research Group, in 1965, were the first to publish details of the earthworks surrounding the farm at Little Givendale.
description_full: Although identified by Beresford as a potential deserted site on the documentary evidence, [1] it seems that the DMV Research Group, in 1965, were the first to publish details of the earthworks surrounding the farm at Little Givendale. [2] To the north these include 'tofts, containing possible building foundations, positioned either side of a north-south hollow way' whilst further related earthworks may also lie to the west. [3] Although a field visit in 1973 identified only evidence of past quarrying, these earthworks were also visible on aerial photographs from 1999. The medieval taxation records usually grouped Little Givendale with Millington, even in the fourteenth century, which may itself be an indication that the settlement retreated at a relatively early date. Beresford noted references to uncultivated land in the township in the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Goxhill
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: The depiction of Goxhill on the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1854-5 suggests that it was, in Beresford’s words, 'much shrunken'.  Although a handful of houses clustered near the church at the northern end of the main street, the area further south contained only a couple of buildings (now removed) and a number of small rectangular fields which could be former tofts.
description_full: The depiction of Goxhill on the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1854-5 suggests that it was, in Beresford’s words, 'much shrunken'. [1] Although a handful of houses clustered near the church at the northern end of the main street, the area further south contained only a couple of buildings (now removed) and a number of small rectangular fields which could be former tofts. The map also marks some ‘old banks’ to the rear of these, perhaps former croft divisions or building platforms. The documentary evidence also makes clear that whilst Goxhill was always relatively small it must have once been larger than the current tiny hamlet. There were 42 poll tax payers in 1377, and as many as 72 burials were recorded in 1588 when the inhabitants suffered from sweating sickness, [2] although one suspects many of these may have been from surrounding settlements. Although Goxhill parish was one of only two in the East Riding excused taxation in 1428 on account of having fewer than ten householders, [1] this was perhaps a reflection of the small parish size (the smallest in north Holderness) as much as depopulation in the village. Nevertheless only 12 tax payers were recorded in 1543-4 and a survey of 20 years later recorded only three tenants holding open field land, [1] so it seems significant depopulation can probably be attributed to the fifteenth or sixteenth century. The site is not recorded by the NMR, but is classified as a shrunken medieval settlement by the Humber HER. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Greenoak
e179_last: 1624 Three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The settlement of Greenoak is limited to a handful of buildings, including one marked in 1855 as the Manor House. About 300m north along what may have been the village street is a moated site which could have been an earlier manor.
description_full: The settlement of Greenoak is limited to a handful of buildings, including one marked in 1855 as the Manor House. About 300m north along what may have been the village street is a moated site which could have been an earlier manor. [1] The observed physical evidence for a former village at this site is limited to a 'ditched enclosure...at the southern end, [which] may form part of a field system associated with the original medieval settlement'. [2] Despite this, the documentary evidence points to a significant medieval population, which seems very likely to have been situated in a village given the small territory surrounding Greenoak. The settlement is indicated from the late twelfth century with presentations to the Sheriff in 1199. [3] The 1379 Poll Tax listed 101 people, with 64 tax payers. By the early sixteenth century Greenoak was grouped for the first time with Bellasize in taxation records, making a comparison difficult, although perhaps this implies a population reduction had already occurred. After 1624 Greenoak was no longer listed as a taxation unit in documents within the E179 database. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Grimston in Garton
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: Grimston is a deserted site which has suffered from the depletions of the plough and significant coastal erosion. The layout of the medieval village remains unclear, but may only have been loosely nucleated, in common with neighbouring Garton. Moat Farm (c.
description_full: Grimston is a deserted site which has suffered from the depletions of the plough and significant coastal erosion. The layout of the medieval village remains unclear, but may only have been loosely nucleated, in common with neighbouring Garton. Moat Farm (c. TA 284 356), contains two moats, the larger of which might date from between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries and represent the site of the medieval manor house. [1] The main village area seems to have been about 500m further west - an area of cropmarks on an air photo of 1946 shows a small north-south street with houses either side, [2] and this appears to be the same street shown on a seventeenth-century map of the area. [3] The medieval village probably also extended further west into the adjoining field, into the area marked on the 1855 6 inch Ordnance Survey map as ‘Old Garths’, showing possible foundations. This area is also now cultivated although modern vertical air photographs show a dark soilmark in the general vicinity. Further areas of settlement appear to have existed to the east of the moated manor house in an area that has rapidly receded into the sea since 1946. Field investigation in 1974 identified 'two possible garths and a mutilated fragment of sunken road' in this area at TA 285 356. [4] The settlement in Grimston shown further south on the 1855 Ordnance Survey map appears to be post-medieval – the new ‘Grimston Hall’ was built between 1781-6 whilst the cottages marked as the ‘Village’ probably also date from this time or shortly after. [3] A refined grid reference is used by the website instead of the 1968 original (TA 290 350). The medieval documentary evidence suggests that Grimston was a smallish village, and always smaller than neighbouring Garton, with which it was grouped in some taxation records of the sixteenth century and most of the seventeenth century. In 1517 two houses were said to have been lost as a result of enclosure, [3] and it seems likely that Grimston experienced depopulation in both the late medieval and post-medieval periods. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Grimston, Hanging
e179_last: 1624 Three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The well preserved earthworks of this scheduled DMV indicate the presence of a moderately sized village where now a single farm and cottage stand. The NMR and the Historic England scheduling report appear to offer different interpretations of the earthworks, [1, 2] but the more detailed and convincing description of the village layout is supplied by the latter.
description_full: The well preserved earthworks of this scheduled DMV indicate the presence of a moderately sized village where now a single farm and cottage stand. The NMR and the Historic England scheduling report appear to offer different interpretations of the earthworks, [1, 2] but the more detailed and convincing description of the village layout is supplied by the latter. The village may have contained as many as 20 tofts, mainly aligned in two rows either side of a main north-south street (or narrow green). A further row of smaller tofts is positioned to the north-west, perhaps a secondary addition to the plan. [2] At the far north of this area are more substantial buildings, more akin to the main village street, [2] although the NMR interpretation raises the suggestion of a manorial enclosure in this vicinity. [1] On the eastern side of the main street, south of the modern farm, the earthworks are suggestive of a fifteenth-century courtyard farm, [2] which may reflect late medieval economic changes and the growing importance of enclosure and sheep farming, perhaps even the process of depopulation. The documentary evidence for the size of the village is somewhat compromised by the grouping of Hanging Grimston with a number of other vills. In 1334 it is recorded with Uncleby, Painsthorpe, Thixendale, Kirby Underdale, Raisthorpe and possibly Anlaby. The 1381 Poll Tax figure of 79 tax payers is ostensibly for Hanging Grimston alone, although the entry perhaps still silently includes tax payers from some other vills. [3, 4] Hanging Grimston was recorded in the taxation records of the E179 database only until 1624, but the period of significant depopulation may have come earlier – some enclosure was reported in 1517, and by 1563 there was only one landowner recorded in a survey. [5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Grimthorpe
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll tax for one year

The treatment of the vill in medieval taxation records follows an unusual pattern. Although mentioned in the Domesday Book, Grimthorpe was mentioned only once (in 1340-1) in the fourteenth and fifteenth-century records of the E179 database.
description_full: Although reduced to a single farm by the mid nineteenth century, earthworks to the west and south-west of Grimthorpe Manor are thought to represent a medieval village. [1] The treatment of the vill in medieval taxation records follows an unusual pattern. Although mentioned in the Domesday Book, Grimthorpe was mentioned only once (in 1340-1) in the fourteenth and fifteenth-century records of the E179 database. It was however referred to as a vill in 1316 and a deed of 1485 suggests there were 'other houses than the manor and the mill'. [2] Grimthorpe is then regularly recorded in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, sometimes grouped with nearby Great and Little Givendale. Possibly the settlement was always relatively small. Beresford noted that a map of 1717 shows the township ‘enclosed but with a significant Chapel Close'. [2] There is also a chapel field in the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map. The chronology of depopulation at Grimthorpe therefore remains unresolved. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Gunby
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: The classification of Gunby as a DMV seems doubtful. There were no discernable village earthworks at the small hamlet when inspected in 1957, although there is a moat on the site of the former hall, thought to be demolished in the late eighteenth century.
description_full: The classification of Gunby as a DMV seems doubtful. There were no discernable village earthworks at the small hamlet when inspected in 1957, although there is a moat on the site of the former hall, thought to be demolished in the late eighteenth century. [1] Presumably the marshy ground to the west, as noted on the 1854 Ordnance Survey map, would have restricted the likelihood of former settlement on this side of the present settlement. Gunby is recorded as a manor in Domesday Book, and as Beresford noted a late eleventh-century charter makes reference to the place as a ‘vill’, [2, 3] but the documentary evidence does not seem consistent with a lost medieval village, unless it disappeared at a very early stage. Gunby does not appear in the E179 database of taxation records until 1563 (which would seem to contradict its published listing in the 1524 Lay Subsidy by Sheail [4]), and then appears in a number of seventeenth-century documents, always grouped with nearby Breighton. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hartburn
description_snippet: The 1854 6 inch Ordnance Survey map places the site of this drowned village at c. TA 170 613, just south of the mouth of the ‘Earl’s Dike’ and further north than the grid reference suggested by Beresford (TA 170 600).  Documentary sources refer to grants of tofts in the village c. late twelfth century, [1, 2] but the settlement was never mentioned in the medieval taxation records of the E179 database.
description_full: The 1854 6 inch Ordnance Survey map places the site of this drowned village at c. TA 170 613, just south of the mouth of the ‘Earl’s Dike’ and further north than the grid reference suggested by Beresford (TA 170 600). [1] Documentary sources refer to grants of tofts in the village c. late twelfth century, [1, 2] but the settlement was never mentioned in the medieval taxation records of the E179 database. It is assumed that the settlement had been depopulated or drowned by the fifteenth century. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hilderthorpe
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll tax for one year
description_snippet: Although now hemmed in by housing development and overrun by a golf course, a significant proportion of the earthworks of the medieval village have survived and are scheduled, despite their sporting use. The sweeping east-west hollow way that formed the main village street can still be seen, snaking its way between greens and fairways.
description_full: Although now hemmed in by housing development and overrun by a golf course, a significant proportion of the earthworks of the medieval village have survived and are scheduled, despite their sporting use. The sweeping east-west hollow way that formed the main village street can still be seen, snaking its way between greens and fairways. The village consisted of at least 13 tofts, three north of the road and 10 to the south, along with a suggested manorial site. [1] Remains of buildings are said to have been discernable in some of the tofts. [2] An excavation on the main street in 1954-5 found a fifteenth-century pot sherd in a re-cut and sealed ditch, confirming that the street was in use in the medieval period. [1] Other features uncovered included a number of walls from toft boundaries and possible buildings. [3] The documentary evidence suggests that Hilderthorpe was always a modestly sized village. It received a 63% taxation relief in 1354, [4] but by 1377 still seems to have been a viable community with 56 tax payers. By 1525 the Lay Subsidy assessment for Hilderthorpe (5s) suggests that the population of the vill (and therefore probably village) had declined relative to surrounding settlements. Hilderthorpe’s continued decline in the post-medieval period seems to have been slow and gradual. In 1539 13 men were noted on a military muster, whilst eight households were recorded in the Hearth Tax of 1670. [1] By the mid-nineteenth century the village seems to have contained just two farms. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Holm Archiepiscopi
e179_last: 1446-8 one and a half fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: The site of this deserted site is marked on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1850-5, in a field just north of a what is believed to be a Bronze Age linear boundary dyke. Beresford noted that the 1946 aerial photograph showed the site already under the plough, appearing as 'a neat row of houses and garths'.
description_full: The site of this deserted site is marked on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1850-5, in a field just north of a what is believed to be a Bronze Age linear boundary dyke. Beresford noted that the 1946 aerial photograph showed the site already under the plough, appearing as 'a neat row of houses and garths'. [1] This soilmark is still discernable on modern vertical aerial photographs, and suggests Holme was a relatively small village. The documentary evidence for Holme is somewhat muddied by potential confusion with other settlements in East Yorkshire of the same name. This site was a prebend of York Minster, and sometimes referred to as Holme Archiepiscopi. An extent of 1295 recorded a total of 11 tenants farming land in the village, two of whom leased demesne land belonging to the Manor House. [1] The village also had a chapel, recorded in the Taxatio of 1291. Based on the identifications in the E179 database, Holme seems to have been recorded throughout the fourteenth century, being only slightly below the average size according to the 1334 Lay Subsidy. The 1377 Poll Tax entry for Holme (identified with this village by Beresford, although the E179 database is curiously uncertain on the question) lists only 11 tax payers, one of the lowest in Buckrose. Possibly the village did therefore see a fourteenth-century decline, perhaps associated with the plague. The last certain entry in the E179 database for the village is for a taxation of 1446-8, although the general lack of documents from the later fifteenth century means that this should not be viewed as providing a precise indication of the village’s extinction. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Houghton
e179_last: 1692 quarterly Poll Tax for one year
description_snippet: The site of this deserted site was marked by the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1855, near Houghton Lane south of a lake and park belonging to Houghton Hall. By 1855 no houses remained in the village. Houghton Lane formed (latterly at least) the southern boundary to the park associated with Houghton Hall,  and the land to its north has remained under pasture.
description_full: The site of this deserted site was marked by the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of 1855, near Houghton Lane south of a lake and park belonging to Houghton Hall. By 1855 no houses remained in the village. Houghton Lane formed (latterly at least) the southern boundary to the park associated with Houghton Hall, [1] and the land to its north has remained under pasture. Field investigation in this area in 1969 found 'amorphous remains which probably represent building sites'. [2] The land south of the road has been cultivated and a thin strip adjacent to the road has produced 'a profusion of potsherds and building materials' under ploughing. [2] These findings are thought to indicate Houghton was a linear village, laid out along Houghton Lane. Houghton’s tax assessment in the 1334 Lay Subsidy suggests a below average sized village, and the vill was already being grouped with nearby Sancton in the 1377 Poll Tax and the 1446-8 ‘tenth and fifteenth’ subsidy, although it was also recorded alone as late as 1606, perhaps because of scribal anachronism. Houghton Hall was built c. 1760 and its parkland laid out according to a design of 1768, [1, 3] although the village may already have disappeared by this stage. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hundeburton
e179_last: 1606 six fifteenth and tenths
description_snippet: Although the evidence is somewhat tenuous, there is a suggestion of a hamlet or small village called Hundeburton in the area named ‘Burtonfields’. The most likely location for a settlement appears to be immediately to the south and south-east of Low Burtonfields Farm, the grid reference used here instead of the 1968 original of TA 725 557.
description_full: Although the evidence is somewhat tenuous, there is a suggestion of a hamlet or small village called Hundeburton in the area named ‘Burtonfields’. The most likely location for a settlement appears to be immediately to the south and south-east of Low Burtonfields Farm, the grid reference used here instead of the 1968 original of TA 725 557. Aerial photographs of 1951 appear to show linear banks and ditches of possible fields or settlement plots, although the area also had evidence of later drainage. [1] The site was under cultivation by 1962, but linear features in the area can still be seen as soilmarks on vertical aerial photographs of 2002 and 2003. The documentary evidence for this settlement is uncertain. Beresford believed that ‘Hundburton’ could have been an earlier name form for ‘Stamford Bridge’. [2] Although the vill was recorded separately in 1332, it was generally thereafter grouped with East Stamford Bridge. The E179 database includes references to Hundburton until 1606, although the majority of these are probably identifications of the manor named ‘Burtonfield’, perhaps a development or alternative version of the name. [3] The grouping with East Stamford Bridge means it is difficult to discern whether we are dealing with a single manorial site or a small village. Possibly the vill included a number of farms in addition to any manor house or settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Hunsley
e179_last: 1667 various acts to raise money
description_snippet: The site of this deserted village was marked on the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of the 1850s, in a pasture field between Hunsley House and Hunsley Cottage suggesting a linear village along the east-west path between them.
description_full: The site of this deserted village was marked on the 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of the 1850s, in a pasture field between Hunsley House and Hunsley Cottage suggesting a linear village along the east-west path between them. The uneven quality of the field surface observed in 1969 probably reflects its former use, and Beresford and the 1969 field investigator both reported local knowledge that 'worked stone' and 'footings' had been disturbed in the area, the latter example suggesting the area had been ploughed in the past. [1, 2] The documentary evidence for Hunsley suggests the village was of below average size in the fourteenth century. Although it was not recorded in the early sixteenth-century lay subsidies, the vill was mentioned in lay taxation returns until 1677, usually individually, but more often grouped with other places, including Little Weighton, in the later seventeenth century. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Keeling, Nun
e179_last: 1692 Feb 24 quarterly poll tax for one year
description_snippet: There are no clear visible earthworks at the site, although features have been plotted in the past. The area is now covered by an extensive farm complex. Recorded in Domesday, most of the land was granted to the Benedictines for a nunnery in the 1140s.  There are 12 tofts recorded in 1256.  However the settlement paid an average amount in the 1334 Lay Subsidy.
description_full: There are no clear visible earthworks at the site, although features have been plotted in the past. The area is now covered by an extensive farm complex. Recorded in Domesday, most of the land was granted to the Benedictines for a nunnery in the 1140s. [1] There are 12 tofts recorded in 1256. [2] However the settlement paid an average amount in the 1334 Lay Subsidy. It does not appear in the later fourteenth-century records, but does appear recorded with other settlements in the sixteenth century. This may suggest continued settlement in the area, but the picture is not clear. Traditionally it is suggested the settlement antedated the nunnery. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Kelleythorpe
e179_last: 1671 subsidy for king's extraordinary occasions (with Elmswell)
description_snippet: Although included in his listing , no physical evidence for a deserted village at Kelleythorpe was noted by Beresford, and neither the HER nor the NMR contain any subsequent evidence of this nature. The first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of the 1850s shows the site as a probable farm and outbuildings to the south of the Driffield-Kirkburn road.
description_full: Although included in his listing [1], no physical evidence for a deserted village at Kelleythorpe was noted by Beresford, and neither the HER nor the NMR contain any subsequent evidence of this nature. The first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map of the 1850s shows the site as a probable farm and outbuildings to the south of the Driffield-Kirkburn road. The settlement is recorded in Domesday Book as well as the 1334 Lay Subsidy and 1377 Poll Tax returns (albeit with very low assessments in the latter two cases). The vill was separately recorded for taxation purposes as late as the early seventeenth century, but as the NMR has noted it is possible the site was always a hamlet. [2] Neave confirms this was probably never more than a hamlet. [3] In the 1672 Hearth Tax 12 households are recorded at Kelleythorpe and Elmswell and the area was enclosed in the late sixteenth or early seventeenth century. [3] The site is today covered by a large farm, with the wider surrounding area having been subject to modern development. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Kettlethorpe
description_snippet: Although the sum total of evidence for a former village at Kettlethorpe is limited there are hints of a once larger settlement. The site is today, and was in the mid 1800s, represented by a farm, situated by the parish boundary between North and Save Cave on a road that perpetuates a former Roman route.
description_full: Although the sum total of evidence for a former village at Kettlethorpe is limited there are hints of a once larger settlement. The site is today, and was in the mid 1800s, represented by a farm, situated by the parish boundary between North and Save Cave on a road that perpetuates a former Roman route. About 400m along this road to the south-east of the farm the former site of a chapel was marked on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map. The area between the farm and the former chapel, which might seem a candidate for the location of the former settlement, has been at least partially affected by quarrying. Kettlethorpe appears as a manor in the Domesday Book, but not in any of the subsequent taxation records consulted for this database. Beresford notes however that evictions were recorded from the settlement in 1533. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Kilnwick Percy
e179_last: 1692 quarterly poll tax for a year
description_snippet: Beresford noted earthworks here situated between the isolated Hall (a nineteenth-century rebuild of an earlier property) and the church (of twelfth-century origins), but an aerial photograph from 1999 has suggested that the main focus of the medieval settlement may have been to the south and south-east of the church, where a hollow way, tofts or crofts and potential buildings were identified.
description_full: Beresford noted earthworks here situated between the isolated Hall (a nineteenth-century rebuild of an earlier property) and the church (of twelfth-century origins), but an aerial photograph from 1999 has suggested that the main focus of the medieval settlement may have been to the south and south-east of the church, where a hollow way, tofts or crofts and potential buildings were identified. [1] Beresford’s study of private muniments for the area led him to believe the village 'had gone by the end of the sixteenth century, possibly earlier'. [2] A comparison of the number of poll tax payers for the vill in 1377 (35) against those for the subsidies of 1524-5 and 1543 (10 to 12) hints at a late medieval depopulation. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Kiplingcotes
e179_last: 1606 six fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: Much of this site, as marked on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map in the field west of Kipling House Farm, has subsequently been ploughed out. However the fields to the south of the Farm do still retain earthworks, some appearing quite regular (perhaps ridge and furrow) but also some which may be toft/building remains to the south-west of the Farm at c. SE 900 497.
description_full: Much of this site, as marked on the first edition 6 inch Ordnance Survey map in the field west of Kipling House Farm, has subsequently been ploughed out. However the fields to the south of the Farm do still retain earthworks, some appearing quite regular (perhaps ridge and furrow) but also some which may be toft/building remains to the south-west of the Farm at c. SE 900 497. The remaining earthworks were surveyed in 1972. [1] Although Kiplingcotes did not feature in the lay subsides reported in this database or the poll taxes it did regularly feature in taxation records, initially as a separate unit. The two tax payers recorded in 1297 suggest a relatively small settlement [2], but it was not until the sixteenth century onwards that the vill was grouped with Middleton on the Wolds in the E179 taxation records. Beresford has also noted a document of 1689 in which witnesses claimed knowledge of a former village and church or chapel. Four gravestones at Middleton are also said to have come from the former graveyard here and human remains are also said to have been found in the vicinity. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Kirkham
e179_last: 1692 quarterly poll tax for one year
description_snippet: Within Kirkham Park, a mainly flat area within a loop of the River Derwent it seems possible that a settlement once existed north of the site of Kirkham Priory ruins, perhaps a hamlet. Surviving earthworks within the park suggest the vestiges of ridge and furrow as well as seven small enclosures, perhaps house plots or small closes which might be medieval.
description_full: Within Kirkham Park, a mainly flat area within a loop of the River Derwent it seems possible that a settlement once existed north of the site of Kirkham Priory ruins, perhaps a hamlet. Surviving earthworks within the park suggest the vestiges of ridge and furrow as well as seven small enclosures, perhaps house plots or small closes which might be medieval. [1] It has been suggested that any settlement survived until at least 1650, [1] and ‘Kirkham’ does feature in the E179 taxation record database down to the end of the seventeenth century. Although occasionally the taxation returns (e.g. the 1377 Poll Tax) refer to the settlement as ‘Kirkham Abbey’, more often the vill is simply styled as ‘Kirkham’, and the tax payers of the lay subsidies were presumably from the nearby settlement and any outlying farms. Further investigation of the relationship between the Priory and the potential settlement (which would perhaps have been unusually close to the ecclesiastical buildings) and the history of the later park (said to be potentially eighteenth to nineteenth century) [2] may also throw further light on this site. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Linton
e179_last: 1628 June 16 x 29 five subsidies
description_snippet: It is thought that the present Linton Wold Farm – and perhaps the Grange buildings before it – occupy the central one of three earthwork enclosures,  with some of the earthworks surviving, particularly to the south-east. [1, 2] The farm is also set within a wider landscape of (possibly prehistoric) earthworks and cropmarks and the relationship of these to the presumed medieval features needs further investigation.
description_full: It is thought that the present Linton Wold Farm – and perhaps the Grange buildings before it – occupy the central one of three earthwork enclosures, [1] with some of the earthworks surviving, particularly to the south-east. [1, 2] The farm is also set within a wider landscape of (possibly prehistoric) earthworks and cropmarks and the relationship of these to the presumed medieval features needs further investigation. As to the size of the settlement, whether before or after its acquisition by the Priory, Beresford commented that 'it can never have been very large'. [3] Linton is mentioned in Domesday Book, and subsequently came into the ownership of Malton Priory, eventually being described as a Grange. Although recently in private hands it was still described as ‘Linton grange’ on the 1549 Lay Subsidy return. The small number of subsequent tax returns of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth century in the E179 database which mention this place list it as ‘Linton’ and group it with Wintringham and Newton. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: East Linton
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths (Linton)
description_snippet: There are no visible remains at the site apart from two arms of the moated site. The documentary history of the settlement would appear to be always combined with West Linton as Linton although Beresford had suggested they were viewed as separate settlements by the Exchequer in the fourteenth century.
description_full: There are no visible remains at the site apart from two arms of the moated site. The documentary history of the settlement would appear to be always combined with West Linton as Linton although Beresford had suggested they were viewed as separate settlements by the Exchequer in the fourteenth century. [1] Recent research has shown that in all likelihood the references to Linton refer to this settlement and West Linton was recorded as Linton in Balkholme. [2] At East Linton, the moated site was in the hands of William Linton, subtenanted from the Haye’s of Aughton. [3] In the 1334 Lay Subsidy Linton contributes an average amount. In 1379 there are 28 people listed, of whom 21 were taxed. The settlement does not appear in the sixteenth-century lay subsidies used by this website although it does continue to appear on the E179 database. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: West Linton
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths (Linton)
description_snippet: There are no visible features at this location apart from the ploughed-out remains of a very large moated site. The documentary history of the settlement would appear to be always combined with East Linton as Linton although Beresford had suggested they were viewed as separate settlements by the Exchequer in the fourteenth century.
description_full: There are no visible features at this location apart from the ploughed-out remains of a very large moated site. The documentary history of the settlement would appear to be always combined with East Linton as Linton although Beresford had suggested they were viewed as separate settlements by the Exchequer in the fourteenth century. [1] This settlement has been identified as Linton in Balkholme and appears in the mid-fourteenth century, and is the later of the two Lintons. It is possible that this was never recorded separately in the tax records but is included with Balkholme. [2] The moated site was the original manor but may have been supplanted with Linton Chapel by 1388. [2, 3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Lund, Garth
description_snippet: Clear evidence for settlement earthworks have been seen from the air located to the west of Preston around Lund Garth. Whether this is a separate settlement or whether it shows shrinkage of the settlement at Preston is unclear. There is no evidence for this settlement from the documentary sources. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.
description_full: Clear evidence for settlement earthworks have been seen from the air located to the west of Preston around Lund Garth. Whether this is a separate settlement or whether it shows shrinkage of the settlement at Preston is unclear. There is no evidence for this settlement from the documentary sources. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Meaux
e179_last: 1692 Feb 24 quarterly poll tax for one year
description_snippet: No clear earthworks are visible on the ground at this site. Mentioned in Domesday as Melsa and as a berewick of Aldbrough, the settlement was destroyed when the Cistercian Abbey was founded in 1151-4. The Chronicle of Meaux records the settlement as being close to North Grange.
description_full: No clear earthworks are visible on the ground at this site. Mentioned in Domesday as Melsa and as a berewick of Aldbrough, the settlement was destroyed when the Cistercian Abbey was founded in 1151-4. The Chronicle of Meaux records the settlement as being close to North Grange [1]. Excavations at North Grange moated site revealed evidence of tile kilns associated with the Abbey but no evidence of earlier settlement was uncovered. [2] This seems to be truly a deserted settlement, with no documentary evidence apart from Domesday Book as it is such an early desertion. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Menethorpe
e179_last: 1692 Feb 24 quarterly poll tax for one year
description_snippet: Located to the east of the River Derwent, these extensive settlement remains include upstanding areas of ridge and furrow. The road through the area runs east-west then makes a dog-leg to the north. Also running east-west is Menethorpe Beck. Parallel to this stretch of road and the Beck are earthworks of house platforms and property boundaries.
description_full: Located to the east of the River Derwent, these extensive settlement remains include upstanding areas of ridge and furrow. The road through the area runs east-west then makes a dog-leg to the north. Also running east-west is Menethorpe Beck. Parallel to this stretch of road and the Beck are earthworks of house platforms and property boundaries. The properties to the south of the road have been curtailed by modern ploughing. These earthworks mirror buildings which are shown on Jeffery’s 1775 map. The earthworks have been plotted during the NMP Howardian Hill project. This identified 12 enclosures to the south of the road. [1] To the north of the road are an indeterminate number of enclosures. [1] A recently discovered map of the village from 1723 also confirms this evidence and lists 12 tenants and two freeholders. [2] Recorded in Domesday as two manors, with a minimum population of 18, it is then recorded in the 1297 Lay Subsidy with four people paying, and there is a sizable population of 34 in the Poll Tax of 1377. [2] There are still 21 people taxed in the sixteenth-century taxations. It has been reported that houses were finally cleared to make way for a park associated with the local hall. [1] However recent research by Cookson has shown the settlement was deserted c. 1872. [2] She has suggested this is a shrunken settlement due to the number of continously occupied farmsteads in the area but for the purposes of this website it continues to be classified as a DMV. The manor was enclosed in the mid-eighteenth century, but reorganisation of agricultural practice in the 1870s saw the old families leaving the village. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Metham
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: Not many clear earthworks are seen at the location. The modern Metham Hall and Metham Hall Farm are located in the area, and much of the surrounding land is under plough. A vague sign of a hollow way or boundary running east-west can be seen to the north of the Hall. A moated site forms part of the area and was the location of the medieval manor.
description_full: Not many clear earthworks are seen at the location. The modern Metham Hall and Metham Hall Farm are located in the area, and much of the surrounding land is under plough. A vague sign of a hollow way or boundary running east-west can be seen to the north of the Hall. A moated site forms part of the area and was the location of the medieval manor. Beresford suggests the settlement was not settled until the thirteenth century on the evidence of the place name history, although the taxation records suggest a sizable settlement by this time. [1] There are deeds recording Metham from the early thirteenth century. [2] It is recorded on the Nomina Villarium of 1316. [3] The fourteenth-century tax records would suggest a sizable settlement with 34 people taxed in 1379, and a total of 45 people recorded. There is a reduced number in some of the sixteenth-century tax records, but by this time it is taxed with Saltmarshe and Cotness. The last record on E179 is 1624 suggesting that the settlement had started to decline by this time or that it was being subsumed into the surrounding settlements' tax records. The current Metham Hall is early nineteenth-century and Metham Hall Farm is dated from around 1800. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Monkwith
e179_last: c. 1377 Feb 16 x 19 poll tax
description_snippet: No physical evidence of this settlement still remains. The settlement has been described as a hamlet, being completely lost to the sea by the seventeenth century.  However Poulson in 1841 records ‘the manor lies along the sea-cliff.... it has suffered materially from the devastations of the sea, and not many years hence will be entirely gone’, suggesting it had not completely disappeared until a later date.
description_full: No physical evidence of this settlement still remains. The settlement has been described as a hamlet, being completely lost to the sea by the seventeenth century. [1] However Poulson in 1841 records ‘the manor lies along the sea-cliff.... it has suffered materially from the devastations of the sea, and not many years hence will be entirely gone’, suggesting it had not completely disappeared until a later date. [2] Extensive areas of ridge and furrow have been plotted in the area from aerial photography. [1] The settlement is recorded in Domesday as a berewick, but missing from the Lay Subsidy of 1344. There is a reasonably sized population in 1377 of 28 people taxed. However this is the last entry on the E179 list. This perhaps suggests that a sizable settlement became depopulated and became a simple hamlet sometime after the late fourteenth century, to then be lost to the sea in the seventeenth century. There is evidence of enclosure in 1517 which may help to establish a timeframe for depopulation with four people evicted. [3] The land was fully enclosed as Tunstall’s common land in 1779. [4] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Moreby
e179_last: 1677 April 16 act to raise £584,978 2s 2½d to build 30 ships
description_snippet: No physical remains are visible at the site which is currently occupied by Moreby Hall and associated park. To the south of the Hall ridge and furrow can be seen in the parkland. Moreby is recorded in Domesday as a berewick. In the Lay Subsidy of 1301, Moreby was recorded with nine people paying separately but after this date is always recorded with Stillingfleet.
description_full: No physical remains are visible at the site which is currently occupied by Moreby Hall and associated park. To the south of the Hall ridge and furrow can be seen in the parkland. Moreby is recorded in Domesday as a berewick. In the Lay Subsidy of 1301, Moreby was recorded with nine people paying separately but after this date is always recorded with Stillingfleet. [1, 2] From Domesday onwards there is a complex manorial history with at least two estates in existence in the sixteenth century. One of the estates was based on the current Moreby Hall and by 1529 there are four houses and tofts, and the estate had been fully enclosed. [3] The current Moreby Hall is dated 1828-33 with a pre-Elizabethan staircase tower. [4] The centre of the other estate was near to Home Farm, about 600m to the south, but is not mentioned after 1612. [3] The evidence for the village would seem to suggest a settlement between two manorial centres, however it is this area that has evidence of ridge and furrow on aerial photographs. The village may have been emparked and any sign of it removed. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Mowthorpe
e179_last: 1662 May 19 hearth tax
description_snippet: Earthworks are visible of this small site, lying between Duggleby and Kirby Grindalythe.  All these three settlements are located in a linear pattern along the Gypsy Race.  Various earthworks are still visible in the area but some of these have been identified as evidence for sixteenth-century farmsteads.
description_full: Earthworks are visible of this small site, lying between Duggleby and Kirby Grindalythe. [1] All these three settlements are located in a linear pattern along the Gypsy Race. [2] Various earthworks are still visible in the area but some of these have been identified as evidence for sixteenth-century farmsteads. [1] Earthworks had been in existence to the east and west of Low Mowthorpe, but those to the west, at least seven buildings, were levelled by ploughing in the later twentieth century. [2] The monastic houses at both Malton and Kirkham record gifts of land as well as tofts and crofts at the settlement, while in 1290 a messuage and six tofts were granted to St Peter’s in York. [1] Within the parish of Kirby Grindalythe this settlement is part of a pattern of smaller settlements, perhaps hamlets, surrounding the clear centre of Kirby Grindalythe. [2] Although the VCH only describes Mowthorpe as deserted on some occasions, but not all, it does describe a settlement that by the early seventeenth century was just a handful of houses, and a single farm by the early eighteenth century. [2] In the 1297 Lay Subsidy four people paid the subsidy. [3] In 1377 there are 21 tax payers recorded, with this decreasing to 15 in 1381. The settlement becomes subsumed with Kirby Grindalythe in later taxations. Beresford suggests this is a Black Death casualty. [1] However there would appear to be a population hanging on until later and it really only becomes deserted in the seventeenth century. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

By the Hearth Tax of 1672 25 households are recorded. [3] This decline continues with in 1764 only eight families recorded as living in the settlement and a 1779 map shows Newick Hall and two farms. [4] The settlement appears to have been cleared by emparking in the early eighteenth century when Neswick Hall was built. [5] Neswick Hall was demolished 1954. description_full: Clearly visible earthworks of a manorial complex can be seen on the aerial photographs between two farm complexes. Earthworks to the south of this showed tofts and boundary ditches, but some of these were levelled in the 1960s. [1] The chapel of St Michael’s is recorded from between 1180-1210. [2] It is last mentioned in 1400. [2] It was located to the south-west of the earthworks, and is shown on the Ordnance Survey first edition map of 1854 and first revision of 1892. On later maps it is simply shown as ‘site of’. It can still be seen from the aerial photographs. One of the present houses is a small brick and chalk cottage and one of the very best examples of cruck-framed buildings in East Yorkshire with seventeenth-century trusses present. [3] A number of religious houses had landholdings in Octon including the Knights Hospitallers, nuns of Wykeham, St Leonards York and Kirkstall Abbey. [2] Octon is recorded in Domesday and in the fourteenth-century tax records, either independently or with Swaythorpe. From the fifteenth century it is assessed with Thwing, and it is suggested that it was only at this time that the village diminished. [2] On the Tithe Maps of 1769 there were 20 crofts along the street, but with only eight houses present. [2] With these and the present hamlet at the site, this is more of a shrunken settlement than a fully deserted settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

e179_last: 1624/5 Three fifteenths and tenths

description_full: Beresford suggested this lost ‘hamlet’ might be to the west of Welwick. [1] The approximate grid reference of TA 345 210 used here and given in the 1968 Gazetteer is at the eastern edge of the village of Welwick, an area shown by recent aerial photographs to contain the remains of medieval ridge and furrow. [2] A series of cropmarks thought to mark the site of a DMV in the western part of Welwick parish are more likely to be the site of Welwick Thorpe. A medieval moated site at Moat Farm does survive at the western edge of the village of Welwick itself. [3] Writing in 1841, George Poulson stated that Penisthorpe ‘adjoined the Humber’, although it appears this statement could only be applied with confidence to the lands of the township or hamlet rather than the settlement itself. Poulson noted evidence that 46½ acres of land within this township called ‘Orwithfleet’ had been lost to the Humber in 1313, whilst a field called ‘Green Close’ ‘lying in Pensthorp’ survived at the Humber edge at a later date. [4] A further location has been suggested at TA 332216 recorded in the archive of the MVRG but there is no further evidence at this location. In 1297 five people paid the Lay Subsidy. [5] Penisthorpe was grouped with Welwick Thorpe (‘Thorpe Hill’) in the taxation records of the late thirteenth to fifteenth century. The 107 tax payers recorded in the 1377 Poll Tax for the two places suggest one or both of them were well populated. For a time in the early sixteenth century Penisthorpe was grouped with the farm called Ploughland at TA 339 217. In 1524/5 only one tax payer from the two places met the taxable threshold. Although occasionally taxed individually, Penisthorpe was again more commonly grouped with Welwick Thorpe in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth century. The vill disappears from the E179 database after 1624/5. Whether the settlement has been lost to the Humber estuary or the location of a settlement on terra firma has been lost from memory is not known. By 1841 only small pieces of land still bear the name. [6] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: This is one of two settlements that developed in the shifting sands of the Humber around Spurn Point. This settlement was also known as Ravenser Odd and replaced Ravenser (also known as Ravenser Old). The locations of both these settlements have been lost to the sea and are not firmly located. Also the similarity in the names has often caused confusion and made the two settlements hard to distinguish. Sheppard has it located to the east of Spurn, while Boyle has it to the west. Both have it closer to the current Spurn Head than Ravenser Old. [1, 2] By the fourteenth century it was approached by a sandy approach road and was located about a mile from the mainland. The current marker is therefore just a rough indication and should not be taken as firm evidence of its location. Ravenserod was founded in around 1230 on an island and becomes a town. It was first described as a borough between 1241-1249. [3] It gained its first grant for quayage in 1297, and another in 1310. It gained a royal charter in 1299, but erosion began soon after 1300. [3] In the 1297 Lay Subsidy 36 people paid 113s 7d, and in Ravenser Old, 44 people paid. [4] By 1346 two thirds of the town was destroyed. [3] A record of 1347-8 suggests that there were at least 300 buildings. [5] By 1350 the chapel was in ruins. [6] The residents had moved to Hull and taken up residence in the town. [5] For a full description of the history of the town see Boyle. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: Most of the area of this settlement has been heavily ploughed and the earthworks are no longer visible. It appears in the 1334 Lay Subsidy and in 1377 when 10 people paid the tax. Meaux Abbey and Warter Priory had land here. [1] It is not recorded in the sixteenth-century subsidies used by this website although it does appear in other records on the E179. Beresford suggested that it was a hamlet of Leconfield and was depopulated when Leconfield Park was expanded, however the village itself falls outside the park. [1, 3] The park was expanded on a number of occasions in the sixteenth century and so may have extended further than is plotted. This would also match the pottery evidence. description_full: Earthworks of the settlement can be clearly seen in the fields surrounding Riplingham House. A hollow way runs east-west with crofts and tofts to the north and south. Excavations in 1956-57 were undertaken to the west of Riplingham House. The first house excavated was found to date from the late fifteenth or early sixteenth with phases of reconstruction up to the middle of the eighteenth century. [1] The second house excavated was built in the thirteenth century and rebuilt twice before becoming completely ruined in the late fourteenth century. [1] A further house site was excavated in 1966. [2] Riplingham is recorded at Domesday as an outlier of North Ferriby. It has an above average contribution to the 1334 Lay Subsidy and 27 people paid the tax of 1377. By 1524 it was recorded with Weighton with only nine contributors. The excavated evidence shows a decline by the fifteenth century, and it would seem that there were attempts to revive the settlement well into the eighteenth century. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: Earthworks are visible from the air. A possible east-west hollow way is visible to the west of the modern farm, with slight indications of tofts. [1] Parts of the earthworks have been levelled and some buried under the current farm. [2] Around 30 sherds of pottery have been recovered from the ploughed areas dating to the thirteenth and fourteenth century. [3] The area also contains the earthworks of the Jacobean gardens to Risby Hall. The Hall was constructed in the seventeenth century and demolished in the eighteenth century. [4] A chapel was recorded at Risby in the fifteenth century, but was recorded as demolished by 1640. [5] Risby is mentioned in the Domesday Book. In 1297 two people paid the Lay Subsidy. [6] It does not appear separately in 1334 as it is entirely subsumed in two entries for Liberties of Chapter of Beverley & Provost of Beverley. In 1377 there are 55 tax payers. By 1524 there are 16 people recorded, six households paid the 1672 Hearth Tax, and the development of the park in the seventeenth century probably brought the end to the settlement. [7] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: There are extensive areas of upstanding earthworks visible. They are complex, appearing on either side of the modern road to the south-east of the modern farm. A hollow way runs roughly east-west with a number of property boundaries visible on either side. The earthworks were surveyed in 1989 and the plan published in the same year, with a larger scale plan appearing in 1990. [1, 2] The main hollow way takes two routes and it is suggested that they be could be different phases with the more sinuous route replaced at a later date. [1] Rotsea is recorded in the Domesday Book and 52 tax payers are recorded in 1377. A rental of Guisborough Priory in 1300 lists 31 or 40 tofts depending on the source [1, 3] By 1524 only seven paid the Lay Subsidy, the settlement could only present four men in the muster of 1539 and Hearth Taxes of 1672 and 1675 record only six houses. [1, 4] A medieval chapel is recorded as newly built in 1328, and bequests were made to it in 1509. [1] The survey and combined documentary evidence has shown that the nucleated medieval village became reduced to a number of substantial farms and was finally deserted with dispersed farms being developed. [1] It is suggested that the change from village to individual farms came about by the early sixteenth century possibly with the conversion to pasture. [1] A map of 1784 shows the settlement had been completely depopulated by this time. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Rowley
e179_last: 1662 May 19 hearth tax
description_snippet: No clear evidence of the settlement can be seen on the ground. The church and the eighteenth-century rectory survive. description_full: No clear evidence of the settlement can be seen on the ground. The church and the eighteenth-century rectory survive. The rectory is now called Rowley Hall, and in the later eighteenth century parkland close to the Hall was improved and if any settlement evidence had survived perhaps this may have removed it from the landscape. [1] The church is recorded from c. 1150. [1] There are no clear individual tax records for Rowley, although there are records for the separate hamlets and villages in the parish. The church though acted as a key focus for the parish. It was the most valuable living in the East Riding. [2] This has made interpretation difficult – a very rich parish but no settlement evidence at the church. Also no manorial information is available apart from the rectory land. Some have suggested that there was no settlement at Rowley and that the surrounding villages provided the wealth of the living. [2] The church was therefore isolated although this is not common in this part of the country. Rowley is well known for the story surrounding the seventeenth incumbent Rev. Ezekiel Rogers. He went to America in 1638 and founded Rowley, Massachusetts, and some have claimed that the parish registers show that many of the parishioners went with him and depopulated the village. [2, 3] However it is now known that many of the people that went with Rev. Rogers were from further afield. [1] A later record in the parish register states that ‘Jeremiah Northand dyed April 12, 1702, he went with Mr Rogers in to America when about 12 years old, and staid there about 9 years. The enclosure at Rowley was made in his absence’, suggesting enclosure by c. 1647. [4] It must be a possibility that there never was a village at Rowley, although it is clear that settlements in this parish did suffer in the medieval period, with two other deserted settlements (Riplingham and Risby) in the parish. Currently this is recorded as a doubtful settlement until more concrete evidence of a village is found. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Rowton

name: Scorborough
e179_last: 1692 Feb 24 quarterly poll tax for one year
description_snippet: This complex site is more a shrunken settlement than deserted. Beresford hesitated to include it in his lists, but it appeared in the 1968 gazetteer. description_full: This complex site is more a shrunken settlement than deserted. Beresford hesitated to include it in his lists, but it appeared in the 1968 gazetteer. [1] A manorial complex of church and manor house still exits although the current manor is not the original manor house. A number of earthworks are visible around the church and surrounding fields. To the north-west of the church a hollow way is visible with property boundaries. These earthworks possibly continue to the north-east of the church running alongside the current road. A moated site exists to the north-east of the church. The early seventeenth-century home of the Hothams stood to the south-east of the church in another moated site but burnt down in 1705-6. [2] This was replaced by the current house in the late eighteenth century. [2] A park was created around the Hall between 1488 and 1517, and enlarged in 1616. [3] This included part of the area with earthworks so these had been abandoned by 1616 at the latest. Neave has shown that by 1670 there were still 19 households, but also three empty cottages. [4] From this time onwards she has plotted the gradual shrinkage of the village to three cottages by 1723. [4] There is a record in Domesday. Scorborough is often recorded in two parts in the fourteenth-century taxation. It pays a high 1344 Lay Subsidy and 128 are taxed in 1377 (along with Holme on the Wolds). In 1379, only the record for the part in Howdenshire survives and records 43 people listed and 28 taxed. By the sixteenth century the lay subsidies have become less complex and it is just recorded in Harthill. In the 1672 Hearth Tax, 19 households are charged. [5] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: High Skirlington
description_snippet: There is nothing visible on the current aerial photographs and the area of the settlement has been encroached upon by the development of caravan parks. Earlier aerial photographs had shown a small settlement with a clear plan.  A geophysical survey in 2004 revealed features such as pits which may be part of the settlement.
description_full: There is nothing visible on the current aerial photographs and the area of the settlement has been encroached upon by the development of caravan parks. Earlier aerial photographs had shown a small settlement with a clear plan. [1] A geophysical survey in 2004 revealed features such as pits which may be part of the settlement. [2] Fieldwalking on the edges of the settlement has uncovered pottery dating to the twelfth to sixteenth centuries. [3] Skirlington is rarely mentioned in the taxation records and if it is, then it is with Atwick. It is recorded as a jurisdiction of Hornsea at Domesday. In 1228 there are six tofts reported. [1] By the thirteenth century there is evidence that much of the land was put over to pasture, particularly parts owned by Bridlington Priory. [4] There are only seventeenth-century references on the E179 database. In 1517 enclosure is reported near to Atwick and it may well be this area. [5] One cottage and one toft were left by the late seventeenth century. [1] It would appear that the settlement was never large and may have disappeared early on with only single farms remaining. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Sledmere

description_full: The grid reference used by this website is not that in the 1968 Gazetteer (SE 930 648). It has been refined to the location of buildings in the eighteenth century at SE 931 642. A number of linear earthworks can be seen in this area, but no clear settlement evidence. A map of c. 1774 shows the remaining houses of the medieval settlement located to the south-east of the church. Sledmere is mentioned in the Domesday Book as waste, but by the fourteenth century it was one of the wealthiest settlements on the Yorkshire Wolds. [1] The Black Death did have an impact on the settlement with the area uncultivated in 1350. [1] It had recovered by 1377 having 196 tax payers. By the early sixteenth century the settlement had declined in prosperity. [1] However the settlement rebounded once again and 52 households were recorded in the parish in the 1672 Hearth Tax. [1] A real reduction in population begins in the 1740s. Sledmere House was built in 1748 and at the time was at the north-western edge of a sizeable village. With the construction of this new house any houses on the higher ground to the south-east which interrupted the view were cleared [1, 2]. This included 20 garths or former houses and parts of four others. [1] The remaining houses were hidden behind plantations to the north-east and south-west. In the 1770s the gardens were remodelled and the remaining villagers moved to the new village laid out to the north of the House. [1, 2] This is a migrated settlement. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.
