name: Sunderlandwick
e179_last: 1692 Feb 24 quarterly poll tax for one year
description_snippet: Clear evidence from aerial photography is present of a linear settlement along Old Sunderlandwick Road. At least 13 tofts are visible, but some of the area is now covered by trees, has been ploughed or has been landscaped as a golf course. The only surviving habitation is a farm at the southern end of the settlement earthworks. The village earthworks are surrounded by ridge and furrow.
description_full: Clear evidence from aerial photography is present of a linear settlement along Old Sunderlandwick Road. At least 13 tofts are visible, but some of the area is now covered by trees, has been ploughed or has been landscaped as a golf course. The only surviving habitation is a farm at the southern end of the settlement earthworks. The village earthworks are surrounded by ridge and furrow. Mentioned in Domesday, it also has a reasonably high yield in the fourteenth century with 38 people taxed in 1377. By the sixteenth century there had been a dramatic reduction with only 9 people taxed in 1524.There are nine houses paying the 1672 Hearth Tax, and six houses are recorded in the eighteenth century. [1, 2] Throughout the eighteenth century there are mentions of a small struggling population which included a shoemaker and a butcher. [3] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Sutton
e179_last: 1673 March 29 grant of £1,238,750 for supply of extraordinary occasions
description_snippet: A number of house plots and a hollow way were visible in 1951 but have since disappeared.  The area to the north has been heavily encroached upon by development. An old trackway was marked on earlier Ordnance Survey maps. Sutton appears in Domesday. However, in later records it is recorded with nearby settlements making its true size difficult to plot.
description_full: A number of house plots and a hollow way were visible in 1951 but have since disappeared. [1] The area to the north has been heavily encroached upon by development. An old trackway was marked on earlier Ordnance Survey maps. Sutton appears in Domesday. However, in later records it is recorded with nearby settlements making its true size difficult to plot. It disappears from the E179 record after 1380 and reappears in 1545 for a small number of mentions. This suggests that the settlement did disappear in the later fourteenth century and that the later records are for the remaining farms and hall. Jeffery’s map of 1771 omits the settlement and by 1884 it is mentioned as old foundations. Robinson suggests an eighteenth-century desertion but evidence could suggest an earlier one. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Swaythorpe
e179_last: 1624 May 13 or later three fifteenths and tenths
description_snippet: Clear earthworks are visible from the air and on the ground, to the north of modern farm buildings. An east-west hollow way is apparent with tofts to both the north and south (at least eight) and at the eastern end of this hollow way runs a further north-south hollow way with more crofts to the east (at least four). description_full: Clear earthworks are visible from the air and on the ground, to the north of modern farm buildings. An east-west hollow way is apparent with tofts to both the north and south (at least eight) and at the eastern end of this hollow way runs a further north-south hollow way with more crofts to the east (at least four). Several building foundations are visible. A triangular green area is apparent at the junction of these two with a possible dew pond at the centre. It is clear that the earthworks once extended further north and south. In the western area there is evidence of small quarry pits. A chapel site is present on the Ordnance Survey map to the north of the village and would now be under the plough. [1] A trial excavation by Bridlington School discovered chalk building foundations and medieval pottery. [2] Swaythorpe is recorded as a manor at Domesday. After this there are no clear indications of size as it is nearly always included with other settlements. In the fourteenth century much of the land at Swaythorpe has been incorporated into land holdings at Kilham. [3] A yeoman had a plough there in 1437 and in 1482 a toft and croft were recorded. In 1545 a ruined house and four tofts are mentioned. [3] By the early seventeenth century the whole area seems to be pasture. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

The First Edition Ordnance Survey map of 1854 has a number of areas of old buildings highlighted. The buildings located to the south-east of Thoroughby Hill on this map may be those of the settlement. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

On the First Edition Ordnance Survey map of 1855 a field to the north is called Chapel Flat, on a revised version of the map an area to the north-west has a record of pottery found in 1860 to 1890 but there is no indication of date, and the main road is Roman in origin. Much of the road and surrounding area has been remodelled to a dual carriage way and this may have destroyed much of the evidence. Thorpe is mentioned in the Domesday Book and has an average 1334 Lay Subsidy combined with Harswell. In 1377, 23 people were taxed. In the 1672 Hearth Tax five households pay. [1] There is no indication of a complete abandonment of the site and it has been described as a shrunken settlement on Pastscape. [2] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

name: Tranby

description_full: Nothing is visible from the air and the area has gradually been encroached by the villages surrounding Kingston upon Hull. The grid reference used by this website is the location marked on the first edition Ordnance Survey map as the location of the village (TA 025 278). The 1968 Gazetteer had located the site at Tranby Croft. This now a school, but the earlier landscaping around the house would have destroyed any remains. There is very little evidence of a truly medieval settlement here. It was not mentioned in the Domesday Book, and does not appear in the fourteenth-century tax records. Its first mention on the E179 database is 1487, it then does not appear until 1540 and thereafter appears only sporadically. It is hard to estimate if there was truly a medieval settlement here and for the time being it is being classed as a deserted hamlet. Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.

description_full: This is probably the most well known deserted settlement, due mainly to the research and excavations carried out for over 40 years. There are clear earthworks visible at the site. A roughly north-south hollow way is bounded on either side by house plots, around 30 in total. Two manor house sites have been uncovered; one that was abandoned in the thirteenth century, and indications are that the northern one was abandoned some time in the fourteenth century. At the south of the village is the church which was in use until 1949. To the south of this is the mill pond. Close to the church are the only surviving buildings – a row of three cottages, which were finally vacated in the 1970s. The excavations at the site have revealed an extensive occupation from at least Roman times. Further information on the village can be found on the Beresford pages of this website. The excavations have been published in a series of 13 volumes – see the Bibliography below. Wharram Percy was mentioned in the Domesday Book, paid an average amount in 1334 and 30 people were taxed in 1377. A record of tenant holdings from 1368 also records 30 farmhouses and cottages in the village. [1] By 1435 only 16 are recorded showing the decline of the settlement had begun. [1] It does not appear in the sixteenth-century tax records. Further reduction in population is noted in the 1517 enquires into enclosure. These record that after 1488 four cottages had been removed. [1] It has been well established that the fate of Wharram was the conversion to pasture. Over time more and more land was removed from arable production. A legal case that was heard in 1555 helps date the final stage of conversion to 1527. [1] Appears in the Gazetteer of Deserted Medieval Villages known in 1968.
